The resolution of this difficulty is that Abdullah ibn Ubayy used to pretend that he was with the believers, ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], while in reality he was one of the hypocrites. So he is counted among them according to outward appearance, not according to the reality and the fact.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not think it bad for you; rather, it is good for you﴾ [al-Nur: 11]. ﴿Do not think it﴾: do not suppose, O believers, that it, [the slander, being] other than the band, is bad for you; rather, it is good for you.

First: Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿Do not think it﴾, and He forbade us from supposing that this slander is an evil for us before it becomes clear that it is good. Why? Because there is no doubt that when this slander occurred, the believers were struck by what afflicted them of harm, and they supposed that this was evil. So Allah, exalted is He, wanted to remove this supposition from their souls before clarifying their situation. He said: ﴿Do not think it bad for you﴾, because this is the first thing that should be addressed, and it is the beginning of dealing with this slander: removing what some believers imagined, that this slander is evil. After this removal, the treatment follows.

They say: clearing comes before adorning (al-takhliyah qabl al-tahliyah). That means clearing a thing of ugliness and defect before adorning it with what is beautiful, because when you remove thorns before spreading the carpet, is that not so? Therefore Allah forbade us to think this evil until this is first uprooted from our souls, and then we are prepared for the adornment and for establishing what is established concerning this slander. It becomes clear from this that when treating matters one should first remove harm to open the way for good to enter.

﴿Do not think it bad for you﴾ [al-Nur: 11]. In it there is also the statement: one should begin with the most important thing, and the most important thing in this matter is that the supposition that this slander is an evil against the Prophet ﷺ, and against the family of Abu Bakr, and against the believers in general, be removed from the souls. For the reality of the matter, were this to occur, and far be it from Allah that it should occur, it would be an evil with respect to the family of Abu Bakr and with respect to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ.

Therefore it is not truly possible for the believers to suppose this, and the eminent believers among the Companions denied it. It was said: it is not possible that it should be. Among those who denied it was Usamah ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, and others denied that it could be. But some people, because of the great spreading of rumours and gossip, and because Satan also whispers into their hearts, some doubt arose in them. The believing Companions were divided on this into three groups:
One group fell into the deviation that occurred in this matter; another group denied it with utmost denial and said: this is not possible; and a third group hesitated and doubted the matter. But the eminent Companions and the majority of them denied it, as the scholars have mentioned.

﴿Do not think it bad for you; rather, it is good for you﴾ [al-Nur: 11]. First: how could we not think it bad? We believe in this, because Allah said: ﴿Do not think it bad﴾. Although a person may at first suppose that it is bad, and this is well known: someone slanders your family, and you suppose something, you know that this is evil directed at you. This is an accepted matter. So when Allah said: ﴿Do not think it bad for you﴾, this problem came to an end, and it was settled by the prohibition of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who knows what will be, because it is not evil.

It remains to say: ﴿rather, it is good for you﴾. We believe this as well, that it is good for us. But what is the good that appeared in this slander?

We say: the good that appeared in the slander is a good without equal, in that the innocence and purity of the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, became manifest, a manifestation that nothing equals. Allah testified to her innocence from above His Throne, blessed and exalted is He.

Second: thereby there appeared the purity and cleanliness of the bed of the Prophet ﷺ, and that it is not possible for the bed of the Prophet ﷺ to be defiled by this.

Third: among the good is the great reward that resulted from what befell the believers in this incident of harm, hardship, and great exertion. Indeed, it is from the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that revelation ceased for a full month; no revelation came down to the Prophet ﷺ. This was so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, so that the believers' longing for Allah's clarification in this great and important matter would intensify, and so that their reward would increase during that period. Moreover, there is also among the good the elevation of the status of the Prophet ﷺ, and this is above our saying: the innocence and purity of his bed is an elevation of his station, and that Allah, exalted is He, Himself defends him.

Then there is also among the good the disciplining and admonition of the believers with what they ought to be upon, namely not uttering words carelessly, and not daring to attack the honour of the chaste, and other things that will become clear, Allah willing, in the course of this great story.

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Rather, it is good for you﴾: Allah will reward you for it, and Allah will make manifest the innocence of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and of the one who came with her, who is Safwan. She said: I was... to the end.

This is also among the good for Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, may Allah be pleased with him: when Allah sent down the innocence of 'A'ishah from that, and he was the one whom the hypocrites accused with it, what does this make manifest? The innocence of Safwan, may Allah be pleased with him.

"'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: I was with the Prophet ﷺ on a campaign after the veil had been revealed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2661), and Muslim (2770/56), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. This campaign is called al-Muraysi' and the Campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq. The author did not state when this campaign was, but it becomes clear to us when it was. When? After the veil had been revealed. When was the veil revealed? In the sixth year of the Hijrah. The veil was revealed in the sixth year of the Hijrah, and accordingly this campaign was in the sixth year, at its end or in the seventh.

As for the statement of some historians that it was in the fifth or the fourth, this is a mistake, a mistake on their part. The correct view is that it was in the sixth year, at its end, because she stated that it was after the veil had been revealed. Also, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, consulted Zaynab concerning it, and the verse of the veil was revealed at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Zaynab. So we say: it was in the campaign of al-Muraysi', which is the Campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq, and it was in the sixth year, at its end. She, may Allah be pleased with her, says: "Then he finished with it," what?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, "in a campaign after the veil had been revealed. Then he finished with it, returned, and drew near to Madinah, and gave permission to depart one night. So I walked and attended to my need, and returned to the saddle-bag."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2661), and Muslim (2770/56), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]

And Zaynab's verse of the veil was revealed at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to her. So we say: in the campaign of al-Muraysi', which is the Campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq, and it was in the sixth year, at its end. She, may Allah be pleased with her, says: "Then he finished with it..."
* Student: And he returned and consummated the marriage with her.
* Shaykh: No, "in a campaign after fighting had been revealed. Then he finished with it, returned, and drew near to Madinah, and gave permission to depart one night. So I walked and attended to my need, and came to the saddle-bag. Then my necklace was broken — [ 'iqd, with a kasrah on the unpointed letter: the necklace] — so I returned to search for it. They lifted my howdah — that is what one rides in — onto my camel, thinking I was in it, for the women were light; they only ate the 'ulqah — [with a damma on the unpointed letter and a sukun on the lam] — of food, meaning a little."

'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, spoke about the story of the slander. She says: when the Prophet ﷺ returned from this campaign, one night he gave permission to depart. So she went to attend to her need, as a person does when he wishes to ride, or wishes to sleep, or the like, to free himself.

She went to attend to her need, that is, to urinate or defecate. When she returned, the necklace had been broken, so she went back to look for it, and the scholars have mentioned that this necklace was a loan to her from her sister Asma'. So she went to search for it, seeking it, and she found the necklace. When she found the necklace, she returned to her place, and behold, the people had lifted her howdah, and they did not suppose she was not in it, because, as she said, may Allah be pleased with her, the women were light; the flesh had not shown on them, for they only ate a little food. Moreover, the howdah was not lifted by one or two men, so that they would notice its lightness; rather, a group carried it, and it is customary that a group does not feel the weight of a thing, it does not concern them. So they supposed she was in it, and they set off.

When she returned and did not find them, she knew that the people would miss her and would come back for her. This is well known. From her intelligence and good sense she did not go right or left, nor did she set off; she said: "Fine, let me catch up with them, let me search," but she remained in her place. And, remarkably, from her tranquillity and composure she fell asleep in that place. When she slept, Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the last of the people. He was a man who slept much and slept heavily as well. When he awoke, he caught up with the people, and when he came to their place he saw the dark form of a person, so he came towards it, and what happened, happened.

Now we read the story. She says: ('ulqah — with a damma on the unpointed letter and a sukun on the lam — of food, which is a little. I found myself after they had set off, so I sat down in the resting place where I was, and I thought the people would miss me and return to me. Then my eyes overcame me and I slept. Safwan had halted behind the army, and he set out in the last part of the night [adlaja], both with a shaddah on the ra' [i.e., 'arrasa] and on the dal [iddalaja], meaning he dismounted in the last part of the night to rest. This is the meaning of 'arrasa: he dismounted in the last part of the night to rest.)

She says: (He set out from his place — that is, from his place — and in the morning he was in his resting place — that is, the army's resting place — and he saw the dark form of a sleeping person, that is, her figure, and he recognized me when he saw me, for he had seen me before the veil. So I awoke at his saying "Inna lillah wa inna ilayhi raji'un" when he recognized me — that is, his words: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return" — and I covered my face — that is, I concealed it — with my outer garment; by Allah, he did not speak a single word to me, and I heard from him no word other than his saying "Inna lillah," until he made his mount kneel and stepped on its foreleg, and I mounted it. He set off leading the riding beast with me, until we reached the army after they had halted in the blazing heat.) And so on to the end.

May Allah be pleased with him: when he saw the dark form, he came towards it. When he came near, behold, it was the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, sleeping, and she had not covered her face, because there was no one around her. He recognized her, may Allah be pleased with him, for he had seen her before the veil, so he recognized her and said: "Inna lillah wa inna ilayhi raji'un." Then he made his camel kneel and stepped on its knee until she mounted, and he did not speak a word to her. He only said "Inna lillah" out of fear of what had happened; he anticipated a matter and it occurred, for a woman alone in the wilderness, and a man coming to her who was late from the army while she too was late, this is undoubtedly a calamity and a trial from Allah. For this reason he saw it as a disaster, may Allah be pleased with him, and so he said "Inna lillah." But out of his chastity and his reverence for the Prophet ﷺ and his reverence for the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, he did not speak to her a word at all, not even saying "Mount," nor "What kept you behind?", nor "There is no harm upon you." He did not utter a single word at all, out of respect for the bed of the Prophet ﷺ and honouring it. He only made the camel kneel and stepped on its knee until she mounted, may Allah be pleased with her. Then he went leading her until he reached the army. When did he reach it?

She says: ("in the blazing heat at midday" — that is, from awghara, standing in a place where the heat is intense — this is the meaning of al-waghirah: intense heat. Even now in our colloquial language people say: "By Allah, today is waghirah," meaning: intensely hot.)

She says: ("So whoever perished, perished on my account, and the one who took the greater part of it among them was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul." End of her words...) What?

* Students: (Narrated by the two Shaykhs).
* Shaykh: (Narrated by the two Shaykhs).

When this happened, Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his fellow hypocrites found an outlet through which to breathe freely in order to disparage the Prophet ﷺ. They began saying: "What brought him? What kept him behind? What kept 'A'ishah behind?!" Then they began to spread the account, shape it, and embellish it, until the news spread and became widely known.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was pained, and he had to be pained. He was pained in truth in two respects. First: 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was his bed and the dearest of his wives to him, and he loved her and she loved him. The second: she was the daughter of the person most dear to him, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. How could this matter occur, and how could it happen?!

Therefore the affliction weighed heavily upon the Prophet ﷺ, so much so that, despite his great patience and his understanding of his family and their purity and their distance from what they were accused of, something of what had entered him did enter him. He began to consult some of his companions on whether he should part from 'A'ishah or not. Some of them advised him not to part from her, and said: "Your family, O Messenger of Allah; we know nothing but good."

Others advised him to part from her, in view of what they saw of his distress, peace and blessings be upon him, and they said that if he parted from her he would be at ease. Among those who gave this advice was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, the cousin of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, because he was a close relative of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and he saw from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, great hardship and great distress, so he said: "Perhaps if he divorces her he will be at rest and reassured."

But the senior Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "This is not possible." Among those who advised him was Usamah ibn Zayd, to keep her and not divorce her.

In any case, the matter remained in this state of agitation, unease, and hardship until the end of the month. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, did not know what the people were discussing, and she knew nothing of it, because she was ill and was in her father's house, and she learned nothing until the very end. She went out to attend to her need, and she stumbled, and her mother Umm Ruman said to her: "Mistah has come to ruin!" For her mother also had in her heart only what had occurred. She singled out Mistah ibn Uthathah from among those who said what they said, because he was a cousin of Abu Bakr, a near relative of his, and it was supposed that a man like him would defend this matter because of his kinship. But Allah's decree was a determined decree.

When she said, "Mistah has come to ruin," 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was surprised at Umm Ruman: she says about Mistah what she says, although he is the cousin of Abu Bakr? So she asked: "What is the matter with him, what is the affair?" Her mother told her the matter, and said: "The people have been gossiping about this matter for such-and-such a time." Her pain increased, her illness grew worse, until she began to weep, and she did not sleep, may Allah be pleased with her, and it was right for her to do this, because the matter was great.

Then one day the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, came to them. She says that she too had noticed something unusual in the Prophet ﷺ, because she was accustomed from him to gentleness and to solicitude when she was ill, and he would come in asking after her and making sure of her condition. But this time he did not make sure of anything; rather, he would say: "How are you?" [kayfa tikum?], sit for a little while, and then leave.

For the rest of the Commentary — the translation covers the passage as given.

Translation:

One day he (ﷺ) came, and said, "How are you?" as was his custom. While he was sitting, the revelation descended upon him with the relief from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and with the innocence of 'Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). When it was lifted from him, he was smiling, peace be upon him, and he said to her, "Rejoice, O 'Aisha." She said, "From you, or from Allah?" He said, "Rather, from Allah." She said, "Praise be to Allah."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (2661) and Muslim (2770 / 56) from the narration of 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah from 'Aisha, and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (173) from the narration of Ka'b ibn Malik.]]

Then the story of the slander ended, but what occurred in it of this great trial had occurred.

* * *

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿For every man of them﴾, i.e., upon him, ﴿is what he earned of sin﴾ in that matter).

﴿For every man of them﴾, i.e., of these group, ﴿is what he earned of sin﴾. The author said: (i.e., upon him), so the lam (ل) carries the meaning of (على, upon). This is what the author saw: that the lam means (upon).

If it implies the meaning of (على), then why was it turned away from to the lam? To convey entitlement (al-istihqaq), and that they deserve what is upon them of sin. So the lam here is for entitlement, meaning: to clarify that these group, who committed what they committed, deserve what is upon them of sin.

His saying: ﴿For every man of them is what he earned﴾ contains in it the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in recompensing evil deeds, and that a person bears only what he earned, no more. It also contains evidence that they are not partners in one sin in this matter; rather, each one has his full sin for what he participated in of this affair.

His saying: (﴿And he who took upon himself the greater part thereof among them, for him is a great punishment﴾; ﴿he who took upon himself the greater part thereof﴾, i.e., bore most of it, for he began the gossip and spread it, and he was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, ﴿for him is a great punishment﴾, which is the Fire in the Hereafter).

Note ﴿he who took upon himself the greater part thereof﴾: He stated the sentence in this form for emphasis. He did not say, "And for those who took upon themselves the greater part of it among them is a great punishment," but rather said: ﴿And he who took upon himself the greater part thereof among them, for him is a great punishment﴾. In reality it made it two sentences within one sentence, because ﴿he who﴾ is the subject, ﴿for him﴾ is the preposed predicate, and ﴿a great punishment﴾ is a second subject. It is as if the sentence became two sentences, to show its importance, to affirm it, and to indicate that his taking up this matter is a grave thing.

﴿Took upon himself the greater part thereof﴾: taking up a thing means to be devoted to it and give it his care. His saying ﴿kibrahu (greater part)﴾ means its greater part, so the "kibr" of a thing means its greater part, i.e., he initiated it, nourished it, made it grow, mentioned it in gatherings, and inflamed hearts with it. That was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and he was deserving of such baseness, because he was a hypocrite, indeed the head of the hypocrites. He wished that such a matter would occur so that he might find an opening to attack the Prophet (ﷺ), his bed, and especially his companions, may Allah curse him.

He says: ﴿for him is a great punishment﴾. What is the meaning of "punishment" (ʿadhab)? A penalty. And "great" (ʿazim) means great in its measure, great in its kind and type, and great in its duration, because he — and we seek refuge in Allah — is in the lowest level of the Fire. No one among the people of the Fire is lower than the hypocrites. And who is the head of the hypocrites in this Ummah?

* Students: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy.

* The Shaykh: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy. So he is the lowest of those in the lowest level of the Fire. Therefore his punishment is great, and we seek refuge in Allah, in its form, its duration, and its measure. So this one who took upon himself the greater part of it among them, for him is a great punishment.

We still have to ask: were these who spoke slanderously given the prescribed punishment (hadd)? What is the answer? The Prophet (ﷺ) only applied the hadd to the believers among them, namely Hassan ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him), Mistah ibn Uthathah, and Hamnah bint Jahsh. Hamnah bint Jahsh, who was she? She was the sister of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and Zaynab was the wife of the Messenger (ﷺ), as a co-wife of 'Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). When the Prophet (ﷺ) asked her about 'Aisha, she praised her well, but her sister was destroyed among those who were destroyed. So the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave them the hadd for slander: eighty lashes.

As for the hypocrites, the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not apply the hadd to them. This is either because the hadd is a purification and an expiation, and the hypocrites are not fit for purification or expiation. This is a clear reason in meaning, but in reality it may not be clear, because the hypocrites show that they are Muslims, so the outward rulings of Islam should have been applied to them, and their inner states left to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Others said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) did not apply the hadd to them because they did not state it explicitly. For example, they did not state explicitly that Safwan did something with 'Aisha. Rather, they gathered the talk and phrased it in expressions that convey this meaning, but without explicit statement. It is known that one who does not explicitly accuse of fornication is not subject to the hadd for slander, so the Prophet (ﷺ) did not apply it to them.

It is also possible that the Messenger (peace be upon him) left their hadd for this reason and for others. For instance, he may have left the hadd for 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy because he was the head of the hypocrites and a leader among his people, and he feared that it would cause a great fitnah. And the hadd for slander, according to the view that it is a right of a human being, may be waived if the one entitled to it waives it.

But what appears — and Allah knows best — is that the reason is that the hypocrites, as is their custom, the hypocrite (...), and he cannot state explicitly; their habit is deception in everything. So you find they do not state explicitly, but hover around the matter until they fill people's hearts with it. For this reason, the companions, who were forthright, stated explicitly what they assumed, even though it was a false assumption. But in any case they assumed this and stated it, so the Prophet (ﷺ) applied to them the hadd for slander.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 12:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾. ﴿Why﴾: the author says: (Hallā, "why did ... not," and ﴿when﴾ at the time ﴿you heard it, the believing men and believing women thought well of their own kind﴾, i.e., some of them thought well of others, ﴿and said, "This is an obvious lie"﴾, a clear falsehood. There is a shift (iltifāt) in it.

﴿Why, when you heard it﴾. The commentator says: (﴿Why﴾ means hallā). It is a particle of exhortation (taḥḍīḍ), and in it there is some reproach, since they thought something that ought not to have been, meaning: why, when you heard it, that is, when you heard this report that spread and has no basis.

﴿The believing men and believing women thought well of their own kind﴾. First: ﴿the believing men and believing women thought﴾. The author says: (there is a shift from address), meaning to the third person noun phrase. Had the context required it, it would have said: "when you heard it, you should have thought well of your own kind." But it said ﴿the believing men and believing women thought well of their own kind﴾, so it shifted from the second person to the apparent noun. From what has been said before, the shift (iltifāt) has at least two benefits. What are they?

* Student: Alerting the listener.

* Shaykh: Alerting, that is one.

* Student: Challenge.

* Shaykh: No, challenge is not always the benefit. The second benefit is determined by the context. So the shift always has the certain, definite benefit, which is alerting. Why? Because when the course of address changes, what does it require? It requires that a person pay attention. This is why some speakers change their style, from report to command, or from question to affirmation, and the like, even in voice and delivery, so that people will pay attention. When people are addressed in one unvarying tone, they may become distracted, but when the style or manner of delivery changes, that attention is achieved. So what is the benefit of the shift? Alerting. That is a definite benefit in every shift. The second benefit?

* Student: Determined by the context.

* Shaykh: We say the second benefit is determined by the context. We cannot specify or determine it here right now; the context determines it. So let us look at the second benefit here: ﴿the believing men and believing women thought﴾, and it did not say "you thought." This is an indication that this thought takes them out of faith, because if they were believers they would only have thought well. It did not say "you thought well," because by this thought they had left faith. Yet this is not a complete exit except after the verses were revealed.

The second benefit, after alerting, is an indication that in this thought they were not believers, because believers think only well. A second benefit is that they ought to have thought this way because they are believers. They say they are believers, and they are truly believers, so it was incumbent upon them to think what? To think well. So now they thought what they thought, and by that they were not believers, since believers think only well.

Second: it was incumbent upon them, because of their faith, to think well.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the believing men and believing women﴾: because the reality is that the matter concerned a man and a woman, namely Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal and 'Aisha, mother of the believers, may Allah be pleased with her. So it covers both sexes, and for this reason He said ﴿the believing men and believing women﴾, specifying both sexes, because the accusation concerned both of them: Safwan, who is among the believing men, and 'Aisha, who is among the believing women. For this reason He said ﴿the believing men﴾, those who are in the position of Safwan, and ﴿the believing women﴾, those who are in the position of whom? 'Aisha.

And His saying: ﴿of their own kind﴾. Does it mean that I myself think well of my own self, and that the accusation of 'Aisha is one where a person thinks evil of himself? Or is the meaning of "selves" here the kind, because the believers are like a single soul? The meaning would then be: they thought well of their own kind, that is, they thought well of Safwan and 'Aisha, and even of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Which is intended, this or the first? Do you understand the question now? Is the intended meaning of ﴿of their own kind﴾ their own selves, that is, themselves, or is it ﴿of their own kind﴾: 'Aisha, Safwan and the Prophet ﷺ, whom Allah made as selves, because all the believers are like a single soul, as in His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:128]? Which of the two meanings is intended?

* Student: The last one.

* Shaykh: Yes, the last one is clear: that they thought well of one another, as the author said, that is, they thought well of their own kind, namely of these people falsely and wrongfully accused, because they are of their own kind, they know them and know their circumstances, and they are their brothers in faith. Or the meaning we pointed to: "of their own selves" means themselves, that is, they think well of their own selves. It is as if, were they accused of this matter while knowing themselves, what would they think of themselves? Good and innocence. That is, just as you would not accuse yourselves if this were said about you, so it is obligatory that you think well of 'Aisha and Safwan, may Allah be pleased with them. So we explained the meaning of "selves" as the self of the one who thinks.

How does the meaning descend? The meaning: they think well of themselves, that is, that if this matter were something accused of them, they would know themselves, and it would be impossible for them to believe this matter, because they know that they are free of it and innocent of it.

In any case, both meanings are possible, and each has a sound aspect. 'Aisha and Safwan are among the selves of the believers, because the believer with his brother is like a single soul. Whoever thinks of the mother of the believers and Safwan something contrary to what is fitting, it is as if he thought it of himself. That is, just as you know yourself and do not think such a thought of it, so you must know the mother of the believers and Safwan, and not think of them except what you think of yourself. Just as you think of yourself only good, so you should think of the mother of the believers and Safwan only good.

﴿...thought well of their own kind, and said, "This is an obvious lie"﴾. His saying ﴿and said﴾ is conjoined to ﴿thought﴾: ﴿the believing men and believing women thought﴾ and ﴿said﴾. In this is that it is obligatory for the believer to refute falsehood in his heart, and what else? And with his tongue. It is not enough that you believe this is not true; rather, you must show the falsehood of this thing, because whoever believes this matter is untrue and remains silent, what is his position? In reality his position is passive; at most he has cleared himself, but the obligation is to refute falsehood.

For this reason He said: ﴿thought well of their own kind﴾, and what else? ﴿and said, "This is an obvious lie"﴾. It is necessary from thinking and speaking. It is not enough that you believe what was said about 'Aisha and Safwan is a lie; rather you must say it, why? So that we may confront this falsehood with refutation. As for our remaining silent and saying, "By Allah, we disown it before Allah, this is not true at all," this is not enough; we must think well, and what else? And refute it. What do we refute? Falsehood.

﴿And said, "This"﴾: ﴿and said﴾ is conjoined to ﴿thought﴾, so it falls under the exhortation. That is, Allah, exalted is He, says: it is obligatory that they think well, and what else? And that they refute (...). It is more forceful in reproach, for when you speak to your companion in the third person it becomes gentler and easier, and when you then come with the second person it becomes more forceful, whether it is praise or commendation. Of praise is: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:2-4], then He said: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:5]. So He praised Allah; the one praying praised Allah first in the third person, ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾, then in the second person, ﴿You alone we worship﴾, as if after praise he had become present before his Lord, so he said: ﴿You alone we worship﴾.

So the shift here from the third person to the second person has the benefit of alerting and greater force of reproach, because the address is more forceful. Consider His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would have purified himself﴾ ['Abasa 80:1-3]. At first ﴿he frowned﴾ is in the third person, then He said: ﴿And what would make you know?﴾, because He, may Allah be exalted, did not wish to address him with this wording, "you frowned and turned away," but ﴿he frowned and turned away﴾, until it became clear, then He said: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would have purified himself﴾. This is similar.

The main point is that when one moves from the third-person form to the second-person form, it has the benefit of alerting, and an additional benefit derived from the context.

﴿

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 24, verse 15:**

﴿إِذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ﴾: meaning, some of you narrate it from others. Talaqqa (to receive) means to welcome and take something, so they receive it with their tongues, and say with their mouths what they have no knowledge of. The difference between ﴿وَتَقُولُونَ بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ﴾ and ﴿تَلَقَّوْنَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ﴾: talaqqi is taking it from its source, as in talaqqahu, like the reception of the caravan (talaqqi al-jalab), meaning welcoming it, so talaqqi is for receiving speech.

﴿وَتَقُولُونَ بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ﴾ that is, for uttering speech to others. It indicates that this saying does not reach the heart; it is merely speech by the tongue. This is because many of the Companions doubted this report, and it has already been mentioned that most of them and their distinguished men denied it from the very beginning.

﴿إِذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ وَتَقُولُونَ بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ مَا لَيْسَ لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾. There is great rebuke in this: that a person says with his mouth (afwah, plural of fah, meaning mouth) what he has no knowledge of. You say with your mouth what you have no knowledge of.

If someone asks: Is speech not by the mouth? Why does He say "say with your mouths," when speech can only be by the mouth?

* Student: For the benefit you mentioned, meaning: it is mere words, and not...

* Shaykh: That is, it is not settled in their souls. Yes, that is it, because it is mere speech by the tongue and mouth, but it has not settled in the heart, because it is not based on knowledge.

It may also be said that this is for emphasis, as in the saying: "He walked with his foot to so-and-so," to affirm the walking. That is, it is a firm statement that you say plainly, and not a suspicion in the soul, for qawl (saying) may also be applied to suspicion. Similarly: ﴿وَلَا طَائِرٍ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ إِلَّا أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ﴾ [al-An'am 38], for a bird flies with its wings, and it is known that a bird does not fly except with its wings: ﴿وَلَا طَائِرٍ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ إِلَّا أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ﴾.

In any case, we say: His saying ﴿بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ﴾ either means to affirm the statement, that it is not mere suspicion or imagination, but that you say it openly with your mouths; or it may be said that this statement is only on the mouth and does not reach the depths of the soul, because although they say it, it is as if they consider it unlikely and doubt its truth.

His saying ﴿مَا لَيْسَ لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾: how often this happens among people! It indicates that a person must not say anything unless he has knowledge of it. It is not enough to say something on mere suspicion, nor on mere delusion or imagination. Do not say, especially in grave matters, except what you have knowledge of. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said in Surah al-Isra: ﴿وَلَا تَقْفُ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾, meaning: do not follow it, ﴿إِنَّ السَّمْعَ وَالْبَصَرَ وَالْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُولَئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْئُولًا﴾ [al-Isra 36]. You will be held accountable for your hearing, your sight, and your heart, which is the place of suspicion and belief.

So do not say what you have no knowledge of, and do not follow what you have no knowledge of. A person must have knowledge, and this is an upbringing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, indicating that a person should verify what he says so that his speech is trustworthy and he is safe from the sin of speaking without knowledge, especially if the speech is about Allah; for none is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or if the speech concerns such grave matters that involve disparaging the Prophet ﷺ, his household, and his Companions, and consequently disparaging the religion; for if he disparages the Messenger who brought it, it is a disparagement of the very religion that this Messenger brought (...) in it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَتَحْسَبُونَهُ هَيِّنًا﴾: there is no sin in it, ﴿وَهُوَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَظِيمٌ﴾ in sin. In this sentence there is much magnification of this matter. That is: you think the speech on this matter is trivial, and that these are words said and passed on, but it is great in the sight of Allah, and it grows greater the further the person spoken about is from what was said about him.

For this reason, slander against a chaste person (muhsan) carries the prescribed punishment (hadd), while slander against one who is not chaste carries discretionary punishment (ta'zir). That is, if he slanders a person accused of adultery who is not chaste, he is only given ta'zir; but if he slanders a person known for chastity, the full hadd is obligatory. For this reason He said: ﴿تَحْسَبُونَهُ هَيِّنًا وَهُوَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَظِيمٌ﴾.

We have said that it grows greater according to what? The condition of the one slandered and spoken about. Likewise, if the speech is not slander, it is greater according to the state of the statement. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرَى عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾ [al-An'am 21]. The greatest lie is lying against Allah, then against His Messenger ﷺ. Thus a lie grows greater according to the one to whom the speech is attributed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 16:

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander"?﴾ (It is) for amazement. ﴿Slander﴾: a lie. ﴿Tremendous﴾.

﴿Lawla﴾ means "halla" (why not), and it is for urging mixed with reproach.

﴿When you heard it﴾: what is the pronoun that refers back to it? It refers to the slander (al-ifk). ﴿You said﴾: this is the answer to ﴿lawla﴾.

﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾. ﴿Ma yakun﴾: the author says, "ma yanbaghi lana" (it is not proper for us). Know that the phrases "ma yakun" and "ma yanbaghi" are used for something that is impossible. When we write in the books of jurisprudence, "it should not be done such and such," what is meant? That it is not merely disliked.

But when "ma yanbaghi" appears in the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger ﷺ, what is meant by it is impossibility to the utmost degree, that which is not valid and not fitting, as in His saying: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam 92]. What does "ma yanbaghi" mean here? It means: it is impossible to the utmost degree, not fitting and not valid.

And as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not befitting for Him to sleep"[[Narrated by Muslim (179/295) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]. What is the meaning of "it is not befitting for Him to sleep"? That it is impossible, not fitting and not valid for Him, glory be to Him and exalted, to sleep, because of the perfection of His life.

In any case, ﴿It is not for us to speak﴾ means: it is not proper for us, and it is not valid for us, to speak of this. Why? (...)

Because what?

* Student: Impossible.

* Shaykh: Why is it impossible? Because it is not possible that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, would allow this matter to occur from the family of the Prophet ﷺ. It is absolutely impossible. According to what the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, requires, it is impossible that Allah, glory be to Him, would let this matter happen from the family of the Messenger ﷺ, because of what that entails that is not fitting for the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾, because of the gravity and the magnitude of the matter (...).

As for His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾: it is for amazement here? This is not correct, that it is for amazement. Rather, it is for absolute declaration of His transcendence (tanzih), meaning: we declare You far above, O our Lord, that this should happen from the family of Your Messenger ﷺ. ﴿Glory be to You﴾ means: exalting You above what is not fitting for You, and among that is that the like of this should occur from the family of the Prophet ﷺ.

So the phrase ﴿Glory be to You﴾ in this context is among the finest that could be said; indeed, it is in reality the finest that could be said. ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾: why? Because that contradicts Your transcendence. For this reason they said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, that is: glory be to You that this should happen from the family of Your Prophet ﷺ. It is not an expression of amazement at what was said, as if they were astonished at it. No, rather they declare Allah, glory be to Him, far above what was attributed to His people. Meaning: exalted are You, O our Lord, above such a thing occurring in the house of Your Messenger ﷺ. This declaration of transcendence in this position is among the finest that could be, indeed it is the finest.

﴿This is a lie﴾: ﴿slander﴾ (buhtan) means a lie, ﴿tremendous﴾. ﴿This is a lie﴾: a lie, because it contradicts what the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, requires. And ﴿tremendous﴾: why was it described as tremendous? The position, O people. What is its position? It concerns the family of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. What slander is greater than slander in which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, his family and his companions are defamed?

﴿Tremendous﴾: its magnitude is clear. If this were a false accusation against so-and-so, or so-and-so, or so-and-so, it would be great, but not like the magnitude of this, not like the magnitude of what was attributed to the family of the Messenger ﷺ. Therefore it was described as tremendous. Because its place is?

* Student: Slander (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever, if you are believers﴾: He forbids you. Or we dropped a sentence earlier in the explanation, which is His saying: ﴿you received it with your tongues﴾. He said: (one of the two taa's has been dropped from the verb). Its original form is: when you were receiving it with your tongues. We cannot say here that "talaqqa" is a past-tense verb. We cannot say that it is a past-tense verb. ﴿Then I warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [al-Layl 14]: in that one it can be said to be a past-tense verb, but it is a present-tense verb; originally it is "tatalaza" (it blazes). But here, can we make "talaqqawnahu" a past-tense verb, since "talaqqa" is past tense? If it came unaccompanied: "talaqqaytu al-hadith" (I received the saying). Here, ﴿talaqqawnahu﴾, can we make it a past-tense verb or not?

* Student: No, it cannot.

* Shaykh: No, it cannot. Why?

* Student: Because "idh" is followed by the present tense.

* Shaykh: No, because "idh" here is for specifying time.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: Because he said after it: ﴿and you say﴾.

* Shaykh: No. Its original past-tense form does not take the waw and the nun. It takes the waw, yes, ("talaqqaw"), but it does not take the nun, because the nun belongs to the five verbs in the present tense. Here there is a nun, or not? ﴿talaqqawnahu﴾ (you receive it). Therefore, here it cannot be a past-tense verb. It is certain that one of the two taa's has been dropped from it.

Then the author said: (And "idh" is in the accusative governed by "massakum" or "afadtum"). Here: "lamassakum idh talaqqawnahu" or "afadtum idh talaqqawnahu." It is understood from the author's words that "idh" here is a noun, although we have already passed that many grammarians treat "idh" in the sense of causation as a particle, not a noun, because the meaning is: because of such and such.

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ..

* Student: (...) ﴿you receive it with your tongues﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes, meaning: it does not reach your hearts. The most that happens is that it reaches the tongue and you utter it.

* Student: The "ba'"?

* Shaykh: This "ba'" is for transitivity. The essential meaning of "talaqqi" is actually by hearing, receiving speech by hearing. But on the basis that as soon as one receives it, one pours it out and says it. That is the reason.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 17:

He said: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it﴾. Al-wa'z (admonition). The author says: (Allah forbids you to return). Commands and prohibitions are admonition; for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾, then He said: ﴿Excellent is that with which He admonishes you﴾ [an-Nisa' 58]. So He made the command an admonition, because a person is admonished by it. Likewise here.

﴿Allah admonishes you﴾ means: He warns you with admonition, and warning includes prohibition. On this basis, we must understand that the author's words "(He forbids you)" are not an explanation of the wording itself, but of what the meaning implies. Otherwise, al-maw'izah (admonition) is warning with that which softens the heart, through fear or through encouragement. So the meaning of ﴿yaʿiẓukum﴾ is: Allah, glorified and exalted, warns you.

﴿That you return to the like of it﴾ means: that you go back to its like. ﴿Ever﴾ means: as long as you are alive.

﴿If you are believers﴾: is it a condition for the admonition ("He admonishes you") or not, or is it an independent clause, the implied meaning being: "If you are believers, then be admonished by that"? The author says: "(If you are believers)" — what else? "(You heed this)." This clause, in truth, if you say it is a condition for His saying ﴿admonishes you﴾, ﴿Allah admonishes you﴾ ﴿if you are believers﴾, then the admonition here must be interpreted as beneficial admonition, not merely the mention of admonition, because admonition benefits only with the condition of faith.

As for if we say that admonition is the clarification of that by which a person is admonished, then faith is not a condition for that, for Allah's admonition is presented to everyone, whether believing or not, but only the believer benefits from it. ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord and a cure for what is in the breasts﴾ — this is general — ﴿and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus 57].

The conclusion is: we say, ﴿If you are believers﴾: if it is a restriction on His saying ﴿admonishes you﴾, then the intended admonition is beneficial admonition, for it is that which benefits the believer.

And if admonition is the presentation of that by which people are admonished, whether they benefit or not, then His saying ﴿If you are believers﴾ is independent, and its response is omitted, meaning: "If you are believers, then heed what Allah has admonished you with."

In it is an indication that only the believers benefit from admonition. On either possibility, it is a clear indication that none benefits from Allah's admonition except the believer; as for the non-believer, he does not benefit.

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, in the commands and prohibitions, ﴿and Allah is Knowing﴾ of what He commands and forbids, ﴿Wise﴾ in it).

﴿Yubayyinu﴾ means: He makes manifest. And ﴿al-ayat﴾ means the signs that point to Him, glorified and exalted be He. It has passed with us that the verses are divided..?

* Student: The verses are divided into two types: the cosmic verses (ayat kawniyyah), which are all (...), and the legislative verses (ayat shar'iyyah), which are (...), and they are the Qur'an.

* The Shaykh: What His revelation sent down to His messengers contains, whether the Qur'an or other than the Qur'an. The cosmic verses are what Allah created in the universe and decreed, and these are apparent to the believers and others. Even the believers know that these are signs that no human can replicate. The legislative verses are not made clear and manifest except to the believers: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are called from a distant place﴾ [Fussilat 44]. What is the point of this? The legislative verses contained in His revelation sent down to His messengers benefit only the believer. As for the disbeliever, may Allah protect us, it increases him in filth upon his filth, and he dies in disbelief.

The cosmic verses, even for those who do not believe in Allah the Exalted, meaning those who do not submit to and comply with His laws, they believe that such matters cannot be brought about by any human, despite the differences of their paths.

Therefore we say: ﴿Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, i.e., He makes them manifest so that they become clear, and there is no difference in this between the cosmic verses and the legislative verses. For this reason, when the sun eclipsed in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, what did he say? "Indeed the sun and the moon are two signs among the signs of Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1044), and Muslim (901/3) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. Even their eclipse is among the signs of Allah, because if all of mankind gathered to eclipse the sun, could they? No, they cannot.

So it is from the signs of Allah, because a sign (ayah) means that which indicates what it is a sign for, meaning that no one can bring it about except the one for whom it is a sign.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah makes clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing﴾, the commentator's statement (in the commands and prohibitions) seems to restrict them to the legislative verses, while the reality is that they include both the legislative and the cosmic verses.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾, ﴿Knowing﴾ means: possessing comprehensive, all-encompassing knowledge regarding His own actions and the actions of the creatures, and Allah the Exalted knows what has occurred and what will occur of His own actions and of the actions of the creatures.

And ﴿Wise﴾: it has passed with us that it is derived from where?

* Student: From wisdom (hikmah) and judgment (hukm).

* The Shaykh: From wisdom (hikmah) and judgment (hukm), correct. And it has passed with us that wisdom is found in..? That is what is required.

* Student: Wisdom is of two types..

* The Shaykh: No, its place?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the place of wisdom: the Shari'ah and the qadar. It is first found in the Shari'ah and the qadar. So everything Allah legislated conforms to wisdom, and in the qadar, everything Allah created conforms to wisdom. Its locus, then, is the Shari'ah and the qadar. As for wisdom itself, it is in three things, in what?

* Students: In origination (ijad), form (surah), and purpose (ghayah).

* The Shaykh: In origination, form, and purpose. The bringing of a thing into existence is wisdom; were it not that wisdom lies in its existence, it would not have come into being. Its being in this specific shape or this specific form is also wisdom, and its purpose is also wisdom. ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115].

If we multiply two by three, how much is it? The Shari'ah and the qadar, and each of them is either in origination, or in form, or in purpose, the total is six. As for judgment (hukm), it is also divided into two types: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). An example of the cosmic?

* Student: His saying: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah﴾.

* The Shaykh: The cosmic? Is this cosmic? Notice that it was mentioned after Allah said: ﴿O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. Allah knows best their faith. If you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them. And give them what they have spent. And there is no blame upon you if you marry them when you have given them their due compensation. And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women, and ask for what you have spent and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. What does this become? Legislative, because all the preceding matters are legislations. This is an example of the legislative. An example of the cosmic?

* Student: ﴿Until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the saying of my brother Yusuf: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me, and He is the best of judges﴾ [Yusuf 80].

If judgment, whether cosmic or legislative, is entirely in conformity with wisdom, is it necessary for us to know this wisdom, or is it not necessary?

* Students: It is not necessary.

* The Shaykh: It is not necessary. But it is obligatory upon us to believe that there is nothing Allah has originated or legislated except that it has a wisdom; however, due to our deficiency, much of these wisdoms remain hidden from us.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 19:

Then Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, those who love that immorality (al-fahishah) should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know" [al-Nur 19].

"Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread" by the tongue, "will have a painful punishment."

We have said that when such a construction comes in a sentence in two clauses, it conveys emphasis: "Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread, for them..." He did not say, "Indeed, for those who love that immorality should spread there is a punishment." He made the matter into two clauses: a minor (sughra) and a major (kubra). So his saying, "Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe, for them there is a painful punishment," is the major clause, and his saying, "for them there is a painful punishment," is the minor clause. It is called "minor" because it stands in the place of a single noun, since it is a predicate (khabar), and the original state of the predicate is that it be a single word. I hope we pay attention to this, for I forgot yesterday to research it.

"Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe": "alladhina" here is the first word. "Inna alladhina," what is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)? It is the noun of "inna," so it is in the position of the subject (mubtada'). "Yuhibbuna" is the relative clause (silat al-mawsul). "An tashi'a al-fahishah fi alladhina amanu" is the object of "yuhibbuna." "Lahum" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "'adhab" is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). The clause is the predicate of "inna."

So we say that this sentence contains two clauses: a minor and a major. The major is the whole: "Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe, for them there is a painful punishment." The minor is: "for them there is a painful punishment."

We call it minor even though it consists of a subject and predicate, because it is a predicate, and so it stands in the place of a single word, since the original state of the predicate is to be a single word. For example, you might say: "The student is understanding" (fahim), where "fahim" is a single-word predicate. You say: "The student has understanding," and it has now become a clause. Together they are two clauses: the major, which is both of them together, and the minor, which is the clause that became a predicate. And Allah knows best.

(...) It may be denied, because they are cosmic signs (ayat kawniyyah) which are witnessed by people: the night, the day, the sun, the moon. Fine, and the legal ones (shar'iyyah)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Has Allah made them clear, while they are apparent to everyone or not?

* Student: He made them clear (...).

* Shaykh: He made them clear, but they are not apparent to the one whose insight Allah has blinded, as Allah the Exalted said: "Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are being called from a distant place" [Fussilat 44]. So the clarity and manifestness of the signs, whether they are cosmic or legal, is clear, and no one doubts them. If they are legal, they are clear in themselves, but some people are blind to them. Yes indeed.

Moreover, it may also be said that even cosmic signs may be missed by some people upon reflection, because some people think that these signs are not produced, or are not the act of the Creator, but are natures that interact and some arise from others, without any Manager or Creator for them. On this basis, the cosmic signs too are like the legal signs, contrary to what we established previously.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter."

"Inna alladhina yuhibbuna": "alladhina" is one of the relative nouns (asma' mawsulah). It is known in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence) that the relative noun conveys generality (umum), so "inna alladhina yuhibbuna" is general.

His saying "yuhibbuna an tashi'a al-fahishah": "tashi'a" means spreads and becomes apparent. The author's saying "by the tongue" (bi-al-lisan) is an explanation of the spreading, meaning it spreads by speech and becomes apparent, and people circulate it.

However, the more apparent view is that it is more general than spreading by the tongue, and that it spreads by action, such that people witness it, and by speech, such that it is reported about them.

So these people who love that immorality should spread, whether they love that it spread by speech, as the author indicated with "by the tongue," or they love that it spread by action, meaning that their affair becomes apparent, becomes clear, and they are seen and witnessed.

His saying, "for them there is a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter": this is a clause that we call what? A minor clause, because "inna alladhina," "alladhina" is the noun of "inna," and it is in the position of the subject, and "lahum 'adhab alim" is a declarative clause functioning as the predicate of "inna." This conveys more emphasis than if it were said, for example: "Indeed, for those who love that immorality should spread, there is a painful punishment," because that would be more eloquent, since it would be two clauses that seem repeated.

The author's saying "by attributing it to them" is based on the view that spreading means the spreading of the tongue. The more correct view is that it is more general, that is, by attributing it to them in what is said about them, or by seeing it from them in what they do.

The author's saying "and they are the 'usbah" is not correct, because he wanted to explain the general by the specific. Is "those who love that immorality should spread" specific to the 'usbah who brought the slander, or is it general for everyone?

* Students: General for everyone.

* Shaykh: General for everyone until the Day of Resurrection. Even, for example, whoever wants or loves that immorality spread among the believers in his time, he is included in this verse.

Restricting the verse to something for which there is no evidence is not permissible. The scholars have said: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause (sabab). However, we must know that the case of the cause is definitively included, meaning: if a general wording comes for a specific cause, then the cause for which it was revealed is definitively included in this generality, while its other instances are not definite but apparent in it.

The explanation of this is that the indication of a general wording on each of its individual instances is definitive or speculative? It is a speculative indication, meaning not definitive, since it is possible that some individual instances have been specified by a ruling that contradicts this generality. For this reason we say that the indication of a general wording on its generality is speculative. Have you understood? Why do we say speculative? Because of the possibility that some of its instances have been specified, except the case of the cause, meaning the instance which is the cause of this generality is definitively included, because it is not possible to exclude it from the generality while it was revealed on account of it.

For example, if someone says: "Those among you who divorce their wives by zihar, they are not their mothers..." [al-Mujadila 2], and so on to the end: if someone said that Aws ibn al-Samit, who made zihar with his wife and was the cause of revelation, is not included in it, what do we say to him? We say: this is not correct, he is definitely included.

If someone said: the man whom the Prophet (ﷺ) saw being shaded, with people around him, while he was fasting on a journey, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1946), Muslim (1115/92), from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, and the wording is al-Bukhari's], and someone said: this man is not included in this hadith, we say: this is not correct, and it is not possible, because the instance which is the cause of revelation is definitively included, and other instances are not definite but speculative.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, now explained this general wording by the specific. Is that permissible or not? It is not permissible. When a general wording is found, it must be taken according to its generality, even if its indication on all its individual instances is speculative, as you have heard. But it must be taken according to its generality until evidence for specification arrives.

So we say: this verse is general to the 'usbah and others.

* * *

("For them there is a painful punishment in this world" by the prescribed penalty (hadd).)

* Student: By the hadd for slander (qadhf).

* Shaykh: I have: "by the hadd for slander," and the meaning is one.

("And the Hereafter" by the Fire, for the right of Allah the Exalted.)

"For them there is a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter": in this world there is punishment as the author mentioned, and it may be a more severe punishment. But now what occurs to us is that the painful punishment in this world is the penalty (uqubah).

"'Adhab," as we indicated earlier, means punishment, and "alim" means painful. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is also with Allah.

The author's saying, "the hadd for slander, and the punishment of the Hereafter is for the right of Allah," is problematic, because it is established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that: "Whoever commits any of these sins and is punished for it in this world, it is an expiation for him" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (18), Muslim (1709/41), from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit]. For this reason they said: the hudud (prescribed penalties) are expiations for those upon whom they are carried out. The hudud, such as the hadd for fornication, the hadd for theft, and others, are expiations for their people, since Allah the Exalted does not combine two punishments upon him. So on this basis we say: this verse is about those who love that immorality should spread, not about those who spread it, because if it is about those who love that immorality should spread, but he did not spread it, is there a hadd for him in this world?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: There is no hadd for him. Merely loving that immorality spread among the believers is not slander, so the hadd is not carried out on him. But he is punished or chastised by what the scholars call ta'zir, a discipline that deters him and the like from this act.

As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is said: since the matter is not a hadd, he may not be chastised, and then the punishment for him is in the Hereafter. As for the one upon whom the hadd is carried out for some act of disobedience, it is an expiation for him, as established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If this threat is for those who love that immorality should spread among the believers, what then is the state of the one who spread the immorality? Which of them is greater?

* Student: The one who spreads it.

* Shaykh: The one who spreads it is worse than the one who loves that it spread, because the one who spreads loves and does. He loved and did, for he only spread the thing out of love for its spreading. So he has loved and done, whereas one who loves may not do, and yet he has a painful punishment. Is that clear, I think?

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: "And Allah knows, while you do not know."

("And Allah knows" their absence from them; "and you," O 'usbah, "do not know" its presence among them.)

* Student: And you, O 'usbah, by what you said of sin, do not know it.

* Shaykh: It is not with me. By what did you say?

* Student: (...).

It is obligatory upon the ruler (imam) to establish it. As for ta'zir, some scholars say it is not permissible, unlike the obligation of the hadd. The hudud are obligations, and they must be established. As for ta'zir, some of them hold that it returns to the judgment (ijtihad) of the ruler. If he sees that it should not be established, he does not establish it. So if we suppose the ruler exercised judgment, whether he erred in his judgment or was correct, and did not establish the hadd upon him, this means he will be punished in the Hereafter without doubt.

* Student: We say: the hadith is general and the verse is specific.

* Shaykh: Which of them?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, the hadith is general according to its generality, and the verse likewise. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he is combined for him in both matters.

* Student: And the hadith.

* Shaykh: And the hadith indicates that the two matters are not prescribed for him together. Yes. The correct understanding is this: that if the punishment of this world escapes him, he is afflicted with the punishment of the Hereafter.

* Student: So if he is chastised for his love of immorality?

* Shaykh: If he is chastised for his love of immorality, he is not punished in the Hereafter, because Allah does not combine two punishments upon a servant for one sin. But if the ta'zir escapes him, either because the judge exercised judgment, or because he concealed himself, or something similar, the punishment of the Hereafter remains.

* Student: How do we know their love of immorality (...)?

* Shaykh: We know it by their displaying it. If he says, "Perhaps Allah will expose so-and-so," then if he himself spread it, he becomes a spreader. And if he did not spread it but loves it, we know that he loves this. He follows it up and says, "The people have spread this, and what have they done?" Then we know that he (...) in it is immorality.

* * *

As for His saying, "And Allah knows, while you do not know" [al-Nur 19], the author says: "(He knows their absence from them)." Whether this or another matter, because the correct view in general is that the absence of the immorality which these people loved to spread among the believers, Allah the Glorified and Exalted knows whether it is absent from them or present in them.

"And you do not know": is this negation absolute, meaning you know nothing, or: you do not know what Allah knows?

The latter, meaning you do not know what Allah knows. Otherwise, a person has knowledge; a person has knowledge. "And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight, and hearts" [al-Nahl 78]. "Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" [al-Zumar 9]. But you do not know what knowledge Allah has, and you do not know as Allah knows, because the knowledge of Allah is vast, comprehensive, and complete, while the knowledge of a human being is limited and deficient, meaning restricted and incomplete, unlike the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. In this there is an indication that it is not permissible for a person to speak of such matters until he has knowledge. And if he has knowledge, he must also weigh the interests in that matter. Suppose I know that this man committed immorality. Is it commendable for me to refer it to the ruler so that it is made clear and exposed? Or is it commendable that I do not refer it?

The answer: this depends on the interest. If the one who committed the immorality is a man known for chastity and righteousness, and the matter came from him as a lapse, then he should not be referred to the ruler and publicized. Rather, it should be concealed from him and he should be advised. If the man is known for evil and corruption, then it is obligatory that his affair be made clear, revealed, and publicized.

Likewise is the matter of pardon: is pardoning the offenders better than taking the right, or is taking the right better than pardon? Yes, it is based on this detail. If there is righteousness in pardon, then pardon is better; otherwise, taking the right is better. All the verses that encourage pardon are restricted by His saying, "So whoever pardons and reforms, his reward is with Allah" [al-Shura 40]. "Whoever pardons and reforms." Yes, Allah the Exalted restricted pardon by reform. And also, in terms of meaning, it may be said: pardon is a kindness, and reform is obligatory, is it not? Reform is obligatory, and seeking righteousness is obligatory, and pardon is a kindness. When the obligatory and the kindness conflict, which one takes precedence?

The obligatory. So on this basis, if the reform of people conflicts with pardoning this criminal, we say: reform takes precedence. If you pardon this criminal, he goes on to commit crime against someone else, and if he is pardoned he goes on to commit another crime, and so on. So we say: pardon is not appropriate here, if we do not say that it is forbidden. On this basis, the conduct of some people now is explained. Some people, for example, when someone hits them, or runs over their property or their person, immediately rush to pardon, and this is a great mistake. People must be told that the obligation is to reflect: is this man who acted recklessly, for example, and ran over this human being, or this animal, or damaged this property, a reckless and wicked person? Then it is not appropriate to pardon him. And is it also in the interest to pardon him? Or perhaps if we pardon him, people will no longer care about this matter. That is, if everyone who did such a thing were chastised, imprisoned, and fined, people would not be in the state you see now. But unfortunately, some brothers are seized by emotion, and they are seized by asceticism toward the world in the face of the great shock that has struck them. Then immediately they renounce it. When, for example, a grave calamity afflicts them, the whole world becomes cheap in their eyes. Yes, they say, for example: "If this dear one of mine has gone, what concern is it of ours? The whole world has become nothing to me..." (...) for anything, then immediately (...). This is an error, and the obligation is wisdom.

Indeed, acting on emotion without reason is truly a trait of women, not a trait of men, nor a trait of the people of reform. In these matters, the obligation is to consider what is most beneficial for this particular person and for the public in general.

(Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah an-Nur, verse 20)

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you, O assembly [of believers], and His mercy, and that Allah is Kind and Merciful﴾ [An-Nur: 20] toward you, He would have hastened the punishment for you.) Here Allah, glorified and exalted, establishes ﴿Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ and so on to the end; because the whole context is a grave matter. In the first [instance], it is the verse that comes before the incident of the slander (al-ifk), concerning false accusation (al-qadhf), which is a serious matter and a defilement of the honor of the Muslims. So were it not for Allah's favor upon the Muslims and His mercy in establishing the prescribed punishments (hudud) that deter them and restrain them, what happened would have happened. Likewise, ﴿Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ is mentioned in the story of the slander. How many times has it come up for us?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Three?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: This is the third? Good.

﴿And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Kind and Merciful﴾. ﴿Ra'uf (Kind)﴾: al-ra'fah is the mercy that includes intense tenderness. That is to say, it is more specific than general mercy: mercy and something additional. For this reason He said ﴿Raheem (Merciful)﴾, combining what is more specific in meaning with what is more general. Mercy (rahmah) is more general than kindness (ra'fah): every ra'fah is a rahmah, but not vice versa, because ra'fah, i.e. kindness, is a special type of mercy that entails an increase in mercy and special care for the one shown it. And ar-Raheem has previously been mentioned as one of the names of Allah, the Exalted.

The scholars have divided mercy into two types: general (ʿammah) and specific (khassah). The general mercy is that which encompasses every person: believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, human and animal (...). For this reason, if someone asks you: "Is the disbeliever shown mercy or not?", we say: in the general sense, yes, he is shown mercy; were it not for Allah's mercy he would not eat, drink, clothe himself, marry, or have children, and so on. Yes. As for specific mercy, it is that which is particular to the believers, which includes the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. As for the general mercy, it is happiness in this world only, whereas the specific mercy is happiness in this world and the Hereafter. This is specific to whom? To the believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 21:

Then Allah the Exalted says: (﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [An-Nur: 21], meaning his paths of adornment). ﴿Do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Al-khutuwat (the footsteps) is the plural of khutwah (a step), which refers to the distance between the two feet in walking. The intended meaning of "the footsteps of Satan" is his paths, so the step is used to express the path, because a path is the trace of footsteps. The author's statement, "his paths of adornment," is correct: all of Satan's paths are repugnant to souls, but he adorns them for the person so that he enters into them. Satan's paths, in general meaning, are denial (al-takdhib) and arrogance (al-istikbar). These are Satan's general paths. Satan is a denier and an arrogant one. An example of his arrogance is that he refused to prostrate to Adam, and his denial is that he claimed he was better than Adam, which necessarily implies that he denied that Adam was better than him. So this is Satan's path in general: denial and arrogance.

Now, denial corresponds to what? It corresponds to the reports (al-akhbar), and arrogance corresponds to the obligations (al-taklif), the commands and prohibitions. If you reflect on all sins, you will find that they do not go outside these two matters: either denial or arrogance. So his path, that of Satan, is built on these two matters: denial, concerning reports, and arrogance, concerning obligations of commands and prohibitions.

Now, when we come to details, for example, is stinginess (al-bukhl) among the footsteps of Satan or not? Yes?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, because he commands it.

﴿Satan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 268]. Many people of knowledge said that what is meant by indecency here is stinginess, because the verse is in the context of spending, although the more appropriate (...). Now, eating with the left hand and drinking with the left hand?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is also among his footsteps, because the Prophet ﷺ informed that "Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand"[[Narrated by Muslim (2020/105) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Accordingly, eating with the left hand and drinking with the left hand is prohibited, because Allah forbade following the footsteps of Satan, and "the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also forbade a person from eating with his left hand and drinking with his left hand"[[Narrated by Muslim (2099/70) from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. From this we derive the danger of people's negligence today regarding this matter, because many people, we ask Allah to guide them now, eat with the left hand and drink with the left hand, and they claim that this is progress and civilization. The cause is a feeling of inferiority, because a person, unfortunately, whenever he feels his deficiency, must imitate whoever he sees as more perfect than himself. These deranged people thought that others among these disbelieving nations are more advanced and stronger in progress. It is true that they are more advanced than us in industry and in worldly matters, but in the morals and manners to which Islam has guided us, they are not more advanced than us. However, looking at the condition of Muslims today, there is no doubt that they have some of the Islamic manners which they practise not intentionally, but merely because they are virtuous morals, not as worship of Allah. This is better than him. Unfortunately, the Muslim who was commanded to apply these manners and morals is the one who has fallen short of them, although when a Muslim applies them he is characterized by these virtuous morals, and these are without doubt nobility and honour.
