In addition, he is rewarded because he does them in obedience to the command of Allah and His Messenger. Do those people, when they do them, receive reward or not? They do not receive reward; they only do them because they are virtuous morals. For example, they have honesty in dealing, clarity, no deceit, and fulfilment of promises. All of these are among the qualities that Islam commanded. Many Muslims now have abandoned these qualities, but when a Muslim possesses them, he is praised for them and is also rewarded for them, because he does them in obedience.

I say: The footsteps of Satan are his paths which he follows and which are his method of conduct, and this revolves around two matters: denial and arrogance. The footsteps of Satan may be specific and particular, as we said regarding the matter of eating with the left hand and drinking with the left hand.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And whoever follows the footsteps of Satan — indeed, he﴾ meaning the one who follows, ﴿commands indecency﴾ meaning the ugly, ﴿and wrongdoing﴾ according to the Sharia, by following them).

﴿And whoever follows the footsteps of Satan﴾: how do we parse (man)? It is conditional; (man) is a conditional noun, and conditional (man) requires a condition and a response, meaning a conditional verb and a conditional answer. Where is the conditional verb? ﴿follows﴾. And the response of the condition is ﴿fa-innahu﴾ [indeed, he], the clause ﴿fa-innahu yamuru bil-fahsha'i wal-munkar﴾ [indeed, he commands indecency and wrongdoing]. Now we have ﴿man yattabi'﴾ and we have Satan, ﴿khutuwat ash-shaytan﴾. Does the pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ return to which of them? If we look at the basic structure and subject, we say it returns to ﴿man﴾, meaning the speech now: the response of the condition returns to what the conditional verb returns to. And if we look at the context and the nearest mentioned item, we say it returns to Satan, so the meaning becomes: whoever follows the footsteps of Satan falls into indecency and wrongdoing, and the clause ﴿fa-innahu...﴾ is then indicative of the response of the condition but is not itself the response.

As for the view the author took, he says: ﴿fa-innahu yamuru﴾, so it is itself the response of the condition, exactly the response of the condition. Is this clear, I think, or is it not clear? If we say the pronoun returns to ﴿man yattabi'﴾, meaning whoever follows, the follower, as the exegete said, then the clause is the response of the condition.

This interpretation is preferred because the basic principle is that what is mentioned is the response of the condition, and that the pronoun in its response returns to what the conditional verb returns to. This is the basic principle. As for the second opinion, it says: ﴿fa-innahu yamuru bil-fahsha'i wal-munkar﴾, saying: indeed Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing, and this indicates the response. This opinion is supported by the fact that the context is about forbidding following what? The footsteps of Satan. So it is as if he says: whoever follows the footsteps of Satan falls into indecency and wrongdoing, because Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing. This is more apparent for two reasons: first, the context indicates it; and second, the one who follows the footsteps of Satan may not command indecency and wrongdoing. He may commit indecency and wrongdoing without commanding it, so it is not necessary that whoever follows the footsteps of Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing. Yes, whoever follows absolutely, meaning absolute following, must command indecency and wrongdoing, because Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing.

In any case, the more preferred view is that the pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-innahu yamuru﴾, yes, the more preferred is that it returns to Satan, not to the follower. Two matters support this. First: the context indicates it, because Allah forbade following the footsteps of Satan, then mentioned what supports this prohibition by warning, showing that Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing. Whenever any sensible person knows that Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing, would he permit himself to follow his footsteps? The answer is no.

The second matter supporting this is that the one who follows the footsteps of Satan may not command indecency and wrongdoing. He may follow it himself but not command it. You will find that many people of misguidance are misguided themselves, but they have no call to what they are upon. Yet we also find that many people of misguidance have a call and command indecency and wrongdoing, meaning to what they are upon. So the correct view is that the pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-innahu﴾ returns to Satan. If we say it returns to Satan, the question remains: where is the response of the condition?

* Student: Could the punishment be immaterial (...)?

* The Shaykh: It is possible that the punishment is immaterial, by what happens to him of regret, anxiety, and what is similar to that. It is possible.

* Student: The prohibition (...).

* The Shaykh: For prohibition, yes. The prohibition is for prohibition, and for this reason, when it is for prohibition, there is what justifies it. Some people now do this: "By Allah, I am eating, I fear I drank with the right hand, and I am eating, I fear I have defiled the vessel."

Sometimes forgiving (ṣafḥ) occurs without pardoning ('afw). A person turns away from the wrong done to him, yet his heart is still full of resentment toward the one who wronged him and he has not pardoned him. And sometimes pardoning occurs without forgiving: a person overlooks the offence and does not punish the wrongdoer for his sin, but he has not turned away from that sin and mentions it whenever the occasion arises. On this basis, Allah the Exalted commanded both together: ﴿that they pardon and forgive﴾. This is similar to the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [At-Taghabun 14]. Here Allah distinguishes between pardon ('afw) and overlooking (ṣafḥ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nur 22]. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Yes, I love that Allah should forgive me," and he returned to Mistah – or he resumed (wa-rajjaʿa) to Mistah – what he used to spend on him.[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq ʿalayh); al-Bukhari (4141) and Muslim (2770/56), from the hadith of ʿAʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her).]]

As for His saying ﴿Do you not like﴾: is this an offer (ʿarḍ) or an urging (taḥḍīḍ)? It is an offer in form, but it carries the meaning of an urging (taḥḍīḍ), meaning it urges us to love this thing. But the intended meaning is not merely that we love it; rather, that we strive for its causes, because whoever loves something pursues the means of obtaining it. Every person may claim, "I love that Allah should forgive me," yet he is absorbed in sins, abandoning obligations and committing what is forbidden. Is his love then sincere?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is not sincere, because whoever loves something strives to reach it. That is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do you not like that Allah should forgive you?﴾, meaning: if you love that, then pardon and overlook the faults of others, for whoever pardons and overlooks the faults of another, Allah will forgive him.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) is derived from forgiveness (maghfirah), which is the concealing of a sin together with overlooking it. It is not mere concealment; it is concealment with overlooking. Concealment without overlooking is not forgiveness. We say that forgiveness is concealment with overlooking because overlooking is what provides protection from punishment. Its root is from al-Mighfar (the helmet), since the helmet covers the head, what? And it protects it. What also indicates this, that forgiveness is concealment together with protection, is the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah will draw near to His believing servant on the Day of Resurrection, and will make him confess his sins. When he admits them, Allah will say: 'I concealed them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him).]] This shows that forgiveness is other than concealment; otherwise forgiveness would have existed already in the world. Forgiveness is one thing and concealment is another thing. But every forgiveness includes concealment, and not every concealment includes forgiveness, because whoever forgives you and does not punish you means that he concealed it for you; for if he punished you, he would have exposed you. Now, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): the author says that he "rajjaʿa" or "rajaʿa." Do we say rajaʿa or rajjaʿa?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, but my question is: do we stress the jīm or not?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Is lightening not acceptable? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them﴾ [At-Tawbah 83]. "Rajjaʿaka" here means "radda-ka" (returned you). This is because rajaʿa in reality is used both transitively and intransitively. Rajaʿa is a past-tense verb used both transitively and intransitively. If you say "rajaʿtu min kadhā" (I returned from such-and-such), it is intransitive. If you say "rajaʿtu ilā fulān mā istaʿartuhu minhu" (I returned to so-and-so what I had borrowed from him), it has become transitive. So "rajaʿa ilā Mistaḥ mā kāna yunfiquhu ʿalayhi" means "radda" (he returned), and so it may be read with lightening (taḥfīf).

* Student: If we say that forgiveness is other than concealment?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not other than concealment in the sense of being entirely separate from it. It is not merely concealment.

* Student: The hadith indicates (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes? What does it indicate?

* The Student: "I concealed them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you." Does it not indicate (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, it indicates. Yes, it indicates that it is not merely concealment, because if forgiveness were only concealment, this would have happened in the world. Rather it is concealment together with the absence of punishment, meaning concealment together with overlooking.

* Student: Now, a person may commit a grave sin, such as drinking wine, and Allah forgives him but does not conceal it; everyone knows he has done these things.

* The Shaykh: In this case, if he is exposed and then forgiven, that becomes concealment, because if he is exposed among his contemporaries and those around him, and is not forgiven, that means he is exposed to all people. Is that not so? When he is exposed among his people and then forgiven, it means he is concealed from most people, because most people are not his contemporaries. Yes.

* Student: Pardon (al-ʿafw) in the sense of (...)?

* The Shaykh: Pardon in the sense of overlooking. It means that Allah pardoned them, that is, overlooked them.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, Allah does not say "ṣafaḥtu ʿankum" (I overlooked you). Overlooking (ṣafḥ) is what we are commanded to do. As for Allah, I do not recall now that Allah says "ṣafaḥa ʿanhu" (He overlooked him); rather He says "ʿafā ʿanhu" (He pardoned him), and He does not say "ṣafaḥa." So when pardon and overlooking are combined in the case of a created being, pardon is interpreted as such-and-such: not holding the sin against him; and overlooking as turning away from it entirely as if it had never happened. Thus overlooking completes pardon.

* Student: That pardon should be (...).

* The Shaykh: No. If we consider its original meaning of pardon, that it is not holding a sin against someone, it does not necessarily follow for Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. I do not know; perhaps pardon in relation to Allah can be understood as including both. That is, Allah overlooks it completely and places no lingering consequences after this pardon. So we may say that pardon with regard to Allah includes overlooking. Yes.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: We mentioned that the hadith refers to the prescribed legal penalties (ḥudūd). But this case is outside the prescribed penalties, because love of spreading immorality, or the spread of immorality, is not the degree that requires a ḥadd. That only requires a discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), and taʿzīr may be omitted. Yes. For example, those who deserve punishment in the Hereafter, which is the taʿzīr, but they may not be disciplined; it may be omitted for some reason. As for their punishment in the Hereafter, it remains. In other words, if the punishment of this world is omitted, the punishment of the Hereafter is not omitted.

Some brothers said yesterday that perhaps what is meant by punishment is something more general than flogging and the like: it may be a punishment in that Allah places in his heart pain, sorrow, anxiety, and the like.

* Student: If he is disciplined (...) the ruler.

* The Shaykh: No, if the ruler disciplines him, we say that by the principle that a ḥadd expiates, taʿzīr also expiates. Taʿzīr expiates if it is fully carried out, because the reality is that with regard to taʿzīr, the ruler may leave it altogether even though it is obligatory, may carry it out while being lax about it, or may carry it out perfectly, meaning he punishes this transgressor with a complete punishment, like the prescribed penalty, because we know that the prescribed penalty is a complete punishment since it comes from Allah. But taʿzīr may fall short of the offence or crime; it may be less, and so it is deficient. It may be equal, and then it is complete. And the person may not be held to account at all, such as when the ruler is either unjust or related to this person and shows him favouritism.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: We said on this basis: the "ʿarḍ" which means "taḥḍīḍ" (urging): that is, Allah urges us to love the forgiveness of Allah, and love of forgiveness necessarily requires striving for its causes.

* Student: (...) and you promised us (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. It seems it has ended. I promised you that I would say: I would like you to review the benefits contained in it and write them down. Yes. If you wish, mention the verses first, then list the benefits without explanation where explanation is not needed. And if you wish, mention each verse on its own and say: "From this verse is derived such-and-such," and so on. That is fine. Yes. So let us see, perhaps we will obtain more benefits. Al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on him) derived a thousand benefits from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Abu ʿUmayr, what happened to the nughayr?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6203) and Muslim (2150/30), from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him).]] It is a hadith of two words, and in meaning it is comparable to ten verses of the Qur'an, which would require you to bring us ten thousand.

Well, in any case, fear Allah as much as you can, and the bounty of Allah is given to whomever He wills. That is why when "a man said to ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib: 'Did the Prophet (ﷺ) entrust you with anything?' He said: 'He did not entrust us with anything except an understanding which Allah gives in the Book, and what is in this sheet,'"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6903), from the hadith of ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him).]] and he mentioned what was in this sheet. The point is that people differ in their acquisition of knowledge, not only according to how much they read, but according to how much they read and according to their understanding. For you find some scholars who take one verse and derive from it many benefits, though it is one verse, through implicit indication, direct indication, and necessary implication. These indications, as you know, are: indication by inclusion (tadammun), indication by correspondence (muṭābaqa), and indication by necessity (iltizām).

The indication of a statement on its complete meaning is called indication by correspondence (muṭābaqa). Its indication of a part of its meaning is called indication by inclusion (tadammun). Its indication of a matter that necessarily follows from its occurrence is called indication by necessity (iltizām). For example, if you say: "This is a house," this word indicates the whole house with its rooms, chambers, and roofs by what kind of indication? Correspondence. That it indicates there is a room in it and a chamber in it and a roof in it, what kind of indication is that? Inclusion. That it indicates that it has a builder who built it, this is indication by necessity, because it necessarily follows from its existence that it has a builder. These three indications differ greatly among people, and according to this difference the knowledge of a person broadens.

Therefore the student should train himself to draw out many rulings from the texts, because from a single text you may take a page of benefits and rulings, while another person may not derive from it even two lines. So the student of knowledge, just as he trains himself in much reading and study of books, should also train himself in deriving rulings (istinbāṭ). Deriving from where? From the evidences. How many a single piece of evidence indicates hundreds of rulings according to a person's understanding, so he is spared from many texts and does not need to exhaust himself in acquiring and reading them. Yes.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: "O Abu ʿUmayr, what happened to the nughayr?" The nughayr is a small bird with which a child plays. It was with a boy who was known by this kunya, and he would play with it. When it died, the boy was distressed, as is customary: a child holds a sparrow and rejoices in it, and when his sparrow dies, yes, he is grieved over it, to the point that sometimes he plays with it while it is dead. So when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered one day and found the boy grieving over the loss of this nughayr, he said to him: "O Abu ʿUmayr, what happened to the nughayr?"

﴿to the near of kin, and the needy, and the emigrants in the way of Allah﴾ [An-Nur 22]. It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Mistah ibn Uthathah, his maternal cousin. But the lesson lies in the generality of the wording, not in the specific cause.

Then Allah the Exalted said: (Indeed, those who accuse ﴿الَّذِينَ يَرْمُونَ﴾ with adultery ﴿الْمُحْصَنَاتِ﴾ the chaste women, ﴿الْغَافِلَاتِ﴾ those heedless of immoral acts, in that it does not occur to their hearts to do them, ﴿الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾ who believe in Allah and His Messenger, ﴿لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [An-Nur: 23]).

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَرْمُونَ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ﴾ Ramy (accusation) means false accusation of adultery, and it is called ramy (casting) because it resembles casting stones in that it inflicts pain on the one accused.

As for His saying ﴿الْمُحْصَنَاتِ﴾, it has already been mentioned that it means the chaste women who abstain from adultery, and that the word muhsan (chaste, protected) in the Qur'an is used with several meanings, among them this one: women chaste from adultery; and among them: women who are married, as in His saying ﴿وَالْمُحْصَنَاتُ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ إِلَّا مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ﴾ [An-Nisa: 24]; and among them: free women, ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ مِنْكُمْ طَوْلًا أَنْ يَنْكِحَ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾ meaning free women, ﴿فَمِنْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ﴾ [An-Nisa: 25]. We have also mentioned in this discussion that for shared words which are applied to multiple meanings, the context determines the intended meaning; context is what specifies the intended meaning.

﴿الْغَافِلَاتِ﴾ He says: (heedless of immoral acts, in that it does not occur to their hearts to do them). This is what is meant by ghafilat (heedless), and this qualifier is not a condition, meaning it is not a condition that the woman accused be heedless. So some scholars have said, on the evidence that whoever accuses a muhsana (chaste woman) of adultery incurs the legal penalty for slander even if she is not heedless. But the default principle regarding a qualifier is: what is the default? It is that it is binding, and that its implied meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the reverse implication) is included in it. This is the principle. Whoever says that this qualifier is not binding, for example on the basis that it describes what is typical or the like, we may demand of him what? Evidence. We say: bring evidence that this qualifier is only to describe what is typical and is not intended; otherwise the principle is that qualifiers are intended to exclude what contradicts them, meaning that what contradicts them differs from them in ruling. Do you understand this or not?

﴿الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْغَافِلَاتِ﴾ Some scholars say that (ghafilat, heedless) is a qualifier describing the actual situation and is not intended. The meaning is that whoever accuses a muhsana incurs this curse even if she is not heedless. What is his evidence? He said: because whoever accuses a muhsana incurs the legal penalty for slander even if she is not heedless. And the ghafila, as you understand the meaning, is one in whose mind this matter with which she was accused does not occur; and this is more emphatic than her not having done it and not having been suspected of it. The heedless woman is more perfect than the one who is merely not suspected of it, because she may not be suspected, yet this thing may occur to her heart though she does not do it. So the heedless women are more complete in condition than merely what? The muhsanat.

So this speaker, who holds that (ghafilat) is a descriptive qualifier with no implied meaning, supports his view by saying that accusing a muhsana obliges the accuser to the legal penalty even if she is not heedless. Is this understood or not?

Our reply to his statement and his argument: your claim that "heedless" is a typical qualifier with no implied meaning, and your evidence for it, namely that accusing a muhsana with adultery makes the penalty obligatory even if she is not heedless, is not accepted. Why? Because the default regarding a qualifier is that it is binding, and that it excludes everything else by mafhum al-mukhalafa. This is the default: the qualifiers that occur in the Qur'an or the Sunnah are by default qualifiers that exclude their opposites from this ruling. So if we say that "heedless" is a typical qualifier that does not exclude its opposite, this goes against the default, and upon the one who claims it lies what? The evidence.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What? Upon the one who claims it lies the evidence. He argued for it by saying that accusing a muhsana makes the penalty obligatory even if she is not heedless. Is that correct or not? It is correct: the chaste woman not suspected of adultery, if the accuser accuses her, the penalty is obligatory on him even if she is not heedless. We reject this argument, or this support he gave to his statement, on the ground that the ruling is different: there is the legal penalty for slander, and here there is the curse, ﴿لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾. Whoever accuses a muhsana deserves the penalty for slander, but cursing is only for whoever accuses a heedless muhsana. This is the default, and therefore we affirm that "heedless" is a binding qualifier, not a typical one, and that the ruling of cursing in this world and the Hereafter applies only to whoever accuses a heedless muhsana. This is because the default, according to what you have heard in this derivation, is that qualifiers are what? Binding, excluding their opposites from the ruling. This is the default, and whoever departs from it must be held to produce evidence.

Now, as for whoever says that the intended meaning of this verse is, for example, A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), that A'isha is meant and she was heedless of this matter: this is correct, A'isha was heedless. But we also reject his statement on this basis: the verse is general. This is like the first view: restricting the general to the specific requires evidence, so whoever claims it must provide evidence, otherwise the generality must be followed.

﴿الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾ (who believe in Allah and His Messenger). ﴿الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾: If someone asks: why did Allah mention the description of chastity before faith? Because faith is greater and is the principle, so why did He place it first?

We say: the reason for placing it here is clear, because accusation of adultery breaks chastity and contradicts it. So He began with the attribute that negates what was attributed to them, which is chastity: because a believing woman may be a believer without being chaste, but the chaste woman, who is furthest from what she is accused of, is not only a believer but also chaste. So the reason for placing the chaste before the believing, even though faith is more complete and more deserving of consideration, is that the matter concerns the rebuttal of a claim related to chastity, so it fits to mention the ruling connected with it first, which is the attribute of chastity before the attribute of faith.

As for His saying ﴿لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾: what is its place in the grammatical structure?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What is it? It is not a conditional response, since there is no condition here.

* Student: Predicate.

* Shaykh: The predicate of (inna): "Indeed those who accuse... are cursed."

﴿لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾. Here He did not say "Allah cursed them," but said ﴿لُعِنُوا﴾ so that it includes the curse of Allah and of others besides Him, the Exalted. ﴿لُعِنُوا﴾ is like His saying: ﴿يَلْعَنُهُمُ اللَّهُ وَيَلْعَنُهُمُ اللَّاعِنُونَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 159], meaning that Allah curses them and likewise those who curse curse them.

Building the verb in the passive has among its benefits generality (...) among the benefits, but in a verse like this it includes generality, like ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ (٦) صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [Al-Fatiha: 6-7]. He did not say "other than those with whom You are angry," just as He said ﴿أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾. Why? Because blessing comes from Allah, while anger comes from Allah and from others: everyone who is arrogant towards the truth is angry-at, not only from Allah's side but also from others' side. Likewise the cursing here comes from Allah and from others, and therefore it is built in the passive: ﴿لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾.

Cursing means expulsion and distance from Allah's mercy. As for Allah's curse, they are, may Allah protect us, expelled from Allah's mercy, the Exalted, in this world and the Hereafter. As for others' curse, in this world they are reviled, spoken of with contempt, and kept at a distance from association, and people withdraw from them, and what is the reason? Because they are despised and avoided; everyone shuns them and fears they will be accused of what they accused so-and-so of.

Now, this verse: ﴿الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْغَافِلَاتِ﴾. Are the chaste heedless men like them? Yes, by consensus, the chaste men are like the chaste women in this ruling.

So what is the reason for mentioning women only and not men, since they share the ruling? Because accusation of women is more frequent than of men: women are accused and suspected of adultery more often than men. Therefore women were mentioned, and men are included by agreement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 24:

The Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ to the end of the verse [An-Nur: 24]. He said: (﴿On the Day﴾: its governing element is the settled state (al-istiqrar) attached to ﴿for them﴾.) ﴿And for them there is a great punishment﴾ (23). ﴿On the Day﴾: the author did not make it dependent on ﴿They are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾; he made it dependent on (﴿for them﴾), (...) a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur). What is it dependent on? On the settled state to which the prepositional phrase is attached, because ﴿for them there is a great punishment﴾. We want the brother to give us its i'rab (grammatical analysis).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) ﴿great﴾. Analyse ﴿for them there is a punishment﴾. Who will analyse it? Yes?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. The prepositional phrase ﴿for them﴾ is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), ﴿punishment﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿great﴾ is an adjective. Now, when a prepositional phrase is the predicate of a subject, they say it is permissible to make it dependent on a verb, and it is permissible to make it dependent on an active participle. Ibn Malik said:

*"They have reported a adverb or a prepositional phrase, intending the meaning of 'existing' or 'settled'."*

So here we say: ﴿for them there is a great punishment﴾ means "a painful punishment has settled for them." We make the predicate a clause. Or: "existing for them." We make it an active participle. Either way, (existing) can take the adverbial phrase as its dependent, and (settled) can also take it. On this basis we say: ﴿On the Day [when] their tongues testify against them﴾. When will the great punishment be theirs? It will be theirs ﴿on the Day when their tongues testify against them﴾ [An-Nur: 24] to the end.

﴿for them﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate. Did you understand? But is the prepositional phrase itself the predicate, or is what the prepositional phrase depends on the predicate? The answer: what it depends on. However, they say the prepositional phrase is the predicate by way of leniency and figurative usage. The predicate is the deleted element on which the prepositional phrase depends. What is its estimate? (Settled) or (settles): "Settled for them is a painful punishment," or "Settled for them is a great punishment." The author indicates this in his tafsir when he says: (its governing element is the settled state to which ﴿for them﴾ is attached). Where is the settled state? It is what we estimated and said: "settled for them," or its estimate: "settled for them." So the word ﴿On the Day﴾ is an accusative adverb. What governs it? The settled state. Instead of saying "the settled state," we say: its governing element is the implied element to which the prepositional phrase is attached, whether you estimate it as (settled) or as (settles). So ﴿On the Day﴾ is attached to it, that is, to what the prepositional phrase in ﴿for them﴾ is attached to, whether you estimate (settled) or (settles).

Now we have finished the explanation of the verse.

This is because if the predicate is a prepositional phrase, it must depend on an implied element. Either you estimate it as a verb or as an active participle. You say: "settled for him" or "settled for him" [as an active participle]. You have heard the verse we recited for this rule in the Alfiyya:

*"They have reported a adverb or a prepositional phrase, intending the meaning of 'existing' or 'settled'."*

(Existing) here is an active participle, and (settled) is a verb.

When will this great punishment be theirs? ﴿On the Day when they [their tongues] testify against them﴾, (﴿testify﴾ with the feminine and masculine prefix). ﴿Testify﴾ and ﴿testifies﴾ are both read. (﴿their tongues, their hands and their feet testify concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 24], meaning in word and deed, and that is the Day of Resurrection.) That is, the Day on which these body parts testify is the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: (﴿testify﴾ with the feminine and masculine prefix) means that there are two readings, ﴿tashhadu﴾ and ﴿yashhadu﴾. This is because (ألسنة, "tongues") is a plural. Is it a broken plural or a masculine one? It is a broken plural. A broken plural may take either masculine or feminine agreement. You say: "qala al-rijal" and "qalat al-rijal" ("the men said"). Is ﴿tashhadu﴾ feminine or masculine? Feminine. And ﴿yashhadu﴾ is masculine. Both are permissible.

﴿Their tongues﴾ is the plural of "tongue" (lisan), ﴿their hands﴾ is the plural of "hand" (yad), and ﴿their feet﴾ is the plural of "foot" (rijl). ﴿Concerning what they used to do﴾. The author said: (in word and deed). We benefit from the words of the author, may God have mercy on him, a great benefit: that ʿamal (action) includes speech and deed, unlike fi'l (deed). For this reason we make speech the first, and what is its counterpart? You say: "speech." What is the counterpart that stands opposite to it? "Deed." You do not say "speech and action." If you want to be fully precise, you say "speech and deed." (...) "speech and action," but this is figurative usage.

So we understand that ʿamal is applied to speech and to deed. Indeed, the people of the Sunnah and the community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah) said in their discussion of faith that ʿamal includes the action of the tongue, which is speech, the action of the limbs, which is deed, and the action of the heart as well. The action of the heart is like its fear, hope, love and the like, meaning the movement of the heart, the inner movement. So when it is said "ʿamal" it includes speech and deed. If you want to make a division, you say "speech and deed."

If you hear or come across an expression that includes "speech and ʿamal," know that this is figurative usage: ʿamal is used figuratively for fi'l (deed). Otherwise the basic principle is that fi'l is the counterpart of qawl (speech), not that ʿamal is the counterpart of qawl.

* Student: Is there a difference in meaning?

* Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference, it is well known. When you say ʿamal, it includes speech and deed. When you say fi'l, it is specific to deed, the action of the limbs, while speech is the action of the tongue. So ʿamal includes the speech of the tongue and the deed of the limbs, but fi'l is specific to the deed of the limbs only.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No. When it is said "speech and ʿamal" as a division, it is figurative in applying ʿamal to one of its two meanings, namely deed. We say it is not a general term placed over a specific one (...) the division.

So, I say: ﴿On the Day their tongues, their hands and their feet testify against them﴾. The tongue testifies against the person. How does it testify? It says to the one who slanders a chaste, heedless, believing woman: "You slandered her." His own tongue says: "You slandered her," even though the act was done by it in this world. The deed was the tongue's deed, and yet it testifies against its owner with this speech, which is slander. Their hands also testify against them, their feet testify against them. God the Exalted has mentioned that these organs testify against a person on the Day of Resurrection. He also mentioned that the skins testify too, and that there will be an exchange between a person and his skin: ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "God has made us speak, He who makes everything speak, and He created you the first time"﴾ [Fussilat: 21].

* In this verse: an affirmation of resurrection and an affirmation of recompense, and that recompense is of the same kind as the deed. What is the evidence? His saying: ﴿concerning what they used to do﴾; they testify to what they used to do, neither more nor less.

* It also contains: the completeness of God's power, the Mighty and Majestic, since these organs speak, although speech is ordinarily through the tongue. Yet there can be speech by everything when God the Exalted wills. For this reason the skins say: ﴿God has made us speak, He who makes everything speak﴾.

* In this is a proof of the gravity of slandering chaste, heedless, believing women. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that it is among the major sins. He said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and he mentioned among them: "slandering chaste, heedless, believing women" [Agreed upon (Bukhari, 2766; Muslim, 89) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him].

* In this is a proof of God's jealousy (ghayra), of the perfection of God's jealousy, and that He, the Majestic and Exalted, is jealous. The sound hadith says: "There is no one more jealous than Allah, that His servant should commit adultery, or that His female servant should commit adultery" [Agreed upon (Bukhari, 1044; Muslim, 901) from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her]. Likewise the story of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, when the verse was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes and never accept their testimony, and those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [An-Nur: 4]. Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, questioned how a man might find another man with his wife, then go and seek four witnesses, who would not come to him until the act was over. He said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "By Allah, I will strike him with the sword, not with the flat side." That is, I will strike him with its edge until I kill him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do you not marvel at Sa'd's jealousy? By Allah, I am more jealous than he, and Allah is more jealous than I" [Agreed upon (Bukhari, 7416; Muslim, 1499) from Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah]. Yes, and what shows this is that God made it obligatory for these slanderers to be cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and that they have a great punishment. For this reason the Shari'ah came with what Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, desired. If a person finds, God forbid, another man with his wife, he may kill him, whether that man is married or unmarried. He does not need to seek defence. He does not need to say that if he cannot (...) then he may kill him. Rather, he may kill him immediately, because this is not a matter of repelling an aggressor, but of protecting his sacred honour.

For this reason the story occurred in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and they brought the case to him, and they acknowledged that the slain man... meaning they did not deny the husband's claim that he had found him with his wife. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I only struck the thighs of my wife. If there was anyone between them, I have killed him." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, took the sword and said to him: "If they return, return [as well]" [Ibn Qudamah cited it in al-Mughni (11/462; 12/135) from Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Sunan, but we have not found it in the printed Sunan available to us]. He did not object to this act, because a man cannot bear to find someone violating his sacred honour to this degree and not kill him.

In any case, in this verse I say: an affirmation of the jealousy of God, the Mighty and Majestic. Its meaning is that He, the Glorified and Exalted, protects the honour of His believing, chaste, heedless servants by this severe punishment, which is being cursed in this world and the Hereafter.

Now, does the verse imply the permissibility of cursing the one who slanders a chaste, heedless, believing woman, from His saying: ﴿They are cursed in this world﴾? Or is this a description of the actual situation, that people curse them, despise them, and keep them away from their gatherings and from mixing with them? What is your opinion?

In truth, the verse is open to both readings, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Beware of the three cursing places: relieving oneself in watering places, in the path of people, and in the shade" [Abu Dawud (26) and Ibn Majah (328) from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him]. In Muslim's version: "Beware of the two cursers." They said: "What are the two cursers?" He said: "The one who relieves himself in the path of people or in their shade" [Muslim (269/68) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. So he called that cursing.

So is the meaning that these people who do this deed are shunned and kept away by people, and people withdraw from their conduct? Or may we curse them, saying: "O Allah, curse the one who relieves himself in the path of people or in their shade," and here we say: "O Allah, curse the one who slanders a chaste, heedless, believing woman"?

It appears that the ruling covers both: it covers the actual situation that people do curse them in fact, and keep away from them and exclude them from their gatherings, and that it is permissible for a person to curse the one who slanders a chaste, heedless, believing woman, because God has cursed him. Therefore, invoking a curse upon him is a matter of realizing what God has informed of.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 25:

Allah the Exalted said: ("On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense, the true one," meaning He will repay them with the recompense that is due to them, "and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth," for He fulfils for them the recompense they used to doubt. Among them was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The chaste women (al-muhsanat) here are the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and no repentance is mentioned for slandering them, whereas those mentioned at the beginning of the surah as slandered are other than them, and for them repentance is mentioned.)

He says: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense﴾. "Yuwaffihim" means He gives them in full. You say "waffaytu-hu haqqahu," meaning I gave him his right in full. His saying "dinahum" means their recompense. The word "din," as we have mentioned many times, is used for the deed and for the recompense of the deed. An example of its use for the deed is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida 3]. What is meant here: your recompense? No. What is meant is the deed by which you worship Allah.

Similarly, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatiha 4]. What is meant here? The recompense. So "din" is used to mean the deed and the recompense for the deed, and from it comes the saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged," meaning as you act, so you will be repaid.

So "dinahum al-haqq" means "their recompense for their deeds."

His saying "al-haqq" means justice. This is because "haqq," if it is said in contrast to a report, means truthfulness, and if it is said in contrast to a ruling, whether an explanatory ruling or a recompensatory one, it means justice. Here it is said in contrast to a recompensatory ruling, so what is meant by "haqq" is justice, free of injustice or oppression. Likewise, Allah the Exalted's recompense is always true, meaning just, without any oppression.

Does not Allah's recompense for good deeds, which is ten times their like up to seven hundred times and up to many multiples, contradict this verse or not? The answer is: it does not contradict it, because this is justice and more. For Allah to repay the doer more than his deed is justice plus bounty. But if a person repays another for a good deed by punishing him more than he deserves, that is oppression, is it not? It is oppression. Allah is exalted above this latter case, because it is oppression. But the former is bounty from Allah, and Allah the Exalted is the Owner of Great Bounty.

﴿Allah will pay them their full recompense, the true one, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾: in this sentence there are two emphasizers (mu'akkidan). If we wish, we may say there are three. 

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: "Inna" and the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl). Are these two?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No. This sentence, who knows? What is the third emphasizer?

* Student: The lam.

* Shaykh: Where is the lam? Is there a lam in it?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: This "al" is the definite article.

* Student: (...) "ya'lamun."

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, it is not a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya)? (...) The sentence is composed of a subject and a predicate, both of which are definite. The fact that both the subject and the predicate are definite gives emphasis and restriction (hasr) as well. It gives emphasis and restriction. So Allah the Exalted is the Truth, emphasized by these three emphasizers. And what is the meaning of Allah being "the Truth"? First: His existence is true. What is due to Him of rights is true, such as worship, for He is the true God. Whatever proceeds from Him, whether a report or a ruling, is true. So He is the Truth in His essence, in existence and in entitlement, and likewise in His rulings. He, the Exalted, exists in truth, and He is the one entitled, in truth, to what is specific to Him, and no one shares it with Him. He, the Exalted, from whom nothing proceeds but truth, meaning His rulings and His actions are all true.

So the sense in which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Truth is in three respects:

First: in His existence. His existence is true, and He is the most truly existent of things. For this reason all sound natural dispositions (fitar) bear witness to it, and likewise pure intellects, meaning those free of doubts and desires, bear witness to it. Likewise, whatever proceeds from Him is true. Whatever He reports is true, and whatever He rules is true, whether these rulings are legislative, which is what He prescribes for His servants, or recompensatory, which is what He repays His servants with. And what is the third meaning?

* Student: What He is entitled to of worship.

* Shaykh: What He is entitled to as well. Whatever He is entitled to is true. That is, that Allah is specific to things that no one shares with Him, this too is true. For this reason Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is because Allah, He is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah, He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [Luqman 30]. So the truth on Allah's side, the Exalted, takes the following forms: existence, entitlement, and what proceeds from Him. His existence, His entitlement and what proceeds from Him. Is that understood? So His existence is true, and what He is entitled to of matters is true, meaning of perfect attributes, worship and other things. Third: whatever proceeds from Him, blessed and exalted, is true, whether a report or a ruling, and a ruling is either recompensatory or legislative.

Alright, shall we say: or decreed (qadariyy)? Because decreed rulings are also considered rulings, as we said: a ruling is of two kinds, cosmic (kawni) and decreed (qadari). In reality, yes, it must be added, because whatever proceeds from Him of rulings, whether recompensatory, cosmic or legislative, is true.

* Student: Is "qadariyy" the same as "kawniyy"?

* Shaykh: "Qadariyy" is "kawniyy," yes.

﴿Allah is the Truth﴾. As for His saying "al-Mubin," it derives from "abana," meaning from the quadriliteral verb. Does "abana" mean "to make clear" or "to become clear"?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That works. This quadriliteral verb "abana," they said, is used both intransitively and transitively. It is used intransitively in the sense of "bana," and transitively in the sense of "bana," meaning "to become clear."

Now here, does "al-Mubin" mean the one who is clear in His truth, or the one who made clear to His creatures that He is the Truth?

* Student: Both.

* Shaykh: Or both, or both? In reality, Allah the Exalted has made the truth clear, and He has made clear to His servants that He is the Truth.

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Ya-Sin 69]. What is the meaning of "mubin" here? Is it "clear" (bayyin), or "mubin" in the sense of "making manifest" (muzhir)?

* Student: Clear.

* Another student: In the sense of clear.

* Shaykh: Is the Qur'an "bayyin" or "mubin"?

* Students: Bayyin.

* Students: Both.

* Shaykh: Or "bayyin" and "mubin" in reality. But "mubin" here is more apparent, because of His saying: ﴿So that he may warn whoever is alive, and the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾ [Ya-Sin 70].

In the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, they were before in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran 164], what is the meaning of "mubin"? It is "bayyin," in the sense of "clear." The conclusion is that the word "mubin" is used both intransitively and transitively, because its root is a quadriliteral verb, "abana," which is used intransitively and transitively. If it is intransitive, it means "clear" (bayyin), and from it comes His saying: ﴿Indeed, they were before in clear error﴾. If it is transitive, it means making something manifest, making its clarity apparent. "Abantuhu" means I made it manifest until it became clear. From it comes His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Ya-Sin 69], meaning "manifesting," as shown by His saying: ﴿So that he may warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin 70]. Likewise: ﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara 195], meaning "manifesting." And although it follows that whatever manifests is itself apparent, "al-mubin" in the sense of "the manifesting" must necessarily be clear in itself, otherwise it could not make anything manifest.

﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾. Do you apply this verse to "mubin" in the intransitive sense or the transitive sense?

* Students: Both.

* Shaykh: In reality, both. Because Allah the Exalted has made the truth clear, He has made clear the truth of it, and He has made it manifest to His servants. How has He made clear to His servants that He is the Truth? First, by what He has placed in them of natural dispositions and intellects, the sound natural dispositions and the intellects. For this reason, Allah the Exalted always refers these matters to reason, saying: ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqara 44], which is evidence that reason is a reference point. But what is meant by reason is sound reason, which has no doubts and no desires. As for reason that has been overpowered by doubts or desires, that is corrupted reason, which judges nothing.

Also, the Blessed and Exalted made the truth clear by means other than reason, by natural disposition, for the sound natural disposition bears witness to the truth. And He made reason clear through the revelation sent down by the messengers. So Allah the Exalted's making the truth clear is by these three means. What are they? Reason, natural disposition and revelation. The truth is made clear through all three of these means. For this reason Allah sets forth parables for people, and why? So that they may take heed. The "mawrid" (the source) and "madrab" (the context) of the parable: they take heed by this in respect of that. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) Allah the Exalted says: (...).

* Shaykh: Read what follows it, read the verse you forgot.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes (...). What is meant by sealing the mouths is that they will not deny. It does not contradict that the tongues bear witness to what is seen of their intention. Is that understood? Or it may be said that the Day of Resurrection has stages, because the Day of Resurrection is fifty thousand years, so at one time it is thus and at another it is thus. Just as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) reconciled between His saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa 42], this is one state, "and they will not conceal from Allah any statement," meaning everything (...). And He said in another verse: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am 23]. And this is denial, is it not? This is denial. So how can we reconcile the two verses? We say: the Day of Resurrection has stages. Likewise some scholars reconciled His saying: ﴿And We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾ [Ta-Ha 102] with His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran 106]. Here there is blackness and there is blueness. Some said this is according to the stages of the Day of Resurrection. Some said blueness is in the eyes and blackness is in the faces. Some said people differ: among the disbelievers some are blue-eyed and some are black.

In any case, my purpose is that the people of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on them, resorted to reconciling the verses whose apparent meanings conflict regarding the Day of Resurrection, because the Day of Resurrection is not a single hour in which verses could conflict. The Day of Resurrection is fifty thousand years, during which conditions vary.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, this is what is meant, meaning it defends them, but (...). The tongue becomes two tongues: a tongue that bears witness and agrees with the limbs, which is what is meant by this verse, and another tongue that denies, which agrees with what its owner intends. The interpretation is: as if a person were to deny with the tongue that follows his will, the same tongue would bear witness against him. The wisdom here, and Allah knows best, in mentioning the tongue is that slander occurs by means of it, and for this reason it is mentioned before the hands and the feet.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 26:

﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ [al-Nur: 26]

Among the wisdom of Allah, glory be to Him, is that He made things corresponding and similar: everything with what suits it, in this world and also in the Hereafter, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses (azwajahum), and what they used to worship﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. ﴿Azwajahum﴾ means their likes and their counterparts. So every thing, by the wisdom of Allah, glory be to Him, is made to resemble its counterpart and to incline towards it. Among the particulars of this general principle, which Allah mentioned after relating what preceded of the story of the slander (al-ifk) and what took place from those who wished to defile the bed of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to impugn his family and his Companions, as has passed before us, it is known that the best of the best of creation is the Prophet ﷺ. So it is impossible that Allah, glory be to Him, would place beneath him a wicked woman. For this reason He, glory be to Him, said: (﴿The wicked women﴾ of women and of words ﴿are for wicked men﴾ of people, ﴿and wicked men﴾ of people ﴿are for wicked women﴾ of what has been mentioned, ﴿and good women﴾ of what has been mentioned ﴿are for good men﴾ of people ﴿and good men﴾ of them ﴿are for good women﴾ of what has been mentioned, i.e., what is fitting for the wicked is its like, and what is fitting for the good is its like).

He said: (﴿The wicked women﴾ of women and words ﴿are for wicked men﴾). The meaning is that a wicked man will have a wicked woman, and it is not possible for a good woman to be with a wicked man. Likewise, it is not possible for a wicked woman to be with a good man. An example of the latter is the matter of the slander: were it supposed that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, had done what she was accused of, she would have been a wicked woman under a good man, and this is impossible; for to whom do wicked women belong? To wicked men: ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men﴾.

As for his saying (of women and of words): "of women" is clear. "Of words" means likewise that wicked words are not attributed to, nor deserved by, anyone except one who is wicked. So ʿĀʾishah, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, cannot be described with what she was described with, because she is good, and only good words befit the good. Similarly ﴿wicked men are for wicked women﴾: if a person were to accuse a righteous man before a good woman, accusing him of fornication, we would say: this too is impossible, because a wicked man can only be with a wicked woman; this is the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore, among the particulars of this matter, the general rule is: lavatories and places of filth have become the abode of whom? Of the devils, while mosques and good places are the abode of the angels. Moreover, we add: a good soul is accompanied by goodness, and angels support it, while a wicked soul is accompanied by wickedness. For example, a bad, deviating person has his companion (qarin) empowered over him, so that he keeps company with him in a way that misleads and misguides him; whereas Allah, glory be to Him, helps a good soul against its companion so that it is safe, and so that evil does not command it. All of this is based on this principle, which accords with the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿The good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾: ﴿The good women﴾ of women and of words as well.

[The text here repeats the preceding sentence on the wicked soul and the companion, in the form found in the transcript.]

﴿The good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ [al-Nur: 26]: ﴿The good women﴾ of whom? Of women and of words as well. ﴿For good men﴾ means: nothing befits them except this; only good words and good women befit the good.

For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, is good and accepts only what is good,[[Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurayrah.]] so if a person gives in charity much wealth from unlawful earnings, will Allah accept it or not? He will not accept it, because it is wicked, and Allah, the Exalted, is good and accepts only what is good.

Reflect on this general principle and you will find it in everything: the good is suited by the good, and the wicked is suited by the wicked.

* A student: Shaykh, what happened to the Companions (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, but in such a case it is not established that they were wicked; and if it were established, that would be a rare matter. This is a rare matter that is taken into account, as has passed us in the matter of li'an: when a husband performs li'an, the penalty is established even if he does not bring four witnesses, because Allah made his accusation of his wife a testimony unlike any other. If this is established, it is rare. We should also know that general rules and universal principles are not refuted by a single instance of their particulars, for the causes may exist while impediments exist that prevent that cause, impediments that override the cause. Just as it often happens to us that the Lawgiver made this a cause for that, and then we find it does not take effect, why? Because of an impediment stronger than the cause. Likewise in the legal rulings: the conditions of validity exist, and the conditions of entitlement exist, and then an impediment among the impediments arises. Yes, this is very common and consistent in rulings, reports and general principles, and in other things.

* A student: This verse narrates the reality (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this verse narrates the reality and also contains a command, because if you reverse the matter which Allah made a sunnah for it, you have disobeyed.

He said: ﴿And the good women are for good men, and the good men are for good women. Those﴾ (the good men and good women, among whom are ʿĀʾishah and Safwan, may Allah be pleased with them both) ﴿are cleared of what they say﴾, i.e., the wicked men and wicked women among them say ﴿for them﴾, for the good men and good women, ﴿is forgiveness and an honourable provision﴾ in Paradise.

﴿Those﴾: the demonstrative refers to whom? To the nearest preceding mention, namely the good women and the good men.

﴿Cleared of what they say﴾: i.e., cleared of what is said about them.

The author gave as an example ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and Safwan ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, who was accused with her, as mentioned earlier in the story. Likewise we say: ʿĀʾishah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for as we indicated previously, the story of the slander was not an impugning of ʿĀʾishah and Safwan alone, but an impugning of ʿĀʾishah, Safwan, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and Abu Bakr.

All of this is undoubtedly included in this wicked statement; so these good people are ﴿cleared of what they say﴾, i.e., of what these wicked people say about them.

﴿For them is forgiveness and an honourable provision﴾: ﴿For them﴾ means these good people; ﴿forgiveness﴾ concerns sins, and ﴿an honourable provision﴾ concerns acts of obedience. Do you understand? ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾ for their sins, ﴿and an honourable provision﴾ for their acts of obedience.

We have divided it this way because sin is suited by what? Forgiveness; and righteous deeds are suited by an honourable provision, since whoever does a good deed is rewarded with ten good deeds up to seven hundredfold, up to many multiples.

It thus becomes clear that these people who were spoken of received through that the expiation of misdeeds, forgiveness of sins, and likewise elevation of ranks. This is also a particular of the general principle: no person is afflicted with distress, grief or harm without Allah expiating his sins by it, even a thorn that pricks him, Allah expiates by it. But is it also raised in rank for him? That is, these harmful things, distress, grief and physical harm and other things, expiate sins; but does Allah raise ranks through them?

* A student: (...) if he is patient.

* The Shaykh: If he is patient, yes. When patience accompanies them, he gains, along with the expiation of sins, additional good deeds; otherwise they are merely an expiation of his sins. The reason is this: are these afflictions that befall him by his choice? No, they are not by his choice; therefore they are punishments from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by which Allah expiates his sins, and He does not combine two punishments for him. But if he is patient, an act occurs from him, and then he is rewarded for it.

This is the verified position on this matter: afflictions that befall a person are not only rewarded, but sins are also expiated by them; and if patience accompanies them, or better still, contentment, then he is rewarded along with the expiation.

Now here: ﴿For them is forgiveness and an honourable provision﴾. Let us see: these people were in truth struck by a great calamity. Did they endure it or not?

* Students: They endured.

* The Shaykh: There is no doubt they endured until Allah relieved them and removed this distress from them. In exchange for what they were afflicted with of harm in this affair, forgiveness was granted to them, and in return for their patience, an honourable provision.

As for "honourable" (karim) when said of provision: it is not that provision has feeling so as to be described as generous; for example, one says "this man is generous" because he gives, meaning he has a will and bestows generosity on people. But how can something without will be described as generous? We say: the meaning of generosity for what has no will is what? It means the good and the fine; as the Prophet ﷺ said to Muʿadh: «Beware of their choicest possessions» [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1496) from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muslim (19/29) from Muʿadh ibn Jabal.]]. The word karāʾim is the plural of karīmah.

So the honourable provision is the good and the fine, and this includes much, for it is of goodness and excellence.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) this contains blame directed at them.

* Among the benefits of this verse:

* First: the great wisdom established for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, both legislatively and in decree. These statements and principles are both legislative and decreed. Allah, exalted is He, has made, in the decreed sense, for everything what suits it; likewise, in the legislative sense, we should also place people in their proper ranks: the wicked has his wickedness, and the good has his goodness.

* From this is derived: the explanation of Allah's wisdom legislatively, and what else? And decreed; legislatively and decreed.

* The second benefit derived from it: a person must place people in their proper ranks; he must place people in their ranks. He should not describe the good with wickedness, nor the wicked with goodness, because that opposes both the decree and the Law. It also entails harms: when you describe a wicked person with goodness, what does that mean? You have falsely and deceitfully removed the description from him, and you have also deceived people with it.

A good man is described as good, and a wicked man as wicked, and it is not permissible for a person to exceed that, because Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men﴾, and so on to the end.

* This also shows that Allah, glory be to Him, clears the family of the pure, chaste man, clearing them of wickedness, through the statement that good women are for good men and good men for good women. And a hadith states: «Whoever commits adultery, his family will be committed against; and whoever is chaste, his family will be chaste». This is part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: whenever a person is good, pure and clean, Allah prepares for him a family of this same standing, ﴿a recompense in full measure﴾ [al-Naba: 26]. The matter is the reverse if he is wicked, especially regarding chastity. If a person reflects on this he will find it frequently, though we do not say a hundred percent, because Allah brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living; but generally this is the reality: a man of defiled character, Allah makes for him a family likewise, and does not protect him, because he did not protect himself, so Allah does not protect him.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Decreed: that Allah, glory be to Him, makes for the good person good family members, and for the wicked person wicked family members.

* A student: And legislatively?

* The Shaykh: And legislatively also: it is not permissible for you to place the wicked in the position of the good, or the reverse.

* This shows that Allah, glory be to Him, in His mercy, defends those who do not deserve the wicked descriptions attributed to them; indeed this verse is, in reality, like a clear and manifest defence of whom? Of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: a clear defence.

* Also in it is evidence that whoever is afflicted with a calamity, whether verbal or practical, Allah forgives him; and if he endures it, he is given a reward as well, he is given a reward.

Among Allah's protection of the good person is that Allah keeps the causes of evil away from him, so that he does not expose himself to them; for the reality is that exposing a person to trials may cause him to be tested. So among Allah's protection of His servant who intends good is that Allah, glory be to Him, protects him from the causes of trials. Let me now relate a story to you:

A man who was known in this town for piety, a piety considered among the most perfect, one day went to carry wood from his family's property, ʾathl wood, and his neighbour was also cutting his ʾathl, and there were two piles of wood there. This man made his camel kneel beside his neighbour's wood and loaded the wood onto the camel. Then, when he wanted to make the camel rise, it would not rise at all; he refused completely. He tried and tried, and it refused; he unloaded the whole load, and the camel rose. When the camel rose, Allah opened his understanding, he stood up (...) and reflected, and behold, the wood was not his; it was the second pile, his neighbour's. This is from...

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) there is nothing in it. But look how Allah, glory be to Him, prevented him; otherwise, if the camel had risen at once, it would have walked off with him. But this is from Allah's protection of His servant: when Allah knows from his intention purity and chastity, He protects him, glory be to Him. In contrast, may Allah protect us, a person whom Allah knows to incline towards evil and corruption may have the causes of evil and corruption prepared for him until he falls into them.

(ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, took pride in several things, among them that she was created good, and was promised forgiveness and an honourable provision.) That is: it seems she, may Allah be pleased with her, understood that a verse like this was revealed concerning her, so she took pride in it. Pride here means speaking of Allah's blessing, not displaying superiority over people, because pride is of two kinds:

The first: a person takes pride in Allah's blessing, speaking of it. This is the pride which is permissible and which Allah has commanded.

The second: a person takes pride in order to display his excellence over others and to exalt himself over them. This is not permissible. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [al-Hadid: 23]. This pride is from self-conceit: the pride whereby a person intends to show his superiority over people and his exaltation over them; this is the self-conceit that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not love.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, like the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: «I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3340) and Muslim (2278/3) from Abu Hurayrah.]], and as ʿĀʾishah took pride in this, if the story is authentic, and as Zaynab took pride over the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in that Allah married her in the heavens, and other things that are said.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you ask permission and greet their occupants﴾ [An-Nur: 27] (The one seeking entry says: "As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?"[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (5177) and Ahmad (23127) from a man of the Banu 'Amir.]] As is reported in the hadith. "That is better for you" than entering without seeking permission. "That you may remember" — with the second taa' assimilated into the dhal — its goodness, so that you act upon it.)

This is among the etiquettes which are in reality a protection of honour. Most of this surah concerns this matter, chastity and what relates to it of protecting honour, and other things. Among the etiquette with which Allah has taught us when we wish to enter houses other than our own is what He says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾. We mentioned earlier that introducing a ruling with the vocative indicates its importance, because the purpose of the vocative is what? Alerting the addressee. If you say, "O so-and-so," he will certainly pay attention. Now, if you saw one of you being heedless or dozing or something, and you said, "O so-and-so," would he pay attention or not? He would pay attention. So the vocative is intended to alert the addressee. And introducing a ruling, whether a command or a prohibition, or even a report, with the vocative indicates its importance, and that a person should be alert to it and attentive to it.

Then the address to the believers by the name of faith: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. What does this indicate?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It indicates that this action is part of faith, and that opposing it is something that diminishes faith, understood? It also intends encouragement (al-igra'), meaning that addressing with the description of faith is intended to urge strongly to adhere to the ruling. Igra' means strong urging to adhere to the ruling. For example, if I say, "O man, do such-and-such," what does it mean? Urging and encouragement, because the requirement of your manhood is that you do such-and-such. "O believer, do such-and-such" means encouragement, because the requirement of your faith is that you do such-and-such or leave such-and-such.

So the purpose of addressing the believers with the description of faith is what? Strong urging and encouragement to adhere to this ruling.

It is as if it were said: "If you are a believer, then do not do such-and-such," if it is a prohibition, or "then do such-and-such," if it is a command.

This also indicates — meaning that addressing them with the description of faith, apart from the matter of purpose — that what is mentioned is among the requirements of faith and that opposing it diminishes faith.

Let us now look at the ruling to which Allah guides: ﴿do not enter houses other than your own houses until you ask permission﴾.

﴿لَا﴾ (do not) is a prohibitive particle, and the prohibition here is for prohibition (tahrim), because that is its basic meaning.

And His saying ﴿بُيُوتًا﴾ (houses) is general. What is the form of generality in it?

* Student: An indefinite noun in the context of prohibition.

* The Shaykh: It is an indefinite noun in the context of prohibition, and an indefinite noun in the context of prohibition conveys generality. That is: do not enter any house other than your own houses that you own, except after two things: ﴿until you ask permission and greet their occupants﴾.

The author explained ﴿تَسْتَأْنِسُوا﴾ as (seek permission).

Explaining it as seeking permission is an explanation by some of its instances, because istі'nas (seeking familiarity/assurance) is more general than istі'dhan (seeking permission). A person may seek familiarity and have no sense of unease about entering this house even without asking permission, and then only the greeting remains. Like if someone invited you to his house after the noon prayer, and when you came you found the door open — what remains for you now?

* Student: You greet.

* The Shaykh: What remains for you is to greet, because the reality of the matter is that seeking permission here has no place, since the man has invited you, specified the time, and when you came you found the door open. That means permission. Therefore Allah the Exalted said: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, meaning: until there is no unease among you from seeking familiarity. And what is the opposite of familiarity? Unease. This is why it is said: "insi" and "wahshi" — wild game and domestic game; and it is said: "wild donkey" and "domestic donkey." And sometimes it is said: "insi."

In any case, istі'nas is more general than istі'dhan, so explaining it as istі'dhan is in the manner of explaining a thing by some of its instances, so that this serves as an example.

By this we know that this Sab'i recitation is more correct than the reading attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, in His saying: ﴿until you seek permission﴾.

We also wish to note that in this report narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ﴿حَتَّى تَسْتَأْذِنُوا﴾ and said: the phrase ﴿حَتَّى تَسْتَأْنِسُوا﴾ is an error of the scribe. This is in reality not authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, and even if it was mentioned in the same report, it is not authentic. The reason is that it is impossible for a scribe to err in a letter of the speech of Allah and then the Ummah receive it with acceptance; because if this were supposed, it would necessitate that Allah did not preserve this Remembrance, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [Al-Hijr: 9]. How could it be an error of the scribe that the Ummah receives with acceptance, recites in its prayers, and teaches to its children?! This is impossible.

For this reason, when such a report comes, it can be declared defective (mu'all) even if its chain is sound, because among what indicates the weakness of a hadith is that it contradicts what is known necessarily from the Sharia. If it is known necessarily from the Sharia that this hadith is not authentic, we must judge it false, why? Because it is impossible for an individual or narrators to bring something that contradicts what is necessarily known from the religion of Islam.

In any case, returning to our matter, we say: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾ is more general than what? Than (until you seek permission). The author's explanation and that of others as permission is in the manner of explaining a thing by some of its instances, only as an illustration.

Sometimes scholars explain a verse by one of its instances as an illustration, as some said regarding His saying: ﴿Then We gave the Book to those whom We chose of Our servants, and among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32]. He said: "The one who wrongs himself is the one who withholds zakat; ﴿and among them is one who is moderate﴾ is one who pays obligatory zakat; ﴿and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ is one who gives charity beyond zakat." So what do we call this?

* Student: An example.

* The Shaykh: We call it explanation by example, explanation by example only, not that the verse only means what was mentioned; rather this is in the manner of explanation by example.

* Student: A Sab'i recitation?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not Sab'i; the Sab'i reading is only: ﴿تَسْتَأْنِسُوا﴾.

As for His saying ﴿وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَى أَهْلِهَا﴾ (and greet its occupants): Allah began with seeking permission before greeting, and this is the natural order. This is the natural order, because you seek permission, and when it is granted you know that someone is in the house, and then you greet — meaning you knock on the door, for example, and say, "O so-and-so," and when he addresses you, you greet him.

So the verse is now arranged in the natural order: seeking permission first, then greeting second, before the person speaks, before he says anything at all.

The author's statement: (The one seeking entry says: "As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?") as is reported in the hadith. This reported hadith is to be understood as applying when the one seeking entry knows that its occupant is present; then he greets him and says, "May I enter?" But if he does not know, he should seek permission first, and then when he knows there is someone there, he greets.

For this reason the scholars differed on this matter: Should one seek permission first, or greet first? There are two opinions: Some hold that seeking permission precedes greeting, based on the apparent meaning of the verse: ﴿until you seek familiarity and greet﴾.

Others hold that greeting comes before seeking permission, based on hadiths reported on this: greet first, then say, "May I enter?"

Others made a distinction, saying: if one knows that the occupant of the house is present, he greets first and then seeks permission; and if he does not know, he seeks permission first and then greets.

This opinion is the most correct, the most preferred of the three opinions, because it combines the verse and the reported hadiths, and because it fully accords with reasoning. Reason requires this: if you know someone is there, you greet; otherwise, how would you say, "As-salamu 'alaykum," while you do not know, perhaps there is nothing there but walls? But if you know there is someone there, because he invited you, or you heard a voice, or you saw a person, then greet and then say, "May I enter?"

And His saying: ﴿That is better for you﴾: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾ (that) — the address is to whom? To the believers.

﴿خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ (better for you): We will now examine the goodness that results from seeking permission before entering. Before we speak of this, we speak of a grammatical point in which the reciter erred, saying: "dhalika khayrun lakum." The kaf is for address, correct or not? And dha is a demonstrative. The demonstrative follows what is pointed to, and the address follows the addressee, do you understand?

As for the first rule: the demonstrative follows what is pointed to. This is a consistent rule that cannot be broken.
