As for the kaf following the addressee, this is according to the most famous and most common usage: the kaf follows the addressee. So if you are pointing to a single masculine person while addressing a group of males, what do you say? A single masculine person, addressing a group of males: what do you say? Dhalikum. (Dha) refers to a singular masculine, so: dhalikum. If you are pointing to a woman while addressing a group of males?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, you point to a woman while addressing a group of males.

* Student: (talkum).

* The Shaykh: (Talkum). But for this address-kaf there is a second dialect: it remains singular, open-vowelled for the masculine and kasra-vowelled for the feminine. So if you address a masculine, whether plural or not, you say: dhalika. If you address a feminine, whether plural or not, you say: dhalika (with kasra).

And in a third dialect it is always fixed with fatha, meaning you always make it masculine addressee. These are three dialects, the first being the most famous, then the second, then the third.

﴿خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾: What is the goodness in our seeking permission and then greeting when we wish to enter houses other than our own? If we wish to enter houses other than our own, do you know any good in this?

* Student: Among the goods, first, is that we do not expose the mahram women of the house from our faces.

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is a goodness here: that if you seek permission you do not expose the mahrams of the owner of this house; because if you entered while they were (...), they may be in a state in which they do not wish anyone to look at them. That is one. The second?

* Student: Displaying the symbols of faith, an example being seeking permission (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, but this is after we know the goodness in it; (...) it may walk on one foot, there is with him (...). Yes.

* Student: The owner of the house may be sleeping, for example (...), so if you seek permission...

* The Shaykh: Meaning, embarrassing the owner of the house?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: So if you seek permission, this embarrassment is removed. Is this the first, or another?

* Student: No, another (...), but the owner of the house (...), so we seek permission (...).

* The Shaykh: Apart from exposing the mahrams, good: that the owner of the house not fall into embarrassment, because there is (...). If you open the door and enter, whatever the owner is busy with, he receives you as he is; perhaps he is occupied with something that embarrasses him if you come in upon him.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: From what?

* Student: Preparing the room of the house.

* The Shaykh: Preparing for whom?

* Student: Receiving the guest.

* The Shaykh: Preparing the owner of the house?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes; because it is closer to his preparation and readiness, so that the entrant does not think he has been humiliated; because when he enters without permission and finds nothing corresponding to it, he says: "This has humiliated me or honoured me," and so on.

Also in it: the innocence of a person from suspicion, and this is among the most important things: that the entrant is cleared of suspicion by it, because if he enters a house without permission he may be suspected of something, of something improper; but if he seeks permission he has entered with insight. So among the most important goods in it: the entrant is cleared of suspicion, so that he is not made a thief, or one who intends immorality, or the like. Because as is known now, if for example someone entered your house straight away without seeking permission, would you suspect him or not?

* Students: We suspect him.

* The Shaykh: You suspect him of stealing, or of committing immorality, or of killing, for example.

For this reason, among the most important goods in this matter is that a person is cleared of suspicion.

And in the greeting too: ﴿تُسَلِّمُوا﴾ — in it also (...) the Sunnah, but in it there is: securing the occupants of the house, together with praying for their safety.

As for securing the occupants: if you say, "As-salamu 'alaykum," your invoking peace upon them is more fitting and more deserving that they know that no harm will come from you; that it is impossible that harm comes from you, since as long as you ask Allah for peace for them, how could you then transgress against them?

For this reason the scholars said: if a man greets a disbeliever, this is considered a securing of him, because he says, "Peace be upon you," meaning: now I have greeted you, I am safe from you. So in greeting there is also, beyond what was previously mentioned, goodness: securing the occupants from the evil of this entrant, which is additional to the matter of clearing him of suspicion.

Also in it: kindness to them by greeting them.

Also in it: that you earn a reward, because when a person says to his Muslim brother, "As-salamu 'alayka," how many good deeds come?

* Student: Ten.

* The Shaykh: Ten good deeds come to him.

Subhan Allah! That is, one of us — may Allah forgive us — if someone said: "You get ten piasters if you say, 'As-salamu 'alaykum,'" would we neglect greeting or not? Never.

If it were said to these good-for-nothings who neither greet nor return greetings when standing up: "Each time you will get ten piasters," yes, at least ten halalas, they might never abandon greeting, besides the ten good deeds which may be multiplied to seven hundredfold. Truly, people are made to shun this, and we do not know whether this is ignorance on their part or negligence.

In any case, there is also in it this goodness: that you invoke blessings for your brothers whom you greeted, and thereby you are doing good to them, and also you are doing good to yourself, because you have gained ten good deeds for it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَى أَهْلِهَا﴾ after His saying ﴿بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكُمْ﴾: if we say ﴿بُيُوتًا﴾ is general, then ﴿وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَى أَهْلِهَا﴾ also requires generality.

If its occupants were disbelievers, would you greet them or not? The apparent meaning of the verse says you greet. But is this apparent meaning specified by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Do not initiate greeting with the Jews or the Christians»[[Recorded by Muslim (2167/13) from Abu Hurayrah.]]? Or do we say: that is in encountering, and this is in seeking permission, because you are the one coming to his house?

* Student: In encountering.

* The Shaykh: I (...) have it that if we look at the verse as general, and the general may be specified, we say: yes, this may be specified, that if he is a Jew or a Christian and you seek permission to him, do not say, "As-salamu 'alaykum." And if we look at the prohibition regarding (...).

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. It has passed that Allah the Exalted, by His legislation and His decree, made the wicked things for the wicked and the wicked for the wicked, and that everything returns to what resembles it, the good to the good and the wicked to the wicked. From this general rule the following is derived:

The innocence of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from what she was accused of. The reasoning is that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was married to the best of the good among creation, the Prophet ﷺ, and it does not befit the wisdom of Allah or His legislation that she be wicked.

It has also passed that if someone accuses the good of wickedness, Allah the Exalted clears him: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾; He clears him by legislated means and by decreed means. This is from Allah the Exalted's care for the people of goodness: that Allah must defend them, legislatively and by decree.

For example, we find that Allah the Exalted cleared the good from the speech of the people of wickedness legislatively, by prescribing the hadd for slander. This — the hadd for slander — is undoubtedly a clearing of whom? Of the one slandered. A clearing of the one slandered, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, it is they who, with Allah, are the liars﴾ [An-Nur: 13].

We also find that Allah the Exalted clears the good by decree, meaning He decrees among the worldly causes what makes his innocence evident.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 2 of 2):**

And among them is the companion of Jurayj, who spoke while in the cradle. Allah the Exalted cleared Jurayj of what he had been accused of, by way of *qadar* (divine decree, meaning what occurs through Allah's will and decree). This child spoke in the cradle and said: "My father is so-and-so, the shepherd."

It is narrated: "Jurayj was a worshipper from the Children of Israel. One day his mother called to him, but he did not answer her, because he was praying. So she became angry with him and said, 'O Allah, do not let him die until he sees the faces of prostitutes.' Then Allah the Exalted decreed what He decreed, until a woman accused him of having had relations with her, and claimed that the fetus, or the child she had given birth to, was his. He said, 'Bring me the child.' They brought it, and he said, 'Who is your father, O (...)?' The child said, 'My father is so-and-so, the shepherd.' Thus Allah cleared Jurayj by this."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3436) and Muslim (2550 / 7), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] Was that by *qadar* or by *shar'i* (legislated ruling)?

* Student: By *qadar*.
* Shaykh: By *qadar*.

In any case, ﴿They are cleared of what they say﴾. We say: it is by *shar'i* and by *qadar*. As for *shar'i*, it is by the *hadd al-qadhf* (the prescribed punishment for slander). As for *qadar*, it is by what Allah the Exalted brings about of cosmic events in which the innocence of this pure person becomes manifest. Is this clear or not?

We have also previously mentioned that Allah the Exalted forbade the believers to enter houses other than their own until after two things. What are they?

* Student: First, *al-istinas* (seeking companionship, i.e., making one's presence known and seeking the household's sense of ease).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The second thing: greeting its people with *salam*.
* Shaykh: *Al-istinas* and the greeting of its people. And which of the two comes first? *Al-istinas* first, then the *salam* second. Is that always the case, or is there a distinction? What is the distinction?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is necessary to ask permission, it is necessary to knock on the door. But does one greet first or ask permission first?
* Student: One asks permission first.
* Shaykh: One asks permission first, absolutely. Yes.
* Student: There are three opinions on it.
* Shaykh: There are three opinions on it, and we preferred?
* Student: The last.
* Shaykh: You have not told us so that we know which is the last. What is it that made us prefer it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The distinction.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, because of the narrations that are related on this matter. And the third?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, if he sees someone, or hears a voice inside the house, then he greets first and then asks permission; otherwise, he asks permission first. This distinction is the preferred view, because reflection also indicates it.

Is this verse ﴿and greet its people﴾ general in its scope, or is there a restriction in it?

* Student: There is a restriction in it.
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: If (...), then he does not greet him.
* Shaykh: Then he does not greet him; he asks permission to enter without a greeting. Good. What is the general evidence?
* Student: His saying ﷺ: "Do not initiate the greeting of salam to the Jews."
* Shaykh: "Do not initiate the greeting of salam to the Jews and the Christians." And this is general, is it not? Correct.

This verse is restricted to those who are among the people of *salam* (those to whom the greeting is due). As for those who are not among the people of *salam*, one makes one's presence known to them, but one does not ask permission to enter upon them.

There is a reading attributed to Ibn 'Abbas in place of ﴿tasta'nisu﴾ (seek companionship). What is it?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿tasta'dhinu﴾ (seek permission) in place of ﴿tasta'nisu﴾.

Which of the two is preferred, of course? Or is that one irregular (*shadhdhah*) and not one of the canonical (*sab'iyyah*) readings?

* Student: (...), because it is general.
* Shaykh: Because it is general.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Correct, because *al-istinas* is more general than *al-istidhan* (seeking permission). So this one is more preferred and more appropriate. As for the irregular one, it is not to be recited with.

As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The scribe made an error in it," this is a lie. It is impossible for this to be authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, because this is a canonical reading upon which the Muslims have reached *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). Is it possible for the Muslims to agree upon an error in the speech of Allah? It is absolutely impossible: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42].

Then we say: is the means of transmission of the Quran writing only, or writing and speech together?

* Student: Writing and speech.
* Shaykh: Writing and speech, especially in the first generation. Speech is more prevalent. Receiving the Quran by speech, especially in the first generation, was more common than receiving it by writing. And with this it becomes clear that this report from Ibn 'Abbas is false. We have only pointed it out, and it was not present with us, so that you will not be deceived by it.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿That is better for you﴾. The goodness here, some of it has been explained to us.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The second interpretation (...) the house.
* Shaykh: The tranquility of the owner of the house.
* Student: Then supplicating for him.
* Shaykh: And supplicating for him with peace.
* Student: And gaining reward.
* Shaykh: And gaining reward from this greeting.
* Student: Removing suspicion from...
* Shaykh: Removing suspicion from the one who enters. Yes. That makes four?

Yes.

* Student: Protecting private matters.
* Shaykh: Protecting private matters. That makes five.
* Student: Preparing the place...
* Shaykh: Yes, that is it. That is, the host's readiness for the guest, his preparation, so that the guest does not enter upon him while he is in a state that embarrasses him.
* Student: Avoiding embarrassment.
* Shaykh: Yes, avoiding embarrassment. Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We have mentioned them. These are what we know. As for what we do not know, it may be more than this. The main point is that it is good for us. And before that, that is, this goodness that we know is the reason the Lawgiver commanded this. However, after the Lawgiver commands something, the goodness in it that we do not dispute is what? It is compliance with the Lawgiver: doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. This is the greatest goodness found in the legal rulings: complying with the command of Allah and avoiding His prohibition, for which creation was created: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

And His saying: ﴿so that you may remember﴾.

This is separate from what precedes it. That is, one should not read it as ﴿That is better for you, so that you may remember﴾. For ﴿so that you may remember﴾: when *la'alla* (perhaps / so that) comes in the speech of Allah, it indicates causation (*ta'lil*). That is, We commanded you to do that and We explained it to you, and We explained that it is good. Why? So that you may remember.

The author says: (with the second *ta'* assimilated into the *dhal*, its goodness, so that you act upon it).

Regarding the word ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ (*tadhakkarun*): its original form is *tatadhakkarun* (تتذكرون).

He says that it is (with the second *ta'* assimilated into the *dhal*). So the reading, according to the author's statement, is ﴿تَذَّكَّرُون﴾ (*tadhdhakkarun*) with the *dhal* doubled. Its original form was *tatadhakkarun*, and the second *ta'* was assimilated into the *dhal*, so it became ﴿تَذَّكَّرُون﴾.

The meaning of ﴿تَذَّكَّرُون﴾ is that you take admonition, because *tadhakkur* is a person's taking heed, and the matter being present in one's mind so that one does not neglect or forget it.

The author's statement: (its goodness, so that you act upon it) indicates that the object of ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ is omitted, its implied sense being "its goodness." However, the truth is that this verb does not appear to me to be transitive; rather, the apparent view is that it is intransitive. One says *tadhakkara*, meaning he took admonition. So the apparent view is that it is intransitive, and the meaning is: you take admonition.

Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿And if you do not find anyone therein, then do not enter until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you.﴾ [An-Nur 28] — that is, permission is given to you. ﴿So do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you﴾ — after seeking permission. ﴿Go back﴾ — that is, returning. ﴿It is purer﴾ — that is, better ﴿for you﴾ than sitting at the door).

"And if you do not find anyone therein": that is, in the houses other than your own. For example, suppose you want to go to a friend of yours, you come and do not find anyone in the house. We have a sign that no one is in the house: if the house, for instance, is locked with its two locks, it is known that its owner is not in it.

As for His saying: ﴿do not enter until permission is given to you﴾ — how can permission be given to us when we have not found anyone in it? In other words, if no one is in it, can permission exist?

* A student: With prior permission.

* The Shaykh: Prior permission? How? That is, that he has already given you permission? That is not valid; the statement does not hold together.

* A student: The owner may have given permission to this person while he was not present.

* The Shaykh: And he was not present?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That is, prior permission; but this is prevented by... ﴿until permission is given﴾. He did not say, "unless he has given you permission"; the meaning is that you wait.

The meaning is that if you do not find anyone, entering is impossible. Just as there is no permission when no one is present, there is no entering with permission. However, it has come in this form — and Allah knows best — to indicate that the cause for entering or not entering is permission: ﴿So do not enter them until permission is given to you.﴾ Of course, if I know that no one is in it, there is no permission; but the meaning of "do not enter" is that there is no permission. So if you wait until the owner comes and gives you permission, then enter; and if you leave, there is no blame on you.

The possibility that the permission is prior, a previous permission, is mentally conceivable; it is possible. But the expression does not support it, because He said: ﴿And if you do not find anyone therein, then do not enter until permission is given.﴾ "Do not do such-and-such until such-and-such occurs" — so this occurrence must come after the prohibition was stated, and this negates that the permission was prior.

* A student: The representative of the owner?

* The Shaykh: Yes. Known: if there is a representative of the owner, then we have found someone.

* A student: It may cause harm to (...) if he wants (...).

* The Shaykh: It does not contradict; we are not saying there is a prior permission. We are saying: a representative of the owner, so he has the owner's standing. But if a person finds no one at all and seeks permission, and no one is there, he does not enter until permission is given to him: ﴿So do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back.﴾

If you ask permission of the owner of the house and he says: "By Allah, go back, brother, I do not want sitting (with you), or I do not want to open (the door)," would you say: "No," and feel offended at his turning you away, saying: "By Allah, I have come, it is not possible that you do not open"? What is the answer?

The answer: he says to him: ﴿Go back﴾. ﴿And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back.﴾ In this is evidence that Islam is forthright: there is no harm if the owner of the house says, "Go back, I am not opening the house," and whoever is told this must return, without taking offense. (...) "I cannot but enter," Allah says: ﴿Go back.﴾

Since this returning is difficult for souls, Allah encouraged it by His saying: ﴿It is purer for you.﴾

(﴿Then go back; it is purer﴾ — that is, returning ﴿is purer﴾ — that is, better ﴿for you﴾ than sitting at the door.)

In sum: He has contrasted the preferred option with the less preferred, which is sitting at the door. But we should say that the verse is general: ﴿it is purer for you﴾ absolutely, whether you sit at the door or persist and embarrass the owner of the house. The point is that this sentence is an encouragement and exhortation to return, because returning in reality is hard on the soul. If the owner of the house tells him, "Go back," and he returns — especially if he has come from afar, it is hard on him. But Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that this act, which is returning, is purer for the human being, meaning more purifying. Purity (zakāʾ) is the refinement of character and elevation of manners, and likewise in terms of worship. So a person's purity is the growth of his character, manners, and religion as well — his religion.

Some of the righteous predecessors said: "I have wished to attain this once in my life." Why? For the sake of purity. But this is rarely found.

In this verse there is much of the explanation of Islam's forthrightness and Islamic etiquette, and that a person should be forthright, not devious.

That is, for example: if I want you to enter, I say, "Enter"; if I do not want you, I say, "Go back." Many people do not do this, but the Shari'ah permits you to do it. It permits you to say to one who seeks permission from you: "Go back." Do not say, "By Allah, this is a difficult thing, a hard thing, and I cannot bring myself to say it." We say: the Shari'ah does not embarrass you. If it is not suitable for him to enter your house, and you have important business, or this man needs a large lavish hospitality and you are not prepared for it, then there is no blame in your saying, "Go back." And if he returns, that is purer and cleaner for him.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, it occurs in his soul if he has not read this verse. But if you have read this verse and he says to me, "Go back," and I return, everyone seeks purity; every person wants purity. For this reason, we said: the wisdom in Allah's saying ﴿it is purer for you﴾ is the exhortation and encouragement to return and to avoid arrogance, and that there should be nothing in the heart. These are Islamic manners that we should adopt and be forthright. Which is better: that he permits me grudgingly, under embarrassment, and I may miss many interests? Which is preferable? The first is preferable.

This, as it appears, has happened to you: sometimes a person seeks permission to enter upon you while you do not wish him to enter at all, either because of urgent work, or a matter at home he cannot witness, or something else. In any case, this matter is part of Islamic etiquette: a person should be forthright, with no trace of duplicity in his action or speech.

He said: ﴿It is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ (﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ — of entering with permission or without permission; ﴿Knowing﴾ — so He will recompense you for it).

﴿What you do﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun. Do you agree?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: That is, of that which you do. And a relative pronoun conveys?

* A student: Generality.

* The Shaykh: Generality. Restricting it to entering with or without permission is not appropriate in reality, although it occurs in the context of that; but the consideration is the generality of the wording. So Allah, glorified and exalted, knows all that we do: entering with or without permission, returning when told "Go back," not returning, and other of our deeds. ﴿Knowing﴾ — ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾. Even deeds that no one perceives, such as deeds of the heart, Allah, glorified and exalted, knows them.

What is the benefit of Allah informing us that He knows our deeds?

The benefit is clear: caution, as Allah, exalted, says: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾ [Al-Baqarah 235]. Caution regarding Him, blessed and exalted, if we have committed a sin; and desire for what is with Him if we have done an act of obedience. That is, when I believe that Allah knows what I do, this obliges me to beware of opposing Him, and it also obliges me to desire conformity to His law, because He will know that and will recompense me for what I have done.

So the conclusion is that Allah's informing His servants that He knows what they do includes two matters: a warning and an encouragement. A warning against what?

* A student: Against opposition.

* The Shaykh: Against opposition. And an encouragement toward conformity, conformity to the Shari'ah, because that is not lost; it is known to Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's Commentary (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 24, Verse 29**

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what you do.﴾ (﴿There is no sin upon you for entering houses not inhabited in which there is provision [matā'] for you﴾ [al-Nur 29], meaning benefit for you, such as taking shelter and other uses, like caravanserais (rubut) and public inns (khanat al-musabbala). ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal﴾, what you show, ﴿and what you conceal﴾, what you hide when entering other than your own houses, whether with a good intention or otherwise.) And so on to the end.

* Student: He means (...) there.

* Shaykh: With permission.

* Student: With taking shelter.

* Shaykh: What?

* Student: With the letter kaf, "with taking shelter."

* Shaykh: "With taking shelter and other"? Good. Actually, it has become a bit jumbled for me.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no sin [junah] upon you﴾. Junah means sin (ithm).

From what has preceded, it is deduced that the commands there are for obligation (wujub), because they are what a person incurs sin by violating. Allah's saying ﴿There is no sin upon you﴾ indicates that what preceded would involve sin if violated.

﴿for entering houses not inhabited in which there is provision for you﴾. Matā' (provision): the author says it means benefit. The more correct view is that it is more general than that, whether it is a benefit of taking shelter, as the author said, or other. Matā' means what is a source of enjoyment for you, of benefits and of material things. Even if the house, for example, contains things that belong to me, such as being a storehouse in which I keep wealth, there is also no sin on me in entering it without seeking permission, even if the house belongs to someone else. The reason is that the presence of my need in it, or my goods in it, is itself a permission for me to enter. The fact that this man gives me a part of his house in which to place my goods indicates that he has permitted me to do so; there is no need for me to seek fresh permission. Also, the permission that the Lawgiver required in this case does not appear to be obligatory, because the house is uninhabited. When it is uninhabited, the basic purpose of seeking permission was for the sake of oversight, and oversight is absent here because there is no one in it. But since it belongs to someone else, a person may feel scrupulous, because He said: ﴿But if you find no one therein, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾. If we took the generality of this verse, we would say: uninhabited houses, even if they contain our goods, we may not enter until we are given permission. But in this case, if they are uninhabited and not places of residence, and contain our goods, whether benefit or material, there is no blame on us for entering them without seeking permission.

His saying ﴿in which there is provision for you﴾ is evidence that if there is no provision of ours in them, we do not enter them even if they are uninhabited. The wisdom in this is clear: when a man enters a house that is not his, and which is uninhabited, and he has no benefit or provision in it, this leads to suspicion of him. What is the result? Corruption. As happens now in houses that are sometimes unoccupied and become a refuge for wrongdoers. So if a person has no provision in this house, he does not enter it at all. But if he has provision in it, even though it is uninhabited, there is no blame on him for entering it, whether he seeks permission or not. Yet seeking permission here does not apply, because it is not inhabited. However, were it not for this exception, we would say that the generality of His saying ﴿But if you find no one therein, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾ also governs this case. But this is a blessing from Allah.

So the conclusion now: houses are of three categories. Inhabited houses in which people live: what is obligatory? Seeking permission and greeting. Houses in which there is no one, but which are inhabited, but we did not find anyone in them: here too seeking permission is necessary; we may not enter until we are given permission.

Uninhabited houses: if there is provision of ours in them, there is no sin on us in entering them. Apparently, if there is no provision of ours in them, it is not permissible to enter them, and there is sin on us in that.

The reason is that if they are uninhabited, and they are not our property (if they were our property it would be clear), but they are not ours; if we enter them and have no provision in them, this gives rise to suspicion. This is one aspect. It also leads to dispute with its owner, because the owner says: "Why do you enter my house? Is that not so?" If you say to him, "It is uninhabited, and there is no need to seek permission because there is no one in it, no resident," he says: "But the house is mine; it is not lawful for you to dispose of it by entering." Therefore Allah the Exalted stipulated that there be provision for us in it.

* Student: O Shaykh, the provision is for what?

* Shaykh: No, the provision, the author says: (meaning benefit).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Either benefit or material thing.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The benefit is as the author said: with taking shelter or the like.

Taking shelter and the like are benefits. For example, suppose heavy rain falls, there are uninhabited houses around you, and you enter in order to take shelter from the rain, or from intense heat, or because an enemy is chasing you, or the like. This is a benefit. The material thing is as we have pointed out.

﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾.

* Student: So, if the interest (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿in which there is provision﴾ means: something that gives you enjoyment.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, as He said here: ﴿provision﴾, meaning what you enjoy of material things or benefits.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾.

Notice the difference between the two expressions. There He said: ﴿Allah is All-Knowing of what you do﴾, and ﴿All-Knowing﴾ is a noun. Here He said: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal﴾, and ﴿knows﴾ is a verb; the sentence is a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah).

The difference between them is that the first, ﴿All-Knowing of what you do﴾, is in terms of describing Allah with knowledge. Allah's knowledge is an attribute necessarily inherent in Him, pre-eternal and everlasting. Or is it newly arising?

* Students: Pre-eternal.

* Shaykh: Pre-eternal and everlasting, and not newly arising at all. Allah's knowledge does not renew, glory be to Him; rather, He has always been and always will be knowing of what has been and what will be. Here He said: ﴿And Allah knows﴾, and the scholars have said that a verbal sentence indicates renewal and occurrence: a verbal sentence indicates renewal and occurrence. Then this presents a problem for us, because we have established the principle that Allah's knowledge is pre-eternal and everlasting.

So we say: what is meant here is the linking of knowledge to action, linking Allah's knowledge to action. Linking Allah's knowledge to action occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We make evident those who strive among you and the patient﴾ [Muhammad 31], and ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove﴾ [Al 'Imran 142], and what is similar to them, which indicates that Allah's knowledge is joined with action.

It is not joined with action because it renews after the action occurs. No, but Allah knows a thing before it exists, that it will occur, and He knows a thing after it exists, that it has occurred. So the accompanying knowledge is not the same as the prior knowledge. The accompanying knowledge is what consequences are based upon, while the prior knowledge does not entail consequences. That is why He said: ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove﴾ [Al 'Imran 142], and ﴿And We will surely test you﴾, what after that? ﴿Until We make evident﴾. So the meaning is accompanying knowledge. And what does it entail? Recompense: reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience.

Notice, brothers, because this is really a problem. The expression of knowledge through the verb, or like the other verse ﴿until We make evident﴾ and similar things, creates difficulty for a person. The difficulty is that he says: Allah's knowledge does not renew; this is what is settled in our souls and our creed, and it is the reality. Allah's knowledge does not renew, yet these verses apparently indicate that Allah's knowledge renews.

What was our answer? The answer is that Allah's knowledge is pre-eternal and does not renew, but there is knowledge prior to existence and knowledge accompanying existence. Do you understand? So the knowledge prior to existence is knowledge that the thing will...?

* Students: Occur.

* Shaykh: Will exist or will occur. And the knowledge accompanying existence is knowledge that the thing has occurred. The knowledge accompanying existence is what entails recompense: reward in obedience and punishment in disobedience.

With this, this great difficulty is removed. Whoever believes the apparent meaning of these verses is a disbeliever, because Allah, glory be to Him, does not have renewing knowledge; rather He is knowing of everything. ﴿Do you not know that Allah knows what is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ [al-Hajj 70]. ﴿No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid 22]. Could Allah write what He does not know? It is impossible. It is impossible for Him to write except what He knows, and it is impossible for anything to occur except what agrees with the Record.

In any case, ﴿He knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾. Here He joined knowledge with what a person reveals and conceals, because it is the knowledge upon which what? Recompense. That is why He said: ﴿what you reveal and what you conceal﴾.

He says: (﴿What you reveal﴾, you show; ﴿and what you conceal﴾, you hide; when entering other than your own houses, whether with a good intention or otherwise. And it will come that when they enter their own houses they greet themselves.)

This too, in reality, concerns entering other than your own houses. As we pointed out earlier, this is the context, as the author said. But the lesson is in generality: whatever we reveal of speech and action, and whatever we conceal, Allah the Exalted knows it.

The purpose of stating Allah's knowledge of this is what? Warning against disobedience and encouragement toward obedience. As for it being a warning against disobedience, this is clear. As for it being an encouragement toward obedience, when I know that whatever good I do, Allah the Exalted knows it and will reward me for it, I become more active in acting and say: nothing of mine will be lost.

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower some of their gaze﴾ [An-Nur 24:30]) from what is not lawful for them to look at, and "min" (some of) is superfluous, ﴿and guard their private parts﴾ from what is not lawful for them to do with them.

﴿Say to the believers﴾: The address is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah commanded him to say it.

A rule has already passed us on this subject, which I hope is on your minds now. What is it? That when Allah says to the Messenger in a specific matter: ﴿Say﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey the entire Qur'an to the people, all of it: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:67]. But what is introduced by ﴿Say﴾, whether rulings or reports, is in reality a text specifying its conveyance in particular. And a text specifying its conveyance in particular indicates what?

Its importance. That is, it is a message specifically for that particular matter, separate from the general message of the whole Qur'an. The Messenger ﷺ was already commanded to say the whole Qur'an to the people, ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾. But when something specific is introduced with ﴿Say﴾, whether it is informative or prescriptive, what does that indicate? Its importance and the obligation to take care of it.

An example of this in reports: ﴿Say, O people, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:158]. This is a report.

And an example in rulings is this verse: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower some of their gaze﴾ [An-Nur 24:30]. So the conclusion?

* Student: The conclusion is that (...).

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: (...) to indicate its importance.

* Shaykh: Its importance and the obligation to take care of it. Why?

* Student: Because of its importance.

* Shaykh: No, I am saying: why does it indicate? What is the reason? You just said: this is evidence for such-and-such. Why?

* Student: Because it (...).

* Shaykh: Because he sent a special message with it: "Say such-and-such." So Allah's command to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to convey this particular thing is a special message about that thing, so that this is evidence of its importance and the obligation to take care of it. What is mentioned here in the verse is without doubt worthy of care.

Allah's words: ﴿Say to the believers﴾.

* Student: You mean at the beginning of the verse (...).

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: This is clear. It is clear that it is a response. I am saying: it is clear that what is meant here is a response, so this rule does not apply to it, because it is a response to this.

* Student: This is a response.

* Shaykh: This is a response...

* Student: ﴿Say﴾ because it is a response.

* Shaykh: Because it is a response. And His words ﴿to the believers﴾: ﴿Say to the believers﴾. Why did He not say "Say to the people"? Because faith is what requires acceptance, so the believer is the one who accepts what he is charged with. Also, there is in it an encouragement to comply with what it contains, an encouragement to comply. (...) ﴿Say to the believers﴾, just as one says "Say to the men such-and-such," meaning that because of their faith they are the ones deserving of this care. This divine direction contains encouragement, and it is evidence that the believer is the place of compliance, because the non-believer, may Allah protect us, does not comply. Whoever does not believe does not comply.

Some of the brothers told me yesterday about a person among those who imitate America, who came from America, saying that he advised me in matters and said: "Train yourself in this thing, for when a person gets used to something it becomes his disposition and nature." So our companion said to him: "Why do you not train yourself to pray in congregation in the mosque?" The answer of this man who imitates America, or who is astonished (perhaps he is not from America, I do not know, but in any case he is one of those sent abroad), was: "I am not convinced of congregational prayer." What is your opinion of this statement? Would it be disbelief or not?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: If the man had said, "I am not convinced of the obligation of congregational prayer," we would say: this is a man who followed others blindly, and Allah knows his intention, whether he imitated them out of ignorance or to trust their opinion. But when he says, "I am not convinced of congregational prayer," it means: I am not content with it (...).

His words ﴿lower﴾ (yaghuddu): what is in (...)?

We mentioned a witness for this, which is: "Muhammad, ransom yourself, every soul," meaning: so that he may ransom. This is a response to the existing command, which is ﴿Say﴾. We raised against this an objection that weakens it, namely that mere speech does not necessarily require lowering the gaze, unless it is assumed that the believer, when told, must lower his gaze at once.

The third view: it is a response to an implied command. Say to the believers: "Lower your gaze," and they will lower their gaze. "Lower" (ghuddu), "they will lower" (yaghuddu). What is the meaning of lowering (al-ghadd)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Restraint and reduction.

﴿from their gaze﴾: The author considers "min" superfluous, and the correct view is that it is partitive, not superfluous. Is that so? What weakens what the author held?

* Student: Three aspects.

* Shaykh: Three aspects. Three aspects weaken what the author said.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: It is well known that "min" is not added except in negation (...), and this is in an affirmative context. Second?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And if it is said to be superfluous, the meaning becomes the same.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Now, that lowering the gaze is not forbidden or not always obligatory, but rather it is permissible. Why is it permissible while guarding the private parts is entirely obligatory? They said: because lowering the gaze falls under the category of obligating means, meaning under blocking the means to harm (sadd al-dhara'i'). Forbidding the unrestricted gaze is by way of blocking the means to harm. For this reason it is permissible when there is a benefit in doing it, unlike guarding the private parts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 6):

His saying: ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying: ﴿Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾.

His saying: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾. What is meant by it?

* Student: According to the author's opinion?

* The Shaykh: According to the author's opinion and according to other than his opinion. According to the author's opinion, what does he say?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Al-Khuluqiyyah or al-Khilqiyyah?

* The Student: Al-Khilqiyyah.

* The Shaykh: Al-Khilqiyyah (...). Specify what he sees.

* The Student: What he sees (...).

* The Shaykh: The face and the two hands. According to the author's opinion, that what is meant by the adornment ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, what is meant by the exception here, or the excepted item, is: the face and the two hands. The second opinion?

* Student: The second opinion regarding His saying ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: it is clothing.

* The Shaykh: Clothing that must necessarily be visible.

The author's explanation of the adornment as the innate adornment with which God adorned the body: is this correct or incorrect?

* Student: Incorrect.

* The Shaykh: Incorrect. And the reason?

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...). What we want is this: to weaken the view that what is meant by the exception is the face and the two hands; we weaken the view that the adornment meant is the adornment with which God created the woman.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Look, the meaning of adornment in the sound (reports) is external adornment, which is what a woman adorns herself with, not the innate adornment with which God created the woman. What is the evidence?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants?﴾ [al-A'raf 32]. Yes. And at the end of the verse: ﴿and let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment﴾ [an-Nur 31]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And the horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [an-Nahl 8]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf 46]. Everyone who reflects on the word "adornment" finds it refers to external adornment, not to what God has adorned the woman with.

On this basis, the exception refers to what appears of the garments, which must necessarily be visible; for if the woman were forbidden even the garments that appear and must necessarily be visible, she would have to remain in her house, since this command cannot be applied except in that way, and this is something God has not obligated anyone to.

So it has become clear that His saying ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, the preponderant view regarding it is what? What appears of the clothing, meaning the thing that must necessarily be visible and whose visibility is unavoidable; this is permitted. This is also supported by other evidences: that the word "adornment" is only used for what a person adorns himself with, such as clothing and other things. It is also supported by His saying ﴿except what appears﴾; and if the intended meaning were the face and the two hands, He would have said, for example, "except what is made to appear" (إلا ما أُظهر), because here it is left indefinite; "except what is made to appear thereof," for example. Alright, is there anything else besides this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes; because jewelry is among the things that can be concealed, unlike the cloak (ʿabaʾah), the jilbab, and the like.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and let them draw their khumur over their juyub﴾. ﴿Wal-yadribna﴾: "daraba bi-l-shay' ʿala l-shay'" means: to cast the thing upon the other thing, but with adhesion.

"Daraba bi-l-shay' ʿala l-shay'" means to cast the thing upon the other thing, adhering to it. From it: I struck my hand upon my hand, for example, or upon my thigh, or the like. This is the meaning of "ḍarb ʿala l-juyub."

﴿wal-yadribna bi-khumurihinna﴾: plural of khimar, which is what a woman covers her head with.

﴿ʿala juyubihinna﴾: plural of jayb, which is the neckline (ṭawq) of the garment. This jayb is the neckline of the garment; it is called jayb, and people still call it by this name today.

God, the Exalted, has commanded ﴿wal-yadribna﴾. The lam is the lam of command, as is well known. The sukun in His saying ﴿wal-yadribna﴾ is not a sukun of i'rab but a sukun of binaʾ (fixed form), because the verb is joined to the feminine plural nun, so it is built on sukun whatever the command.

Here God, glorified and exalted, commanded that the woman strike her khimar upon her neckline, and it necessarily follows that it should come down from her head to the neckline.

So is the meaning of striking the khimar upon the neckline that it be beneath the face, such that the face remains uncovered and the neckline covered? Or is the meaning that she casts the khimar upon the neckline passing over the face? The latter is closer, because the khimar comes down from above, since it is over the head; then, if the neckline must be covered, the face is more deserving of covering.

Among the women of the Jahiliyyah, according to what some exegetes said, they used to let the khimar hang down behind them, and it would not come near their face or their neckline; therefore God commanded the women to draw their khumur over their juyub.

According to those who hold that the adornment meant is the face and the two hands, she draws her khimar over her neckline from below, pulling it like this, thus covering the neckline and uncovering the face. Yet the face is a greater source of temptation than the neckline!

(﴿And let them draw their khumur over their juyub﴾, i.e., they should cover the heads, necks and chests with the maqani (head coverings).)

It is the plural of miqnaʿah, which is what a woman wears to cover her head; what a woman covers herself with, which is what we now call the ghutrah.

(﴿And let them not display their adornment﴾: the hidden adornment, which is what is other than the face and the two hands, ﴿except to their husbands﴾: plural of baʿl, meaning husband.) And so on to the end.

Note the first: ﴿let them not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, where an exception is made from the adornment; and here: ﴿and let them not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, where an exception is made from those to whom the adornment may be displayed. There the exception concerns the adornment itself, and here it concerns the person to whom the adornment is displayed; and there is a difference between them.

Now, if we take the apparent meaning of ﴿and let them not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, we say: the adornment meant is the first adornment, so it becomes: "let them not display their adornment except what appears thereof," and let them not display this adornment either except to their husbands. Then we would have specified the general scope of what preceded in the verse. Please pay attention: we now have a prohibition on displaying adornment in two places:

An exception was made in the first place regarding the adornment, and in the second place regarding the person to whom the adornment is displayed. So shall we make the two exceptions govern a single action and say: "and let them not display their adornment except what appears thereof, to their husbands," etc., and then those other than these who are excepted would be forbidden from seeing the adornment absolutely, whether visible or hidden? The answer: this is a possibility, meaning.

Another possibility: we say that adornment is of two kinds: external adornment, which may be displayed to everyone, and hidden adornment, which may be displayed only to these people. On this basis the author proceeds, holding that the adornment meant here is other than the first adornment. So the first adornment is general, and what appears of it is permitted to everyone.

The second is not general; rather, what is meant by it is the hidden adornment, the adornment that is not displayed or that it is not necessary to display. This is what the author says:

(And it is what is other than the face and the two hands.)

This is based on the interpretation of the first: on the interpretation of His saying ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, by what? By the face and the two hands.

But the correct view is that what is meant by the hidden adornment is that which it is not necessary to display; that is, the inner garments, as the common people say. These may not be displayed except to those mentioned here: ﴿except to their husbands﴾, etc.

The bu'ulah (ُbuʿūlah): plural of baʿl, which means husband.

﴿or their fathers﴾: this includes the nearest father and whoever is above him, such as the grandfathers. Know that the category of prohibition is not the category of inheritance:

In the category of inheritance, fatherhood and sonship include only those who relate to you through the father; that is, through the male line. So a daughter's son, for example, and a mother's father have no connection to inheritance.

But in the category of prohibition, in the category of the prohibition of marriage and what is connected to it: it includes fathers on the father's side and on the mother's side; that is, there is no difference between those between whom and you there is a female and those between whom and you there is no female.

There, in the category of siblings and descendants in inheritance, those between whom and you there is a female among the fathers do not inherit and are not counted among the fathers; but here, those between whom and you there is a female and those between whom and you there is no female are on an equal footing.

Accordingly we say: ﴿or their fathers﴾ includes: the nearest father, and the grandfather on the father's side and on the mother's side.

﴿or the fathers of their husbands﴾: the same thing; it is permissible for a woman to display to the fathers of her husband the hidden adornment just as she displays the visible adornment to everyone.

The fathers of the husbands here include: the husband's father, his grandfather on the father's side and on the mother's side. For this reason the husband's father is a mahram to whom?

* Student: To the wife.

* The Shaykh: To the wife. The husband's father, however high he goes, is a mahram to the wife, and the wife of his son, however low he goes, is a mahram to him, whether he married her and consummated the marriage, or married her and divorced her before consummation, or she was widowed by him; his fathers are mahrams to her.

﴿or their sons, or the sons of their husbands﴾:

Regarding the son here, we say what we said about the father; that is, there is no difference between the son by blood who connects to a person through the male line and the son who connects through the female line. So a daughter's son, for example, enters among the sons, or not? He enters.

Likewise ﴿the sons of their husbands﴾: the husband's son is permissible for the wife to display the hidden adornment to, and the husband's daughter's son likewise. On this basis, all who descend from the husband, male and female, however low they go, are mahrams to the wife of their grandfather. However, in this matter, the condition is consummation with the woman, because they are stepchildren (rabaʾib), and for stepchildren consummation is required.

So if a man married a woman, contracted marriage with her, then divorced her, or she was widowed by him before consummation, his children are not mahrams to her; the reason is that consummation is a condition for that, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated with them, there is no sin upon you﴾ [an-Nisa 23].

﴿or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers﴾: ﴿their brothers﴾: full brothers, or paternal half-brothers, or maternal half-brothers, whether full, paternal, or maternal.

﴿or the sons of their brothers﴾, and however low they go. ﴿The sons of their brothers﴾: what do they become to them? Paternal aunts. So an aunt may display to her brother's son the hidden adornment, since he is among her mahrams.

﴿or the sons of their sisters﴾, and they have maternal aunts. So the maternal aunt may display to her sister's son the hidden adornment, since he is among her mahrams.

Is there any remaining relative who is a mahram and was not mentioned in this verse?

* Students: The paternal uncles.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the paternal uncles; the paternal uncles were not mentioned in this verse.

* Students: And the maternal uncles.

* The Shaykh: And the maternal uncles, yes. The paternal uncles and maternal uncles were not mentioned in this verse, although they are mahrams, and the verse is explicit in its exception: ﴿and let them not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾. Therefore: a paternal uncle or maternal uncle, it is not permissible for a woman to display to him the hidden adornment, because the verse restricted it: ﴿and let them not display their adornment﴾ except to these.

On this basis, not every mahram is one to whom it is permissible to display adornment. Why? They said: because her displaying adornment to the paternal uncle or maternal uncle is feared to lead him to describe it to his son, since a paternal cousin may marry his paternal cousin's daughter, correct? And a maternal cousin may marry his paternal aunt's daughter. Therefore they said: she should not display adornment to the paternal uncle or maternal uncle, even though they are mahrams.

In this there is an indication or clear evidence that what is meant by adornment here is not, as the author said, "other than the face and the two hands," because it is permissible to display other than the face and the two hands to the paternal uncle and maternal uncle, since they are mahrams. Rather, this is the hidden adornment of clothing, and on this basis a woman may not beautify herself in front of her paternal uncle or maternal uncle.

Foster-relationship (al-radaʿ) was not mentioned here. Does its ruling equal the ruling of those mentioned here or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: It is not "yes." We want you to bring me evidence.

* Student: "What is forbidden by nursing is what is forbidden by lineage" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645), and Muslim (1447/13), from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas].

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is known: "What is forbidden by nursing is what is forbidden by lineage." But the matter here is not from the category of prohibition; for this reason the paternal uncle and maternal uncle were dropped (...). The matter is not from the category of prohibition.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Adornment is a different matter from whether he sees her face or sees her hand.

* Student: If, for example, (...).

* The Shaykh: Why the paternal uncle? Is it permissible for the paternal uncle to look at a woman at the same level as a brother does in terms of mahram status?

* Student: No, it is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: In terms of mahram status, not in terms of adornment?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, there is no doubt; he is a mahram to her, he may travel with her, be alone with her, and she may uncover her face to him.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because the reality is, O people, that displaying adornment is a different matter from the question of mahram status. The verse indicates that displaying adornment is separate from the question of mahram status. If the paternal uncle and maternal uncle were not mentioned, although they are mahrams, this shows that the question of displaying adornment is other than mahram status; for the matter here is in reality sensitive, very sensitive.

For this reason, foster-siblings, according to (...) and according to all people, it is permissible for the woman to beautify herself (...), although the matter is in reality serious, very serious. How many people, God forbid, have committed immorality with their foster-sisters, because the bond is not a bond of kinship and lineage but a bond of nursing, and it is weaker than the bond of lineage and kinship.

For this reason, among some people, God forbid, who do not fear God, arousal of desire and enjoyment through looking occur toward their foster-sisters or foster-aunts, as is known. Therefore some scholars disliked that a woman display her adornment to her foster-mahrams, and said that this involves error.

For this reason God, glorified and exalted, did not address foster-relationship in this verse at all, not at all; and this is not from the category of prohibition, otherwise the prohibition would be as the Prophet ﷺ said: "What is forbidden by nursing is what is forbidden by lineage." But the matter here is the display of adornment.

It is now known from this restriction that it has no connection to the question of mahram status; there is no connection. This is shown by the fact that He excepted things that are not mahrams, such as "those whom your right hands possess," and the male attendants who have no desire (ghayr ulil-irbah), and the children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private matters. This shows that this matter has no connection to the question of mahram status; rather it is an independent matter that returns to a sensitive, delicate issue; for we said that this entire surah (...) concerns what?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The protection of honor, the purification of souls, and keeping them far from defilement; for this reason you find in it extremely important precautions. What appears to me from the context of the verse is that it must be kept on its general scope and also on its specific scope, and that what is excepted in it has the ruling of the exception, and what is not mentioned in it remains under the prohibition: ﴿and let them not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, etc., and the rest remains under the prohibition.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, they are in reality seeking (...) from this.

* The Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: I say: some scholars said thus (...). We may accept it and we may not; for not every maternal uncle is in this position, nor is the majority of maternal uncles in this position, so as to say that a rare case has no ruling. Rather we say: God did not except them, so they remain under the general rule: the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle may not be shown the hidden adornment, unlike those mentioned.

And I tell you: there is no connection between this verse and the question of mahram status; the proof is that things were mentioned that are not mahrams, such as those whom the right hand possesses and the attendant; displaying adornment to them was permitted, while mahrams, namely the paternal uncle and maternal uncle, were left out.

Someone may say: if displaying adornment to the sons of a brother and the sons of a sister is permitted because the paternal aunt or maternal aunt is their aunt, then why is it not the reverse? Because the paternal aunt and maternal aunt are (...) what? They are the aunt of the son of her brother or son of her sister; the paternal uncle is the father of the brother's daughter, and the maternal uncle is the father of the sister's daughter.

Ibn 'Uthaymin, *Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim*, on Surah 24, verse 31 (part 2 of 6):

If it is permissible for her to display her adornment to her brother's son and her sister's son, why is the reverse not permissible, since the relationship is the same? We say: No, because she feels that she has superiority over them, since she is their paternal aunt (ʿammah) and maternal aunt (khalah). They respect her, and she does not respect them.

But the matter of the paternal uncle and maternal uncle, what is (...)? Because of the high rank of the two of them over their brother's daughter and sister's daughter. She respects them, and they do not respect her. Therefore the analogy (qiyas, reasoning from one ruling to a similar case) is not sound here. The verse leaves no room for analogy at all, because it specifies individuals specifically: "except to their husbands, or their fathers..." These are not general rules.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, what is this adornment? We said: adornment is the clothing of beautification. That is, we say: she should not appear before her paternal uncle or maternal uncle in beautiful clothing. That is what it means. Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: There is nothing wrong with it, because we said that adornment originally means not what God has created the woman with, but what the woman adorns herself with, such as clothing.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: For a mahram (a person one may never marry, such as a close blood relative) it is permissible, for example, for her to show him her face, her palms, and what normally appears. But on the matter of clothing, we have taken the position that the stronger view regarding adornment is not the natural adornment with which God created the woman. The meaning of adornment here is clothing. So we say: the hidden adornment, which custom holds that a woman adorns herself with only in specific circumstances, is not for these people, namely the paternal uncle and maternal uncle.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "Except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands." "Their husbands" is clear. "Their fathers" is clear. "The fathers of their husbands" means the husband's father, however high up (...). You would say: this is the wife of his son, however low down. The wife of his grandson is also included in this. In the matter of mahram, we said that marriage makes no distinction between those who relate through the mother and those who relate through the father.
* Student: The husband of the daughter (...), the mother of the wife, how (...)?
* Shaykh: The husband of the daughter?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: "The sons of their husbands": if this man becomes a man, marries a woman, and she has children, what is he to him? He is one of the sons of the husband.

In any case, this verse in reality has no connection to the matter of mahram. We must understand this difference neither by inclusion nor by exclusion. How is that neither by inclusion nor by exclusion? Because we have considered that paternal uncles are mahrams, yet they are not mentioned. That is the case regarding inclusion. Conversely, we have considered that there are people in the verse who are not mahrams. On this basis, the ruling in this verse is independent of the matter of mahram. Whoever God has exempted from the display of adornment to them must be exempted, and whoever He has not exempted, is not.

God the Exalted says: "or their women" (*nisaihinna*). Regarding this, the exegetes differ. Some said that the possessive (*idafah*) is one of type (*li-l-nawʿ*). Others said that the possessive is one of genus (*li-l-jins*).

Those who said the possessive is one of type said: the meaning of "their women" is believing women. Its parallel is: "Say to the believing women" (Surah al-Nur 24:31 is itself the context, but compare Surah al-Ahzab 33:59). So the meaning of "their women" is: those of their own type. The possessive is therefore of the kind "the thing to its type": the women of the believers.

Some said: it is of the kind of the genus. That is, the women are attributed to them with regard to genus, meaning: the women who are of their kind, i.e., women.

According to the first view, a Muslim woman may not display her adornment to a disbelieving woman, and the reason is that she is not of her type. So it is not permissible to display it to her. Also, in reality, a disbelieving woman is not trustworthy. She may tempt sinners and disbelievers if she sees her beautifying herself and displaying adornment.

The second view is that the meaning of "their women" is the genus, meaning the women who are of their kind. On this basis, it is permissible for a woman to display her hidden adornment to all women, whether believers or not. This is the closer view. The possibility that a disbelieving woman may tempt sinners and disbelievers is a real concern, but this possibility also exists with Muslim women, for a Muslim woman who is not a believer (i.e., not righteous) may also do this. These matters are in reality very subtle.

It may even occur among women themselves. That is why musahaqah (lesbianism between women) exists. Women may love one another and become attached to each other, just as a man becomes attached to a woman, and this wrong inclination arises.

In any case, now "their women" (*nisaihinna*): I say that the possessive here has been disputed by the exegetes. Is it of genus or of type? If we say it is of genus, then the meaning is women, and the possessive is attributed in the sense of genus, because women are like them. If we say it is of type, we say: only the women of believers. The author may address this later.

("Or their women, or what their right hands possess.") It is permissible for them to look at her except between the navel and the knees. It is forbidden for them to look at her if they are not husbands.

The author follows the view that the meaning of adornment here is what God has adorned the woman with, and we said that these are the ones who are exempted.

("What their right hands possess") means (slaves).

Likewise, the female slaves whom the women own. The ownership must be complete. If she has a slave held in partnership, it is not permissible for her to display her adornment to him. What is the reason? Because she has not owned him. She owns only part of him. For this reason, a man may not take a jointly owned female slave as a concubine. If a slave-girl is jointly owned between him and another person, he may not have intercourse with her, because she is not wholly his property. Likewise, a woman may not display any of her hidden adornment to a slave owned jointly between her and someone else, because it is not true that he is hers. He is rather shared.

He says: "It is permissible for them to look at her except between the navel and the knees; it is forbidden for them to look at her if they are not husbands."

The author follows what we indicated earlier, that the meaning of adornment is what God has adorned the woman with. He says that these exempted people may be shown what lies between the navel and the knees. This is according to one opinion. For example, it would be permissible for her to show her brothers, her brother's son, her sister's son, and her husband's son her chest, belly, breasts, and everything except what lies between the navel and the knees. That is: she could come in trousers and appear before her husband's father and the like!

But this is subject to scrutiny, and it would bring great temptation. If we said this were permissible, a great temptation would arise. A young woman, for example, the wife of his son, would come to him in such a state! And suppose he is a young man too. No one says this!

Yet, brothers, notice that it is conditional on the temptation being secured. Even by the author's view, the security from temptation must be assured. If temptation is not secured, it is forbidden. But even if temptation is secured, this clearly opens a door to it.

For this reason, the correct view on this matter, setting aside whether or not this is what the verse means, is that a woman may not uncover before mahrams except what custom has made normal. Custom is what is not considered shameful or regarded as a concern in our culture.

Now she shows her palms, forearms, shins, head, and neck. All of this is customarily shown to mahrams. If you went beyond this, you would find people objecting (...). That is: if uncovering the shin is permissible, then uncovering the forearm is more so. A person's thoughts move from the shin to what is above it more readily than from the forearm to what is below it.

In any case, the correct view on this matter is that the matter should be referred to what custom has established, except for what cannot be uncovered without an anticipated or inevitable temptation. That is not permissible.

There remains the question of non-mahrams, those with whom a woman is tested, non-mahrams with whom she is tested, such as her husband's brothers. If a man has a brother in the house, and each of the two brothers has a wife, the well-known position of the school is that she may not show either her palms, face, feet, or anything else, and that this man is like the man in the market!

If we took this view in reality, great hardship would befall people. We would say to the woman: if your husband's brother is present, not a nail nor a strand of hair may appear from you! This in reality involves difficulty and hardship.

For this reason, the correct view on this matter is that the matter of the palms and feet, which are difficult to guard against, is permissible. As for the face, it is not permissible, because guarding against it is possible, unlike the palms and feet. This woman works in the house. She cooks, for example, spreads things out, and sweeps. How can she guard herself from her husband's brother? And he says: if you want to wash the dishes while your husband's brother is with you, you must be (...) on the hands! This involves difficulty.

So we say: what is difficult to guard against, such as displaying the feet and palms, is correctly permissible. Some Hanbali jurists followed this, and in *al-Insaf* (a major Hanbali work by al-Mardawi) it is said: people cannot manage except by this. This is correct. People cannot manage their work except by this. And God grants success.

The author's words: (and included those whom their right hands possess, the male slaves):
That is, "those whom their right hands possess" includes male slaves. How does it include male slaves, and is there anyone else it means besides male slaves? The answer: yes, it is meant, according to the opinion that "their women" means Muslim women, like those whom their right hands possess, even if they are from disbelievers. So it is permissible to display adornment to them. That is, it is not specific to female slaves but includes even male slaves, meaning males. Have you understood now or not? That is, if someone said: how does the author say that "those whom their right hands possess" includes male slaves, and is there anyone other than male slaves? What is the answer?

* The Shaykh: The answer is yes: according to the view that "their women" means Muslim women, then "those whom their right hands possess" includes a disbelieving female slave, and it is permissible to display adornment to her even if she is not among "their women," because she is a slave.
As for if we say "their women" means all women, then His saying "those whom their right hands possess" is restricted to males only, because women are already known from His saying "or their women." If a forbidden matter is feared, that is a different thing; but these matters are without any forbidden matter.

(﴿of men﴾ who have no erection.)
﴿أَوِ التَّابِعِينَ﴾ The author says: (the "followers" are those who take the leftover food).
By "the followers" are meant servants and the like who follow the people of the house; this is what is meant by "the followers." Also ﴿أَوِ التَّابِعِينَ﴾ refers to those who come to people to eat from their leftover food, even if they are not their servants. It includes both of these. The follower is one who follows the household either because he is a servant among them, or because he receives leftover food from them. But it is permissible to display adornment to followers on a condition: that they have no physical desire, meaning need for women.
The author's words: (that the erection of each ... ) — what is the sign? The sign is not that his erection does not occur; rather the sign is that no inclination toward women is known from him, because some people incline toward women even if their erection does not occur; that is not necessary. So the sign is that there is no inclination toward women at all, neither when his member is erect nor when it is not.
The matter is that he has no desire for women and no inclination toward them. This is like a woman. Because of the difficulty of guarding against him, God, glorified and exalted is He, permitted women to display their adornment to him. So the follower means: one who follows the people of the house to receive their leftover food, either because he is a servant among them or not a servant.
But God, glorified and exalted is He, made a condition for the follower: that he have no physical desire for women. And what does physical desire mean? It means need. Is the sign what the author mentioned? No, what the author mentioned is not the sign; rather the sign is that it is known he has no inclination toward women and no desire for them. Usually his member does not become erect, but this is not required; a person may incline toward women and love and be fond of them without his member becoming erect.
Therefore the sound view in this matter is that we know his lack of need by his lack of inclination toward women. "For this reason, in the houses of the family of the Prophet ﷺ there was a effeminate man (mukhannath), that is, one of those without physical desire, and they did not perceive anything from him, until one day he said to a man of the mahrams of one of the Prophet's wives, peace and blessings be upon him: When you conquer al-Ta'if, then take the daughter of Ghaylan, Ghaylan al-Thaqafi, for she comes forward with four and turns back with eight."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4324) and Muslim (2810 / 32), from Umm Salamah.]]
The first one, they had not sensed anything from him, but this one who describes a woman in this manner, what does that indicate? It indicates that he inclines toward women, so the Prophet ﷺ forbade him from entering upon the household, since it became clear that he inclines toward women. So if it is found that this follower describes women and mentions their beauty and the like, it is known that he is one with need. As for the matter of the erection of the member, that is not the sign.
