And His saying ﴿or the child who have not yet attained knowledge﴾, "attained knowledge" meaning "come to know" ﴿of women's private parts﴾ for intercourse.
The meaning is that they do not know what relates to the private parts. So His saying ﴿have not attained﴾ means they have not come to know, in the sense that they do not understand what is done with the private parts; this is what is meant, not seeing with the eye, because seeing with the eye occurs in children and others. Rather, what is meant by knowing is that they do not understand what is done with the private parts and it does not occur to them. These children are permitted to be shown the adornment.
The author's words: (it is displayed to them what lies between the navel and the knee) are based on the view that the adornment meant here is that with which God adorned the woman, not clothing.
﴿وَلَا يَضْرِبْنَ﴾ How many do we now have? Twelve? They have become twelve:
﴿except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or those whom their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no physical desire, or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private parts﴾: twelve categories.
These are the ones to whom the hidden adornment may be displayed, and others are not to be shown it; this is the apparent meaning of the verse, because God, glorified and exalted is He, says ﴿and they shall not display their adornment except to﴾, and this exception is an exclusive (mufarragh) one, which requires that anyone other than these may not be shown the adornment. But some scholars added to them the remaining mahrams by marriage, lineage, or fosterage, because there are some things: among the mahrams by lineage there are those not mentioned, such as:
* Students: The paternal uncles.
* The Shaykh: The paternal uncles and the maternal uncles. Also among the mahrams by marriage there are those not mentioned; because He said ﴿or the fathers of their husbands﴾, meaning a wife of a son; ﴿or the sons of their husbands﴾, meaning a wife of a father; that is, a father's wife displays adornment to her husband's sons, and a son's wife displays adornment to her husband's fathers. Is that right or not? Is a daughter's husband permitted or not? The daughter's husband is not mentioned, and he is a mahram by marriage, so some scholars say he is added to those mentioned.
We also have fosterage, in all its kinds, which is not mentioned; some scholars added it, claiming that the mention of some implies the rest, and that Arabs sometimes limit themselves to mentioning some as a reminder of the rest. But this is not sound. The reason is that mentioning some, intended to add the rest, is satisfied with mentioning one, and this one is by way of example; but mentioning a number from a category and omitting the rest, in an exclusive manner, is not accepted.
However, there remains the question of displaying the adornment that God has adorned the woman with, meaning the face, the hands, and the like. This has evidence other than this verse. So we say: this verse concerns the adornment of clothing and the like, and it must be kept as God mentioned it. As for the display of the face, the two palms, the shin, the neck, and the like, this is derived from other evidence.
Are these twelve equal in what may be displayed of the adornment, or are they not equal? They are clearly not equal; for this reason God began with the husband, because he is the highest of those to whom adornment may be displayed in full. As for the rest, it may be said that they are in order, and it may be said that they are not in order, but rather one considers what custom and habit require; because the reality is that, for instance, a brother who is always in his sister's house is not like one who comes only rarely. Which of the two states is more modest for her? She is more shy and modest with him when he comes only rarely than when he is always with her.
So for such matters one should say: their assessment varies; as for the husband, he is at the top in every case; and as for the rest, it depends on what custom and habit call for regarding the display of adornment, whether complete, moderate, or the least that is called adornment.

* The Shaykh: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze﴾: this matter has a difference among the scholars.
Some of them said: it is not permissible for a woman to look at a man, just as it is not permissible for a man to look at a woman, because the verse is one: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾ and ﴿say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze﴾. They supported this view with the hadith of Umm Salamah and the other woman, when Ibn Umm Maktum entered, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Veil yourselves from him." They said: "O Messenger of God, he is a blind man." He said: "Are you two blind?!"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4112) and al-Tirmidhi (2778), from Umm Salamah.]]

This passage contains a repeated section of the commentary, so I render the full text as it stands.

When they objected to him that he was blind, he said: "Are you two blind?" and ordered them to veil. However, this hadith is not authentic according to the scholars, because it comes through the narration of Nabhan, the freedman of Abu Salamah, and he is unknown (majhul). For this reason Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) declared it weak. Furthermore, this hadith cannot be [accepted]. Therefore, the correct view is that it is permissible for a woman to look at a man if there is no fitna (temptation) or desire, and this is indicated by clear and authentic hadiths, among them:

The hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) when she used to look at the Abyssinians while they were playing in the mosque, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was screening her while she looked at them.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (454) and Muslim (892/18) from 'A'ishah.]] Indeed, it was she who stopped looking at this. This is clear evidence for the permissibility of a woman looking at a man.

Likewise, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Fatimah bint Qays: "Observe your 'iddah in the house of Ibn Umm Maktum, for he is a blind man; you may put your clothes down at his place."[[Recorded by Muslim (1480/36) from the hadith of Fatimah bint Qays.]] This too is a clear and explicit statement that a woman may look at a man.

Also, our jurists (may Allah have mercy on them) said: If it were forbidden for a woman to look at a man, then it would be obligatory for men to veil, just as a woman veils from a man lest he look at her. So we say: likewise, a man veils from a woman lest she look at him, because the obligation is not fulfilled except by this. Is that not so? Because if a man is uncovered, the woman will inevitably glance at him, it is necessary that she glances; it is impossible that she not see him unless he veils just as she veils.

No scholar says that a man is obligated to veil from a woman. Therefore, the correct position on this question is the view of Imam Ahmad, that it is permissible for a woman to look at a man. But all these matters, this and others, are on what condition?

* Students: Safety from fitna.

* The Shaykh: On condition of safety from fitna. As for when there is fitna, it is not permissible for her to look, nor at a picture of a man, even a picture on an identity card, or one that appears, for example, on television. It is not permissible for her to look at it if fitna is feared. The same applies to a man as well. This is a matter we may research independently: is it permissible for a man to look at a picture of a non-mahram woman or not? What is your opinion?

Some people say that the picture on television is more intense than the picture on a card, because it conveys movement and sound, so the fitna through it is greater. But I also hold that it differs from the card picture in that it does not last, while the picture on the card lasts. A person can keep the picture on the card and whenever he wishes to enjoy looking at it, he goes to it and looks; but this is not possible with television, because it has passed and the television is switched off and it is gone from him.

* Student: (...) lowering the gaze from women (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is what we say: we do not equate them. In my view...

* The Shaykh: The described thing, however great it is, can never be like the picture; there is no doubt. The picture is a stronger depiction of reality. But in our discussion, if there is no fitna and no harm, and describing the women of the Muslims to the disbelievers is a great harm. Therefore there is no doubt that pictures have become degraded, and letting a picture of so-and-so's daughter, for example, fall into the hands of the immoral is undoubtedly among the forbidden things.

For this reason we see that among the greatest dangers is what is being done now with brides: photographing women, even if the one photographing is a woman, because these pictures remain in the hands of women, and who can be sure they will not give it to so-and-so, or to someone else, or to her son, or her husband? But perhaps you will argue against this with the hadith I mentioned, the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of a woman describing a woman to her husband as if he were looking at her. So if the Messenger prohibited describing a woman to a man, then this is like it.

The picture may be stronger; this is what could be said: that the picture falls under it, because describing, in reality, is mentioning attributes, and does not convey the woman as the picture conveys her. When the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) "forbade that a woman should touch a woman and describe her to her husband as if he were looking at her,"[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (5240) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] then this is like it. But what appears to me is that, because in reality describing the attribute is more enticing, especially when the Messenger says: "describes her to her husband." If this phrase "to her husband" is a restriction that is not meant to state the usual case, because her describing her to her husband leads to harm:

First: the husband may think that his wife dislikes him and describes this woman so that he might marry her.

Second: perhaps when she describes her to her husband, his heart becomes attached to this described woman, and that becomes a cause for the separation from this wife.

It may be said: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "describes her to her husband" is not to state the reality, and the usual case is not that a woman describes women unless she has neglected her husband. It may be said: it is not to state the usual case, but because of the harms that follow from it, where the husband thinks this woman does not want him, and so she describes women to him, perhaps he will become attached to them. This is one aspect.

And another aspect: perhaps the husband himself, when his wife describes this woman to him, his heart becomes attached to her and he turns away from the wife he has and moves toward the new one.

In any case, I cannot be certain. I tell you my opinion after this discussion, because I cannot be sure to prohibit looking at a woman on television or in a picture, if there is no prohibited matter in it. If there is a prohibited matter in it, then there is no doubt it is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: This is correct, because such a matter varies according to the incitement of fitna: either it is far-fetched, so a person's soul may not become attached to it, especially an intelligent person, because how can a person desire what cannot be attained? This is unlike things that are attainable. For this reason, and Allah knows best, it is permitted for mahrams to uncover their faces before a mahram, because his soul can never become attached to them, except for a person, may Allah protect us, whose nature has been reversed. But as for non-mahram men, no. This is part of the wisdom: a person's soul cannot become attached to one of his mahrams. For this reason uncovering was permitted for them. But what I have said supports (...) on fear of fitna, or on fear of it.

As for when a person is normal and his heart does not stir and his feelings are not moved by what he sees, then forbidding it and declaring people sinful for it is a matter with difficulty.

You know that now pictures of women are widespread, like some fabrics, I think they have pictures of women, and a card with a woman's picture is stuck on them, and likewise some...

* The Shaykh: In newspapers as well. This is a problem; that is, declaring people sinful for something a person cannot verify is difficult. As for something he doubts, he should not declare people sinful for it. There is no doubt that caution in this is better, but the matter is not one of mere caution (...) the priority is the question of prohibition: do we say it is forbidden for you to look, or is it not forbidden?

As for when a person may look at the woman herself, it is clear that he may look at her picture, just as the brother said, in the matter of the suitor: if a man wanted to propose to a woman, and instead of going to see her he says, if there is a picture of her, show me her picture. This is not objectionable, even though the picture in reality does not convey the reality completely as it is witnessed. Now you see pictures of one person: sometimes his picture comes out distorted, sometimes it comes out better than the reality, and sometimes the picture is better than the reality, and sometimes the picture matches the reality. The truth is that these pictures do not completely convey the reality.

* Student: This is not consistent.

* The Shaykh: No, it is consistent. Everything prohibited as a means is permitted by benefit, not necessarily by necessity, because what is prohibited in itself is only permitted by necessity, while what is prohibited as a means is permitted by benefit. For example, you have the prohibition of riba al-fadl, which is prohibited as a means, and need permits it, as in the matter of al-'araya. The matter of looking is prohibited as a means, as the scholars said, and for this reason benefit and need permit it, such as: a physician looking at a patient, a suitor looking at the woman he proposes to, a witness looking at the woman who is the subject of testimony, and a dealer looking at one he deals with. Even a dealer may look at one who deals with him, such as a woman who is accustomed to buying and selling from a shop; you may say: uncover your face, perhaps someone else will come (...), if I doubt, let me see your face again. This is permitted; the scholars affirmed the permissibility of this matter, because this is not from the category of prohibition in itself, but prohibition as a means. What shows that this is prohibited as a means is this: regarding mahrams, why is it permitted for a woman to uncover to her mahram? Because this means is almost nonexistent.

For this reason, if it were supposed that there is a reversed mahram, may Allah protect us, who looks at his mahrams with the gaze of non-mahram women, he must be prevented from them.

Do not be surprised that one of the men looks at his mahrams with the gaze of non-mahram women. Do not be surprised at that, for I was asked these days about a man who has a half-sister, young, seven or eight years old. The female questioner says, Allah knows best, that she is truthful or not. She says: her brother from her father, may Allah protect us, took her to his house and committed fornication with her. May Allah protect us.

That is, is it strange that some people have the nature of dogs, who mount their own mothers without caring!

The conclusion is that we say: the prohibition of looking is not, in its origin, a prohibition in itself, because what is prohibited is adultery and indecency; but the prohibition of approaching adultery is to prevent us from seeking a means to it, or from having a means to it. Therefore the prohibition of looking is for this reason, a matter of prohibiting means.

* Student: ﴿And let them not reveal their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur 31].
* The Shaykh: Ten. What we discussed is ten.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾.

(And "excluding their women" includes the disbelieving women, so it is not permissible for Muslim women to uncover before them; and "what their right hands possess" includes male slaves.)

The Shaykh's words: "excluded" and "included". "Excluding their women the disbelieving women" is based on the idafah (possessive construction) being specific (nau'iyyah) rather than generic (jinsiyyah).

And that what is meant by "their women" is the Muslim women.

As for the second view: that "women" is an idafah of the genus to its own genus,

i.e., those of your kind, who are women, so the disbelieving women are not excluded, but both disbelieving and Muslim women are included.

They mention that when the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) conquered the cities, there were midwives among the disbelieving women who delivered women, and the Companions approved of them in this.

This indicates that what is meant by "their women" is women generally, not specifically Muslim women. Yes, if harm is feared from them, that is a separate matter, and the fear of harm applies even to Muslim women.

("And 'what their right hands possess' includes male slaves.") ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ includes slaves. How does it include slaves, and is something other than slaves intended?

The answer: yes, on the view that "their women" means Muslim women, "what their right hands possess" includes the disbelieving female slave, so it is permissible to display adornment to her, even though she is not among "their women." It is not limited to female slaves; it even includes male slaves, meaning the males. Have you understood now, or not?

That is, if someone says: how does the author say "and includes what their right hands possess, the male slaves," when is there anyone other than slaves? What is the answer?

The answer: yes, on the view that "their women" means Muslim women, "what their right hands possess" covers a disbelieving female slave, and it is permissible to display adornment to her, even if she is not among "their women," because she is owned.

But if we take "their women" to mean all women, then the phrase "what their right hands possess" applies to whom?

To males only, since women are already known from "or their women." However, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, was compelled to say this for this reason. Some scholars restricted "what their right hands possess" to disbelieving women only, saying that a male slave may not display adornment to his mistress; rather, "what their right hands possess" is for the purpose of including a female slave if she is disbelieving, because she has left "their women" and entered "what their right hands possess." But the correct view is that "their women," as we indicated earlier, means the genus, and all women, Muslim and disbelieving, may have adornment displayed to them, unless a forbidden matter is feared. For example, if a Muslim woman describes another woman to her husband, the Prophet ﷺ forbade a woman from describing a woman to her husband in such a way that it is as if he were seeing her [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5240) from Ibn Mas'ud.]]. That is, she says to him, for example: so-and-so is such-and-such, and describes her to him until it is as if he were looking at her, because the Messenger ﷺ forbade a woman from describing a woman to her husband in this manner. If a forbidden matter is feared, that is a separate issue, but these things are without prohibition.

He said: (﴿or male attendants﴾ [who are] surplus of food, ﴿who have no physical desire﴾ — with a genitive (jarr) as an adjective, and an accusative (nasb) as an exception: ghayra and ghayri.)

(﴿who have no physical desire﴾: those with need of women.)

"Those with" is the explanation of "ulī," and "al-irbah" is the need for women.

(﴿of men﴾ by the fact that his member does not rise.)

﴿or male attendants﴾: The author says: "(who are the surplus of food)." ﴿At-tabi'in﴾ refers to servants and the like who follow the household. This is what "at-tabi'in" means.

Or ﴿at-tabi'in﴾ also refers to those who come to people to eat from their surplus food, even if they are not servants to them. It includes both these and those. The follower is one who follows the household, either because he is a servant among them, or because he receives the surplus food from them.

But it is permissible to display adornment to the attendants on the condition that they have no physical desire, i.e., need for women.

The author's statement: "(by the fact that his member does not rise)" — this is not the sign. The sign is not that his member does not rise; rather, the sign is that no inclination toward women is known from him at all, because some people incline toward women even if their member does not rise; that is not necessarily the case. So the sign is that no inclination toward women exists in him at all, whether his member rises or not.

The point is that he has no desire for women and does not incline to them. Like the woman, Allah the Mighty and Majestic permitted women to display their adornment to him because guarding against him is difficult. So what does "attendant" mean now?

He who follows the household in such a way, to receive their surplus food, either as a servant among them or not a servant. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic stipulated for the attendant: that he have no physical desire for women. What does "physical desire" mean? That is, need. And is the sign what the author mentioned?

No, what the author mentioned is not the sign; rather, the sign is that it is known he does not incline to women and has no desire for them. Usually his member does not rise, but this is not necessary: a person may incline to women, love them, and be fond of them, yet his member does not rise. Therefore, the correct position in this matter is that we know his lack of need from his lack of inclination to women.

For this reason, in the households of the family of the Prophet ﷺ there was an effeminate man (mukhannath), i.e., one of those without physical desire, and they did not perceive anything from him. Then one day he said to a man from the close relatives (mahram) of one of the Prophet's wives, peace and blessings be upon him: "If you conquer al-Ta'if, then take the daughter of Ghaylan, Ghaylan al-Thaqafi, for she comes forward with four and retreats with eight." They, at first, did not sense anything from him. But this description of a woman, what does it indicate?

It indicates that he inclines to women. So the Prophet ﷺ forbade him from entering upon the household [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4324) and Muslim (2180/32) from Umm Salamah.]], because it became clear that he inclines to women. So when it is found that this attendant describes women, mentions their beauty, and the like, it is known that he has need. As for the matter of the member rising, this is not the sign. You have "(the member) rises" in your text; look at the margin and see what it says.

He said: (﴿or the child﴾, meaning children, ﴿who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private parts﴾, i.e., who have not come to know them for intercourse. So it is permissible to display to them what is other than what lies between the navel and the knee.)

﴿or the child﴾: The author says "in the sense of children." So it is a collective noun meaning children. The proof that it means children is that it is in the sense of children.

His statement "(﴿who﴾)": since it is described with the plural, and a singular is not described with the plural. But there is evidence here that a generic noun preceded by "al" (the definite article) indicates generality, even if it is singular.

And his words: ﴿or the child who have not yet attained﴾.

(﴿have not yet attained﴾ meaning have not come to know the women's private parts for intercourse.)

The meaning is that they do not know what relates to the private parts. So his words "have not attained" mean they have not come to know to such a degree that they do not understand what is done with the private parts. That is what is meant, not seeing with the eye, because seeing with the eye occurs in children and others. Rather, what is meant is knowing: that they do not understand what is done with the private parts and it does not occur to them. These children — it is permissible to display adornment to them. The author's statement "(display to them what lies between the navel and the knee)" is based on the view that "adornment" here means what Allah adorned the woman with, not clothing. ﴿And let them not strike their feet﴾ — how many do we now have? Twelve.

﴿except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or what their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no physical desire, or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private parts﴾ — twelve categories. These are the ones to whom the hidden adornment is displayed, and to others it is not displayed. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿and let them not reveal their adornment except to﴾, and this exception is complete (mufarragh), requiring that anyone other than these may not be shown adornment.

But some scholars added to them the remaining mahrams by marriage, lineage, or nursing, because there are, from lineage, mahrams not mentioned, such as paternal and maternal uncles, and there are, from marriage, those not mentioned, because he said: ﴿the fathers of their husbands﴾ — does that mean a wife of a son, or ﴿the sons of their husbands﴾ means a wife of a father, or not? That is, a stepmother displays adornment to her husband's sons, and a daughter-in-law displays adornment to her husband's fathers, and so on, is that right?

Good. Is it permissible for the husband of a daughter, or not? The husband of a daughter is not mentioned, and he is by marriage; so some scholars say he is added to those mentioned.

We also have nursing, all its types, which is not mentioned; some scholars added it, claiming that mention of some indicates the rest, and that Arabs sometimes limit themselves to mentioning some, as a hint toward the rest. But this is not sound. The reason is that mention of some, intended to include the rest, is satisfied by mentioning one, and that one is by way of example. But that a number from one category be mentioned and the rest omitted, by way of restriction, is not accepted.

But there remains for us the consideration of displaying the adornment which Allah made the woman's, i.e., the face, the hands, and the like. This has a proof other than this verse.

We say: this verse concerns the adornment of clothing and the like, and it must remain as Allah the Mighty and Majestic stated.

As for displaying the face, the two palms, the shin, the neck, and the like, this is derived from other evidences.

Are these twelve equal in what may be displayed of adornment, or are they not equal?

They are not equal without doubt. That is why Allah began with the husband, because he is the highest of those to whom adornment may be displayed in its entirety. The rest can be said to be in order, and it can be said not to be in order, rather one looks at what custom has established; because the reality is, for example: a brother who is always in his sister's house is not like one who comes only rarely. Which of the two states is more modest for her?

If he comes only rarely, she is shy before him and more modest than when he is always with her. So for such matters it is said: by their order. As for the husband, he is at the top in any case.

* * *

The hidden adornment is for none except those mentioned in the verse. We reached their number yesterday or in the previous lesson: twelve categories. Those other than them may not be shown the hidden adornment.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And let them not strike their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾. Whom does the pronoun in ﴿let them not strike﴾ refer to?

To the believing women. ﴿With their feet﴾: striking with the foot is known; that is, moving it forcefully on the ground.

(﴿So that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾: such as an anklet that jingles.) That is, it makes a jingling sound; because when a woman wears an anklet, and trousers cover it so that it is not shown to people, but some women, for temptation, may Allah protect us, strike their feet until the anklet is heard, meaning that she has an anklet. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbade the believing women from doing this: that they strike their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known.

And is the "lam" in His words ﴿li-yu'lama﴾ for causation (ta'lil), or for consequence ('aqibah)?

The meaning differs. If you say it is for causation, the prohibition falls only on one who does not intend that; that is, she struck her foot in order that it be known, and accordingly if she struck her foot on an insect, for example a scorpion, or the like, and the anklet was heard, then there is no blame on her in that, because she did not intend that what she conceals of her adornment be known.

If we take the "lam" to be for consequence, meaning: do not strike your feet, for the consequence of this striking is that what she conceals of her adornment becomes known, then the prohibition on striking with the foot is absolute, whether she intends it or does not intend it.

Without doubt, if we look at the forbidden result of this striking, which is the knowing of what was concealed of the adornment, this forbidden result does not differ whether the woman intends it or not.

This forbidden result will occur if she strikes until the anklet sounds, whether she intends this matter or does not.

On this basis, it is preferable that the "lam" be for consequence; because the forbidden result will occur.

And if we look at the fact that when a woman does not intend this, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Actions are only by intentions" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]], and she struck her foot not for this purpose, so she is not sinful for it.

We preferred that the "lam" be for causation, but the first is better: that it be said striking with the foot is not permissible, even for another purpose, because it results in what she conceals of her adornment becoming known.

The "lam" of causation occurs frequently in the Qur'an, such as His words: ﴿And do not hold them back to harm them, that you may transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah 231], and His words: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. They did not pick him up for that; they picked him up that he might be a comfort to their eyes, but the consequence turned out to be this.

So in any case, what appears is that it is better to take the "lam" as for consequence, because the corruption and temptation occur whether she intends it or not.

If it is not permissible for her to strike with the foot out of fear that the sound of the anklet will appear, how much more so for one who displays the anklet itself, displays bracelets on the hands, and displays a necklace on the neck? Is this like that, or more severe?

* Students: More severe.

* The Shaykh: More severe, yes, more severe and more deserving of prohibition and forbiddance. Therefore the practice of women now is without doubt forbidden, and in reality we and they are exposed to this. How is it that we see these women openly violating what Allah the Mighty and Majestic has forbidden, and we find no one forbidding them and saying: this is forbidden?!

I think it is her intention to display the hand so that what is on it of jewelry is seen. For this reason you will sometimes find her showing only the hand that has the jewelry on it. This is also among the blameworthy practices that women engage in: filling one hand with jewelry while leaving the other hand bare. This too is an error, because it apparently belongs to the same category as one who walks with one sandal. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade a man to walk with one sandal[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5856) and Muslim (2097 / 68), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] because of the lack of balance between the two feet, and balance is commanded. So if she fills one hand with jewelry and the other is bare, there is something troubling about this in the soul.

We say: it is better that she wear jewelry evenly on both hands, except if one hand has a watch and she wishes to reduce the bangles by the amount of space the watch takes up. This may be called balance, and there is nothing wrong with it.

But your filling this hand with jewelry while the other is white, or has nothing on it except a watch, or has a strap as well, there is something troubling about this in the soul.

In any case, if Allah, glory be to Him, forbade a woman to strike her feet together, lest what she conceals of her anklet be known through the sound of it, then what we have mentioned, which women do today, is even graver and more serious. For this reason it is not permissible for women to do that, even according to those who say that the face and the palms are not 'awrah. They hold that the forearm is 'awrah, and that it is not permissible for a woman to reveal her forearm adorned with bangles. But the problem is serious.

﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may succeed.﴾ (For what has befallen you of forbidden looking and other things) ﴿that you may succeed﴾: that you may be saved by having your repentance accepted.

﴿Turn to Allah﴾: this is a command from Allah, glory be to Him, to His believing servants, addressed to all people: repent, O believers. The address is directed to everyone because when these abominations are displayed, their trial encompasses everyone. For this reason Allah addressed everyone: turn to Allah all together. Then reflect on the emphasis of this command in His words ﴿all together﴾, His words ﴿O﴾ (the vocative), and His words ﴿believers﴾. All of these are incentives that compel a person, or are meant to encourage a person to repent, so that repentance is collective: it is not enough for one person to repent while the rest openly persist in their sin and opposition.

Second: ﴿O believers﴾, the vocative, what does it indicate?
We have already mentioned its importance. For this reason the address was directed with the vocative to show concern for it. Also, describing them as believers is evidence that faith requires the believer to repent, and that he does not neglect or ignore sins, and that failing to repent is what? A deficiency in faith. What is repentance?

Repentance: it is returning, returning from where? From disobedience to obedience, from disobedience to Allah to obedience to Him. It is of two kinds:

A general repentance, by which the penitent deserves to be described as among the repentant whom Allah loves: it is repentance from all sins, such that a person ceases every sin he commits, whether verbal, practical, or in belief. About this we said: the general repentance whose doer deserves praise and to be among the repentant whom Allah, mighty and majestic, loves.

The second: a restricted repentance from a specific sin. This person has the praise that he deserves, and the correct view is that this repentance is accepted.

So if a person repents from one sin while he persists in another, his repentance from that sin is valid and accepted according to the preponderant opinion, because faith is divisible and deeds are divisible, and Allah, glory be to Him, is a just judge who does not wrong or betray.

So this man who repents from one sin while persisting in another: the correct view is that his repentance is accepted, and there is no barrier to that. But he does not deserve the previous description of being a penitent in the absolute sense, nor of being among the repentant who deserve unqualified praise; he receives praise in proportion to the repentance that he has achieved.

Now, this command ﴿Turn to Allah﴾: which of the two kinds does it point to, the restricted or the general?
* The students: the general.
* The Shaykh: The general absolute one; that is, a general absolute repentance from all sins, in order that success may be achieved. And what is meant by "la'alla" (perhaps) in ﴿that you may succeed﴾? It indicates causation: that repentance is a cause of success. Success, in reality, is not a light word. Success, like triumph, is the deliverance from what is feared and the attainment of what is desired. ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed﴾ [Al-Imran 185]. ﴿Drawn away from the Fire﴾ is deliverance from what is feared, and ﴿admitted to Paradise﴾ is attainment of what is desired. Success here, ﴿that you may succeed﴾, is not restricted by Allah either in this world or in the next, which shows that success through repentance occurs both in this world and in the next, and so it is: the penitent attains success both in this world and in the next.

* From this sentence is derived: the obligation of repentance, from His words ﴿Turn to Allah﴾. There is no need to mention the conditions of repentance, since they have been mentioned several times before; how many conditions are there? Five conditions; the conditions of repentance are five.

* In it is evidence for the obligation of repentance.
* And also evidence for Allah's love for the one who repents, since He commanded it with this emphasis: ﴿all together, O believers﴾. It has been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah is more delighted at the repentance of His servant than one of you would be with his mount" — and he mentioned that — "on which is his food and drink, and he lost it in a barren desert, and he searched for it and did not find it, so he lay down in the shade of a tree awaiting death. While he was in that state, suddenly the rope of his she-camel was hanging from the tree; he took hold of its rope and said: 'O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your Lord,' he erred from the intensity of joy."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6309) and Muslim (2747 / 7), the wording is his, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]

This joy, in reality, we are now saying it, but do we imagine it? We do not imagine it; however powerful our imagination and our grasp of unseen matters may be, we cannot picture its reality. We now imagine it as a great joy, because it is joy at life after death; but when this happens to a person he finds that it has no parallel, and it cannot have a parallel. So Allah, glory be to Him, despite His complete independence from us and our complete need and poverty toward Him, rejoices at the repentance of His believing servant more than this man rejoices at his mount. For this reason Allah commanded repentance with this emphasis in these three aspects.

(...) Allah's love for repentance is among the generosity and grace of Allah. From where do we derive generosity and grace?
From His love for repentance; that is, His wishing that people repent so that He does not punish them. What indicates this?
It indicates His generosity and grace, and that His mercy precedes His wrath, unlike one who has no mercy. For example, suppose a teacher or a king commands something or forbids something; some of those who command or forbid may love for people to disobey so that they can punish them, thereby showing their control over them. This one loves violators so that they know that he is, for example, (...) and for authority and control. Allah, may He be exalted, despite the perfection of this matter and His complete sovereignty, still loves from His servants that they repent so that He does not punish them.

* And by this we derive the perfection of Allah's mercy toward His servants, His grace and His kindness.
* In it is evidence that repentance is among the requirements of faith. From where do we take it?
From His words ﴿O believers﴾. The correct view is that faith must compel its bearer to repentance. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2475) and Muslim (57 / 100), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] When is faith negated from him?
At the time he commits fornication. It is not possible for a person to be truly a believer without leaving what Allah has forbidden him and doing what Allah has obligated him.

Know that if a sin proceeds from you, that is necessarily a consequence of a deficiency in your faith; no sin can occur from you except that it accompanies a deficiency in faith. For this reason the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (may Allah have mercy on them) is that faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience. This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, and we are among them, God willing.

In any case, I say: repentance is among the requirements of faith, and whoever neglects it is evidence of a deficiency in his faith. If the one who neglects repentance is shown by this action to have a deficiency in faith, then the one who commits the sin and actually engages in it is so by a greater degree. For this reason we pointed to the hadith in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2475) and Muslim (57 / 100), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The completion here, because it is apparent that he is not free of faith at some point, otherwise he would be a disbeliever.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where was it taken? We mentioned it. From where did you take it, O brothers?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From His command to it first, and Allah does not command except what He loves; He does not legislate a command except for what He loves, and from His concern for it through these emphases: ﴿all together, O believers﴾.
* And in it is evidence that: whoever does not repent (we said repentance is among the requirements of faith) is deficient in faith, and in proportion to his disobedience his deficiency in faith is.
* And also in it is a sixth benefit: that repentance is a cause of success, from His words ﴿that you may succeed﴾. And what is success? Deliverance from what is feared and attainment of what is desired.
* And also in it is the seventh benefit: the affirmation of causes. Allah made repentance a cause of success, and in this there is a refutation of those who deny causes and say that causes are merely signs, not determinants. And whose doctrine is this?
It is the doctrine of the Ash'aris, who hold that causes are signs, not determinants, to the extent that they say: when a man breaks a glass, it did not break by his breaking it; rather it broke at the time of his breaking it, not because of it. And fire, when it burns, what it burns is not burned by its agency; rather it burned at its presence, not by it. So a person who eats until he is satiated was not satiated by the eating; he was satiated at the time of eating, not by it. I believe that if they put food before him (...) and he did not eat, would he be satisfied or not? He would not be satisfied.

In any case, this is a false doctrine with no basis for correctness whatsoever, and even reason rejects it. But I say: this verse and many verses establish causes, and show that causes are effective in their effects. Would no speaker say: if you make causes effective in their effects, have you not affirmed with Allah a creator and originator, for example? No, we have not affirmed an originator, because we do not say that causes act independently in their influence; rather causes are causes only by the will of Allah, glory be to Him. For this reason a cause sometimes exists complete and yet does not produce its effect, because of a known or unknown impediment. Could no speaker say: if you affirm causes, have you not affirmed with Allah a partner in bringing into existence and in creation? We say: No. The One who made this cause a cause necessitating its effect is Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason we often see effects fail to occur despite the presence of complete causes, which shows that the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, is above everything, and that these causes are not independent. But we cannot deny a matter established by the Sharia and established by reality, that causes do affect their effects: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may succeed.﴾

* A student: This cause precedes the effect.
* The Shaykh: This cause precedes the effect; give me an example of it. Can an effect exist without a cause existing?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It does not contradict; there is nothing wrong with it. This is a regimen (hamiyah), and regimen is established in the Sharia.
* A student: In His words ﴿and let them not stamp﴾?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, the prohibition is for prohibition, which is why He said: ﴿turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If we take the "lam" as indicating causation, it is possible; because if you take it as causation, its meaning is intention: do not do such-and-such for such-and-such a purpose.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. When a thing is prohibited and no reason is mentioned, for example, it is taken at face value. If someone said he wants to eat carrion, not with the intention of eating carrion, we would say: this does not help. Allah did not say: carrion is forbidden to you because of your intention toward it. But when the ruling is given a reason, it becomes dependent on intention.
In this verse, the truth is that the "lam" can indicate causation, and this is supported by "Actions are only by intentions."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907 / 155), from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] But we said: the harm will occur whether you strike with this cause or for another.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And marry off the single among you and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾ [An-Nur 32].

(In the verse, the masculine is given precedence over the feminine.) Why did the author bring this phrase, although this is common in the Qur'an?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because the address in this verse is directed to the women. Had it originally been directed to the men, this phrase that the author mentioned would not have been needed. But since the address in the noble verse is directed to the women, then He said: ﴿Turn to Allah in repentance all together, O believers﴾, and He did not say: "Turn to Allah in repentance all together, O believing women."

We say: this is for the sake of giving precedence to the masculine. There is also in it an indication – and Allah knows best – directing the address here to the men, while it undoubtedly includes the women. It indicates the man's responsibility for the woman, and that he himself must repent and set his family right. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has made one of them to excel the other, and because they spend of their wealth﴾ [An-Nisa 34].

So we say: in this there is a direction of the address to the males, although the whole verse is an address to the women. It indicates the man's responsibility for the woman, and that the woman cannot be upright except through the uprightness of the man. Reality bears witness to this. Now, the negligence of these women among us – what are its causes?

* The students: The men.

* The Shaykh: They, of course, are inclined to this thing, so the direct cause is from them, but the men's failure to look after them and their lack of care for them is what has brought about this for them.

So we say in this: directing the address to the males, although the whole verse is an address to the women, indicates the man's responsibility for the woman, and that the woman cannot be upright except through the uprightness of the man. Reality bears witness to this. Now, the negligence of these women among us – what are its causes?

* Students: The men.

* The Shaykh: They, of course, are inclined to this thing, so the direct cause is from them, but the men's failure to look after them and their lack of care for them, this is what has brought about for them this expansion that the Sharia does not approve. Therefore, if every one of the people had dedicated himself to protecting his wife, this evil would not have occurred. And it is strange that one of us is found (...) himself to protect his wealth, or not? A safe (...) with two keys, and the keys are in (...) always. If he had, for example, one in a thousand fear for this wealth, he would say: put it in the banks for its protection, and he calculates and examines: what decreased today? What increased? The family, who are truly the life of a person, do not concern him. His sons wander about and his daughters wander about, and everything, and he does not look. If we cared for our families even half as much as we care for our wealth, much good would have come about. Yet, do we care for our wealth for ourselves or for others? For others, because this accumulated wealth will not follow you; it returns. But your family, if Allah makes them righteous at your hand, you are in reality making them righteous for yourself. The Prophet ﷺ said: «When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three», and he mentioned among them a righteous child who prays for him.[[Narrated by Muslim (1631 / 14) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And marry off the single among you and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾ [An-Nur 32]. ﴿Ankihu﴾ (marry off) – if someone recited (wa-ankihu), would the meaning differ or not?

* A student: It differs.

* The Shaykh: It differs an enormous difference. Therefore, if anyone errs in this verse and says (wa-nkihu), it is obligatory to correct him, because this is a grammatical error that changes the meaning.

﴿Ankihu⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ means "marry off" (zawwiju), but (inkihu) means "get married" (tazawwaju); a great difference between them. ﴿Ankihu⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ means: marry off the single among you, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿al-ayama⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ – the author says: (al-ayama is the plural of ayyim, who is one without a spouse, whether virgin or previously married, and one without a spouse; this applies to free men and free women).

﴿al-ayama⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ is the plural of ayyim: one who has no spouse, whether she was a previously married woman whose husband died or divorced her, or a virgin; she is called ayyim. Allah the Exalted has commanded their marriage. This is evidence that a woman does not marry herself, because ﴿ankihu﴾ means "marry off." If a woman could marry herself, we would not need to tell others to marry her, since she would marry herself. This is one of the proofs, and among them is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When they have reached their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾ [Al-Baqarah 232].

In any case, this is not the place to expand on the issue of the guardian and the lack of a guardian. Rather, in this address there is a directive to guardians regarding women: that they marry them off – ﴿marry off the single among you﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not specify whom one marries; that is, whom do we marry? Because they are commanded to arrange marriage, but whom do we marry? The Sunnah has clarified that. What is it?

«If there comes to you one whose religion and character you are pleased with»[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (1084) and Ibn Majah (1967) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. So we marry the one of religion and character. Wealth is indeed sought by the Sharia – that is, sought in reality – and the Prophet ﷺ made clear that «a woman is married for her wealth»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5090) and Muslim (1466 / 53) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]], and a man likewise is married for his wealth, but the foundation is religion and character; this is the principle.

As for His saying: ﴿the single among you⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ – this means unmarried women. But unmarried men, how do we marry them off?

Does it mean that if he proposes to me, I marry him off, or that I help him to marry, or both?

Both; because the ayama applies to men and women who have no wives. As for women, it is clear that we are commanded to marry them off; we do not prevent them if a suitable man proposes. But likewise, we are commanded to marry off men: meaning, if an unmarried man proposes to us, we marry him off. Well, and the one who has no wife?

* A student: We do not marry him?

* The Shaykh: So we do not marry him?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: No, we marry him off, but this is of greater concern. For example, if two men propose to me, one of whom has a wife and the other has no wife, and both are equal in religion and character, whom do I give precedence to?

* Students: The one who has no wife.

* The Shaykh: The one who has no wife, it is known, because he is more in need, and it guards his chastity, while the other has already guarded his chastity. So then: ﴿the single among you⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ regarding men who have wives: they are commanded to marry, but the text specifically mentions the single because he is more in need. Likewise, helping the single to marry is included in this: that a person assists them, for this is among the deeds for which a person is rewarded, because marriage is sought by the Sharia and by nature. So when a person marries, he has done what Allah commanded and attained what his soul also seeks. Moreover, if we help them in this matter, we are complying with His saying: ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾, yes, because in reality we have married him; our helping him to marry is a form of marrying him off.

* A student: If the righteous husband refuses (...)?

* The Shaykh: If she refuses the righteous husband and wants an unrighteous husband, that is not accepted from her.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: He does not permit her. But if she requested a suitable match, yet the guardian himself considers that this is better, but she who asked does not have any defect in his religion, she must follow what she wants.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾, meaning: and marry off (﴿the righteous﴾, i.e., the believers, ﴿among your male servants and your female servants﴾, and ʿibād is the plural of ʿabd).

This refers to the owned: that is, this is an address to the masters; meaning, marry off the righteous: marry off the righteous among your servants and your female servants.

The author's statement "(﴿the righteous﴾ – the believers)" takes righteousness here to mean righteousness of religion, and righteousness of religion is by faith and righteous action. But it may include both righteousness of religion and of worldly affairs; that is, if the person is a righteous servant in his religion and righteous in his worldly affairs, meaning he is fit to be married, having reached marriageable age, knowing the matters of marriage, and being sensible so that no harm comes from marrying him and no injury to his wife's rights. The point is that ﴿the righteous⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ should be interpreted as righteousness in religion and in worldly affairs; that is, fit both to marry and to be married. As for one who, for example, is a servant who is insane, we are not commanded to marry him off absolutely; rather, we look: if not marrying him would cause harm, we marry him, otherwise not, because that would be an injury to others.

In summary: the righteous servant is married off unconditionally, and the non-righteous one, if the need to marry him arises – because not marrying him would entail harm – we are commanded, not from this verse, but from where? From averting harms, from the general principle of the Sharia: averting harms.

As for His saying: ﴿from your servants⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ – ʿibad is the plural of ʿabd, and what is meant is those owned by us. Allah called them servants because they are subdued to us and we are their masters; they are subdued by decree and by the Sharia. By the Sharia, it is clear: my servant I may sell, buy, command, and forbid. By decree, as is known, servants – those who are owned – see themselves as falling short of their masters, and this is one of Allah's blessings: that He subdued them to their masters. Otherwise, if one rebels against his master, as they say: "When the camel rages, what then? And the servant when he hunts, and the valley – I don't know what else – and the flood when it runs, there is no one to stop them." Allah the Exalted has subdued the servants by the Sharia and subdued them by decree; therefore He called them our servants.

﴿and your female servants⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ – ʾimaʾ is the plural of ʾamah: the female slave who is owned. This indicates that a servant does not marry himself, from His saying: ﴿ankihu﴾ "marry off." This is if the address is directed to the husbands. But if the address is directed to people in general – meaning a person should not disdain marrying off a servant or a slave woman – this is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that the address here is to the masters: meaning, marry off the righteous who are fit for marriage in their religion and worldly affairs, marry them to female slaves and male slaves.

This verse has a difficulty from two angles. The first angle: in "ʿibad" (servants), and the second angle: in "imaʾ" (female servants). For the Messenger ﷺ said: «None of you should say: my servant and my female servant»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2552) and Muslim (2249 / 15) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. And here He said: ﴿your servants and your female servants﴾. And he ﷺ said: «Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (900) and Muslim (442 / 136) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]]. So is there a contradiction between the hadith and this verse, or not?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of both is indeed a contradiction, but reconciling them is clear. The address here: ﴿your servants⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ is from Allah to the person, calling him a servant of his, his slave. Just as I may say "the servant of so-and-so," I attribute him to so-and-so: I say "this is so-and-so's servant, this is your servant, this is your female servant," and similar. But what is prohibited, and what has been forbidden, is that a person attributes the servitude of these people to himself. This is what is forbidden: that the master attributes servitude and female servitude to himself. Why? Because it involves self-conceit, arrogance over his servant, and looking down on him. He says: "O my servant, come here," "O my female servant, come here," and undoubtedly he feels greatness and superiority, while the other feels humiliation and submission before him, and this should not be so. Therefore the prohibition came. But if the matter is reversed, and the attribution comes from someone other than the master, there is no harm in it. Likewise, the servant is forbidden to say "my lord" to his master, and «let him say: my master».[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2552) and Muslim (2249 / 15).]]

But if you say: "O servant, speak to your lord, pray to your lord for me," is it permissible or not? This is permissible. The same applies when a servant addresses his master with lordship: we say this is forbidden, because the one is becoming great and the other is humbling himself. For this reason, in the hadith, when Gabriel's hadith about the signs of the Hour, he said: «Tell me of its signs.» He said: «That the female slave gives birth to her lord»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9 / 5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. This is established with this wording: «that the female slave gives birth to her lord». The well-known wording is «her mistress» [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4777) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]], but in another narration: «that the female slave gives birth to her lord».

In summary, one must know the difference between attributing to the first-person pronoun (my) and attributing to others. Attributing to the speaker's pronoun is forbidden; for the master, he should not say "my servant" and "my female servant," and the servant should not say "my lord." But attributing to something other than the first-person ya' is permissible, and the difference between them in meaning is clear.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

(﴿If they are⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ – meaning the free – ﴿poor, Allah will enrich them﴾ through marriage ﴿from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing﴾ in regard to His creation, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of them.)

﴿If they are poor⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ means: those who are married.

As for the author's statement "(meaning the free)": why did he restrict it to the free, although the verse says: ﴿the single among you and the righteous among your servants and your female servants﴾, and then said: ﴿if they are poor﴾?

Because female slaves cannot be conceived of as rich or poor. Why? They do not own. The evidence that they do not own is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: «Whoever sells a slave who has wealth, his wealth belongs to the one who sold him, unless the buyer stipulates it»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2379) and Muslim (1543 / 80) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]]: «his wealth belongs to the one who sold him». He did not say "to the one who sold him" as an addition. So the slave does not own; therefore he is poor, and cannot become rich. But it may be said that wealth belongs to his master: you marry your servant so that Allah enriches them from His bounty and widens His provision for them, so they marry. When Allah commanded marriage and explained that if they are poor, Allah enriches them from His bounty, He commanded whoever is poor to seek chastity until Allah enriches him from His bounty; that is, he should not give free rein to forbidden looking, forbidden physical contact, pursuing women, and the like. Rather, he must be chaste regarding adultery, its causes, and its preliminaries. This is what is meant by chastity: keeping away from adultery and its causes and preliminaries.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 33 (part 1 of 3):

The saying of the Most High: ﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur 33]; because when Allah enriches them from His bounty, they marry, since nothing prevents them from marriage except that.

As for His saying ﴿those who find no means of marriage﴾, the author (al-Mu'allif) explained it with his statement: (what they may marry with). The correct view is that the verse is more general than that. This is why He said ﴿those who find no means of marriage﴾, which includes what the author mentioned, and also includes the case where a person does not find a woman to marry. A person may be wealthy, have a dowry, and have maintenance, yet he proposes and is refused. So do we say that this man has found a means of marriage or not?

He has not found a means of marriage. Therefore, restricting the lack of marriage to what the author mentioned is open to question. The verse is more general: ﴿those who find no means of marriage﴾, meaning they find no maintenance for it, and they also find no woman to marry, since this falls within the generality of the verse.

As for His saying ﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾, this is how Allah, glorified and exalted, guided toward chastity for those who find no marriage. Does this contradict the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O assembly of youth, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield for him"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1905) and Muslim (1400 / 1) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]? Is there a contradiction between the verse and the hadith? No. How is that?

* A student: It explains the path to chastity (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, well said. The verse commands chastity, and the Prophet ﷺ explained the path to chastity: that a person fasts, for that cuts off the desire for marriage. When the desire for marriage is cut off, this is one of the greatest causes of chastity, since nothing drives a person to lack chastity except desire. When desire is cut off, the causes of lacking chastity disappear. Through this we know that the hadith does not conflict with the verse, because Allah commanded seeking chastity, and the Prophet ﷺ explained to us one of the means of seeking it. Moreover, the one who finds no marriage may have strong desire, which may lead him to violate what is forbidden, so the remedy for that is fasting. As for the person whose desire is ordinary and unlikely to lead him astray, he need not fast, because if we took the Prophet's saying ﴿whoever is not able, let him fast﴾ literally, we would say that every poor person who finds no marriage and has desire must fast. But the matter is not like that. Rather, if a person finds no path to chastity except fasting, let him fast. As for a person who is balanced and normal and does not fear for himself what is forbidden, he has no need of fasting. This is why he said "فَعَلَيْهِ" (let him), and "عَلَى" here indicates obligation/necessity, which shows that he is in a state needing something to restrain the surge of desire, namely fasting. There is also an indication in this: His saying ﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ points to the fact that chastity is a cause of richness, just as marriage is also a cause of richness. Likewise, when a person is patient, keeps himself chaste, and stays away from what Allah has forbidden him, that is a cause of richness. Allah the Most High has said in the Qur'an: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out (2) and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq 2, 3].

As for His saying ﴿Until Allah enriches them﴾, is the intended meaning richness of wealth or richness of marriage?

* A student: Both: richness of marriage and richness of wealth.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not both. It is richness of marriage, because He said ﴿those who find no means of marriage﴾. We say: richness of marriage, why? Because, as we pointed out, a person may be wealthy but still not find marriage, not be married. So we say: they find no means "until He enriches them", that is, until Allah enriches them with marriage, not with wealth, with the marriage they were unable to find. Thus it includes richness in wealth and richness in a wife.

And how many a person, as you know, has much wealth yet has no wife; so he is like the poor man. So the better way to understand His saying ﴿Until Allah enriches them﴾ is: with what? With wealth or with marriage? With marriage, so that it covers both: if the lack of marriage is due to poverty, then it is by wealth; if it is due to a prohibition, then it is by obedience, for He only eases for him one who obeys Him and marries him.

When Allah, majestic and exalted, mentioned the rulings of marriage and what relates to them, He moved to another important matter, which concerns female slaves, and indeed male slaves in general, saying ﴿and the righteous among your male and female slaves﴾, thus indicating the slaves.

He moved to a very important issue, which is His saying (﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission﴾ meaning contracting (al-mukatabah) ﴿from among those whom your right hands possess﴾, from the slaves and female slaves, ﴿then write it for them if you know any good in them﴾, meaning: trustworthiness and capacity to earn to pay the amount of the contract and its form, for example, such and such).

﴿Those who seek the Kitab﴾: "seek" means "request", and "al-Kitab" means "al-mukatabah" (the contract of manumission). Mukatabah is the master selling his slave to himself: the master sells his slave to himself. This is mukatabah, and it was called that because it generally takes place by a document (kitab) that the master writes between himself and his slave recording this contract. So if the slave asks his master to make a contract of manumission with him, Allah has said: ﴿then write it for them﴾. So we say: "yabtaghun" means "seek" or "request".

﴿al-Kitab﴾: mukatabah, which is the master selling the slave's person to the slave himself.

As for His saying ﴿then write it for them﴾, why did he add the "fa"?

* A student: It is the response of the imperative.

* The Shaykh: The response of the imperative?

* A student: If...

* The Shaykh: "If"? Do we have "if" here?

* A student: The "fa" here is a connecting particle.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the "fa" connects the predicate to the subject. Does linking the predicate to the subject require it or not?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It does not require it. You say: Zayd is standing, the book is beautiful, the sky is high. But if the subject resembles a conditional in generality, then its predicate is linked with "fa". We mentioned to you earlier that the grammarians give the example: "The one who comes to me, for him is a dirham," and that much of this in the Qur'an is this verse: ﴿Those who seek the Kitab from among those whom your right hands possess, then write it for them﴾.

And His saying ﴿from among those whom your right hands possess﴾: this "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah) for the relative pronoun ﴿those who﴾. ﴿Those who seek﴾: since the relative pronoun, even when its clause is present, is in reality indefinite, so "min" is explanatory to clarify what is indefinite in the relative pronoun.

His saying ﴿from among those whom your right hands possess﴾ affirms ownership (al-mulk) for human beings.

If someone says: Does not Allah say ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 189], restricting dominion to Himself? How can this agree with affirming dominion for human beings?

The answer: absolute dominion belongs to Allah, while the ownership of human beings over what they own is not absolute. It is therefore restricted: restricted by the type of ownership, restricted by the type of disposal, restricted in every respect. When I have wealth, am I free to dispose of it entirely? No, I dispose of it in a specific way and within specific limits. Therefore my ownership is not complete in every respect. So we say: absolute dominion belongs to Allah alone, and my ownership is attributed to me, but it is restricted and specific. If you own the thing and its usufruct, you are called an owner; if you own only the usufruct without the thing, you are called a lessee; and so on, each type of ownership has a specific name.

His saying ﴿from among those whom your right hands possess﴾: "al-Aymān" is the plural of "yamin" (right hand), which is the opposite of the left. Does this mean that a person owns his slave with his right hand only, and the left hand does not own?

No. This is a case of prevalence (taghlib), like ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30]. Since what usually prevails in a person's taking, giving, selling and buying is what?

Working with the right hand. He said ﴿from among those whom your right hands possess﴾; otherwise, in reality, I own him entirely, not just with my right hand. But since this is what usually prevails in matters of buying, selling, taking and giving, Allah, glorified and exalted, attributed ownership to the right hand.

﴿then write it for them﴾: we said the "fa" connects the predicate to the subject, and that it connected the predicate to the subject because the subject is a relative pronoun resembling a conditional in generality.

As for His saying ﴿write it for them﴾, this is an imperative. Is the imperative here obligatory or recommended?

Scholars differ on it. The majority hold that the imperative is recommended (istihbab). Their evidence is that the slave is your property, and you are not obliged to release your property except with your consent. Just as a person cannot be compelled to sell his house or his mount, he cannot be compelled to sell his slave. So if he asks me for a contract of manumission, I am free to decide, because he is my property; this is why Allah called him "mulk" (possession).

So the majority view is that the imperative is recommended, their evidence being that the slave is your possession, and a person cannot be compelled to remove his property from his ownership: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his own good pleasure"[[Narrated by Ahmad (21082) from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Yathribi.]]. Since this is so, the imperative here is for recommendation. Some scholars, including the Zahiris, held that the imperative is obligatory, and that if the slave asks for a contract of manumission, the master must respond. This is because the basic principle of an imperative is obligation. As for their statement that the owner cannot be compelled to remove his property from his ownership, this is not absolute: the owner is compelled to remove part of his property in matters Allah has made obligatory. Is it not obligatory for a person to pay zakat, which is removing part of his property? Is it not obligatory for him to pay expiation (kaffarah)? Is it not obligatory for him to spend on others, relatives, wives and others?

So the statement "a person is not obliged to remove his property from his ownership" is not absolute, and there are many matters in which a person is compelled to remove his property from his ownership. Is it not the case that if a person's wealth becomes encumbered with a right, the right of creditors, and his debts exceed his wealth, he is placed under restriction (hajr)?

He is placed under restriction and compelled to sell his property, and it is spent on the creditors. So in any case we say: this matter is not absolute, and many matters have become obligatory though they involve a person removing his property from his ownership.

Moreover, this strengthens that the imperative is obligatory. This is in fact a response to what the majority cited. As for strengthening the imperative to be obligatory, they said: the Lawgiver (al-Shari') is eager for emancipation, and servitude is something that comes upon humans; it is not original to them. Is that not so?

If humans wish to free themselves from this servitude and return themselves to their original state, the Lawgiver is eager for that. This is why you find that the Lawgiver encouraged manumission greatly, even informing: "Whoever frees a slave, Allah will free from the Fire, for every part of him, a part of himself, even the private part for the private part"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6715) and Muslim (1509 / 22) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. This is a great encouragement.

Likewise, Allah, glorified and exalted, made obligatory in several expiations: what did He make obligatory? The freeing of a neck (raqabah), such as the expiation for zihar, the expiation for oath-breaking, and the expiation for killing. All of this is evidence that the Lawgiver has an eagerness to free slaves. So how can we not make this imperative obligatory, especially when the slave himself is the one requesting it, and he knows of himself that he will become independent of his master, and wants to free himself? How can we prevent him?

If the master says: "This is my slave, and I cannot be rid of him," we say to him: If you fear Allah, the Most High, He will make your affair easy. Perhaps you will free him; and if you free him, then hire him if you need him and know him, or Allah will ease for you someone else. In any case, since Allah has commanded it, the basic principle of the commands of Allah and His Messenger is obligation.

He says: ﴿if you know any good in them﴾. This is a condition on the command: ﴿write it for them if you know any good in them﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, made this conditional upon knowledge of good in them. What is good?

The author says: (that is, trustworthiness and capacity to earn to pay the amount of the contract).

Yes. Some of the early scholars explained it as: righteousness in their religion and earning. It may be that his saying "trustworthiness" points to this, but if we say "righteousness in their religion," it becomes more general than the word "trustworthiness," since trustworthiness is part of righteousness in religion, not the reverse. So we say: the intended good is righteousness in religion and earning. Righteousness in religion means we know that he upholds the prayer, upholds fasting, avoids what is forbidden, and is upright. Among righteousness in religion is also trustworthiness: we know that I do not want to free someone who goes around stealing from people; that he is trustworthy. And earning is worldly righteousness: we know that if this slave is freed, he will be able to earn and will not be a burden on others. For if he becomes unable to earn and his master frees him, from where will he eat? He becomes a burden on people, and perhaps he gains strength and steals and plunders. Therefore this condition is necessary: righteousness and earning.

As for the author's statement "to pay the amount of the contract," this is open to question. It is not sufficient that he has earnings to pay the amount of the contract; rather, it must be to pay the amount of the contract and to support himself in the future. So the command is conditional upon our knowing good in them. Now, if I do not know good in him, is it obligatory for me to make a contract with him if he asks?

* A student: It is not obligatory.

* The Shaykh: It is not obligatory. Is it permissible?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: But how is it permissible when I know there is no good in him, I know that if I free him he will want to corrupt? Either he will join the disbelievers if his origin was a disbeliever, or he will corrupt the earth through sins. I have him under control, but once he is free, who will rebuke him? He has no one.
