So the correct view is: if we do not know good in him, we are not commanded to make a contract with him. This is one point, and it is the implication (mafhum) of the verse. Then, if we are not commanded, is it permissible for us to make the contract?

If we know there is evil in him and corruption in responding to him, then responding is forbidden. If we know no evil or corruption in him, responding is permissible. Thus the implication has a distinction.

What remains is the answer to the question the brother asked: if the master says, "I do not know good in him, so it is not obligatory for me to contract with him," what do we say?

We say: you and your trustworthiness. Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who will hold you to account, and He has left the matter to you. If you say "I do not know good in him," then as far as we are concerned, we accept your claim and do not compel you to make the contract. But as far as Allah is concerned, it does not benefit you if you know there is good in him and claim you do not know it. As far as Allah is concerned, it does not benefit him. In any case, the matter of knowing good or lacking it is left to the master.

As far as we are concerned, the rulings of this world are based on the outward. If he says, "I do not know good in this slave, and I know that if I leave him he will go astray and lead others astray," we say: as far as we are concerned, we do not compel you now, and we do not say it is obligatory for you. But if Allah knows that you know there is good in him, then your claim is rejected and not accepted.

And in this verse is there evidence?

* A student: That the imperative is obligatory?

* The Shaykh: Yes, the imperative is obligatory. The correct view is that the imperative is obligatory.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is not necessary: if he does not know good in him, it is not obligatory.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is not necessary, because Allah did not make it obligatory except when we know good. The opposite of that is that we know evil in him, or that we know neither good nor its opposite. But if we know evil in him, the contract is forbidden; and if we know neither this nor that, it is a matter of permissibility. Yes?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this is left to you, unless we know that reality contradicts his claim. If we know that this slave is always righteous, prays, is trustworthy among people, and knows how to earn, then of course we do not accept his claim.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, otherwise the basic principle is left to his trustworthiness.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: With whom?

* The student: With the slave.

* The Shaykh: His earnings belong to his master, and likewise the female slave.

* The student: If the female slave asks for a contract (...)?

* The Shaykh: If she asks for a contract, and she has no earnings, you do not contract with her; it is not obligatory for you to contract with her.

* The student: What prevents you if you free her?

* The Shaykh: No. If she is freed and has relatives, they are her guardians; and if she has no relatives, then he (the master) is her guardian.

Student: (...).
Shaykh: Yes, until (...), and that he marries her off, for example, if she wishes to marry. If he is not fit for that, then the judge is her guardian.
In this is evidence of the Lawgiver's eagerness for emancipation, and that among the causes of emancipation is the contract of manumission (mukatabah) that takes place between a master and his slave. He says: "its formula" (ṣīghatuhā), meaning the contract of manumission, "and its formula, for example: I have contracted with you for two thousand over two months, a thousand each month; when you have paid them, you are free." Then he says: "I accept that."
The author says: "its formula, for example." That is, this is not the only formula; whatever indicates that suffices. But notice his words: "for two thousand over two months." Is the intended meaning that the two thousand fall due together at the end of the two months, or that each thousand falls due in its month?
Students: Each thousand in its month.
Shaykh: The scholars say that it is part of facilitation for the slave that the sum be paid in installments (munajjaman), the money for which the contract is made being paid in two or more due dates. That is, one does not say: "I contract with you for ten thousand, all due after a year," because this would be a hardship for the slave. Rather, he makes it payable in two or more installments. For example, ten thousand: either he says "a thousand riyals every two months," or "a thousand riyals every month," or "five thousand in six months and five thousand in six months." The essential point is that it must be in installments of two or more due dates. And what is the purpose of this? Consideration for the slave's circumstances and gentleness toward him.
The apparent sense of the words of the scholars on this question is that even if it is assumed that the slave has the ability to pay it in a single due date, it is still necessary to have two due dates. That is, if we suppose a person approaches the slave and says to him: "Come, buy yourself from your master, and I will pay you the dirhams immediately," this is not valid. However, in this matter there is room for consideration. The case of 'A'ishah with Barirah, when she made a contract of manumission with her family for nine awāq, and 'Ā'ishah said: "If your family wishes that I pay it for them and that your loyalty (walā') be to me, I will do so," is narrated [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2168), and Muslim (1504/8)]. What does it indicate? It indicates permissibility, even though 'Ā'ishah intended to buy her outright. But it indicates that if someone wishes to hasten what the slave owes his master, and both agree to that, it is valid. In this case, however, the slave must take precaution for himself, because that man may come to him and say this, then retract, although if he retracts nothing harms the slave. And what is the final outcome? If he becomes unable to pay, he returns to his master as a slave, and in reality this does no harm.
Student: The money, shaykh?
Shaykh: The money he earned goes to his master.
Student: If he asks for the money?
Shaykh: If he asks, from now on it begins.
Student: He did not know it?
Shaykh: Nothing takes effect.
Student: He did not write it?
Shaykh: That is, he requested the contract and the master refused; it remains as it was, he remains a slave as he was.
Student: He does not own the money?
Shaykh: No, he does not own it. If he owns it, it belongs to his master according to those who make it obligatory; he is compelled to write the contract. Then the slave goes and earns, and when he earns he hands it over to his master.

God Most High says: ﴿And give them of the wealth of God which He has given you﴾ ("give them" is a command to the masters; "of the wealth of God which He has given you" is what they may use in fulfilling what they owe you; and the meaning of giving includes remitting some of what they owe).
"﴿Give them of the wealth of God﴾": the author says, "the command is to the masters." But it is also permissible that the command be addressed to others than the masters, or to the masters and others; it is permissible that the command be addressed to all Muslims: ﴿give them of the wealth of God﴾.
If the command is directed to the masters, there are two ways of giving:
The first way: if he contracts with him, he gives him money so that it becomes a foundation for his earning.
The second way: when he has paid what he owes, he remits part of it for him. But is it remitted from the first installment, or from the last installment?
Some of the early generations chose to remit from the first installment, because that is easier for him. Others chose to remit from the last installment, saying: "If I remit from the first installment, or give him from the first installment, and then he becomes unable and returns to me, my charity has returned to me. Whereas if I give him from the last installment, nothing of my charity returns to me, because when he pays the last installment, what happens? He is freed." And this is the preferred view: that he gives from the last installment.
So if the command is directed to the masters, there are two ways of giving. The first: that he gives him from the outset, from his own private wealth, giving him money from the beginning. For what purpose?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Yes, to be a foundation for earning toward the contract money.
The second way: when he has paid what is owed, he gives him from what he paid. But we say: the correct view is that it is a command to the masters in the manner mentioned, and also a command to non-masters that they assist the mukatab in his contract. For this reason he was given a share of zakah. So it is permissible for a person to spend some of his zakah on those in contracts of manumission, and this is the correct view. The correct view is that the command in His words ﴿and give them of the wealth of God﴾ includes masters and others; and others, if we say that zakah is distributed to them, then zakah is the wealth of God.
His words ﴿of the wealth of God which He has given you﴾: He did not say "of your wealth." He said "of the wealth of God," indicating that even if you give them, the favor belongs to whom?
The favor belongs to God, Glorified and Exalted; the favor belongs to God, because the wealth is God's wealth. Whether we say it is His legislated wealth, which is zakah, if we say the command is directed (...) as well; or that the wealth which is a person's own is God's wealth in a non-legislated sense, God's wealth by decree, the property of a person which he disposes of as an owner disposes of his possession, it is in reality God's wealth. It is as though the verse indicates that there is no merit for you: by the mercy of God, Glorified, God gave you wealth, so give these mukatabin from the wealth of God which He has given you.
The summary of the matter: in this verse is the legitimacy of the mukatabah. When? When the slave requests it. The command in it is for what? For obligation, according to the correct view. But it is conditional upon what? Upon knowing good in them. And good is: righteousness in religion and earning.
Also in the verse: evidence for the obligation to give the mukatab from the wealth, whether the address is to the master or to people in general. As for people in general, they give from zakah; as for the master, he gives from the wealth in his hand, because God Most High is the One who bestowed it upon him. Then he said.
Student: Does the master give from his zakah?
Shaykh: No, he does not give from his zakah, because if he gives from his zakah, in reality it will certainly return to him.
Student: (...).
Shaykh: (...) he remits from the principal.

He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution﴾. Someone may say: Why do you forbid the master to give his mukatab from his zakah, when you permit him to give it to his debtor or not? That is, if a person asks someone for money and he gives him from his zakah, is there no harm?
It is said: the difference is clear. If you give to a debtor, he may or may not pay; he does not dispose of it as he wishes. But the mukatab will pay in any case: either he pays, or he returns to slavery and the money returns to him. This is the difference between them.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: No, once he becomes a mukatab, you are not obliged to support him; he owns his earnings and everything.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: No, emancipation begins from the start of the contract.
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Yes, it began, but it is not complete until the contract's payment is made.

He said: (﴿And do not compel your slave-girls﴾, i.e., your female slaves ﴿to prostitution﴾, i.e., fornication ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33], seeking to keep themselves chaste; and this desire is the very object of compulsion, so the condition has no mafhum (implied opposite).)
"﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution﴾": "slave-girls" (fatayat), as the author says, means female slaves (al-ima'), and it does not mean young unmarried women here; that is, not even free women, since that is not intended. The intended meaning of "fatayat" is female slaves. "Bigha'" (prostitution) is fornication; it is called bigha' because it is sought (yuṭlab), that is, desired, and bigha' means seeking, and ibtighā' means seeking. So the fornicators, may God protect us, seek this matter.
His words ﴿if they desire chastity﴾: what does this mean? Chastity from fornication, that is, abstaining from it and refraining from it. This desire is the very object of compulsion, so the condition has no mafhum.
When we read the noble verse, it says that God Most High forbade us to compel slave-girls to prostitution on the condition that they desire chastity. That is, if they do not desire chastity, the apparent sense of the verse would permit us to compel them. But the author says that the place of prohibition is the condition: compulsion is only conceivable if they desire chastity, and on this basis the condition has no mafhum. This is what the author held, and there is clear room for objection.
The author, may God have mercy on him, says: "this desire is the very object of compulsion," meaning that compulsion is only conceivable with this desire present, so the condition has no mafhum once compulsion is conceivable only with this desire; the condition is therefore to state the reality, namely the reality of compulsion. This is what the author held, but there is clear objection to it, because a master may compel her to prostitution while she does not desire chastity, but only resents the one he compels her to, such as saying: "You will fornicate with this man," but she does not want this man; she wants another man. If he compels her to fornicate with this man, has compulsion been realized or not?
Student: It has been realized.
Shaykh: Even though she does not desire chastity. So in reality compulsion can occur even if she does not desire chastity. As for their saying that the desire is the place of prohibition, because there is no compulsion without the desire for chastity, we say: No, compulsion can occur without the desire for chastity. For example, she may at that time have no desire for intercourse, or be in a place where she does not wish to be intercourse-d, or at a time when she does not wish to be intercourse-d, or she does not want the one she is compelled with, or the like. So compulsion is not specific to fornication such that we would say this condition states the reality and therefore has no mafhum.

So what is the view on this question? That is, what is the preponderant opinion?
The scholars mentioned three aspects other than what the author mentioned. Among them: that this is based on what is usual, that they compel them while they desire chastity; and it is known that when a qualifier is given to describe what is usual, it has no mafhum. That is, God forbids them from a matter they had fallen into, namely that they compel their slave-girls to fornication while the girls desire to abstain from it; so this is based on what is usual and has no mafhum. This is what Ibn Kathir took: that the qualifying condition describes what is usual, not the actual reality.
Some scholars said: this condition is in the sense of "idh" (since): "and do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution since they desire chastity"; that is, because they desire chastity. This view, in reality, may return to the view before it.
* * *
Student: ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth... God guides to His Light whom He wills, and God strikes the parables for mankind, and God is Knowing of all things (35). In houses which God has permitted to be raised...﴾ [al-Nur: 35-36].
Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. It has passed that God, Glorified and Exalted, commanded the granting of a slave's request for manumission, and that the scholars differed on this: some hold that it is an obligation, and some hold that it is recommended; and that the correct view is that it is an obligation. But God, Glorified and Exalted, stipulated that we know good in them. And what is the good?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Righteousness in religion and earning. Righteousness in religion includes trustworthiness, and earning is evident. It has also passed that God commanded that they be given from the wealth of God which He has given us. What is meant by it?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: That is one view. The second view?
Student: From the master's wealth?
Shaykh: From the master's wealth. How is it from the master's wealth?
Student: The second view: from his wealth.
Shaykh: Yes, that is, from the wealth of the contract: he remits for him from the contract's wealth. The early generations differed on whether it is remitted from the first installment or from the last installment; and the preferred view is from the last installment, because he may become unable, and then what the person remitted for him would return to his ownership. Now, the form of the mukatabah?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: That is, he buys himself from his master; this is the mukatabah. Why was it called mukatabah? Because usually a writing (kitabah) takes place between them: a writing that "I have contracted my slave so-and-so for such and such."
Then it has also passed that God forbade us to compel slave-girls to fornication, to prostitution, and He qualified that by His words ﴿if they desire chastity﴾. And Ahmad, this compulsion explains to us: is it for free women absolutely, or with this qualification?
Student: For free women absolutely.
Shaykh: For free women absolutely, yes. I say: how do you explain this qualification: ﴿if they desire chastity﴾?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: That is, the prohibition came concerning a specific situation, yes. That is one opinion, and the second opinion?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: (...) This condition, that is, now, the ruling is that compelling to prostitution is forbidden whether they desire chastity or not. But how do we explain this condition?
Student: The usual case...
Shaykh: Based on what is usual: that God forbids a specific situation that people used to do in the Jahiliyyah. For this reason it is not permitted, nor is enabling them to fornicate, let alone compulsion; even enabling them to fornicate is not permitted. But the matter is that the prohibition came concerning a specific matter that they used to do in the Jahiliyyah. This is according to the view that this qualification applies to what is usual, or to the state in which they were (...), but there is a second view.
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Then what is the benefit of it?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: That is, exaggeration?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: That is, exaggeration in rebuking them, blaming them and reproaching them: how these slave-girls, who are slaves, desire chastity while you want the opposite?
So this is intended as exaggeration in rebuking those masters who compel slave-girls to prostitution, given that it would be expected that if they desired prostitution, you would be wanting chastity rather than abstinence.
The third explanation followed by the author: that the form of compulsion cannot occur except when they desire chastity. We said this is incorrect, and it is not valid at all. The reason: the form of compulsion occurs outside this desire; that is, he may compel her while she does not desire chastity, but does not want this particular person he compels her with, or does not want this act to occur at this time or in this state, or the like. That is, a girl's refusal of fornication is not confined to the desire for chastity, since it may have other motives.
In any case, the author's view, may God have mercy on him, is not correct, since he claimed the form of compulsion occurs only with this desire. It is said to him: No, it occurs with this desire and with another desire besides it. Suppose she wants to defy the master, not because she wants fornication or chastity, but wants to defy the master and simply not comply with him. Is this not possible?
And in His words, ﴿seeking the transient good of the worldly life﴾, there is an indication of the lowliness of the rank of one who desires that, one who seeks worldly goods; and this is correct, and I think similar applies here.
Is the lam in His words ﴿to seek the transient good of the worldly life﴾ for causation or for consequence? The apparent sense is causation: those who compel their slave-girls to this do so only seeking the goods of the worldly life, that is, its enjoyments. The enjoyments of the world are called "ʿaraḍ" (transient goods) because they pass away. This is a real matter: the enjoyment of the world, as God, Mighty and Majestic, described it, is ﴿little﴾ [al-Nisa: 77], so it departs from you or you depart from it. Thus it is ʿaraḍ, meaning a passing matter that goes away.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 33 (part 3 of 3):

In His saying, ﴿the life of this world﴾, there is an indication that there is another life, which is the life of the Hereafter. Is the word "dunya" (this world, the nearer) derived from nearness in the figurative sense, from nearness in time, or from both? It is from both. It is from nearness in time, because it precedes the Hereafter. It is from nearness in meaning, because it is far inferior to the Hereafter. ﴿But you prefer the life of this world, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [Al-A'la 16-17]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The place of a whip of one of us in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]] "The place of a whip" means about a meter. It is better than this world and all that is in it. Which world is meant? Is it your world, the one you live in, or the whole world?

It is the whole world, from its beginning to its end. However pleasant its life may be, the place of a whip of one of us in Paradise is better than it and all that is in it. Therefore it is lowly in comparison to rank. So the "dunya" is a term of time and also of meaning, or, if you wish, of rank, and this is its meaning. So this is the "dunya." How can a person desire this passing worldly good at the expense of the Hereafter?

There is no doubt that this is a deficiency of intellect, or a deficiency of faith. A believing man would never, in any way, prefer this world over the Hereafter. For this reason, the Commander of the Faithful 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, once delivered a sermon and admonished the people, saying: "O people, if you acknowledge this, while still opposing it, then you are foolish; and if you do not acknowledge it, then you are destroyed."[[Narrated by Abu Nu'aym in Hilyat al-Awliya' (5/289) in similar wording.]]

Is this correct or not?

That is, one who opposes the Sharia of Allah is between two situations. Either he is a man who does not believe in the Hereafter, so he is destroyed; or he is a man who believes in the Hereafter but opposes it, so he is a fool who does not know how to act and does not act well. In any case, it is not befitting for a person to seek the goods of this world at the expense of the Hereafter.

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving﴾ toward them ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them) (It was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who used to compel his slave girls to earn through prostitution).

This may be so: that it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy or concerning someone else. But the author did not cite a chain of narration for it. Some exegetes mentioned it, saying it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy. However, we should know that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

But we also find a second benefit, which some scholars have pointed out: the consideration is the generality of the wording in the circumstance in which it was revealed, or for which the generality was given. It is not its generality in all circumstances. The generality of the wording is regarding its not being restricted to the individual, but in the circumstance in which it came. Do you understand the difference?

That is, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not in all circumstances, but the generality of the wording as regards not being restricted to the person. So it is not specific to the person for whom it came; rather it includes him and others in the circumstance in which it came. An example of this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Fasting while traveling is not righteousness."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1946) and Muslim (1115/92) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]] If we took this in its generality regarding persons and circumstances, a person would not fast while traveling at all, and fasting would not be righteousness. But we do not take it in the generality of circumstances. Rather, we take it in the generality of persons in a situation like the one for which it came. The hadith was narrated when the Prophet ﷺ saw a crowd and saw a man over whom shade had been cast during travel. He said: "What is this?" They said: He is fasting. He said: "Fasting while traveling is not righteousness." So when the fasting person on his journey reaches a state like this man's, we say to him: "It is not righteousness." But apart from that, we do not say that it is not righteous, because the Prophet ﷺ used to fast while traveling,[[Narrated by Ahmad (3813) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] and he did not do anything that was not righteous. He also used to approve of his companions fasting while traveling when they had not reached the state of that man.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1947) and Muslim (1118/98) from the hadith of Anas, whose wording is: "We used to travel with the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not blame the one who fasted for the one who broke the fast, nor the one who broke the fast for the one who fasted." And there are other hadiths on this topic.]] So, the consideration is the generality of the wording: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls﴾. Here, whether it was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy or someone else, the ruling is the same.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. ﴿Whoever compels them﴾: ﴿whoever﴾ here is a conditional particle, and the conditional is general. Is it not so?

The conditional particles are among the forms of generality, just as the relative pronouns are among the forms of generality. Likewise the conditional particles. That is, any person who compels his slave girl, ﴿then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

In His saying, ﴿after their compulsion﴾, there is an indication that the compulsion must be established: ﴿after their compulsion﴾, that is, after confirming the compulsion, and that there is no inclination in her heart toward what she was compelled to do. For Allah, after this compulsion, is Forgiving to whom? To the one who was compelled, not to the one who compelled. The one who compels is disobedient and is not worthy of forgiveness. For this reason we say that the conditional clause here, ﴿then indeed Allah, after their compulsion﴾, did not return to what the verb of the condition refers to. For the verb of the condition refers to what? To the one who compels, or the one who is compelled?

To the one who compels, the one who compels.

But the response of the condition (jawab al-shart, the apodosis) did not refer to the one who compels, but to the one who is compelled. This is because of the mutual dependence between the one who compels and the one who is compelled, since there is no compeller without someone compelled. Therefore, it is correct that the response of the condition does not return to what the verb of the condition refers to. It refers to something connected to it and necessarily linked to it, which is the one who is compelled. We have mentioned the response of the condition. I think it is known to you that the response of the condition refers to what?

* Students: The one who compels.
* Shaykh: No, not in this verse. The general rule is that the response of the condition refers to what the verb of the condition refers to. But this is not necessary. It may refer to what is connected to it and linked to it, as in this verse. For this reason we say: ﴿then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving﴾ toward them, not toward the compellers. That is, toward the ones compelled (the female slaves), ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them.

In His saying, ﴿Forgiving﴾, there is an indication that this sin carries no punishment.

In His saying, ﴿Merciful﴾, there is an indication that Allah will make a way out (faraj) for them, for mercy involves the attainment of what is sought and the removal of what is feared. Therefore we say that this verse indicates relief (faraj) for the one who is compelled to commit a prohibited act, and that Allah the Exalted will make a way out for him. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Know that victory comes with patience, relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease."[[Narrated by Ahmad (2803), and 'Abd ibn Humayd in al-Muntakhab (635) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas.]]

If someone says: We often hear that some people are compelled to do a prohibited matter and relief does not come to them quickly.

We say: This does not contradict the verse. For it may be that among the forms of relief is that Allah makes the matter easy for him in his heart, and that the actual release from this compulsion comes afterward through some cause beyond what we know.

* It is derived from this verse that the one compelled to do something does not bear its sin. Is this so or not?

That the one compelled to an act does not bear sin for it. This is a refutation of those among the scholars who distinguished between compulsion to speech and compulsion to action. Some scholars distinguished between compulsion to action and compulsion to speech, and said: compulsion to speech does not entail its legal consequence, but compulsion to action does entail its legal consequence. The correct view, however, is that there is no difference, and that whoever is compelled to a statement or an act, his act and his statement have no legal effect. This is shown by the saying of Allah the Exalted together with this verse: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who has been forced while his heart remains firm in faith, but those who open their breasts to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [An-Nahl 106]. In this noble verse, ﴿except one who has been forced﴾ to disbelief: is it by speech, by action, or by both?

* Student: By both.

* Shaykh: By both. The verse did not restrict it to speech. Likewise, this matter in our surah: is compulsion to prostitution an action or speech?

* Students: An action.

* Shaykh: An action. Prostitution is an action.

If someone says: What do you say about the hadith of "the companion of the fly," in which a man and his companion passed by an idol, and the people of the idol said to one of them: "Offer something." He said: "I would never offer anything to anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." So they killed him. Then they said to the second: "Offer, even if it is a fly." So he offered a fly, and they did not kill him?[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah (33583) and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (6962) from the hadith of Salman al-Farsi, as a statement of his (mawquf).]]

We say concerning this: this story has no authenticity. Furthermore, even if it were supposed to be authentic regarding the Children of Israel, our religion, praise be to Allah, has removed from it the burdens and shackles that were upon the Children of Israel, which made it necessary for it to be characterized by ease and facility. For this reason, one of the characteristics of the Messenger ﷺ is that: ﴿He permits for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [Al-A'raf 157]. Many of the burdens and shackles that were upon the earlier nations have been lifted from this Ummah.

So in any case, we now say: in this verse there is clear evidence that compulsion to an action has no legal effect, that the one compelled bears no sin, and that there is a clear refutation of those who distinguish between compulsion to speech and compulsion to action. Even if we were to grant, for argument's sake, that His saying in Surat an-Nahl, ﴿except one who has been forced﴾, is specific to compulsion to speech, and even if we granted that, though we do not grant it, this verse cannot be interpreted or divided, because the matter here is an action.

What if a woman is compelled, while fasting, to have intercourse? Her husband has intercourse with her while she is fasting, forcibly against her will, and she cannot escape. What is the ruling? Nothing is upon her. She does not break her fast, and there is no expiation (kaffarah). Likewise, if he compels her to intercourse while she is in ihram, she is in a state of ihram, and nothing is upon her either regarding the rite or regarding the ransom (fidyah). This is a general principle in Islam, an established rule in the Islamic religion.

But notice that in ﴿after their compulsion﴾, we said there is an indication of what? An indication that compulsion has been established. And that if there was any slight inclination in the one compelled, the response of the condition may fail to occur. Forgiveness and mercy may fail to follow if, after being compelled, she inclined toward the act. In this case, the condition is not fulfilled. For this reason, the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, claimed that a man cannot be compelled to commit adultery. They said: if a man is compelled to commit adultery, the legal penalty (hadd) must be established upon him. If he is compelled to have intercourse during Ramadan, he must make expiation and make up the fast. Likewise regarding the rite. What is the reason?

They said: compulsion in intercourse is not possible, because he does not act except from inclination. He does not act unless his member becomes erect, and it does not become erect except when he is inclined. Therefore compulsion is not realized. And Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿after their compulsion﴾. But in particular concerning the hadd, there is the saying: "Avert the legal penalties by doubts."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1424) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, with the wording: "Avert the legal penalties from the Muslims as much as you can."]] This, although it is open to discussion, is in any case the situation. If a man is young and is compelled to commit adultery with a beautiful young woman...

I do not know any good in it for us. We agree with you and do not force you to write. But for Allah: will it benefit you if you know that there is good in it and you claim that you do not know any good in it? That does not benefit him before Allah. The matter is left to the Lord regarding knowledge of good and its absence.

For us, the rulings of this world are based on the outward. If he says: "I do not know any good in this servant, and I know that if I let him go, he will go off, corrupt himself and corrupt others." We say: As for us, we do not compel you. Now we do not compel you, nor do we say it is obligatory upon you. But if Allah knows that you know there is good in him, then your claim is rejected and not accepted.

* * *

If he is young and is compelled to commit adultery with a beautiful young woman, yes. Perhaps, for example, she clings to him, so this may happen from him (...). The truth is that a person, with strong aversion to something, cannot (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that are clear [in their explanation]﴾ [al-Nur: 34]. It is read with a fat-ha on the ya' and with a kasra on the ya' in this surah: "buyyina" (it was made clear) [what was mentioned in it], or "bayyanat" (they made clear). Good. Is it ﴿mubayyanat﴾ (made clear) or ﴿mubayyinat﴾ (making clear), and do we say "bayyanat" or "buyyinat"?
* Student: "Buyyinat."
* Shaykh: "Buyyina fīhā mā dhukira" (what was mentioned in it was made clear), but ﴿mubayyinat﴾ means "they make [things] clear": ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that are clear﴾, or ﴿mubayyanat﴾ means "in which what was mentioned has been made clear."
The lam in His saying ﴿And certainly﴾ (wa-laqad) is the lam of the answer to an oath, and it is for emphasis, and "qad" is likewise for emphasis. ﴿And certainly﴾, and accordingly this sentence is emphasized?
* Student: Four.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Three.
* Shaykh: Three. What are they?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The implied oath preceding (...), the lam, and "qad." Here Allah, glorified and exalted, has emphasized this with these three emphatics because of its importance; for when we know that these are clear verses, this will necessarily require us to attend to these verses.
As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We have sent down to you verses﴾: what is meant by the "verses" here, the legislative (sharʿi) or the cosmic (kawni)?
* Students: Cosmic.
* Shaykh: No, the apparent meaning is that they are the legislative ones, because the sense of "sending down" (inzal) becomes clearer with them than with the cosmic ones. So the apparent meaning is that they are the legislative ones, which is the revelation that was sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ.
And in His saying ﴿We sent down﴾ [is the meaning of] legislative revelation, because it truly descends from the high to the low; for from where does it descend? From Allah upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ. So it is a true descent.
Some of them have distorted this, saying that the intended meaning of "sending down" is the sending down of revelation. He said: "﴿We sent down﴾ means: We revealed." And he said: "Descent occurs only from above, and occurs only in a physical body; it is said: a man descended from the roof to the ground, and the Qur'an is not like that."
Without doubt, what does the one who says this statement deny? The loftiness of Allah. For this reason, the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah) are among those who argued for the loftiness of Allah by the fact that Allah sent down the Qur'an upon the Prophet, and they said: "Sending down necessarily entails that the one who sends down is high."
But [the other group] interprets it as revelation on the argument that the thing that descends is a body, and the Qur'an does not have a body; rather it is a speech that descends. This is undoubtedly a distortion of the words of Allah, mighty and majestic.
We say: the Qur'an descends as Allah said. The word (yanzil, "descends") is not the same as (yūḥā or yūḥā, "is revealed"), but has another, specific meaning. Furthermore, what prevents descent from applying to matters that are non-physical? For example, when descent is attributed to sensory things (...) in bodies, and not to non-physical matters, it has another meaning. Does not Allah say: ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 4]? Is tranquility a stone thrown into the heart, or a non-physical matter? A non-physical matter. ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾. Therefore, descent occurs in non-physical matters.
Then, what prevents the Qur'an from also having a body, though we do not know this body? For Allah says to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. It has been established that "the revelation descended upon him one day while his head was on the thigh of Hudhayfah, until it almost crushed it,"[[Reported by al-Bukhari (2832) from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit; we did not find it from Hudhayfah.]] and that "the revelation descended upon him while he was on his riding camel, so it knelt with him."[[Ahmad reported in al-Musnad (27575) from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid with the wording: "When the whole of al-Ma'idah was sent down upon him, it nearly broke the camel's shoulder from its weight."]] So there is no objection to its being a body, but not like the known bodies; Allah knows best. Allah, glorified and exalted, makes non-physical matters into sensory matters. Do you not see that death on the Day of Resurrection is depicted as what? As a ram, which the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise see and which is slaughtered before them. Likewise, deeds are placed on the scales on the Day of Resurrection, and deeds are originally what? From the meanings; they are not bodies. Allah, glorified and exalted, is capable of all things, and His power, exalted is He, is beyond the grasp of our minds.
In any case, this verse contains clear evidence that Allah sent down the Qur'an from His presence, and that the descent is not merely in the sense of revelation, but a specific meaning more particular than revelation.
As for His saying, ﴿verses﴾, He made it plural: the reality of the matter is that it is so, and the Qur'an is not a single ruling nor a single report; it contains many reports and many rulings, so they are verses. Yes.
Now, ﴿verses﴾ means what? Signs.
Signs of what? Of the greatness of the One who sent them down and of the truthfulness of the one who brought them, peace and blessings be upon him. The way this is so, the manner in which they are verses: when you reflect on the rulings that these verses brought, you find them completely in accord with benefit, benefit in what is commanded and the averting of harm in what is forbidden. You also find that their reports are of the utmost benefit and profit. Yes. And you find that they have a profound effect, among its effects being that those nations who had been opposed to Islam entered the religion of Allah in multitudes merely because they heard the Qur'an and saw its etiquette and morals. Furthermore, this effect upon one who listens attentively, or who has a heart, is an effect for which there is in reality no parallel, when the mind is clear and a person turns his heart fully to the Qur'an, whoever he may be; even if he is not a Muslim, he must be affected. Jubayr ibn Mut'im was among the captives of Badr (...) in Medina, "and he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting in the Maghrib prayer Surat al-Tur, and when he reached ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they are not certain﴾ [al-Tur: 35-36], he said, may Allah be pleased with him: 'My heart nearly flew.' Yes, and from that time Allah cast faith into his heart, and then he embraced Islam afterward."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4854) and Muslim (463/174) from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im.]] This is evidence that the Qur'an consists of great signs that indicate the greatness of the One who sent it down, and what else? And of the truthfulness of the one who brought it. This is due to what it contains of just rulings that dazzle the intellects, which no human can produce the like of, and of truthful and beneficial reports, and reports that delight the soul and bring it comfort, and that are beneficial to the heart as well: ﴿There is certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111].
As for His saying, ﴿clear [in their explanation]﴾, i.e., they make clear the truth from falsehood, distinguish between them, and differentiate between them. Furthermore, they also make the rulings clear by themselves, but some of them need explanation from elsewhere, and some are clear in themselves. This is an indication that in the Shariah, in actual reality, there is no matter that is problematic; rather, the difficulty lies in what? In understanding. For the difficulty that arises in legal questions is not due to deficiency in the texts, but to deficiency in understanding or deficiency in knowledge. A person may have deficient knowledge, not encompassing all the texts, or deficient understanding, and from this difficulty arises. But with complete knowledge and complete understanding, it is impossible for a difficulty to exist in the Shariah.
For this reason, you sometimes find (let me speak about myself): sometimes a question comes before me and its ruling is clear to me like the sun; then at another time the same question comes and there is a difficulty in it. Why? Because clarity of mind and the states of a person have a profound effect on the understanding of the texts, a profound effect.
For this reason I believe that the student of knowledge should, regarding questions that come to him, the rare questions he fears he will forget, that he must write them down. He should not rely on himself, saying: "This verse is clear, there is no need for me to write it down." For a day may come when what Allah granted you to understand yesterday is no longer present now, either because the cause has been lost or an obstacle has appeared. A person is human, and his states change: a child may anger him in his house, so he goes out to people angry and cannot bear even a word from anyone; or he may be pleased in his house and go out to people (...). So a person is human, in all his states he fluctuates and changes.
In any case, I return to this: the Qur'an, praise be to Allah, is clear, and what else? And made clear as well. But the obscurity that enters a person comes only from himself, not from the evidences, and that is due to one of two matters. What are they?
Deficiency in knowledge, or deficiency in understanding. Because of one of these two matters, obscurity arises in the legal rulings. As for the verses that Allah sent down, they are clear and make clear; there is no difficulty in them. May Allah have mercy on him, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah mentioned a statement in al-Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah, saying: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an, seeking guidance from it, the path of truth will become clear to him."
This is in reality a statement that should be written in gold, as people say (...). But my intention is that this statement (...): "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an, seeking guidance from it," two things are necessary, "the path of truth will become clear to him."
﴿Verses that are clear﴾, ﴿And certainly We have sent down to you verses that are clear﴾, ﴿mubayyanat﴾ and ﴿mubayyinat﴾ are two Sab'i (canonical seven) readings.
(﴿And an example﴾: a wondrous report, and it is the report of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, ﴿from those who passed away before you﴾, i.e., of the kind of their examples, meaning their wondrous reports, like the report of Yusuf and Maryam.) This means that Allah has also sent down ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the intended meaning of "example" (mathal) here is more general than the actual event; meaning examples of those who passed away, and this is not specific to the report of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, nor Maryam, nor Yusuf; rather it is more general than that. However, the author restricted it, as is his habit, may Allah have mercy on him, restricting general verses to a meaning according to context. This is in reality a deficiency. It is true that context may restrict the absolute and may specify the general, but only with evidence. If there is no evidence that this is specific, then generality is preferable.
So His saying ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾ in reality may be more general than what the author mentioned of the Qur'anic surahs.
Thus, legal rulings are expressed by the clear verses, and true reports containing lessons are expressed by His saying ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾. So Allah, glorified and exalted, has struck for us examples of those who passed away before us, not concerning chastity and protection alone, nor concerning religion, faith, and disbelief alone. Yes. ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them﴾, and after it ﴿and for the disbelievers are the like of them﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned the story of Lut, He said: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 83]. The intelligent person analogizes, for Allah's way is one, and Allah, mighty and majestic, is the same toward mankind except in piety. So if Allah destroyed a nation of the earlier nations for opposing Him, is it impossible that He would destroy this nation as well?
Yes, it is not impossible, and what is impossible is (...) the righteous, namely the general destruction; this does not save the righteous. Indeed, some scholars said: it did not occur after the destruction of Pharaoh, for they argued with His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43]. They said: after the Torah was sent down to Moses, peace be upon him, none of the earlier nations remained after (...). This is the reality, whether or not the verse indicates it; this is simply the reality.
And His saying: ﴿an example from those who passed away before you﴾ is like the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: he was accused of what he was accused of, and Allah saved him, or not (...), and Allah, mighty and majestic, saved him. Who accused him of immorality? The wife of the minister. Strangely, it was the wife of the minister who solicited him and locked the doors and prepared everything. But he, peace be upon him: ﴿She desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf: 24]. After he desired, with all the means available, the absence of obstacles, and the existence of the demand and the desire, he then restrained himself. This is the highest form of chastity. This is contrary to those who go against the word "hamma" (desired). ﴿She desired him, and he desired her﴾. Strangely, some say: "﴿She desired him﴾ for fornication, and ﴿he desired her﴾ to strike her." This is contradictory. Rather, it is said: the perfection of chastity is to occur together with the presence of demand: ﴿he desired her﴾. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said about those whom Allah will shade under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: "A man whom a woman of rank and beauty invited, and he said: 'Indeed I fear Allah.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1423) and Muslim (1031/91) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] There is no barrier except this, otherwise no one else would be present, desire is abundant, and resolve is present. What is the resolve? The desire. But what prevented him was the fear of Allah, mighty and majestic. He, peace be upon him, after she desired him and he desired her, now found the demand and the cause, and the obstacle was removed; then he saw the proof of his Lord, Allah granted him success, or he perceived and turned away. Finally it became clear who the doer was: the wife of the minister. That became public. Even Yusuf, peace be upon him, from the strength of his patience and his wisdom, when he was summoned to leave prison ﴿He said: "Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands"﴾ [Yusuf: 50]; he did not leave until his innocence was manifest. This is considered great patience; otherwise one might be excused, a person imprisoned who was told: "Come out" (...) before he said: "Come out." Yes, but he, peace be upon him, refused until he would be completely innocent and (...) this is what happened.
As for Maryam, may Allah be pleased with her, it is the same thing. The Jews accused her; they did not say "you are an adulteress," no; they insinuated, saying: ﴿O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman﴾ [Maryam: 28]. That is, from where (...) the same response: your father was not a man of evil and your mother was not unchaste; so from where did this fornication come to you? This is the meaning of their words.
For this reason the scholars differed: is one punished for slander (qadhf) if he insinuates, or is he not punished?
The correct view is that if the insinuation is clear, he is punished, and indeed it is greater, as some scholars say: insinuation of fornication is greater than explicit accusation, because it includes slander and blame, like if (...) and said to you: "Praise be to Allah, I am (...) I commit fornication.."
* * *
Whoever compels his slave-girl into prostitution, Allah, glorified and exalted, will forgive her and have mercy on her, if the compulsion is established. In this is evidence that the one compelled has no legal consequence for his action, just as he has no legal consequence for his speech, and that whoever distinguishes between verbal compulsion and physical compulsion has no basis for this distinction; and we have explained the evidences that they are general in this.
It has also already been explained that Allah, glorified and exalted, emphasized that He sent down ﴿clear verses﴾ or ﴿made clear﴾, making clear what they indicate and manifesting it, whether these verses are verses of rulings or verses of reports. And it was already mentioned that they are signs of what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, of what?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: Of the greatness of the One who sent them down and the truthfulness of the one who brought them, namely Muhammad ﷺ.
And in them also, it was already mentioned, is the striking of examples for this nation with what has already occurred to the earlier nations, and that in striking examples there is great benefit, namely that a person takes lessons from them regarding his own state. This is because Allah, glorified and exalted, has no kinship with anyone, that the noblest of people before Allah is the most pious, and that Allah's way is one with regard to the first and the last, except that the general destruction is excepted from this; the general destruction has been lifted from this nation, but otherwise the basic punishment applies to this nation as to others.
It was also already mentioned that the Noble Qur'an is an admonition, but only the God-fearing benefit from it, those who take a shield against the punishment of Allah by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

Then the author said: (﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ — referring to His words: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah﴾ [An-Nur: 2], ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious lie"?﴾ [An-Nur: 12], and so on to the end, ﴿And why, when you heard it, did you not say﴾ [An-Nur: 16], and so on to the end, ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it﴾ [An-Nur: 17], and so on to the end. He restricted it to the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from it.)

The author -may Allah have mercy on him- mentioned these verses in keeping with his habit, which is restricting the general to its context. As you have seen, his habit was to restrict generality by context. The correct view, however, is that generality is not restricted by context, because it includes what the context contains and other things. Accordingly, it is an admonition for the God-fearing in these verses he enumerated and in others as well.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said: (﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35], i.e., the one who gives light to them with the sun and the moon; ﴿the likeness of His light﴾, i.e., His description in the heart of the believer) and so on to the end.

This verse contains several matters:

First: He said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. Is this sentence to be taken according to its apparent and literal meaning, or does it need interpretation (ta'wil)?

The scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah and others differed over it, as is customary in the rest of the verses about the divine attributes. The people of ta'wil (interpretation) held that the verse has an interpretation, and they made the interpretation either that ﴿Light﴾ means "one who gives light (munawwir)", as the author (al-Mu'allif) went, or that ﴿Light﴾ means "possessor of light (dhu al-nur)", as you say: "a just man" (rajul 'adl), meaning "possessor of justice". So the meaning of ﴿the Light of the heavens﴾ is: the possessor of the light of the heavens and the earth, i.e., the one who creates the light in them. On this, the meaning returns to the first meaning, but the disagreement is in the estimation (taqdir). This is the position of the people of tahrif (distortion), who are called the people of ta'wil; and the more correct name for them is "the people of tahrif", because ta'wil in reality is of two kinds: sound and unsound. What is more fitting for unsound ta'wil is to be called tahrif, because it is turning a word away from its meaning without evidence, and this is tahrif in truth.

As for Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, they said: the verse is according to its reality and its apparent meaning, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, is the Light of the heavens and the earth; but light is of two kinds: a light which is the very essence of the Creator, may He be exalted, and His attributes, signs and rulings, and this is not created; and another light, sensory, created, separate and distinct from Allah. So the light we see in the sun, the moon, the stars and the lamps: which of the two kinds is this? It is the sensory created light. Then created light is also sensory and immaterial: the sensory is what we have just given as an example, and the immaterial is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿the likeness of His light is like a niche﴾ [al-Nur: 35], and so on.

So Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah say: Allah, exalted is He, is the Light of the heavens and the earth; He is light in His essence, and likewise His attributes, and likewise His signs, which Allah called light: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa: 174]. So He, glorified and exalted, is Light. But the people of tahrif, when they thought that light is the substance of illumination, or light itself, they said: this is an accident that passes away, and Allah is far above accidents; or they said: this is a body, meaning it is receptive to illumination, and Allah is exalted above being a body, according to their terminology and their rules.

But we say: what obliges us to deviate from the apparent meaning of the verse and not say "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth"? And the Prophet ﷺ said: «I seek refuge in the light of Your face, by which the darknesses are illuminated»[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (181) and in al-Du'a (1036), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far.]], so he affirmed light for His face.

Rather, the sound path is to say: the light of Allah, glorified and exalted, is not created; it is not like the light of the moon, which Allah placed in them: ﴿and made the moon in them a light﴾ [Nuh: 16]; nor like the light of a lamp, nor like the light that is in the heart of the believer from knowledge, guidance and faith. Rather, light is truly an attribute of Allah, glorified and exalted: He is Light, His attributes are light, and likewise His signs are light, which Allah called light.

The sound division is to say: light is divided into two kinds: uncreated light and created light. The uncreated is the light of Allah, mighty and majestic: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth, He is light, His speech is light, and His attributes are also light; but not like the light that we imagine or picture to ourselves. For the Prophet ﷺ said: «His veil is light; were He to lift it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever His sight reaches of His creation»[[Narrated by Muslim (179 / 293), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]], meaning: the glories of His face would burn everything, because His sight reaches everything.

As for created light, it is divided into two kinds: what are they? Immaterial and sensory. The sensory is what is seen in these bodies, like the light of the sun, the moon, the stars, the lamps and what is similar to them. The immaterial is what is in the heart of the believer of knowledge and faith.

By this distinction the difficulty disappears, and we keep the verse on its apparent meaning fitting for Allah, mighty and majestic, and we say: Allah is light, His attributes are light, and His speech is light too; this is because Allah described Himself with this, so what obliges us to deviate from it? Rather, what would permit it?

So the Light of the heavens and the earth means: He Himself is light in them.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The speech of Allah is light because of the guidance that is achieved by it, since the origin of light is that by which one is guided.
............................. ∗∗∗ as if it were a banner atop its head, a fire
So we say: Allah, exalted is He, is the Light of the heavens and the earth, i.e., light within them; but this light, with which Allah described Himself and which He made one of His attributes and names, does it resemble the light of created things?
What is the answer? No, like the rest of the attributes.
So the author's statement "(i.e., the one who gives light to them)" is not correct; this is tahrif, and it is not correct. Rather its meaning is: light within the heavens and the earth, light in His essence, His attributes and His signs, blessed and exalted is He.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the matter of excuse is something else. We refute the statement and excuse the speaker. We tell the man when he errs: you have erred; but nevertheless (...) if we know good intention from him, rather we love him too. We now know distinguished, eminent scholars who followed this path, the path of tahrif in the names and attributes of Allah, and nevertheless we call Allah to witness our love for them, because we know they only followed it through ijtihad and good intention. Yes, because of their sincere standing in Islam, their sincere counsel to Islam, and their writings in Islam, such as al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, and many others. No one hates them or detests them or thinks ill of them. But there is no harm in saying, if they err: they erred. We say: their statement is an error; we say: their statement is false; but it does not follow from that that we blame this person when we know his good intention and that this is what his ijtihad led him to.
This is the method of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, and therefore you do not find among them enmity or hatred; when their statements differ, each one knows that his companion is excused. But the people of desires, may Allah protect us, are those who do not excuse anyone who opposes them, even if they themselves are upon falsehood; therefore you find them harboring enmity and hatred towards whoever opposes them.
﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, said: (﴿the likeness of His light is like a niche﴾, i.e., His description in the heart of the believer). This, in reality, is "the likeness of His light", i.e., the likeness of the light of Allah is like a niche. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (in the heart of the believer, ﴿like a niche﴾) and so on. Why do we not take ﴿the likeness of His light﴾, which is the light of His essence and attribute? What obliged us to interpret?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is it: because Allah has no likeness; we cannot liken His light, which is His attribute, to anything of His creation, for Allah said: ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So interpretation is necessary.
In reality, if someone says: "Do you not deny interpretation?" we say: we do not deny interpretation absolutely, but we deny the interpretation for which there is no evidence. As for what reason requires, that is a known matter; even now, by reason, can your intellect accept that the light of Allah is of this size, like a niche in which there is a lamp? No, reason itself prevents this.
If reason prevents this, then interpretation is necessary. Allah, mighty and majestic, says about the wind of 'Ad: ﴿It destroys everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25]; by reason, they did not destroy the heavens, nor did they destroy the earth, but they destroyed everything they benefited from, as is evident from His saying: ﴿so that none could be seen except their dwellings﴾.
In any case (...) we say: ﴿the likeness of His light﴾, i.e., the likeness of His light which He places in the heart of the believer.
Some say: ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ is the light by which He guides, and they see this as bringing the immaterial close to the sensory, saying for example: the Qur'an is light, like this light, a niche and so on. But the safer position is that of the author, that by light here is meant the light which Allah places in the heart of the believer.
﴿the likeness of His light is like a niche in which is a lamp﴾: what is the niche? The recess that people call the rawzana; this is the mishkat.
﴿in it is a lamp﴾: a lantern (siraj). (﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾: it is the lantern (qindil); and the lamp is the lantern (siraj), i.e., the burning wick; and the niche is the non-penetrating recess, i.e., the tube in the lantern) and so on.
The niche, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, is "the non-penetrating recess"; people call it the rawzana. If there is a lamp in it and a glass, and the description of this glass will also come, its light will be stronger, because the light is reflected and not dispersed; and this, in reality, is the origin of the mechanism called the "cobs" (reflector), which they call cobs; what reflects the light is taken from the Qur'an, because this niche is in reality the theory of the cobs.
He says: (﴿the glass as if it were﴾ and the light in it ﴿a brilliant star (durriy)﴾, i.e., luminous, with the dal vowelled with kasra and damma, from al-dar' meaning repelling, because it repels darkness.)
* Student: (because it repels it).
* Shaykh: I have (li-dar'ihi) and it is better, because it explains: ﴿durriy﴾.
(with the dal vowelled with kasra and damma, from al-dar' meaning repelling, because it repels darkness; and with damma and shadda on the ya, it is attributed to al-durr, the pearl.)
﴿durriy﴾: this last reading, with damma and shadda on the ya, is attributed to al-durr, i.e., the pearl: ﴿as if it were a star durriy﴾. The second, with kasra on the dal and damma: ﴿dir'iy﴾, he did not mention the hamza in reality; otherwise the hamza must be mentioned. See the continuation in the margin; did you bring it with you?
* Student: Yes, with the hamza.
* Shaykh: There must be a hamza, since it is from al-dar'.
* Student: There is a hamza in the original.
* Shaykh: It is in the original; I do not have a hamza in the original.
﴿dirri'> this is one, and ﴿durri'> this is the second, i.e., fi'
Ah, the readings are three:
﴿durriyyun﴾ without hamza, attributed to al-durr, which is the pearl, for its purity.
And ﴿dirri'> on the pattern of sikkin, intensive from al-dar', meaning: repelling.
Or ﴿durri'> also: from al-dar', meaning: repelling.
And the "brilliant star" means: its meaning is greatly luminous, and its blazing, i.e., its blazing, and its light is great; because describing it with this repelling indicates the strength of its light and its penetration, and the more brilliant it is, the more it repels. For this reason the matter came in the pattern of intensive form, because fi'-ayyil and fu'-ayyil are both intensive forms; since the active participle in this matter would be "dari'," and when it is turned away from the active participle to another form, this becomes an intensive form.
Durri, from where? It derives from al-dar', daraa yadra'u, so he is dari', this is the active participle; but the matter came on the pattern of fi'ayyil and fu'ayyil, why? For intensity; it came for intensity, because every derived form with the meaning of an active participle, when turned from it, indicates one of two things: either intensity or the assimilated quality.
So here intensity, meaning because of the strength of its blazing and the strength of its brightness, it is dir'iyyan, i.e., it repels darkness because of the strength of its penetration; and of course it cannot repel darkness with the strength of its penetration unless it is of great blazing and great light; for if you brought, for example, a lantern or a small bulb, does it repel darkness? It repels only a slight repulsion around it; but if you brought a large and great bulb, it repels darkness strongly, and therefore what is around it is very bright, and likewise wider and farther.
The second reading is ﴿durriy﴾: to what is it attributed? To al-durr, which is the pearl, for its purity, meaning: there is no haze between us and this star that is not very clear like the pearl.
These two readings, I think we have previously noted that the two readings have among their benefits: breadth of meaning. The difference between the two readings has a benefit, a great benefit:
Among them, for example, explanation; like His saying: ﴿so verify﴾ ﴿so clarify﴾.
And also: broadening of meaning; for example ﴿dur'iy﴾ or ﴿dir'iy﴾ and ﴿durriy﴾: what broadens the meaning? That it is itself pure according to durriy, and strong in illumination according to dir'iy.
So this is one of the benefits of the variant readings: that in each reading a meaning appears different from that which appears in the other reading, so it becomes broader and more comprehensive.
* Student: Sab'iyya.
* Shaykh: Apparently it is not sab'iyya (canonical); the author did not mention it. ("Qari'a") is not sab'iyya.
He said: (﴿tawaqqada﴾ the lamp, in the past tense, and in another reading the present tense of awqada, passive, with the yā' underneath: yūqadu (i.e., the glass)).
So there are three readings here: ﴿as if it were a star durriy tawaqqada﴾, this is taken as a past verb (...).
He drew the fuel for a blessed tree, and so on.
Also there: ﴿yūqadu﴾, i.e., fuel is placed in it.
Also there: ﴿tūqadu﴾.
With tawaqqada and with yūqadu, the pronoun refers to what? To the star, because it is masculine: a star durriy tawaqqada, a star durriy yūqadu; but on the reading ﴿tūqadu﴾: as if it were a star durriy that is lit.
The author says on this reading: (i.e., the glass), the pronoun refers to the glass, not the star; and here one does not say, for example, that the pronoun refers to the nearest antecedent; because the rule is: the pronoun refers to the nearest antecedent unless there is a verbal or semantic obstacle.
Here there is a verbal obstacle. What is the verbal obstacle? The return of the pronoun, because (tūqadu) the pronoun refers to a feminine noun, and the star is masculine. This is a verbal obstacle preventing the pronoun from referring to the last masculine noun.
And there may be a semantic obstacle, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the creed of your father Abraham﴾; and what is before this verse: ﴿and strive for Allah with the striving due to Him; He chose you and did not place upon you any hardship in religion, the creed of your father Abraham; He named you the Muslims before and in this...﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. To whom does the pronoun refer?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it refers to Allah: ﴿the creed of your father Abraham; He﴾, i.e., Allah, ﴿named you the Muslims before﴾. Of course Abraham, peace be upon him, did not name us in this; because if it were supposed that it is valid that He named you before, it might be valid that it refers to Abraham; but ﴿and in this﴾ is not valid.
Therefore we say: this is a semantic obstacle, because it is suitable to refer to Allah and suitable to refer to Abraham, peace be upon him, but the meaning prevents it.
In any case, let us return to our reading. We say: ﴿tawaqqada﴾ and ﴿yūqadu﴾, both pronouns refer to what? To the star. As for ﴿tūqadu﴾, the pronoun refers to the glass in which is the lamp, as if it were a star durriy.
﴿from a blessed tree﴾
(﴿from﴾ olive oil, ﴿a blessed tree, an olive, neither of the east nor of the west﴾, but between them, so that neither harmful heat nor harmful cold can reach it).
* Student: The lamp blazed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein glorify Him in the mornings and the evenings﴾, and so on to the end of the verse.

(﴿In houses﴾ is connected to ﴿glorify﴾ which comes next.) What is meant by "connected" (mutaʿallaq)? A verb transitively takes its object directly, and sometimes it takes its object through a preposition. When it takes its object through a preposition, it is said that this [prepositional phrase] is connected to it. In reality, the prepositional phrase is connected, and likewise the adverbial phrase is in reality an object, but the verb does not reach it directly. So ﴿glorify﴾ is connected to his saying ﴿in houses﴾, meaning that the governing element of the prepositional phrase is his saying ﴿glorify﴾.

(﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ means glorified, ﴿and in which His name is mentioned﴾ meaning His oneness.) And so on to the end.

﴿Permitted﴾ (idhn) here means the legislative permission. The meaning of ﴿permitted﴾ is that He legislated that they be glorified. For this reason ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that mosques be built in the neighbourhoods, that is, in the quarters, and that they be perfumed."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (455), al-Tirmidhi (594), and Ibn Majah (758) from the hadith of ʿAʾisha.]]

This is evidence that the permission here means what? The Sharia (legislative ruling). We have already established that permission is divided into two types: universal (kawni) permission and legislative (shariʿ) permission.

An example of universal permission is: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. An example of legislative permission is: ﴿Have they legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21]. This cannot be a universal, decreed permission. Why? ﴿That which Allah has not permitted﴾ cannot be a universal decreed permission, because the universal decreed permission has not been negated: they did legislate, and they only legislated by Allah's permission, universally and by decree. So ﴿that which Allah has not permitted﴾ means legislatively, without doubt.

In any case, now the permission of Allah is divided into two types: universal and legislative. The universal is like His saying the Exalted. 

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And the legislative is ﴿Have they legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾.

Permission may also come in the sense of listening, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Allah has never listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet with a beautiful voice who chants the Quran."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5024) and Muslim (792/232) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] That is, Allah never listened to anything as He listens to this Prophet who chants the Quran aloud.

So ﴿Allah has permitted﴾ in the verse before us, ﴿Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, is which of the two permissions? The legislative.

Must it be the legislative?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And why?
* Student: ﴿In houses﴾.
* Shaykh: Good. ﴿In houses﴾ — your answer is correct, but the reasoning is: if it were permitted by decree, then the mosques would certainly be glorified and certainly raised, because the universal or decreed permission (both meaning the same) necessarily requires that what is permitted occurs. Everything related to universal matters must occur. So if the meaning of permission here were universal permission, raising the mosques would be what? A certainty, even though we find that mosques are sometimes not raised or glorified, but rather are prevented: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of Allah's name in His mosques?﴾ [al-Baqarah 114].

Now, ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted﴾, that is, legislated, ﴿to be raised﴾, meaning glorified. In reality, raising them is more general than glorifying them: they are raised by glorifying and by other means, but it is true that the most evident form of raising is glorifying.

﴿And in which His name is mentioned﴾, that is, the name of Allah. The meaning is that Allah is mentioned by His names, because when the name is mentioned, the one named is mentioned.

In His saying ﴿in which His name is mentioned﴾, by what is it mentioned?
* Student: By prayer.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. By recitation and glorification, as will also come. The point is that His name is mentioned with praise and glorification, and this includes prayer and other than prayer.

Then He said ﴿glorify Him﴾. This is declaring Him free of imperfection. So in the verse there is an indication of two matters: affirmation of perfection in His saying ﴿His name is mentioned﴾, and negation of deficiency in His saying ﴿glorify Him therein in the mornings﴾, and so on to the end.

His Exalted saying: (﴿yusabbaḥu﴾ with a fatha or kasra on the bāʾ, meaning: it is prayed.)

﴿Yusabbiḥu﴾ has two canonical readings: with fatha and with kasra. Their derivations will come, God willing, in their proper place.

As for His saying: (meaning: it is prayed). This needs consideration. If by this one intends to restrict glorification to prayer, then it is problematic. If one intends it as an example, then it is correct, for His saying ﴿glorify Him therein﴾ is more general than people praying; rather, they glorify Allah through prayer and other things by which Allah the Exalted is declared free of imperfection.

His saying: ﴿glorify Him therein in the mornings﴾.

(Prays ﴿to Him﴾, meaning to Allah ﴿therein in the mornings﴾, a verbal noun meaning the mornings, that is, the early hours; ﴿and the evenings﴾, the afternoons after the decline of the sun.)

His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. (al-Ghuduw) — the author says it is a plural, the verbal noun of ghadā yaghdū ghadwan, but it has the sense of a plural, meaning the mornings. The author resorted to making al-ghuduw mean "the mornings" for the sake of correspondence. What is the correspondence? ﴿and the evenings﴾: the correspondence with ﴿and the evenings﴾, because al-āṣāl is the plural of aṣīl, which is the end of the day.

His saying: they are the evenings, plural of ʿashī also, what is after the decline of the sun. In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: "He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in one of the two evening prayers"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (482) and Muslim (573/97) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. The narrator, from Abu Hurayrah, says it.

I say: al-ghuduw is a verbal noun with the sense of a plural, meaning the mornings. ﴿Al-āṣāl﴾ is the plural of aṣīl, meaning the evenings, that is, the end of the day.

Now, where are the prayers if we say ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ means "prays"? What would be in the mornings? The Fajr prayer. The evenings: Dhuhr and ʿAsr. What remains? Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, which are also prayed in mosques. For this reason we hold that the correct view is that glorification is more general than the prayers. Furthermore, it is possible that by al-ghuduw and al-āṣāl is meant the whole time, as in the Exalted saying about the people of Paradise: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 62].
