When it takes its object through a preposition, it is said that this [prepositional phrase] is connected to it. In reality, the prepositional phrase is connected, and likewise the adverbial phrase is in reality an object, but the verb does not reach it directly. So ﴿glorify﴾ is connected to his saying ﴿in houses﴾, meaning that the governing element of the prepositional phrase is his saying ﴿glorify﴾.

(﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ means glorified, ﴿and in which His name is mentioned﴾ meaning His oneness.) And so on to the end.

﴿Permitted﴾ (idhn) here means the legislative permission. The meaning of ﴿permitted﴾ is that He legislated that they be glorified. For this reason ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that mosques be built in the neighbourhoods, that is, in the quarters, and that they be perfumed."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (455), al-Tirmidhi (594), and Ibn Majah (758) from the hadith of ʿAʾisha.]]

This is evidence that the permission here means what? The Sharia (legislative ruling). We have already established that permission is divided into two types: universal (kawni) permission and legislative (shariʿ) permission.

An example of universal permission is: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. An example of legislative permission is: ﴿Have they legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21]. This cannot be a universal, decreed permission. Why? ﴿That which Allah has not permitted﴾ cannot be a universal decreed permission, because the universal decreed permission has not been negated: they did legislate, and they only legislated by Allah's permission, universally and by decree. So ﴿that which Allah has not permitted﴾ means legislatively, without doubt.

In any case, now the permission of Allah is divided into two types: universal and legislative. The universal is like His saying the Exalted. 

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And the legislative is ﴿Have they legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾.

Permission may also come in the sense of listening, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Allah has never listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet with a beautiful voice who chants the Quran."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5024) and Muslim (792/232) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] That is, Allah never listened to anything as He listens to this Prophet who chants the Quran aloud.

So ﴿Allah has permitted﴾ in the verse before us, ﴿Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, is which of the two permissions? The legislative.

Must it be the legislative?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And why?
* Student: ﴿In houses﴾.
* Shaykh: Good. ﴿In houses﴾ — your answer is correct, but the reasoning is: if it were permitted by decree, then the mosques would certainly be glorified and certainly raised, because the universal or decreed permission (both meaning the same) necessarily requires that what is permitted occurs. Everything related to universal matters must occur. So if the meaning of permission here were universal permission, raising the mosques would be what? A certainty, even though we find that mosques are sometimes not raised or glorified, but rather are prevented: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of Allah's name in His mosques?﴾ [al-Baqarah 114].

Now, ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted﴾, that is, legislated, ﴿to be raised﴾, meaning glorified. In reality, raising them is more general than glorifying them: they are raised by glorifying and by other means, but it is true that the most evident form of raising is glorifying.

﴿And in which His name is mentioned﴾, that is, the name of Allah. The meaning is that Allah is mentioned by His names, because when the name is mentioned, the one named is mentioned.

In His saying ﴿in which His name is mentioned﴾, by what is it mentioned?
* Student: By prayer.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. By recitation and glorification, as will also come. The point is that His name is mentioned with praise and glorification, and this includes prayer and other than prayer.

Then He said ﴿glorify Him﴾. This is declaring Him free of imperfection. So in the verse there is an indication of two matters: affirmation of perfection in His saying ﴿His name is mentioned﴾, and negation of deficiency in His saying ﴿glorify Him therein in the mornings﴾, and so on to the end.

His Exalted saying: (﴿yusabbaḥu﴾ with a fatha or kasra on the bāʾ, meaning: it is prayed.)

﴿Yusabbiḥu﴾ has two canonical readings: with fatha and with kasra. Their derivations will come, God willing, in their proper place.

As for His saying: (meaning: it is prayed). This needs consideration. If by this one intends to restrict glorification to prayer, then it is problematic. If one intends it as an example, then it is correct, for His saying ﴿glorify Him therein﴾ is more general than people praying; rather, they glorify Allah through prayer and other things by which Allah the Exalted is declared free of imperfection.

His saying: ﴿glorify Him therein in the mornings﴾.

(Prays ﴿to Him﴾, meaning to Allah ﴿therein in the mornings﴾, a verbal noun meaning the mornings, that is, the early hours; ﴿and the evenings﴾, the afternoons after the decline of the sun.)

His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. (al-Ghuduw) — the author says it is a plural, the verbal noun of ghadā yaghdū ghadwan, but it has the sense of a plural, meaning the mornings. The author resorted to making al-ghuduw mean "the mornings" for the sake of correspondence. What is the correspondence? ﴿and the evenings﴾: the correspondence with ﴿and the evenings﴾, because al-āṣāl is the plural of aṣīl, which is the end of the day.

His saying: they are the evenings, plural of ʿashī also, what is after the decline of the sun. In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: "He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in one of the two evening prayers"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (482) and Muslim (573/97) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. The narrator, from Abu Hurayrah, says it.

I say: al-ghuduw is a verbal noun with the sense of a plural, meaning the mornings. ﴿Al-āṣāl﴾ is the plural of aṣīl, meaning the evenings, that is, the end of the day.

Now, where are the prayers if we say ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ means "prays"? What would be in the mornings? The Fajr prayer. The evenings: Dhuhr and ʿAsr. What remains? Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, which are also prayed in mosques. For this reason we hold that the correct view is that glorification is more general than the prayers. Furthermore, it is possible that by al-ghuduw and al-āṣāl is meant the whole time, as in the Exalted saying about the people of Paradise: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 62]. Is the provision of the people of Paradise continuous, or only in the morning and at the end of the day? It is continuous, but it is expressed this way and the meaning is continuity. So either you take al-ghuduw and al-āṣāl to mean continuity, that is, they glorify constantly, or to mean the beginning and end of the day, and this would point to the glorifications recited at the beginning and end of the day, among them the Fajr prayer and the ʿAsr prayer, for these two prayers are the best of prayers, as in the authentic hadith: "Whoever prays the two cool prayers enters Paradise"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (574) and Muslim (635/215) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari.]], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon, without being harmed in seeing Him. So if you are able not to be overcome in a prayer before the sun rises and a prayer before it sets, then do so"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (554) and Muslim (633/211) from the hadith of Jarir ibn ʿAbd Allah.]]. What does this mean? Fajr and ʿAsr.

In any case, if al-ghuduw and al-āṣāl are intended in their literal sense, that is, the beginning of the day and its end, then this contains an indication of what? Of the glorification, exaltation of Allah, and tahlil (saying lā ilāha illā Allah) recited at the beginning and end of the day, and likewise an indication of the Fajr prayer and the ʿAsr prayer.

And if we say that by al-ghuduw and al-āṣāl is meant the whole of time, and that this is a case of mentioning the two extremes to include everything, as in His saying ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 62], then it includes everything that is glorified to Allah the Exalted in the mosques at the beginning and end of the day, and at night, its beginning, end, and middle.

* * *

His Exalted saying: ﴿Therein glorify Him in the mornings and the evenings (36) Men﴾ [al-Nur 36–37] (the subject of yusabbiḥu with a kasra on the bāʾ; with a fatha, the deputy subject is lahu, and ﴿men﴾ is the subject of a suppressed verb, an answer to a suppressed question, as if it were said: "Who glorifies Him?").

Now, the justification of the two readings ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ and ﴿yusabbaḥu﴾:

If it is ﴿yusabbiḥu lahu fīhā bil-ghuduwwi wal-āṣāl﴾, is ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ in the active or the passive voice?
* Student: Active.
* Shaykh: Active. In that case, is ﴿men﴾ the subject of (yusabbiḥu) or not? Clear.

On the reading ﴿yusabbaḥu﴾, the verb is in the passive voice and needs a deputy subject. ﴿Men﴾ cannot be the deputy subject, because if it were, those who glorify would be whom? The men. This is impossible. So where is the deputy subject?

The deputy subject is the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿lahu﴾: ﴿yusabbaḥu lahu﴾. When the object is absent in a passive verb, it is replaced by an adverbial or prepositional phrase, just as if you said: "It was said, a saying" — no, that is an explicit deputy subject. ("The striking was struck," and similar examples), it substitutes for the direct object.

Ibn Malik says:
"And what is receptive of an adverbial phrase, or of a verbal noun, or of a prepositional phrase, is fit to substitute as deputy (for the subject)."
(The Arabic: وَقَابِلٌ مِنْ ظَرْفٍ أَوْ مِنْ مَصْدَرٍ ∗∗∗ أَوْ حَـــــرْفِ جَـــــرٍّ بِنِيَابَــــــةٍ حَـــــــــــرِي)

What we have now, ﴿yusabbaḥu lahu﴾: if we say ﴿lahu﴾ is the deputy subject, is it the adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase? Look at the verse in the Alfiyya:
"And what is receptive of an adverbial phrase, or of a verbal noun, or of a prepositional phrase, is fit to substitute as deputy."
Of which of the three is ﴿yusabbaḥu lahu﴾? A prepositional phrase.

The problem remains with ﴿men﴾ [al-Nur 37] on the reading ﴿yusabbaḥu﴾. We say: ﴿men﴾ is the subject of a suppressed verb. This suppressed verb was necessitated by the word ﴿yusabbaḥu﴾, because ﴿yusabbaḥu lahu﴾ implies, as if it were said: "who glorifies or who is glorified for Him?" So it was answered: "men." On this, ﴿men﴾ is the subject of a suppressed verb indicated by the verb mentioned, ﴿yusabbaḥu﴾. Clear?

So ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ has two canonical readings, with fatha and with kasra on the bāʾ, and now the justification of each reading has been explained.

(﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah, and the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat; they fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾, meaning: shifted, ﴿therein from fear; hearts between salvation and destruction, and eyes between the right and the left, and it is the Day of Resurrection﴾.)

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts﴾. The word "men" (rijāl) indicates praise and commendation, as one says: "So-and-so is a man," meaning he has the quality of manhood. So the word "men" without doubt indicates praise; for this reason it is applied only to the mature and sensible.

His saying: ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts﴾ does not say "who do not sell or buy," because one who neither sells nor buys may come to the mosque merely to fill his free time. But one who sells and buys, while being occupied with it, [is not diverted]. (...)

(...) to Him, not because he is idle and has no work or occupation. Do you understand now? This is more eloquent in praise: that they do sell and buy, but this trade and buying do not divert them from the remembrance of Allah.

His Exalted saying: ﴿trade nor sale﴾. The author explained "trade" as "buying." Why?
* Student: Explanation by contrast.
* Shaykh: In contrast with "sale." But this explanation is not correct, because buying is understood from selling, since there is no selling without buying. But trade is more general than selling. A person may be diverted by his trade through sorting it, cataloguing it, preserving it, maintaining it, and the like. Is this not so? Perhaps he is not selling or buying, but is diverted by this trade in another way. Therefore we say concerning the verse: the meaning of "trade" is what a person trades in and is diverted by, not merely buying. Rather it is more general. As for buying, it is understood from selling, because when they buy, others have sold to them, and when they sell, others have bought from them.

His saying: ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ means: trade does not divert them from the remembrance of Allah. They give the remembrance of Allah precedence over their trade. But people in this matter fall into three categories regarding trade and remembrance:

The first: one who gives trade precedence over remembrance. This one is a loser, by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, those are the losers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 9]. Even if they profit in wealth and children, they are losers. This is the first category.

The second category: one whom trade, wealth, and children do not divert from the remembrance of Allah, but he does each thing in its place. This one is a winner. He has not lost his wealth or his child, nor has he lost the remembrance of Allah; he gives each its share.

The third category: one who is above this, who makes his trade and his children a part of the remembrance of Allah, such that by this trade he intends to be helped in obeying his Lord and in spending his wealth on what pleases his Lord. The same is true of children: he occupies himself with them for their upbringing and in reflection on the blessing of Allah upon him through them, and the like. This is the highest rank.

On this basis, this man is a winner in both respects, is that correct or not? In both respects at the same time. The second category is a winner in both respects but in alternation: he gains in this and gives it what it deserves, and gains in that and gives it what it deserves. As for the third, his condition is great, but few are found with this quality; very few, extremely rare. And most people today, from which categories are they?
* Students: The first.
* Shaykh: From the first category, which is in reality last in rank yet first in mention. Most people today are like this.
* Student: The third.
* Shaykh: The third: one who makes his occupation with his trade a remembrance of Allah.

I say: ﴿And the establishment of prayer﴾ (iqām) means iqāmah, but the feminine ending was dropped for lightness. And the establishment of prayer is not merely performing it; rather it is a matter beyond the act. What is the meaning of "to establish something"? To make it upright and straight, and that is by performing its conditions, pillars, and obligations. Not every one who prays is one who establishes the prayer. For this reason you find that the praise which Allah mentions in the Quran, and indeed the commands which Allah gives in the Quran, mostly, what do we say? With establishment, because that is the essence, not merely the act of prayer. For this reason we find two men pray behind the imam, their actions are identical, their entry into prayer is identical, and their exit from it is identical, yet between their two prayers is as between heaven and earth. Why? Because one of them established the prayer, while the other merely prayed. But the first established it humbly, present of heart, sincere, hoping for the reward of Allah and fearing His punishment.

The establishment of prayer mentioned frequently in the Quran: how was it explained? It was explained by the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition). There are matters explained in the Quran, but most of that is explained by the Sunnah, the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) Sunnah explained it. By this we know that the Sunnah is necessary in the Sharia, and that whoever denies it has demolished a great part of the Sharia. Some people have been found who deny the Sunnah, may Allah protect us.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 36–38 (part 2 of 3):

We have heard that some leaders among the Arabs have begun confiscating the books of the Sunnah. I was told that they confiscate Bukhari and Muslim from the bookshops so that the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ) will not spread among his Ummah, God forbid. There is no doubt that this is disbelief. That is, whoever permits himself to confiscate the books of hadith that the Ummah has received with acceptance... Even if they confiscated misguiding, weak, or fabricated books, we would praise them for this matter. But they confiscate authentic books that the Ummah has received with acceptance, that the Muslims have taught and regarded as a foundation. These people are undoubtedly disbelievers, because they have disbelieved in the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ), and indeed in the Quran itself, since God says: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21], and He says: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ [al-Nisa 80], and He says: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31], and He says: ﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr 7], and He says: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ [al-Ahzab 36].

In any case, the verses on this are numerous, clear, and evident. The establishment of prayer of this kind is not explained sufficiently except by the Sunnah of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him).

As for His saying: ﴿and giving zakat﴾, that is, giving it. Zakat is known to us; it is the portion that God Most High has made obligatory on our wealth. The recipient is not specified here, but it is specified in the Quran in Surah al-Tawbah in His saying: ﴿Alms are only for the poor, the needy, those employed to collect them, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, to free captives, to those in debt, for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer﴾ [al-Tawbah 60]. These are the ones to whom zakat is given.

﴿and giving zakat; they fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾. His saying ﴿they fear﴾ is a description of ﴿men﴾. Trade and commerce do not distract them, and in these states they also fear a Day; they fear while glorifying Him morning and evening, and while establishing prayer and giving zakat, and while not being diverted by trade and sale. All these deeds are built upon this belief and foundation.

﴿They fear a Day in which﴾: their fear of this Day indicates their belief in it, does it not? It indicates their belief in it, since a person does not fear something he does not believe in. This shows that they have complete faith and certainty in the Last Day; therefore they fear it, they fear this Day.

God described this Day by His saying: ﴿turned about﴾, meaning agitated in it. ﴿Hearts and eyes﴾: ﴿turned about﴾. The turning about is known; it is the change of state from one condition to another. These hearts turn about, become agitated and move from one condition to another. How? The turning of hearts, as the author says: (between salvation and destruction). A person does not know whether he will be saved or destroyed, so his heart is turned about and agitated; sometimes hope predominates over it, and sometimes fear predominates over it. Likewise the eyes turn about.

The author says: (from the right and the left side), because people (...) as if they were not rational. Therefore God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And you see people as drunk, yet they are not drunk, but the punishment of God is severe﴾ [al-Hajj 2]. ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly, hurrying forward with heads raised, their glance not returning to them﴾ [Ibrahim 42–43]. One who sees him thinks he is insane, as if he were drunk from the intensity of the terror. What then do you think of the heart at that time? There is no doubt that in reality it will turn about and be agitated, not knowing its final end. This is what happens on the Day of Resurrection.

He says: ﴿So that God may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur 38]. ﴿So that God may reward them with the best of what they did﴾ (that is, His reward; and "best" means "good"). May God be praised. The lam in His saying ﴿so that He may reward them﴾: is it the lam of consequence, meaning that their outcome is this, or is it also the lam of purpose; that is, they glorify Him and fear Him in order that God may reward them with the best of what they did, so that here they have combined fear and hope according to the view that it is the lam of purpose? Or we say it is the lam of consequence, and that they perform those things out of fear of God, Mighty and Majestic, so that their outcome is complete security together with abundant reward? There are two possibilities: either the lam is of consequence, meaning they glorify and fear, and their outcome is that, namely security from what they feared and the attainment of abundant reward; or it is of purpose, meaning they do that in expectation of the recompense.

﴿So that God may reward them with the best of what they did.﴾ Now here we discuss the author's words.

The author said: (that is, His reward). Why? Because in reality they are not rewarded with the deed itself, but with what?

* Students: The reward.

* The Shaykh: With His reward. The recompense is the reward; therefore the author needed to estimate the deed as the reward of the deed, because that is what the recompense is given with. This is the first point.

The second: he says: ("best" means "good"). Why? Because the author imagined, or perhaps someone might imagine, that recompense falls only on the best of what a person does. In reality, recompense falls on both the good and the best, is that not so? When a person does something good, the recompense is for the good and the better. But this imagined objection does not arise on the author's estimate, which is that the meaning is "that God may reward them the best reward for what they did." Then the meaning becomes: God rewards them the best reward for what they did, and on this basis there is no difficulty at all, and we do not interpret "best" as "good," because interpreting "best" as "good" is distortion. Which is more complete? The best. Therefore we say the verse stands on its apparent meaning, the comparative form remains in its proper sense, and the meaning is that they are rewarded with the best reward for their deed. How so? A good deed is multiplied tenfold, up to seven hundred fold, up to many multiples. If someone does a deed for you and gives you your wage twice, is that the best reward? Yes, but the reward of God, Mighty and Majestic, is better and better, because God multiplies for whom He wills. Therefore it is preferable, indeed obligatory, that "best" remain in its comparative sense.

We say: "best," that is, the best reward for their deed. Here "best" is not applied to the deed; what is "best" applied to? It is applied to the reward.

There remains for us, on the first estimate: ﴿so that God may reward them the best of what they did﴾. Why did God attribute the good to the deed itself, although the good belongs to the reward? This is an indication that the recompense is according to the deed; therefore it is expressed by the deed, as you do, so you will be repaid.

So the person who does not pray, for example, is not rewarded with the reward of one who prays, and one who does not give zakat is not rewarded with the reward of one who gives zakat, and so on. The recompense is according to the deed; therefore the deed is used to express its recompense, indicating that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, but it is recompense in the best form.

And He, Exalted, said: ﴿and increase them from His bounty; and God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ (It is said: "So-and-so spends without reckoning," that is, he is generous, as if he does not count what he spends). His saying ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾ is additional to the reward of the deed, and that is what results from an increase in righteous deeds, an increase in provision in this world, and an increase in what is stored for them with God in Paradise, such as looking upon the Face of God, Glorified and Exalted, as mentioned in the authentic hadith [[Recorded by Muslim (181/298) from the hadith of Suhayb.]], regarding His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best and an increase﴾ [Yunus 26]: that the increase is an increase of provision in this world, and an increase of reward in the Hereafter through looking upon the Face of God, Glorified and Exalted.

His saying: ﴿and God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ means that He, Glorified and Exalted, gives without measure. But what is the meaning of "without measure"? How do we say "without measure" when God, Glorified and Exalted, says: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd 8]?

The answer: this is a metaphor for abundance of giving. Therefore one says, as the author said: "So-and-so spends without reckoning." What does that mean? It means he gives abundantly, without limit. Otherwise God has determined it by His knowledge and wisdom; everything, even a drop of rain when it falls on the earth, is by measure.

So the meaning of His saying ﴿without reckoning﴾ is "without measure," and it is a metaphor for what? For the abundance of what is given. It is not that He gives without being aware of what He gives; rather He, Glorified and Exalted, knows what He provides, how He provides, and where He provides, but because of the abundance of His giving, it is as one who does not count.

* There are many benefits in this verse. Among them: the virtue of mosques. What is our evidence for this? His saying: ﴿God has permitted that they be raised and that His name be mentioned in them﴾. God's permission that they be raised and that His name be mentioned in them indicates their nobility, because a place is ennobled by the nobility of the worship performed in it, just as a time is ennobled by the worship performed in it. Why was Ramadan noble? Because fasting is prescribed in it and the Quran was revealed in it. And why was (...) noble? Because the rites take place in it and the name of God is mentioned over what He has provided them of livestock, and so on.

* From this is derived: the nobility of mosques, because they are places where God, Mighty and Majestic, is remembered and glorified.

* Also in it: the legitimacy of honouring mosques. Among honouring them: that they be perfumed, and also that they be cleaned of filth and dirt.

* Should we say: among that is decorating them? No. That is why the hadith says: "I have not been commanded to build up the mosques," and the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "You will decorate them as the Jews and Christians decorated [theirs]" [[Recorded by Abu Dawud (448) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas.]]. Decoration is something unsuitable for mosques, because mosques are not houses of this world, but houses of work for the Hereafter. However, they should be cleaned of filth and dirt and perfumed. There is a difference between cleaning them of filth and introducing decoration; cleaning of filth is purification, whereas decoration is introducing things that are not fitting for mosques.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, honouring the mosque means: you do not enter with your shoes unless you have cleaned them.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, the clothing I enter with.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, and there is no (...) necessity. We say: the Sunnah is to pray in the sandals, because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded that [[Recorded by Abu Dawud (650) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, in which: "and let him pray in them."]] and also did it himself [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (386) and Muslim (555/60) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]].

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: The houses?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: No, "dur" in the language means quarters; it is said: "this is the dar of the sons of so-and-so," meaning their quarter. Yes, (...) the remembrance of God.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, eating in mosques; that will come, God willing, later.

* * *

Like... may God keep you safe from the terrors when they are mentioned: if a person is given good news, he either forgets what he was given good news of because of the intensity of the terror, or he fears something that will befall him before he reaches what he was given good news of. Is it clear? For example, the King says to you, and to God is the highest example: "See, you do what is incumbent upon you," and you see the skin among people, the captivity and the seizing. Do you not fear? You will necessarily feel fear, although we say this by way of approximation; otherwise the terrors of the Day of Resurrection cannot be imagined by a person.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. The Messengers, peace be upon them, cross the Sirat and say: "O God, grant safety, O God, grant safety" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (806) and Muslim (182/299) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. (...)

We have completed the discussion of what is derived from the noble verse in His saying: ﴿in houses that God has permitted to be raised﴾. Now we begin the benefits all together. We began mentioning the benefits, so we say, and with God we speak, Glorified and Exalted:

* In it: the magnification of the status of mosques, because of His saying: ﴿God has permitted that they be raised﴾, for this is evidence of the magnification of their status.

We have explained that permission is of two kinds: legislative (shar'i) and universal (kawni). The difference between them is that the legislative relates to what God has legislated and loves, while the universal relates to what He has decreed, whether He legislated it or not. We gave examples for that.

* Also in it: the virtue of mentioning God, Glorified and Exalted, in mosques, because of His saying: ﴿and that His name be mentioned in them﴾.

The virtue of cleaning mosques and protecting them from harm, because of His saying, what? ﴿that they be raised﴾, for this is from raising them. Therefore it is reported in the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The rewards of my Ummah were shown to me, even the speck that a man removes from the mosque."[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (461) and al-Tirmidhi (2916) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]

* In it: that the better remembrance is with the heart and the tongue. From where is this derived?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿His name be mentioned in them﴾; because the name cannot be mentioned except by the tongue.

* Also in it: the virtue of glorification (tasbih), because of His saying: ﴿glorify﴾.

* Also in it: combining the affirmation of perfection for God with the negation of imperfection from Him. From where? ﴿be mentioned﴾ and ﴿glorify﴾; ﴿that His name be mentioned in them﴾ is the affirmation of the attribute of perfection, ﴿glorify﴾ is the negation of the attribute of imperfection. Do you understand? I think we have previously mentioned an important rule in the chapter on the Divine Names and Attributes: that negation is not intended as mere negation, but rather it is intended...

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, with negation there is the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. So when God negates injustice from Himself, Glorified and Exalted, this does not mean mere negation of injustice, but rather to establish the perfection of justice; due to the perfection of His justice He does not wrong. Because the negation of injustice may be due to incapacity to do injustice, or it may be due to the place not being capable of being unjust. Do you understand? We said, for example, that one says: "The wall does not wrong." Why?

* Student: It has no capacity.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is not capable of injustice; capacity is absent. And you say, for example, about a weak, humiliated man: "This one does not wrong." 

* Student: Because of his incapacity.

* The Shaykh: Because of his incapacity, so it is not praise. But when you say it of one who is capable and able to be unjust by his very nature, this is evidence of the perfection of His justice. Therefore God negated injustice from Himself, praising Himself by it, blessed and exalted is He. Had He been incapable of injustice, as the Jabriyyah said, the negation would not be valid.

* Also in it: the virtue of glorification in the morning and evening. If we say the intended meaning of "morning and evening" is these two times, then; if we say the intended meaning of "morning and evening" is continuity at all times, then mention of these two was because they are the two ends of the day. There is no evidence in this for restricting these two times, but the apparent meaning of the texts is that these two times have a distinction, because God constantly commands glorification at these two times.

* Also in it: evidence that the more strongly a distraction is present and a person is not diverted, the more perfect he is than one who has no distraction. From where is this derived? What is the point?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Right, correct. For example, these men, if they did not know trade or were unable to trade, we would say their resort to God's houses is out of necessity, that is, to occupy their time and to entertain themselves with that. But they are people who have trade; the distraction from remembering God in the mosques is present, which is trade, yet nevertheless it does not divert them.

* Also in it: evidence for the permissibility of trade. Its basis is that it established that they trade in a context of praise. Had trade been forbidden or blameworthy, it would not be valid to mention it in a context of praise. So trade is not objectionable; one should not say to a person: "Do not trade, do not work."

But in any case, people have different aims in their trade. One wants, through trade, to make it a means to the Hereafter, while others want only this world through trade. The difference among people in this matter is a broad field. Whoever trades in order to earn wealth with which he helps someone in need, draws near to Allah through it, and carries out projects of good, he is praised for this. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) made it a companion to what? He made it a companion to beneficial knowledge when he said: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given wisdom, so he teaches it, and a man whom Allah has given wealth and empowered him to spend it in the right way."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (73) and Muslim (816 / 268) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] This is evidence for the virtue of wealth when it is a help in obedience to Allah.

* And in it is evidence for the virtue of establishing the prayer. What is the reasoning behind that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is it about establishing the prayer that gives it a status and distinction?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Who knows?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...). No, my point is that the prayer has a distinction over other things. Is the prayer part of the remembrance of Allah or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is part of the remembrance of Allah, so He singled it out from among the remembrances, and specifying after generalizing indicates the virtue and distinction of the one specified. ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4]. "The Spirit" is Jibril; He singled him out for mention although he is among the angels, because of his nobility and excellence. So singling out the prayer and its establishment after mentioning what is more general is evidence of its distinction. And likewise the giving of zakat.
These two acts of worship are the best of acts of worship after monotheism and the testimony of the Messengership, because establishing the prayer is the second pillar, and giving zakat is the third pillar. Allah, glorified is He, always pairs them together in the Qur'an.
* And in it is also evidence: that whoever worships Allah out of fear is praised. From where is this taken? ﴿They fear a day﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, has praised those who worship out of fear of punishment, saying: ﴿They fulfil the vow and fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾ [al-Insan 7]. And here He said: ﴿They fear a day in which hearts and eyes will be overturned﴾. And Allah, exalted, praised those who worship out of desire: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29].
In this there is a clear refutation of those Sufis or others who hold that the best worship is for a person not to intend any benefit for himself, but to worship Allah for His own sake alone. That is, when you worship Allah, you should not intend that you want Allah's bounty or that you fear His punishment; they say: worship Allah for Allah's sake.
It is said to them: you are not more perfect in state than the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, and Allah has mentioned of them that they were ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29]. Nor are you more perfect in state than those whom Allah praised among the righteous: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan 5], up to His saying: ﴿They fulfil the vow and fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾ [al-Insan 7]. There is no doubt that a person who worships Allah, glorified and exalted, in order to attain His bounty and be saved from His punishment, wants to reach Allah's approval and to see Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because among the bliss of Paradise is seeing Allah, glorified and exalted.
* And in this is evidence: of the greatness of the Day of Resurrection and its severe terrors, from His saying: ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be overturned﴾.
(...) It is not specific; rather the "al" in it is for generality. That is, all hearts are overturned and all eyes are overturned. Even the prophets, peace be upon them, fear and are apprehensive, but despite that, the people of good are granted security; despite their fear they are granted security. It is known that those who are granted security, there is no doubt that this day is made easy for them. This is why Allah, exalted, said about the Day of Resurrection: ﴿for the disbelievers it will not be easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir 10], and He said: ﴿and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan 26]. From this it is understood that this day, despite its greatness, terrors, and severity, will be easy for the believers, though in itself it is extremely great. ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. The day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, and every pregnant one will lay down her burden, and you will see people as intoxicated, but they will not be intoxicated; but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾ [al-Hajj 1, 2].
* And in it also is evidence: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed, and indeed in the case of acts of obedience it is better than the deed. From where do we take this? ﴿So that Allah may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty﴾; something beyond what they had done.
* And in it is evidence: of the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted. From where do we take it? Because if they are rewarded with the best of what they did, then there is no recompense except after the knowledge of the one who recompenses; he knows what was done and then rewards for it.
* And in it also: the affirmation of power is from the affirmation of recompense, for one does not reward except one who is able. If you do a kindness to a person, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does you a kindness, reciprocate it; if you do not find [means to], then pray for him until you see that you have reciprocated it."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1672) and al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (2567) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]] So Allah, glorified and exalted, in the perfection of His power, is not diminished by what He gives the workers of their reward and their recompense.
* And in it: the affirmation of Allah's will; ﴿and Allah gives provision to whom He wills﴾. Or not? The affirmation of Allah's will regarding Himself, that is, in what relates to His action, is an agreed matter as far as I know; no innovators or others have opposed it. As for Allah's will in relation to what concerns the actions of creatures, a group called the Qadariyyah opposed it, for they claimed that the servant is independent in his deeds and that Allah's will has no connection to them. Some of them even denied knowledge; their extremists denied Allah's knowledge and said that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not know of the servant's deeds until after he does them; before that He does not know, glorified and exalted. They also denied the authentic, explicit texts affirming Allah's knowledge of everything, even the deeds of man.
* And in it also, regarding His saying ﴿without reckoning﴾: the abundance of Allah's provision, glorified and exalted, and that He gives without reckoning. But "without reckoning" does not mean "without measure." Why do we not say that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, because Allah says ﴿Everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd 8]. Even the drop that falls from the sky to the earth is measured with Allah, glorified and exalted; but it is without reckoning, meaning He does not reward a person by calculation, but with abundance without counting. This is well known; it is said: so-and-so spends without reckoning, meaning he spends very lavishly.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. What is established from the Salaf is that they are the mosques, and this is the place; this is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No people gather in one of the houses of Allah reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves..." and so on, and the intended meaning is undoubtedly the mosques.[[Narrated by Muslim (2699 / 38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 39–40 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert (qī'ah)﴾ [an-Nur 39]. When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the deeds of these men, those virtuous deeds, He mentioned the deeds of those who disbelieve and what their state is. This is the method of Allah the Exalted in His Book: when He mentions the description of the believer, He mentions after it the description of the disbeliever, or vice versa; and when He mentions the description of Paradise, He mentions after it the description of the Fire, or vice versa. This is because the Qur'an is mathani (oft-repeated, paired), in which meanings are repeated and set against one another. This is one reason. Another reason is that when a person is told the attributes of the people of goodness and the attributes of Paradise, the aspect of hope may overcome him and he perishes; and when the attributes of the Fire and the attributes of the people of evil are mentioned, what overcomes him is what?
* Students: Fear.
* The Shaykh: Fear, and he perishes too. For this reason the scholars differed: is it better for a person to let the aspect of hope prevail, or the aspect of fear, or to make them equal? Imam Ahmad said: It is required that his fear and his hope be equal; whichever of them prevails, his companion perishes. For if fear overcomes you, you fall into despair of the mercy of Allah, and if hope overcomes you, you fall into feeling safe from the plotting of Allah, and both are paths that do not befit the believer.

Some scholars said: It is appropriate for the sick person to let the aspect of hope prevail, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "None of you should die except while he thinks well of his Lord" [[Recorded by Muslim (2877/82) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]], and it is appropriate for the healthy person to let the aspect of fear prevail.

Others said: When committing a sin, the aspect of fear should prevail, and why? So that he refrains; for if the aspect of hope prevailed, he would say: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, and I hope Allah will forgive me, and he commits the sin. And when performing an act of obedience, the aspect of hope should prevail: that Allah the Exalted accepts it from him and rewards him, so that he does not despair. He said: What indicates this is such as the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Call upon Allah while you are certain of being answered" [[Recorded by at-Tirmidhi (3479) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Likewise, worship Allah while you are hoping that He will accept from you.

In any case, this view, in my opinion, is the most preponderant of the views: that when a person is in the state of worship and performing acts of worship, hope should prevail. This does not mean he is certain of acceptance; for Allah says: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun 60], meaning fearful that it will not be accepted from them. Rather, the meaning is that hope prevails along with fear. As for the state of committing sin, fear should prevail, so that he does not proceed to it relying on hope.

In any case, we have digressed a little, but our purpose is that the noble Qur'an mentions both of these, so that the person's course may be balanced.

He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert (qī'ah)﴾ (plural of qā', meaning in a wasteland; it is a shimmer seen there at midday in intense heat, resembling flowing water). This is an explanation of the mirage; and qī'ah is the wasteland. I think you all know the mirage: in intense heat, when you are in a wasteland of the earth. (qī'ah) means the plural of (qā'), unlike sandy terrain where this does not occur; rather, the qī'ān appear from afar as if there were water on that side, so one thinks it is water and heads toward it. These disbelievers' deeds are like this: like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one takes for water, though it is not water. How so? Because they say: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ [az-Zumar 3], ﴿and they say: These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 18]. They think that this shirk, which in reality distances them from Allah, is what?
* Students: It brings them near.
* The Shaykh: It brings them near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They think these intercessors are the ones who will disown them: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah 166]. They think them to be what?
* Students: Intercessors.
* The Shaykh: They think them to be intercessors. And you know that when the soul attaches itself to a thing as an intercessor or as something that brings it near to Allah, does it follow it or not? It follows it without doubt. These are like the mirage in the level desert.

(﴿He whom the thirsty one thinks to be water﴾: ﴿thinks﴾ means supposes; ﴿the thirsty one﴾ means the parched one; ﴿water﴾.) This is an eloquent simile: meaning that he heads toward it with intense eagerness, believing that it will rescue him. The parched one needs water, does he not? So when he sees something resembling water, he heads toward it with intense eagerness. And why? In order to relieve his necessity with it. Does he think it benefits him or not? Yes, he thinks it benefits him; and were it not that he thought it would benefit him, he would not have gone to it. But the outcome: ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, he finds it to be nothing of what he supposed; when he comes to it, he finds nothing. What do you imagine his state to be then? Immense disappointment, may Allah protect us; no one can imagine it. A thirsty person came to this mirage from afar. And note also that the mirage does not appear in nearby places; in the distance, the farther you see it. From a distant place he wants to drink, and the outcome is that he finds nothing of what he supposed.

The author says: (Likewise the disbeliever thinks that his deed is like charity that will benefit him; until, when he dies and comes before his Lord, he finds his deed to be nothing, meaning it did not benefit him. ﴿And finds Allah with him﴾, meaning with his deed, ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾, meaning He recompenses him for it in this world. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, meaning in recompense.)

This disbeliever thinks his deed benefits him. The author's illustration of this with charity is open to scrutiny, because it should be (...); that is, unless by this he intended to give an example. If he intended an example, then it is correct: this is among the deeds that the disbelievers perform, thinking they benefit them while they do not. But it should be said that it is more general than that: it is not only charity; even the worship of idols they think beneficial. What do they think?
* Students: That they benefit them.
* The Shaykh: That they benefit them: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ [az-Zumar 3], ﴿they say: These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 18]. Yet all of this does not benefit them; they will not find anything of what they suppose and reckon.

As for His saying: ﴿And finds Allah with him﴾: with what? With this mirage? Because he has now reached death; when he dies, he has met Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾. This is the apparent context.

As for the author's view, which makes (﴿And finds Allah with him﴾, meaning with his deed) a consequence of His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, because (those who disbelieve) is general, it is as if He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the disbeliever: his deed is such and such, ﴿like a mirage in a level desert; the thirsty one thinks it water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with it﴾, meaning with that deed, according to His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds﴾, ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾. But the apparent meaning of the verse is that the pronouns refer to what?
* A student: To the nearest antecedent.
* The Shaykh: To the nearest antecedent, which is this thirsty one who reached the water thirsty and found nothing, and so he will perish.

﴿And finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. ﴿His account﴾ means the recompense for his deed. His saying: ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ means the recompense. What is meant by swiftness here? Is it meant as the nearness of the time of recompense, so the swiftness is temporal; or is it meant as the completion of the reckoning, so the swiftness is in action; or both? ﴿Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: does the meaning that He is swift in His reckoning, or that His reckoning of the servants is near?
* A student: It may be either.
* The Shaykh: It may be all of them. The reckoning is near, even if it seems long to a person in this world; it is near. ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [an-Nisa' 77]. Likewise, when Allah reckons all creatures on the Day of Resurrection, He reckons them in half a day, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day will be better in resting place and finer in place of repose﴾ [al-Furqan 24]. The scholars inferred from this that they will take their midday rest in their dwellings during half of that day. But in any case, the day to which Allah pointed is of a measure of fifty thousand years; and whatever the case, Allah is capable of what is even more eloquent than that. Nevertheless, this is a great swiftness and an extreme power, even if the fifty thousand years were twenty-five thousand years: all creatures, from first to last, human, jinn, birds and others, in half a day.

Now, if a person were to reckon with someone he deals with for a year, how long would it remain if the reckoning were exact and extensive? It would remain for a period; and the reckoning may be precise or may not be precise. But the reckoning of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, despite its swiftness, does not leave behind any small or great thing without counting it.

This is an example of a disbeliever who performs a deed wishing to draw near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Or another example: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea﴾ [an-Nur 40]. (Or) here is not for doubt, beyond any doubt, why? Because Allah, glorified and exalted, is free of doubt; doubt arises only from the deficiency of a person's knowledge, or the deficiency of the knower's knowledge. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His knowledge is vast; so it is not possible for Allah, glorified and exalted, to say: the deeds of those who disbelieve are either like this or like that, by way of doubt, as you might say, for example: I saw this thing and it resembles such and such or such and such. This cannot be said of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus (or) in His saying ﴿or like darkness﴾ is for variety: meaning, or their deeds are like darkness, and so on.

(﴿Or﴾: the disbelievers' evil deeds, ﴿like darkness in a deep sea﴾, deep; ﴿covered by waves, above it waves﴾, meaning the waves; ﴿above it waves﴾, meaning the second wave; ﴿above it clouds﴾, meaning cloud. These are ﴿darkness, some above others﴾: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the first wave, the darkness of the second, and the darkness of the cloud.) Four darknesses. (﴿When he brings out﴾, meaning the observer, ﴿his hand﴾ into these darknesses, ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾, meaning he does not come close to seeing it; ﴿and whomever Allah has not given light, for him there is no light﴾, meaning whomever He does not guide, he is not guided.)

This is a second category of disbelievers. The first is the state of the disbeliever who strives, thinking his deed benefits him; this second is the state of the blind follower who does not know that he walks in darkness together with the disbelievers, while he does not know it.

﴿Like darkness in a deep sea﴾: the sea is well known, and lujji means deep; and the deeper the sea, the more intense its darkness. Also ﴿covered by waves﴾: ﴿covered﴾ means overspread; a wave covers this disbeliever, ﴿above it waves﴾, also high waves, ﴿above it clouds﴾.

﴿Waves above waves﴾: what is the boundary of the second wave from the first?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: At the sea?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, I mean its height; for in reality it becomes darker the higher it rises. ﴿Above it waves﴾: water.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where is this?
* The student: From the cloud.
* The Shaykh: The cloud is above; no, I mean ﴿waves above it waves﴾.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, waves. But what prevents it from being the second wave, and what distinguishes it from the first wave?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Good. This is one possibility: that it be by direction, meaning they meet; one comes from here, and the second, higher than it, comes from another direction, so that the height of this over that becomes clear. Or they are successive waves; for example, a wave approaching (...) the mountains, and behind it another wave higher than it; when it overtakes it, there is a wave above it. But if it is a single wave, it cannot precede part of itself. Whoever has seen the sea finds it so: you find successive waves; sometimes, when the wind reverses, they meet head-on, and sometimes they follow one another. But these successive waves, too, you find, glory be to Allah the Mighty, sometimes like steps, meaning one above another. This is what Allah, glorified and exalted, struck as the example.

﴿Above it clouds﴾: clouds in reality are in levels in the atmosphere; we do not suppose they are in one layer. No; they are in very distant layers. A person knows this when he rides an aircraft: he sometimes finds a cloud between himself and the aircraft from below, as far as between the cloud and the earth, and a cloud above it, as far between himself and it as between the aircraft and the earth, while he is between them. This is a known, observed matter. So the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that His saying ﴿above it clouds﴾ is like His saying ﴿above it waves﴾: meaning that the cloud almost clings to these waves. Among this is fog; there is no doubt that fog comes close to the surface of the sea.
* A student: Is it not (...) far from the sea (...), which may obstruct the view (...) whether it is near or...?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it may be; whether it is near.
* The student: (...) so it creates darkness, or near sunset, then it is with it.
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt, but which of them is more intense?
* The student: When it is near.
* The Shaykh: When it is near, it is more intense. It is also possible that by the cloud is meant what includes fog, for the reality is that fog is a cloud, since it spreads along the ground. When this is clear, the darkness becomes very evident because of its abundance.

﴿Darkness, some above others﴾: the amplification in this example; it would have sufficed to say ﴿above it clouds﴾, but for the sake of magnifying it in the soul and showing its greatness, He said ﴿darkness, some above others﴾.

Then He struck an example, saying: ﴿When he brings out his hand, he almost cannot see it﴾. What is closer to you than something? The hand is closer to you than the moving limbs that can be seen; they may come out or may not come out. When you bring out your hand, ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾. What is your opinion: does the meaning of ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾ mean he sees it with difficulty, or he does not see it?
* A student: He sees it.
* Another student: He does not see it.
* The Shaykh: He does not see it. Now, ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 71]: did they slaughter it or not?
* Students: They slaughtered it.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* A student: He sees it.
* The Shaykh: He sees it with difficulty?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The grammarians roughly say: the affirmation of (kāda) is negation and its negation is affirmation. So when you say: "I did not almost do it," it means: I did it, but after great delay. And ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾ according to this rule means: he saw it, but after a great distance and the difficulty of seeing. However, the apparent meaning, as other grammarians said, is that (kāda) is like other verbs: its negation is negation and its affirmation is affirmation; but it means (qāraba), "approached." So if you say: "kadtu af'al," meaning: I approached doing it. Did you do it or not?
* A student: I did not do it.
* The Shaykh: You did not do it, but you approached it. Has the approach been affirmed or negated now? The approach has been affirmed, but we know the non-occurrence of the act from the approach. ﴿He almost cannot see it﴾, meaning: he did not approach seeing it, as the author or the commentator said: he did not approach seeing it. Therefore, if he does not approach seeing it, the non-seeing is by all the more reason and more certain, is it not?

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 71], were it not for His saying ﴿they slaughtered it﴾, the verse would not indicate that they slaughtered it. But the meaning of ﴿they slaughtered it﴾ is: after they had been far from slaughtering it, and had not intended it, nor resolved to comply, but had said to their prophet: ﴿Do you take us for a jest?﴾ [al-Baqarah 67], after this distance from the act, and after their requests had been answered, they slaughtered it. Do you understand now? The verse stands as it is.

Also, (kāda), like other verbs, its negation is negation and its affirmation is affirmation; but since it indicates approach, when a man says "kidtu an af'al" ("I almost did"), it means: he did not do it. For the word "approached" indicates the act; that is, "and I did not do it": "lam akud af'al" ("I did not almost do"). If nothing preceding indicates the act, then certainly he did not do it, like the saying of 'Umar: "I did not almost pray the 'Asr until the sun almost set"; meaning: I did not approach praying the 'Asr. So did he pray it or not?
* A student: He prayed it.

The Shaykh: No, he did not pray it. "I was not even about to pray the 'Asr until the sun was nearly setting"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (596) and Muslim (631 / 209), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]]. That is, he had not come close to praying the 'Asr until the sun came close to setting. When the sun came close to setting, he came close to the 'Asr prayer. He prayed it only after sunset, together with the Prophet (ﷺ). But at the beginning, it was as if he had not been able even to get ready to come close to the prayer, let alone to pray it. The meaning is that he was occupied. The unbelievers kept him busy until the sun was close to setting, so he did not even come close to praying. Coming close to a prayer, my brothers, means getting ready for it. He is saying: he did not get ready, and there was no readiness for the prayer, until the sun was about to set. For this reason, he prayed the 'Asr with the Prophet (ﷺ) after the sun had set.

The conclusion, then, is that the correct view differs from what some of the grammarians (al-nuhat, Arabic grammarians) said: that the affirmative of (كاد, kada, "to almost") is a negation and its negation is an affirmation. Rather, the correct view is that (كاد) is like other verbs. And what is "like other verbs"? Its affirmation is an affirmation and its negation is a negation. But it means "approaching" (al-muqarabah), which is why the grammarians counted it among the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah). Whoever denies that a thing was approached has certainly not done it, and whoever affirms that he approached it has also certainly not done it, because the phrase "I approached the act" means "and I did not do it." That is its meaning.

So if one says, "He almost did not do such-and-such," and nothing has preceded that indicates he did it, then he did not do it. But if something has preceded that indicates he did it, such as ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:71], which means: "So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it," then this shows that before the slaughter they were far from complying and were hardly about to do it. Yet after insistence, and after they said, "Make it clear to us," and it was made clear as they asked, they were answered afterwards. For this reason, in reality, this is an example which a person should take as a lesson for himself: when he is commanded to do a thing, he should not (...) upon himself, going beyond this and that, because this is dangerous. Allah the Mighty and Sublime has said: ﴿وَنُقَلِّبُ أَفْئِدَتَهُمْ وَأَبْصَارَهُمْ كَمَا لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهِ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ وَنَذَرُهُمْ فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ [al-An'am 6:110]. For this reason, when a Muslim knows the Shari'ah, he must submit. There is no harm afterwards in what he commits himself to as being bound by it. There is no harm afterwards in his seeking to learn the wisdom, because asking about the wisdom does not contradict submission. But the important thing is, and what is important? That he submits first, and does not raise objections and doubts, asking "Why this? Why that?" Then after that, he may ask if he wishes.

(...) It has preceded that Allah, glorified and exalted, explained that the deeds of the unbelievers are of two types: one type is like a mirage in a level desert (qi'ah), which the thirsty man thinks is water, and another type is like darkness in a deep sea. This division and this variety are in terms of the condition of the unbelievers. The first, Allah knows best, is for the one who has understanding and effort, and the second is for the one who has ignorance and error, like the common people (...).

A mirage in a qi'ah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, what is it?
* Student: The wasteland of the earth.
* Shaykh: The wasteland of the earth. (Al-qa'ah) is the plural of (qa') and it is the wasteland of the earth, meaning the wide, distant land which is in a qa' (...). Qa' or not? (...) Al-qa': the low-lying land.
What is the mirage (al-sarab)?
* Student: The mirage is (...).
* Shaykh: As if it were water (...).
What is the point of resemblance between the deeds of these unbelievers and this mirage?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He finds that it betrays him at the moment he needs it most.

His saying ﴿وَوَجَدَ اللَّهَ عِنْدَهُ﴾ [al-Nur 24:39], "and found Allah with him." The pronoun in (عِنْدَهُ, 'indahu, "with him") refers to what?
* Student: The deed.
* Shaykh: According to the opinion of the author, it refers to the deed. So here it refers to the thing being compared (al-mushabbah) and not to the thing it is compared to (al-mushabbah bihi). It may also refer to the thing it is compared to, meaning: the thirsty man found Allah with him, that is, with this mirage, when he died of thirst, and Allah paid him his account in full.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, the thirsty man.
What does (al-bahr al-lujji, "the deep sea") mean?
* Student: The deep one.
* Shaykh: The deep one, good.
﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهِ مَوْجٌ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "above it is a wave." How was the upper position of the second wave?
* Student: Either it is (...) from the change of the winds, or it is successive waves: the first is followed by the second and...
* Shaykh: And rises above it, yes, correct.
﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهِ سَحَابٌ ظُلُمَاتٌ بَعْضُهَا فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "above it is a cloud, darkness upon darkness." What are these darknesses, ﴿ظُلُمَاتٌ بَعْضُهَا فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The darkness of the first wave. What else?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the darkness of the first wave, and the second, and the cloud. And if it is at night, the darkness increases.
His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "he could scarcely see it." What is it?
* Student: He did not come close to seeing it.
* Shaykh: Good. And the negation of approach?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but its negation is the negation of the reality. That is, the negation of approaching seeing is the negation of seeing. Is that right or not?
What some of the grammarians said, that the negation of (كاد) is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation, is it correct or incorrect?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but it is so only by necessary implication.
What was their argument by which they established this point?
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:71].
* Shaykh: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾.
Is there in the verse evidence for what they said?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They say: they slaughtered it and they had almost not done it, but they did it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That means the act...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ means: they did not come close to doing it, but they did it.
* Student: In reality, they did it.
* Shaykh: Yes, this answer is not sufficient.
* Student: (...) Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾, meaning it was negated beforehand. It was negated by his saying (...), but it was negated (...), yet they did it. This shows that (...) according to their opinion has a special course (...), because when it is negated it indicates affirmation. When approach is negated...
* Shaykh: Its negation is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation, yes. This is their evidence from the verse. How do we refute them? That is the question.
* Student: In the verse there is a negation of approach, meaning that they slaughtered it after they had come close to not doing it.
* Another student: (...).
* Shaykh: Some grammarians, not all of them.
* Student: Yes, those who say that the meaning of this, the meaning of the saying of Allah the Mighty and Sublime: ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾, is: they had not almost done it before the act; they were far away, and the intended meaning is: they did not come close to doing it before the act; they were far away, they did not come close to doing it.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. I understood (...). They say: did they not do it? Yes, but their doing it is not known from His saying ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾. From where do we know the act?
* Students: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا﴾. That is, were it not for His saying ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا﴾, we would not understand that they slaughtered it. We would understand that they did not slaughter it and did not come close to slaughtering it. So there is no evidence in the verse. When you say, "I almost did such-and-such," it means you did not come close to doing it, and if you did not come close to doing it, you did not do it. But if there is a clue indicating your doing it, then this clue is what indicates the act. If you say, "I reached the town, and I almost did not arrive," this indicates your arrival. But it is not (...). Yet the fact that you arrived at the town... If you say, "I traveled to the town and I almost did not arrive," what happens? Would he be arriving?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: He would not be arriving, nor would he be close to arriving, unless there is evidence.

So ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾, if he brings out his hand in these darknesses, "he could scarcely see it." What is the meaning of ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾? He did not come close to seeing it, and if he did not come close to seeing it, then he did not see it.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُورًا فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light." That is: the one to whom Allah has not granted light has no light.
(﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, "for him there is no light," means: whoever Allah does not guide, will not be guided.)

The author here made the light a spiritual light, that is: whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with knowledge and faith, no one can illuminate his heart; ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾.

Like these verses which Allah, glorified and exalted, mentions: "Whoever Allah guides, none can misguide him, and whoever He misguides, none can guide him"[[Related by Muslim (867 / 45), from the hadith of Jabir, and (868 / 46), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and the like. What is their purpose? Is their purpose to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, as they used them as evidence, or is the purpose something else?
The answer, certainly: their purpose is not to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, because the doctrine of the Jabriyyah is false, refuted by the sound Shari'ah, the intellect, and the natural disposition. Rather, the purpose of these is that a person should not rely on himself, and should always turn to Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, seeking guidance, seeking light, seeking success, and so on. Otherwise, it is known that Allah does not establish a false matter which the intellect and the senses refute. In any case, Allah the Mighty and Sublime says: if Allah does not give a person light by which he is guided, then he has no light. And what sentence did He use? A nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah), which indicates what? Permanence and continuity: ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾. And He emphasized the negation of light from him with the extra ﴿مِنْ﴾ in His saying ﴿مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, because ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra and ﴿نُورٍ﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar); that is, he has no light.

So we know from this that Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and whoever Allah gives light is upon light from his Lord, and whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light. And from where will light come to him when Allah has veiled light from him!

But know also that Allah's veiling light from the servant is not a withholding of His bounty, may He be blessed and exalted, for He is the Possessor of great bounty. Giving is more beloved to Him than withholding, and guidance is more beloved to Him than misguidance. Rather, it is because the person himself is the one who prevented this light from himself. Recite the saying of Allah: ﴿فَلَمَّا زَاغُوا أَزَاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ [al-Saff 61:5], and recite the saying of Allah: ﴿فَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾, meaning: turned away from the truth and withdrew from it, ﴿فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُصِيبَهُمْ بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:49]. It becomes clear to you that Allah's misguiding the servant and veiling light from him is because of himself, which is what, may Allah protect us, has not been guided. In any case, this verse indicates that a person should, indeed must, always turn to Allah by asking Him to illuminate his heart, because ﴿مَنْ لَمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُورًا فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾ is the explicit meaning (mantuq) of the verse. The implicit meaning (mafhum) of the verse is: whoever Allah grants light, no one can veil that light of Allah, the Mighty and Sublime from him. So the noble verse indicates two matters: one explicit (mantuq) and the second implicit (mafhum). The explicit?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The one from whom Allah has veiled light...
* Student: Because of himself.
* Shaykh: No, (because of himself) is not from the verse; we restricted it by that. ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, and we said: it used a nominal sentence, which indicates what?
* Students: Continuity.
* Shaykh: Permanence and continuity. And it emphasized the negation of light from him by what? By the extra ﴿مِنْ﴾, because the extra (min) indicates generality. This is the explicit meaning of the verse.
Its implicit meaning: whoever Allah grants light, no one can veil it from him, so no barrier stands between him and His light, may He be blessed and exalted.

Then He said: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Nur 24:41], "Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾: the hamzah is the interrogative particle entering upon a negation, and when the interrogative enters upon a negation, it conveys affirmation (al-taqrir), like: ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1], "Did We not expand for you your breast?", meaning: We have expanded your breast for you.
﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ means: you have indeed seen. So the interrogative hamzah entering upon a negation conveys affirmation, that is, affirming what was mentioned, not negating it. For example, Allah (...) said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾.
(...) it has no connection to the will of Allah in it, to the point that some of them denied knowledge. Their extremists denied Allah's knowledge and said: Allah, glorified and exalted, does not know the deeds of the servant until after he does them; before that, He does not know. Glory be to Him, and they denied the sound and explicit texts establishing Allah's knowledge of everything, even the deeds of man.
* Also in it, His saying ﴿بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:38], "without reckoning": the abundance of Allah's provision, the Mighty and Sublime, and that He, glorified and exalted, gives without reckoning. And the meaning of "without reckoning" is not "without measure." Why do we not say that?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, because Allah says: ﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ عِنْدَهُ بِمِقْدَارٍ﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:8], "everything with Him is by measure." Even the drop that falls from the sky to the earth is measured with Allah, glorified and exalted. But ﴿بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾ means that He does not reward the person by reckoning, but with abundant, copious abundance (...).

* * *

What is the point of resemblance between the deeds of these unbelievers and this mirage?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He finds that it betrays him at the moment he needs it most.

His saying: ﴿وَوَجَدَ اللَّهَ عِنْدَهُ﴾ [al-Nur 24:39], "and found Allah with him." The pronoun in (عِنْدَهُ, 'indahu) refers to what?
* Student: The deed.
* Shaykh: According to the opinion of the author, it refers to the deed. So here it refers to the thing being compared and not to the thing it is compared to. It may also refer to the thing it is compared to, meaning: the thirsty man found Allah with him, that is, with this mirage, when he died of thirst, and Allah paid him his account in full.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, the thirsty man.
What does (al-bahr al-lujji, "the deep sea") mean?
* Student: The deep one.
* Shaykh: The deep one, good.
﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهِ مَوْجٌ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "above it is a wave." How was the upper position of the second wave?
* Student: Either it is (...) from the change of the winds, or they are successive waves: the first is followed by the second and...
* Shaykh: And rises above it, yes, correct.
﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهِ سَحَابٌ ظُلُمَاتٌ بَعْضُهَا فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "above it is a cloud, darkness upon darkness." What are these darknesses?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The darkness of the first wave. What else?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the darkness of the first wave, and the second, and the cloud. And if it is at night, the darkness increases.
His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾?
* Student: He did not come close to seeing it.
* Shaykh: Good. And the negation of approach?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but its negation is the negation of the reality. That is, the negation of approaching seeing is the negation of seeing. Is that right or not?
What some of the grammarians said, that the negation of (كاد) is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation, is it correct or incorrect?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but it is so only by necessary implication.
What was their argument by which they established this point?
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:71].
* Shaykh: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾.
Is there in the verse evidence for what they said?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They say: they slaughtered it and they had almost not done it, but they did it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That means the act...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ means: they did not come close to doing it, but they did it.
* Student: In reality, they did it.
* Shaykh: Yes, this answer is not sufficient.
* Student: (...) Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾, meaning it was negated beforehand. It was negated by his saying (...), but it was negated (...), yet they did it. This shows that (...) according to their opinion has a special course (...), because when it is negated it indicates affirmation. When approach is negated...
* Shaykh: Its negation is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation, yes. This is their evidence from the verse. How do we refute them? That is the question.

* Student: In the verse there is a negation of approaching (al-muqarabah), meaning that they slaughtered her after they had nearly not done it.

* Another student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Some grammarians, not all of them.

* Student: Yes.
