Those who say that the meaning of this is the meaning of Allah's words, ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾, that is: they had not nearly done it before the act; they were far from it, and what is meant is: "and they were not near to doing it before the act; they were far off, they did not come close to doing it."

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. I understood (...). They say: "Had they not done it?" Yes, they did. But their act is not known from His words, ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾. From where do we know the act?

* The students: ﴿So they slaughtered her﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿So they slaughtered her.﴾ That is, were it not for Allah's words, ﴿so they slaughtered her﴾, we would not have understood that they slaughtered her; we would have understood that they did not slaughter her and did not even come close to slaughtering her. So the verse contains no proof of this. When you say, "I almost did not do such-and-such," it means you did not come close to doing it, and if you did not come close to doing it, you did not do it. But if there is an indicator (qarinah) that points to your doing it, then that indicator is what points to the act. If you say, "I reached the town and I barely arrived," it indicates your arrival. But it is not on (...). Yet your having reached the town is (...). If you said, "I travelled to the town and I did not nearly arrive," what would happen? Would you be one who has arrived?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: He would not be one who has arrived, nor one who has come close to arriving, unless there is evidence.

So, ﴿he could hardly see it﴾: if he brings out his hand in these darknesses, he could hardly see it. What is the meaning of ﴿he could hardly see it﴾? He did not come close to seeing it, and if he did not come close to seeing it, then he did not see it.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light.﴾ That is: whoever Allah has not granted light, there is no light for him.

(﴿For him there is no light﴾: that is, whoever Allah does not guide, will not be guided.)

The author here takes "light" to be spiritual light; that is, whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with knowledge and faith, no one can illuminate his heart: ﴿for him there is no light﴾.

Like these verses that Allah the Exalted mentions, "Whomever Allah guides, none can misguide him, and whomever He misguides, none can guide him"[[Related by Muslim (867/45) from the hadith of Jabir, and (868/46) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and what is similar to that. What is the purpose of them? Is the purpose of them to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah (determinists), as they have used them as evidence, or is the purpose something else?

The answer, with certainty: the purpose is not to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, because the doctrine of the Jabriyyah is false, refuted by the sound religious sense, reason, and the fitrah (innate human nature). Rather, the purpose is that a person should not rely upon himself, and that he should always turn to Allah the Exalted in seeking guidance, seeking light, seeking success, and so on. Otherwise, it is known that Allah the Exalted does not establish a false matter that reason and the senses refute. In any case, Allah the Exalted says: if Allah has not granted a person light by which to be guided, then for him there is no light. He brought the nominal sentence, which indicates what? It indicates permanence and continuity: ﴿for him there is no light﴾. He emphasized the negation of light from him with the added ﴿min﴾ in His words ﴿min nurin﴾, because ﴿min﴾ is extra (zaa'idah), and ﴿nur﴾ is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar); that is, "there is no light for him."

So from this we know that Allah the Exalted is the One who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and that whoever Allah gives light is upon light from his Lord, and whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light. And from where would light come to him when Allah has withheld light from him!

But know also that Allah's withholding light from the servant is not a denial of His grace, blessed and exalted is He, for He is the possessor of great bounty. Giving is more beloved to Him than withholding, and guidance is more beloved to Him than misguidance. Rather, it is because the person himself has prevented this light from himself. Recite the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5]. And recite the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, from the truth and turn away from it, ﴿then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. It becomes clear to you that Allah's misguiding the servant and withholding light from him is because of himself; it is he who, may Allah protect us, did not become guided.

In any case, this verse indicates that a person should, indeed must, always turn to Allah, asking Him to illuminate his heart, because ﴿whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light﴾ is the explicit meaning (manṭūq) of the verse. Its implicit meaning (mafhūm) is: whoever Allah grants light, no one can withhold His light from him. So the noble verse indicates two matters: one explicit (manṭūq) and the other implicit (mafhūm). The explicit?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Whoever Allah withholds light from...

* Student: Because of himself.

* The Shaykh: No, (because of himself) is not from the verse; we restricted it by that. ﴿For him there is no light.﴾ And we said: He brought the nominal sentence, which indicates what?

* The students: Continuity.

* The Shaykh: Permanence and continuity. And He emphasized the negation of light from him with what? With the extra ﴿min﴾, because the extra "min" conveys generality. This is the explicit meaning of the verse.

Its implicit meaning: whoever Allah grants light, no one can withhold it from him, so there is no one who can block His light, blessed and exalted is He, from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 39–40 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert (qī'ah)﴾ [an-Nur 39]. When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the deeds of these men, those virtuous deeds, He mentioned the deeds of those who disbelieve and what their state is. This is the method of Allah the Exalted in His Book: when He mentions the description of the believer, He mentions after it the description of the disbeliever, or vice versa; and when He mentions the description of Paradise, He mentions after it the description of the Fire, or vice versa. This is because the Qur'an is mathani (oft-repeated, paired), in which meanings are repeated and set against one another. This is one reason. Another reason is that when a person is told the attributes of the people of goodness and the attributes of Paradise, the aspect of hope may overcome him and he perishes; and when the attributes of the Fire and the attributes of the people of evil are mentioned, what overcomes him is what?
* Students: Fear.
* The Shaykh: Fear, and he perishes too. For this reason the scholars differed: is it better for a person to let the aspect of hope prevail, or the aspect of fear, or to make them equal? Imam Ahmad said: It is required that his fear and his hope be equal; whichever of them prevails, his companion perishes. For if fear overcomes you, you fall into despair of the mercy of Allah, and if hope overcomes you, you fall into feeling safe from the plotting of Allah, and both are paths that do not befit the believer.

Some scholars said: It is appropriate for the sick person to let the aspect of hope prevail, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "None of you should die except while he thinks well of his Lord" [[Recorded by Muslim (2877/82) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]], and it is appropriate for the healthy person to let the aspect of fear prevail.

Others said: When committing a sin, the aspect of fear should prevail, and why? So that he refrains; for if the aspect of hope prevailed, he would say: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, and I hope Allah will forgive me, and he commits the sin. And when performing an act of obedience, the aspect of hope should prevail: that Allah the Exalted accepts it from him and rewards him, so that he does not despair. He said: What indicates this is such as the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Call upon Allah while you are certain of being answered" [[Recorded by at-Tirmidhi (3479) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Likewise, worship Allah while you are hoping that He will accept from you.

In any case, this view, in my opinion, is the most preponderant of the views: that when a person is in the state of worship and performing acts of worship, hope should prevail. This does not mean he is certain of acceptance; for Allah says: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun 60], meaning fearful that it will not be accepted from them. Rather, the meaning is that hope prevails along with fear. As for the state of committing sin, fear should prevail, so that he does not proceed to it relying on hope.

In any case, we have digressed a little, but our purpose is that the noble Qur'an mentions both of these, so that the person's course may be balanced.

He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert (qī'ah)﴾ (plural of qā', meaning in a wasteland; it is a shimmer seen there at midday in intense heat, resembling flowing water). This is an explanation of the mirage; and qī'ah is the wasteland. I think you all know the mirage: in intense heat, when you are in a wasteland of the earth. (qī'ah) means the plural of (qā'), unlike sandy terrain where this does not occur; rather, the qī'ān appear from afar as if there were water on that side, so one thinks it is water and heads toward it. These disbelievers' deeds are like this: like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one takes for water, though it is not water. How so? Because they say: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ [az-Zumar 3], ﴿and they say: These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 18]. They think that this shirk, which in reality distances them from Allah, is what?
* Students: It brings them near.
* The Shaykh: It brings them near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They think these intercessors are the ones who will disown them: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah 166]. They think them to be what?
* Students: Intercessors.
* The Shaykh: They think them to be intercessors. And you know that when the soul attaches itself to a thing as an intercessor or as something that brings it near to Allah, does it follow it or not? It follows it without doubt. These are like the mirage in the level desert.

(﴿He whom the thirsty one thinks to be water﴾: ﴿thinks﴾ means supposes; ﴿the thirsty one﴾ means the parched one; ﴿water﴾.) This is an eloquent simile: meaning that he heads toward it with intense eagerness, believing that it will rescue him. The parched one needs water, does he not? So when he sees something resembling water, he heads toward it with intense eagerness. And why? In order to relieve his necessity with it. Does he think it benefits him or not? Yes, he thinks it benefits him; and were it not that he thought it would benefit him, he would not have gone to it. But the outcome: ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, he finds it to be nothing of what he supposed; when he comes to it, he finds nothing. What do you imagine his state to be then? Immense disappointment, may Allah protect us; no one can imagine it. A thirsty person came to this mirage from afar. And note also that the mirage does not appear in nearby places; in the distance, the farther you see it. From a distant place he wants to drink, and the outcome is that he finds nothing of what he supposed.

The author says: (Likewise the disbeliever thinks that his deed is like charity that will benefit him; until, when he dies and comes before his Lord, he finds his deed to be nothing, meaning it did not benefit him. ﴿And finds Allah with him﴾, meaning with his deed, ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾, meaning He recompenses him for it in this world. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, meaning in recompense.)

This disbeliever thinks his deed benefits him. The author's illustration of this with charity is open to scrutiny, because it should be (...); that is, unless by this he intended to give an example. If he intended an example, then it is correct: this is among the deeds that the disbelievers perform, thinking they benefit them while they do not. But it should be said that it is more general than that: it is not only charity; even the worship of idols they think beneficial. What do they think?
* Students: That they benefit them.
* The Shaykh: That they benefit them: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ [az-Zumar 3], ﴿they say: These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus 18]. Yet all of this does not benefit them; they will not find anything of what they suppose and reckon.

As for His saying: ﴿And finds Allah with him﴾: with what? With this mirage? Because he has now reached death; when he dies, he has met Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾. This is the apparent context.

As for the author's view, which makes (﴿And finds Allah with him﴾, meaning with his deed) a consequence of His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, because (those who disbelieve) is general, it is as if He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the disbeliever: his deed is such and such, ﴿like a mirage in a level desert; the thirsty one thinks it water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with it﴾, meaning with that deed, according to His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds﴾, ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾. But the apparent meaning of the verse is that the pronouns refer to what?
* A student: To the nearest antecedent.
* The Shaykh: To the nearest antecedent, which is this thirsty one who reached the water thirsty and found nothing, and so he will perish.

﴿And finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. ﴿His account﴾ means the recompense for his deed. His saying: ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ means the recompense. What is meant by swiftness here? Is it meant as the nearness of the time of recompense, so the swiftness is temporal; or is it meant as the completion of the reckoning, so the swiftness is in action; or both? ﴿Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: does the meaning that He is swift in His reckoning, or that His reckoning of the servants is near?
* A student: It may be either.
* The Shaykh: It may be all of them. The reckoning is near, even if it seems long to a person in this world; it is near. ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [an-Nisa' 77]. Likewise, when Allah reckons all creatures on the Day of Resurrection, He reckons them in half a day, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day will be better in resting place and finer in place of repose﴾ [al-Furqan 24]. The scholars inferred from this that they will take their midday rest in their dwellings during half of that day. But in any case, the day to which Allah pointed is of a measure of fifty thousand years; and whatever the case, Allah is capable of what is even more eloquent than that. Nevertheless, this is a great swiftness and an extreme power, even if the fifty thousand years were twenty-five thousand years: all creatures, from first to last, human, jinn, birds and others, in half a day.

Now, if a person were to reckon with someone he deals with for a year, how long would it remain if the reckoning were exact and extensive? It would remain for a period; and the reckoning may be precise or may not be precise. But the reckoning of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, despite its swiftness, does not leave behind any small or great thing without counting it.

This is an example of a disbeliever who performs a deed wishing to draw near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Or another example: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea﴾ [an-Nur 40]. (Or) here is not for doubt, beyond any doubt, why? Because Allah, glorified and exalted, is free of doubt; doubt arises only from the deficiency of a person's knowledge, or the deficiency of the knower's knowledge. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His knowledge is vast; so it is not possible for Allah, glorified and exalted, to say: the deeds of those who disbelieve are either like this or like that, by way of doubt, as you might say, for example: I saw this thing and it resembles such and such or such and such. This cannot be said of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus (or) in His saying ﴿or like darkness﴾ is for variety: meaning, or their deeds are like darkness, and so on.

(﴿Or﴾: the disbelievers' evil deeds, ﴿like darkness in a deep sea﴾, deep; ﴿covered by waves, above it waves﴾, meaning the waves; ﴿above it waves﴾, meaning the second wave; ﴿above it clouds﴾, meaning cloud. These are ﴿darkness, some above others﴾: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the first wave, the darkness of the second, and the darkness of the cloud.) Four darknesses. (﴿When he brings out﴾, meaning the observer, ﴿his hand﴾ into these darknesses, ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾, meaning he does not come close to seeing it; ﴿and whomever Allah has not given light, for him there is no light﴾, meaning whomever He does not guide, he is not guided.)

This is a second category of disbelievers. The first is the state of the disbeliever who strives, thinking his deed benefits him; this second is the state of the blind follower who does not know that he walks in darkness together with the disbelievers, while he does not know it.

﴿Like darkness in a deep sea﴾: the sea is well known, and lujji means deep; and the deeper the sea, the more intense its darkness. Also ﴿covered by waves﴾: ﴿covered﴾ means overspread; a wave covers this disbeliever, ﴿above it waves﴾, also high waves, ﴿above it clouds﴾.

﴿Waves above waves﴾: what is the boundary of the second wave from the first?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: At the sea?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, I mean its height; for in reality it becomes darker the higher it rises. ﴿Above it waves﴾: water.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where is this?
* The student: From the cloud.
* The Shaykh: The cloud is above; no, I mean ﴿waves above it waves﴾.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, waves. But what prevents it from being the second wave, and what distinguishes it from the first wave?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Good. This is one possibility: that it be by direction, meaning they meet; one comes from here, and the second, higher than it, comes from another direction, so that the height of this over that becomes clear. Or they are successive waves; for example, a wave approaching (...) the mountains, and behind it another wave higher than it; when it overtakes it, there is a wave above it. But if it is a single wave, it cannot precede part of itself. Whoever has seen the sea finds it so: you find successive waves; sometimes, when the wind reverses, they meet head-on, and sometimes they follow one another. But these successive waves, too, you find, glory be to Allah the Mighty, sometimes like steps, meaning one above another. This is what Allah, glorified and exalted, struck as the example.

﴿Above it clouds﴾: clouds in reality are in levels in the atmosphere; we do not suppose they are in one layer. No; they are in very distant layers. A person knows this when he rides an aircraft: he sometimes finds a cloud between himself and the aircraft from below, as far as between the cloud and the earth, and a cloud above it, as far between himself and it as between the aircraft and the earth, while he is between them. This is a known, observed matter. So the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that His saying ﴿above it clouds﴾ is like His saying ﴿above it waves﴾: meaning that the cloud almost clings to these waves. Among this is fog; there is no doubt that fog comes close to the surface of the sea.
* A student: Is it not (...) far from the sea (...), which may obstruct the view (...) whether it is near or...?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it may be; whether it is near.
* The student: (...) so it creates darkness, or near sunset, then it is with it.
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt, but which of them is more intense?
* The student: When it is near.
* The Shaykh: When it is near, it is more intense. It is also possible that by the cloud is meant what includes fog, for the reality is that fog is a cloud, since it spreads along the ground. When this is clear, the darkness becomes very evident because of its abundance.

﴿Darkness, some above others﴾: the amplification in this example; it would have sufficed to say ﴿above it clouds﴾, but for the sake of magnifying it in the soul and showing its greatness, He said ﴿darkness, some above others﴾.

Then He struck an example, saying: ﴿When he brings out his hand, he almost cannot see it﴾. What is closer to you than something? The hand is closer to you than the moving limbs that can be seen; they may come out or may not come out. When you bring out your hand, ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾. What is your opinion: does the meaning of ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾ mean he sees it with difficulty, or he does not see it?
* A student: He sees it.
* Another student: He does not see it.
* The Shaykh: He does not see it. Now, ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 71]: did they slaughter it or not?
* Students: They slaughtered it.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* A student: He sees it.
* The Shaykh: He sees it with difficulty?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The grammarians roughly say: the affirmation of (kāda) is negation and its negation is affirmation. So when you say: "I did not almost do it," it means: I did it, but after great delay. And ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾ according to this rule means: he saw it, but after a great distance and the difficulty of seeing. However, the apparent meaning, as other grammarians said, is that (kāda) is like other verbs: its negation is negation and its affirmation is affirmation; but it means (qāraba), "approached." So if you say: "kadtu af'al," meaning: I approached doing it. Did you do it or not?
* A student: I did not do it.
* The Shaykh: You did not do it, but you approached it. Has the approach been affirmed or negated now? The approach has been affirmed, but we know the non-occurrence of the act from the approach. ﴿He almost cannot see it﴾, meaning: he did not approach seeing it, as the author or the commentator said: he did not approach seeing it. Therefore, if he does not approach seeing it, the non-seeing is by all the more reason and more certain, is it not?

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 71], were it not for His saying ﴿they slaughtered it﴾, the verse would not indicate that they slaughtered it. But the meaning of ﴿they slaughtered it﴾ is: after they had been far from slaughtering it, and had not intended it, nor resolved to comply, but had said to their prophet: ﴿Do you take us for a jest?﴾ [al-Baqarah 67], after this distance from the act, and after their requests had been answered, they slaughtered it. Do you understand now? The verse stands as it is.

Also, (kāda), like other verbs, its negation is negation and its affirmation is affirmation; but since it indicates approach, when a man says "kidtu an af'al" ("I almost did"), it means: he did not do it. For the word "approached" indicates the act; that is, "and I did not do it": "lam akud af'al" ("I did not almost do"). If nothing preceding indicates the act, then certainly he did not do it, like the saying of 'Umar: "I did not almost pray the 'Asr until the sun almost set"; meaning: I did not approach praying the 'Asr. So did he pray it or not?
* A student: He prayed it.

The Shaykh: No, he did not pray it. "I was not even about to pray the 'Asr until the sun was nearly setting"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (596) and Muslim (631 / 209), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]]. That is, he had not come close to praying the 'Asr until the sun came close to setting. When the sun came close to setting, he came close to the 'Asr prayer. He prayed it only after sunset, together with the Prophet (ﷺ). But at the beginning, it was as if he had not been able even to get ready to come close to the prayer, let alone to pray it. The meaning is that he was occupied. The unbelievers kept him busy until the sun was close to setting, so he did not even come close to praying. Coming close to a prayer, my brothers, means getting ready for it. He is saying: he did not get ready, and there was no readiness for the prayer, until the sun was about to set. For this reason, he prayed the 'Asr with the Prophet (ﷺ) after the sun had set.

The conclusion, then, is that the correct view differs from what some of the grammarians (al-nuhat, Arabic grammarians) said: that the affirmative of (كاد, kada, "to almost") is a negation and its negation is an affirmation. Rather, the correct view is that (كاد) is like other verbs. And what is "like other verbs"? Its affirmation is an affirmation and its negation is a negation. But it means "approaching" (al-muqarabah), which is why the grammarians counted it among the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah). Whoever denies that a thing was approached has certainly not done it, and whoever affirms that he approached it has also certainly not done it, because the phrase "I approached the act" means "and I did not do it." That is its meaning.

So if one says, "He almost did not do such-and-such," and nothing has preceded that indicates he did it, then he did not do it. But if something has preceded that indicates he did it, such as ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:71], which means: "So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it," then this shows that before the slaughter they were far from complying and were hardly about to do it. Yet after insistence, and after they said, "Make it clear to us," and it was made clear as they asked, they were answered afterwards. For this reason, in reality, this is an example which a person should take as a lesson for himself: when he is commanded to do a thing, he should not (...) upon himself, going beyond this and that, because this is dangerous. Allah the Mighty and Sublime has said: ﴿وَنُقَلِّبُ أَفْئِدَتَهُمْ وَأَبْصَارَهُمْ كَمَا لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهِ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ وَنَذَرُهُمْ فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ [al-An'am 6:110]. For this reason, when a Muslim knows the Shari'ah, he must submit. There is no harm afterwards in what he commits himself to as being bound by it. There is no harm afterwards in his seeking to learn the wisdom, because asking about the wisdom does not contradict submission. But the important thing is, and what is important? That he submits first, and does not raise objections and doubts, asking "Why this? Why that?" Then after that, he may ask if he wishes.

(...) It has preceded that Allah, glorified and exalted, explained that the deeds of the unbelievers are of two types: one type is like a mirage in a level desert (qi'ah), which the thirsty man thinks is water, and another type is like darkness in a deep sea. This division and this variety are in terms of the condition of the unbelievers. The first, Allah knows best, is for the one who has understanding and effort, and the second is for the one who has ignorance and error, like the common people (...).

A mirage in a qi'ah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, what is it?
* Student: The wasteland of the earth.
* Shaykh: The wasteland of the earth. (Al-qa'ah) is the plural of (qa') and it is the wasteland of the earth, meaning the wide, distant land which is in a qa' (...). Qa' or not? (...) Al-qa': the low-lying land.
What is the mirage (al-sarab)?
* Student: The mirage is (...).
* Shaykh: As if it were water (...).
What is the point of resemblance between the deeds of these unbelievers and this mirage?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He finds that it betrays him at the moment he needs it most.

What some of the grammarians said, that the negation of (كاد) is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation, is it correct or incorrect?

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. I understood (...). They say: did they not do it? Yes, but their doing it is not known from His saying ﴿وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾. From where do we know the act?

* Shaykh: ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا﴾. That is, were it not for His saying ﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا﴾, we would not understand that they slaughtered it. We would understand that they did not slaughter it and did not come close to slaughtering it. So there is no evidence in the verse. When you say, "I almost did such-and-such," it means you did not come close to doing it, and if you did not come close to doing it, you did not do it. But if there is a clue indicating your doing it, then this clue is what indicates the act. If you say, "I reached the town, and I almost did not arrive," this indicates your arrival. But it is not (...). Yet the fact that you arrived at the town... If you say, "I traveled to the town and I almost did not arrive," what happens? Would he be arriving?

So ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾, if he brings out his hand in these darknesses, "he could scarcely see it." What is the meaning of ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا﴾? He did not come close to seeing it, and if he did not come close to seeing it, then he did not see it.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُورًا فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:40], "And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light." That is: the one to whom Allah has not granted light has no light.
(﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, "for him there is no light," means: whoever Allah does not guide, will not be guided.)

The author here made the light a spiritual light, that is: whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with knowledge and faith, no one can illuminate his heart; ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾.

Like these verses which Allah, glorified and exalted, mentions: "Whoever Allah guides, none can misguide him, and whoever He misguides, none can guide him"[[Related by Muslim (867 / 45), from the hadith of Jabir, and (868 / 46), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and the like. What is their purpose? Is their purpose to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, as they used them as evidence, or is the purpose something else?
The answer, certainly: their purpose is not to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, because the doctrine of the Jabriyyah is false, refuted by the sound Shari'ah, the intellect, and the natural disposition. Rather, the purpose of these is that a person should not rely on himself, and should always turn to Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, seeking guidance, seeking light, seeking success, and so on. Otherwise, it is known that Allah does not establish a false matter which the intellect and the senses refute. In any case, Allah the Mighty and Sublime says: if Allah does not give a person light by which he is guided, then he has no light. And what sentence did He use? A nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah), which indicates what? Permanence and continuity: ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾. And He emphasized the negation of light from him with the extra ﴿مِنْ﴾ in His saying ﴿مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, because ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra and ﴿نُورٍ﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar); that is, he has no light.

So we know from this that Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and whoever Allah gives light is upon light from his Lord, and whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light. And from where will light come to him when Allah has veiled light from him!

But know also that Allah's veiling light from the servant is not a withholding of His bounty, may He be blessed and exalted, for He is the Possessor of great bounty. Giving is more beloved to Him than withholding, and guidance is more beloved to Him than misguidance. Rather, it is because the person himself is the one who prevented this light from himself. Recite the saying of Allah: ﴿فَلَمَّا زَاغُوا أَزَاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ [al-Saff 61:5], and recite the saying of Allah: ﴿فَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾, meaning: turned away from the truth and withdrew from it, ﴿فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُصِيبَهُمْ بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:49]. It becomes clear to you that Allah's misguiding the servant and veiling light from him is because of himself, which is what, may Allah protect us, has not been guided. In any case, this verse indicates that a person should, indeed must, always turn to Allah by asking Him to illuminate his heart, because ﴿مَنْ لَمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُورًا فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾ is the explicit meaning (mantuq) of the verse. The implicit meaning (mafhum) of the verse is: whoever Allah grants light, no one can veil that light of Allah, the Mighty and Sublime from him. So the noble verse indicates two matters: one explicit (mantuq) and the second implicit (mafhum). The explicit?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The one from whom Allah has veiled light...
* Student: Because of himself.
* Shaykh: No, (because of himself) is not from the verse; we restricted it by that. ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ﴾, and we said: it used a nominal sentence, which indicates what?
* Students: Continuity.
* Shaykh: Permanence and continuity. And it emphasized the negation of light from him by what? By the extra ﴿مِنْ﴾, because the extra (min) indicates generality. This is the explicit meaning of the verse.
Its implicit meaning: whoever Allah grants light, no one can veil it from him, so no barrier stands between him and His light, may He be blessed and exalted.

Then He said: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Nur 24:41], "Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾: the hamzah is the interrogative particle entering upon a negation, and when the interrogative enters upon a negation, it conveys affirmation (al-taqrir), like: ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1], "Did We not expand for you your breast?", meaning: We have expanded your breast for you.
﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ means: you have indeed seen. So the interrogative hamzah entering upon a negation conveys affirmation, that is, affirming what was mentioned, not negating it. For example, Allah (...) said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾.
(...) it has no connection to the will of Allah in it, to the point that some of them denied knowledge. Their extremists denied Allah's knowledge and said: Allah, glorified and exalted, does not know the deeds of the servant until after he does them; before that, He does not know. Glory be to Him, and they denied the sound and explicit texts establishing Allah's knowledge of everything, even the deeds of man.
* Also in it, His saying ﴿بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾ [al-Nur 24:38], "without reckoning": the abundance of Allah's provision, the Mighty and Sublime, and that He, glorified and exalted, gives without reckoning. And the meaning of "without reckoning" is not "without measure." Why do we not say that?

* Shaykh: No, because Allah says: ﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ عِنْدَهُ بِمِقْدَارٍ﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:8], "everything with Him is by measure." Even the drop that falls from the sky to the earth is measured with Allah, glorified and exalted. But ﴿بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾ means that He does not reward the person by reckoning, but with abundant, copious abundance (...).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light.﴾ That is: whoever Allah has not granted light, there is no light for him.

(﴿For him there is no light﴾: that is, whoever Allah does not guide, will not be guided.)

The author here takes "light" to be spiritual light; that is, whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with knowledge and faith, no one can illuminate his heart: ﴿for him there is no light﴾.

Like these verses that Allah the Exalted mentions, "Whomever Allah guides, none can misguide him, and whomever He misguides, none can guide him"[[Related by Muslim (867/45) from the hadith of Jabir, and (868/46) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and what is similar to that. What is the purpose of them? Is the purpose of them to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah (determinists), as they have used them as evidence, or is the purpose something else?

The answer, with certainty: the purpose is not to establish the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, because the doctrine of the Jabriyyah is false, refuted by the sound religious sense, reason, and the fitrah (innate human nature). Rather, the purpose is that a person should not rely upon himself, and that he should always turn to Allah the Exalted in seeking guidance, seeking light, seeking success, and so on. Otherwise, it is known that Allah the Exalted does not establish a false matter that reason and the senses refute. In any case, Allah the Exalted says: if Allah has not granted a person light by which to be guided, then for him there is no light. He brought the nominal sentence, which indicates what? It indicates permanence and continuity: ﴿for him there is no light﴾. He emphasized the negation of light from him with the added ﴿min﴾ in His words ﴿min nurin﴾, because ﴿min﴾ is extra (zaa'idah), and ﴿nur﴾ is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar); that is, "there is no light for him."

So from this we know that Allah the Exalted is the One who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and that whoever Allah gives light is upon light from his Lord, and whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light. And from where would light come to him when Allah has withheld light from him!

But know also that Allah's withholding light from the servant is not a denial of His grace, blessed and exalted is He, for He is the possessor of great bounty. Giving is more beloved to Him than withholding, and guidance is more beloved to Him than misguidance. Rather, it is because the person himself has prevented this light from himself. Recite the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5]. And recite the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, from the truth and turn away from it, ﴿then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. It becomes clear to you that Allah's misguiding the servant and withholding light from him is because of himself; it is he who, may Allah protect us, did not become guided.

In any case, this verse indicates that a person should, indeed must, always turn to Allah, asking Him to illuminate his heart, because ﴿whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light﴾ is the explicit meaning (manṭūq) of the verse. Its implicit meaning (mafhūm) is: whoever Allah grants light, no one can withhold His light from him. So the noble verse indicates two matters: one explicit (manṭūq) and the other implicit (mafhūm). The explicit?

* Student: Because of himself.

* The Shaykh: No, (because of himself) is not from the verse; we restricted it by that. ﴿For him there is no light.﴾ And we said: He brought the nominal sentence, which indicates what?

* The students: Continuity.

* The Shaykh: Permanence and continuity. And He emphasized the negation of light from him with what? With the extra ﴿min﴾, because the extra "min" conveys generality. This is the explicit meaning of the verse.

Its implicit meaning: whoever Allah grants light, no one can withhold it from him, so there is no one who can block His light, blessed and exalted is He, from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 41:

Then He said: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [An-Nur 41]. ﴿Have you not seen﴾: the hamzah is an interrogative particle entering upon a negation, and when the interrogative enters upon a negation it conveys affirmation (taqrir); like His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded for you your breast.

﴿Have you not seen﴾ means: you have indeed seen. When the hamzah of interrogation enters upon a negation it conveys affirmation; that is, it affirms what is mentioned and does not negate it. Allah said to His Prophet ﷺ, for example: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ What is the meaning of ﴿Did We not expand﴾? It means: We have indeed expanded for you your breast. Allah, exalted is He, affirms that He expanded the breast of the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿Have you not known that Allah knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al-Hajj 70]. What is its meaning? It means: you have indeed known.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah is glorified by﴾ means: you have indeed seen.

And regarding His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾, is the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ or to everyone who can be addressed?

* A student: To everyone.

* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning is generality; "Have you not seen, O addressee," not "O Prophet," because that is more comprehensive and general.

And regarding His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah is glorified by Him﴾, is this seeing visual or cognitive?

* The students: Cognitive.

* The Shaykh: If you make it visual, this seeing becomes restricted to what is done, not to what is said or known by reason. If you make it cognitive, it includes what is known through speech, through sight, and through the mind. Then which of the two is preferable?

* The students: Cognitive.

* The Shaykh: That it be cognitive; that is: have you not known; whether your knowledge is through observation by sight, or through hearing by ear, or through inference by reason and thought. Therefore we say: what is meant by seeing here is, what? Knowledge; have you not known, whether this knowledge is from what?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: From seeing with the eye, or hearing with the ear, or inference by reason and thought. These three are the means of knowledge, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned﴾ [Al-Isra 36].

So: have you not known, with knowledge resulting from these three matters or from one of them, that Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens and the earth.

(And among the glorification is prayer.) Is it so in your copies, "ṣalāh" indefinite?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Glorifies Him whoever﴾: He used ﴿man﴾, which is for rational beings, because glorification is more evident among rational beings than among non-rational ones. This glorification includes glorification by speech and by state. By speech we say: Subhan Allah. By state: when you reflect upon His creation and what it has been made to do, you know thereby that Allah, exalted is He, is free from futility and from deficiencies. This is called glorification by what? By state.

If we say glorification by speech, it is known that the disbeliever does not glorify Allah by his speech; that is, he does not say: Subhan Allah. Because he attributes defects to Allah and sets up partners with Him. But he glorifies Allah by his state: his state, what he has been made to be, and his turning away from the truth despite its clarity, and what is similar to that, all of it indicates the glorification of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and His wisdom.

And regarding His saying ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, does it include the angels or not?

* The students: It includes them.

* The Shaykh: It includes the angels. We do not know the glorification of the angels through sight; rather through revelation that is conveyed by hearing. We heard from our Prophet ﷺ that the angels glorify Allah, and we heard the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that the angels glorify Allah, and so on.

* * *

He said: (﴿And the birds﴾ is the plural of ṭā'ir, that which is between the sky and the earth. ﴿In flight, spreading their wings﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); spreading their wings.)

And ﴿and the birds﴾ is conjoined to what? To ﴿man﴾; that is: and the birds glorify Him. And ﴿in flight﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the birds; that is, they too glorify Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in the state of their ranks in flight; that is, the arranging of their wings, that is, their spreading.

Is this glorification by state or by speech?

* A student: By state.

* The Shaykh: We know it as by state, but it may also be by speech; perhaps in the state of extending and spreading their wings they glorify Allah, because birds have speech. Allah said: ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ [An-Naml 16]. So everything speaks, even the pebbles speak, and "the glorification of pebbles has been heard in the presence of the Messenger ﷺ"[[Narrated by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (4040), and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Awsat (1244), from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. Everything glorifies. Indeed, Allah said in another verse: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but that it glorifies [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [Al-Isra 44]. Here He said: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth and the birds in flight glorify Him﴾, and He did not mention the heavens, and did not generalize as in His saying ﴿And there is not a thing﴾; because there He said ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾, whereas here He said ﴿Have you not seen that Allah is glorified﴾, thereby affirming our knowledge of this glorification; and it is not all-encompassing as in the second verse.

As for the glorification of the birds in flight by the tongue of speech, this we do not know; but by the tongue of state we know it. Their ranks in the air between the sky and the earth, their not falling, their direction right and left, and the winds with their violence not preventing them from what they intend; this indicates the perfection of Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic is He.

The winds that shake mountains and vehicles do not prevent the bird from its direction; it heads against the winds, and this is observed, and it is not bothered. This is from the completeness of Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic is He. This small weak bird, which the wind may carry if it is moving, the winds do not turn back; this is from the completeness of Allah's power.

And from the completeness of power also: you find it in the cold, biting winter days, you find it flying between the sky and the earth with this speed and above, and it is not affected by this cold. All of that is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power.

Then, greater than this, He said: (﴿Each has known﴾ [His] ﴿prayer and glorification﴾; ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾.)

﴿Each has known﴾: ﴿known﴾ is a past verb; in it is a hidden pronoun referring to whom?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: The author's words: it refers to Allah; ﴿Have you not seen that Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens and the earth and the birds in flight, each has known﴾, that is: Allah has known ﴿its prayer and its glorification﴾. This is what the author held.

The second opinion: the subject of ﴿known﴾ refers to ﴿whoever﴾ and what is conjoined to it; that is: ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth and the birds in flight glorify Him, each﴾ of these glorifiers ﴿has known its prayer and its glorification﴾, meaning that Allah inspired these things so that they know how to glorify Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and how to pray to Him. As for Allah's knowledge of that, it is understood from His saying ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾.

On the author's view there is something like repetition in the verse: ﴿each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ and ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾. This sentence is the first on the author's view. Therefore the correct view is that His saying ﴿each has known﴾ means: each of these glorifiers has himself known his prayer and his glorification. By what did they know?

As for humans, and likewise the jinn, they knew through the messengers; Allah sent the messengers to teach people how to pray and how to glorify Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for beasts and other animals, they knew their prayer and glorification through what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inspired in them, and each of them has a particular prayer and glorification. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said, on the tongue of Musa in reply to Pharaoh: ﴿Who is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ He said: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation and then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha 49-50]. This guidance, just as it includes guidance to the matters that preserve their bodies, may also include guidance to what Allah, glorified and exalted is He, inspired them of glorification and prayer. So the correct view is that the subject in ﴿known﴾ refers to whom?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: To the one glorifying.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. As for Allah's knowledge of what they did:

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this is understood from His saying: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾. He said: (it contains the predominance of the rational).

﴿And Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾: the author says: (it contains the predominance of the rational). What do you say? Because ﴿they do﴾ has the waw for rational beings, and it is known that "whoever is in the heavens" includes the rational and others; but the verse gives predominance to the rational in both the first and the second: ﴿whoever﴾ in ﴿glorifies Him whoever﴾ is for rational beings, and likewise ﴿they do﴾ is for rational beings; so there is in it the predominance of the rational. The reason for this, and Allah knows best, is that glorification and prayer are more evident in the rational than in the non-rational, therefore the rational was given predominance. Otherwise, non-rational beings on earth are more numerous than the rational, (...) animals and insects.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, except when evidence indicates that it is in the tongue of speech; such as one who says: Subhan Allah, one who glorifies Allah, and what is similar to that; this is by the tongue of speech, like one who glorifies Allah thirty-three times after the prayer.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This is like how sometimes something is mentioned after the general, and sometimes the general is mentioned after it, which indicates that prayer is among the most important acts. But glory be to Allah the Mighty! Look, even animals pray: ﴿each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾. But we do not know their number; whether their prayer is like ours or differs. The point is that they have a prayer and a glorification, but it is particular to them; Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has taught them how to pray and how to glorify, and they have known their prayer and their glorification.

(Verse 42 of Surah al-Nur, with the commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin.)

Ibn 'Uthaymin: "Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return.﴾"

(﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: the treasuries of rain, provision, and vegetation.) (...).

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ First: His saying ﴿lillah﴾ ("to Allah") is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿mulk﴾ ("dominion") is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). It is known from the rule that fronting something whose proper place is to come later conveys restriction (hasr). The rule among the scholars is that when something whose proper place is to be postponed is fronted, this indicates the restriction of the postponed element to the fronted one; that is, restricting the postponed to the fronted. ﴿Iyyaka na'budu﴾ (“You alone we worship”): what does it mean?

* Student: It means: we worship none but You.

* Shaykh: It means: we worship none but You. ﴿Wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾ ("and You alone we ask for help"): we ask for help from none but You. So when something whose proper place is to be postponed is fronted, that is evidence for restricting the thing to it.

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: based on this rule, what do you understand? That the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to whom?

* Student: To Allah.

* Shaykh: Alone, or with something else besides Him?

* Student: Alone.

* Shaykh: Alone. From the restriction, ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾.

His saying ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ encompasses both ownership of the entities and control of their affairs. So ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ — their substances belong to Allah, and the disposal and management also belong to whom? To Allah. To restrict this to the treasuries of provision, vegetation, and rain has no basis whatsoever. Allah the Exalted has the dominion of the heavens and the earth in creation and governance; the substances and the disposal belong to Allah alone. This is shown by the order in them, their lack of disturbance, and their lack of contradiction. For this reason Allah the Glorified argued for His oneness with His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ — that is correct; as long as there is a god, he must have his own dominion alone. And ultimately, ﴿some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun 91]. If some overcame others, then to whom would divinity belong? To the one who prevails, without doubt. We see with certainty that creation is not distinguished by one part over another, and that the upper and lower worlds are all a single unity, one solid mass, some of which is subjected to others, completing one another, not contradicting or repelling one another. Therefore reason and observation are two proofs of the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Furthermore, the multiplicity of gods is impossible; one of them must prevail. For if they opposed each other — this is a very well-known rational proof — and each was unable to overcome the other, what would become of them? They would not deserve divinity, and (...) a lord; as long as each is incapable, the Lord cannot be incapable. And if one of them overcame the other, he alone would be the Lord and God. Therefore there must be one God; for either one prevails, and divinity belongs to him, or both are incapable, and then neither is fit to be lord, because the Lord must be capable. This is among the clearest and most evident proofs.

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ If someone says: Does not Allah say, ﴿except from their spouses or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 6], and say, ﴿And those who seek a writing from among those whom your right hands possess, write it for them﴾? So He affirms ownership to humans, while you say that the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusive to Allah, based on the restriction. How then is the reconciliation?

The answer: This ownership is restricted, not absolute. And who granted you ownership? Allah is the One who made you own this thing, within a limited measure as well. If you own this recorder, for example, you own it, sell it, buy it, and benefit from it; this is clear. But do you own the right to break it?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. With respect to created beings, you own it; but with respect to Allah, you do not own it. It is not permissible for you to break it, because you are forbidden by Allah. But does Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have the power to destroy whoever is upon the earth or not?

Yes: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature﴾ [Fatir 45]. Thus it becomes clear that my ownership of a thing comes from where? From Allah; it is He who made me own it. That is one point. The second: it is a limited, restricted ownership. On this basis there is no contradiction between what Allah affirmed for the human of ownership and what He affirmed for Himself of exclusive dominion. Clear? For this reason some scholars said: Every thing whose ownership is attributed to a human is by way of metaphor (majaz), not by way of reality (haqiqah), because the owner in reality is who? Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. I am an owner metaphorically, because I do not dispose of this thing except as I have been commanded or permitted; I do not dispose of it in absolute terms.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾: the return).

This contains an indication that He, the Glorified and Exalted, is the owner of the first and the last: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ at the beginning, and ﴿to Allah is the final return﴾ at the end.

And in it — Allah knows best — is an indication that since the dominion belongs to Allah and the return is to Him, it is not lawful for us to dispose of things except according to what? What has been legislated for us. As long as we are owned by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic — we are now owned by Allah, are we not? And our return is to whom? To Allah. So as long as we are His possession and our return is to Him, it is obligatory that we do not dispose of anything except where He has legislated for us, because as long as you know that you belong to Him, it is He who governs you: do this, do not do that. And as long as you also know that your return is to Him, you must prepare for that return, for He will call you to account.

And His saying ﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾ also contains what is in His saying ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Good. But ﴿to Allah is the final return﴾ [al-Nur 42]: what is the grammatical position of ﴿ila Allah﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: A fronted predicate, and ﴿al-masir﴾ is a postponed subject. Fronting what should be postponed conveys restriction. Anything whose proper place is to come later, when you front it, means you want what follows it to be restricted to it. So the return is to Allah. However much a person soars, however far he roams in imagination and thought, and however long he remains in this world, his return is to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 223]; ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet it﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]. Meeting Allah the Mighty and Majestic and returning to Him is a necessary, inevitable matter, just as our existence is from Allah, so too our end is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿al-masir﴾ does not mean only the return of people in the Hereafter, but the return of all matters; that is, the return to Allah in everything. Everything returns to Allah, and He, the Glorified and Exalted, is the one who governs and does as He wills.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 43:

Then he said: (﴿Have you not considered that Allah drives the clouds gently?﴾ [An-Nur: 43] — drives it gently).

﴿Have you not considered﴾ — also, to whom is the address? To every addressee: "Have you not considered, O addressee?" And is "tara" (ترى) here in the sense of sight (baṣariyyah) and not knowledge ('ilmiyyah)?

* Student: Sight (baṣariyyah).

* The Shaykh: I do not know. If we say it is so, its meaning is that the blind man does not know anything; its meaning is that he did not take a lesson from this cloud, because he does not see it.

Why did we not say "knowledge"? Because the sense of knowledge includes the sense of sight. That is: "Do you not know?" whether that is through observation or through hearing. So we leave it as "you know" in the sense of knowledge: ﴿tara﴾ means "you know."

(﴿that Allah drives clouds﴾ — drives it gently). Someone says: "drives it." He did not restrict it with "gently." Yes, and perhaps that is better: that we interpret izjā' (إزجاء) as driving, whether gently or not gently, because we observe that clouds sometimes move gently and sometimes move quickly, while being clouds. Al-Mutanabbi says — I think:

"And of the good is the slowness of your gift toward me, / The swiftest of clouds in motion is the barren one (al-jahām)."

The one that has no water.
* * *
(...) Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh: 1]. It is for affirmation (taqrir); that is: We have indeed expanded it for you. Likewise, whenever the interrogative particle enters a negation, it becomes for affirmation of that matter.

Allah, Exalted, says, affirming this visible matter: ﴿Have you not considered that Allah drives clouds﴾, and ﴿have you not considered﴾ (ra'a) means knowledge. Our interpreting it as knowledge is more general than interpreting it as visual sight, because it includes a person's seeing with his eyes, since that leads to knowledge; and a person's hearing about it, since that also leads to knowledge; and a person's reading about this matter, since that also leads to knowledge. The key point is that, since the seeing admits of being in the sense of knowledge, interpreting it as knowledge is preferable, because it is more comprehensive and more general.

And the address in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ — is it to the Prophet ﷺ or to everyone who can be addressed?

The apparent meaning is that it is to everyone who can be addressed; that is: "Have you not considered, O addressee, that Allah drives clouds… " to the end, because that is also more comprehensive.

His saying ﴿drives clouds﴾: the author says: (gently). Some exegetes said: "drives it," and did not say "gently," so as to include driving gently and not gently, because the cloud — as is observed — sometimes moves slowly, slowly, and sometimes moves quickly, swiftly.

(﴿Then He joins it together﴾ — gathers its parts to one another and makes scattered pieces one piece).

This too is observed: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, joins these clouds together and gathers some of them to others until they become one large piece. Sometimes He does not join them; the small piece itself expands and becomes a large piece. But joining is more eloquent, because the joined thing is sometimes of a different kind from that with which it is joined. Sometimes there is a white cloud, a red cloud and a black cloud, then they gather and become one color, and this is more eloquent.

After this joining, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿then He makes it piled up﴾ — some of it upon some).

﴿Piled up﴾ means accumulated: some of it upon some. This too is observed with the eye: you find some clouds above others. If you are in an airplane at height, it appears clearly to you: you find some clouds beneath you and some clouds above you. If you are on the ground, it becomes clear that the clouds are upon one another — by what? By some of them covering others.

And how does it cover others?

Look, for example, at a piece passing beneath another piece and passing beyond it, going past it, which indicates that some of it is above some. This piled-up formation has a wondrous appearance when a person is above it, an appearance that delights and gladdens, and therefore Allah, Exalted, made it one of the signs indicating the perfection of His power.

Then (﴿you see the rain﴾ — the rain ﴿coming out from its midst﴾ — its outlets).

﴿You see﴾ here means "you perceive," because rain is seen with the eye, and ﴿coming out from its midst﴾ means from the midst of this cloud.

But is this seeing something a person perceives, or do some people perceive it and not others?

In reality, only a person with strong sight perceives it. But we know that rain descends from the cloud and passes through it. Some scholars said: it is like a sieve; that is, like the sieve with which wheat is sifted and the like; this rain descends (...) from its midst.

From where does the rain come if it descends from its midst?

From the cloud itself: it is pressed out by Allah's permission, then it passes through it. Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And We send down from the squeezing clouds water pouring forth﴾ [An-Naba': 14]. ﴿And We send down from the squeezing clouds﴾ — by Allah's permission it is squeezed and this rain descends. In any case, the natural causes — we do not know anything about them, but this is what we know by sensory sight.

* * *
﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail within it﴾: (in the sky; it is a substitute for "from the sky" by repeating the preposition. ﴿from hail﴾, that is, some of it ﴿so He strikes with it whom He wills...﴾) to the end.
﴿He sends down from the sky mountains within it﴾ — in the sky. Strangely, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is confused about this: at first he said regarding ﴿from mountains﴾: (﴿from﴾ is superfluous). That is, grammatically superfluous, so according to his statement the sense would be: and He sends down from the sky mountains. Then right after he said: (a substitute for "from the sky" by repeating the preposition). What is the substitute? His saying ﴿from mountains﴾, mountains in the sky.

Now, if it is a substitute by repeating the preposition, is ﴿min﴾ in His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ superfluous or not superfluous?

It is not superfluous, because it is for the starting point; ﴿He sends down from the sky﴾ is for the beginning of the extent; that is, to the earth. The meaning in reality is the last meaning he mentioned: that His saying ﴿from mountains﴾ is a substitute for "the sky"; as if he said: He sends down from mountains in the sky. So it is a substitute for the sky by repeating the preposition which is ﴿min﴾, and in this case ﴿min﴾ is not superfluous but is for the starting point; that is, He sends down from the sky to the earth.

From where does He send down from the sky?

He said: ﴿from mountains within it﴾, that is, in the sky.

(﴿from hail﴾, that is, some of it). This is what would have had a basis if he had said that ﴿min﴾ is superfluous, but he made ﴿min﴾ partitive, because he said: (that is, some of it); that is, some of hail, yes, ﴿from mountains within it from hail﴾.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: You do not have "superfluous"?!

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Strange. ﴿from the sky from mountains within it﴾ — you do not have "superfluous"?!

* Students: Superfluous.

* Other students: Connective (ṣilah).

* The Shaykh: Whether it is from the connective or superfluous, the meaning is one; but do you have "connective" or "superfluous"?

In any case "superfluous" or "connective" have the same meaning, but how can it be superfluous or connective when he says: (﴿from mountains﴾ is a substitute for the sky by repeating the preposition)?! It is known that ﴿min﴾ in His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is neither superfluous nor connective, but has a meaning, which is the starting point: the beginning of the extent.

It remains for us to say: ﴿within it from hail﴾ — the pronoun ﴿it﴾ refers to ﴿the sky﴾; that is, mountains in the sky.

As for His saying ﴿from hail﴾, the author intends that ﴿min﴾ be partitive; that is, He sends down some hail from these mountains. It may also be superfluous; that is, ﴿from hail﴾ means hail: He sends down from the sky, from mountains, hail; so ﴿min﴾ is superfluous. It may also be that ﴿min﴾ is for specifying the kind: that the mountains are of hail, mountains of hail, so the mountains themselves are of hail. On this reading it becomes: He sends down from the sky from mountains of hail, and the object of sending down is omitted; that is, He sends down hail. If He sends down from the sky from the mountains that are of hail, then what does He send down? Hail. So the object is omitted, its estimate being: hail.

In any case, what is the object of ﴿sends down﴾ according to the author's opinion? Its object is ﴿from hail﴾, because he said: (that is, some of it), on the basis that ﴿min﴾ is partitive, meaning "some," and on this basis this is the object of ﴿sends down﴾. As for what is sent down from, what is the thing sent down from? ﴿from the sky from mountains﴾: the mountains that are in the sky, because we said that ﴿from mountains﴾ is a substitute for ﴿the sky﴾ by repeating the preposition, so the thing sent down from is these mountains, and the thing sent down is the hail.

On the last possibility we mentioned, that ﴿min﴾ is superfluous, the thing sent down is also hail, but ﴿min﴾ is not partitive.

On the third possibility we said: ﴿min﴾ is for specifying the kind. What is its kind? The kind of the mountains: mountains of hail, that is, He sends down from mountains of hail. What does He send down? Hail. So in this case the thing sent down, which is the object, is omitted, its estimate being: hail, and the context indicates it.

In any case, the meaning of the noble verse is that in the sky there are mountains of hail from which Allah, Exalted, sends down; from these mountains. This sent-down matter is sometimes large and sometimes small, but by Allah's blessing it is not so large as to demolish buildings; this is very rare. Rather it is large enough to kill some crops or some trees, according to Allah's wisdom, Mighty and Majestic. As for demolishing houses and killing human beings, this is rare, though it may occur, but it is rare. In this is evidence of Allah's power, Glorified and Exalted, that these mountains exist in this sky, these mountains of hail, and what descends from them descends by the will of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and His wisdom, upon this earth. For this reason He said: ﴿so He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills﴾.

Is this sentence for showing favour, or for showing punishment: ﴿He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills﴾, or does it admit of both, since "averts" (yaṣrif)?

It may occur to a person that the intended meaning of "striking" in the first part is the striking of punishment, as one says: "Allah averted evil from you" (ṣaraf Allāhu 'anka al-sū'), and as in the hadith: "And avert from me bad character and bad deeds" [[Recorded by Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and recorded by al-Daraqutni (1139) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and the wording is his.]]. So one does not "avert" and one does not express with "averting" except about something disliked. On this basis the sentence ﴿He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills﴾ is led to show the punishment that occurs through this hail.

It may also be that it is in the category of favour, for hail may be good, and by it the land may be watered, trees may grow, and other things. Thus it becomes in the context of favour: He strikes with this hail whom He wills, so he benefits from it, and He averts it from whom He wills, so he misses the benefit.

There is no objection to using "averting" for averting a beneficial thing; there is no objection, although the more common usage is for averting harmful things. But it is also used for averting things that benefit. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that this sentence is suitable for both aspects: the aspect of punishment and the aspect of mercy. Being struck by hail is sometimes a punishment by which crops are destroyed and livestock die, and sometimes it is the opposite.

* * *
(﴿Almost﴾ — nearly ﴿the flash of its lightning﴾ — its brightness ﴿goes near to taking away the sights﴾ of those who look at it; that is, it snatches them away.)
Because of the strength of this lightning, its flash — that is, its brightness — almost takes away the sights. In this there is an indication that clouds in which there is hail have lightning brighter than others, so this lightning, because of its strength, almost takes away the sights. There is no doubt that this lightning is very great, and they have mentioned that in it there is a great quantity of electricity and that this equals such-and-such kilowatts. This matter is a reality; now you find, for example, airplanes that are not as far away as this cloud, and despite the lights in them you can barely see them, but this, as you observe, almost snatches away the sight and fills the earth with light, which indicates the abundance of electrical energy in this lightning, even though it is in Allah's hand, in an instant, as if it were a single stroke. This is the apparent meaning, by way of friction, as it has been mentioned that it is (negative) and (positive), and from their meeting this lightning is produced. And there is no objection — if the hadith is sound — that this is also among the causes of the striking of the angel who drives the cloud [[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (3117) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. If the hadith is sound, it does not contradict what is established from the scientific standpoint concerning this matter, that it is the gathering of (negative) and (positive) by which this brightness occurs; for the gathering of the negative and positive may occur through causes such as the striking of what, the angel's striking, if the hadith is sound about that. So there is no contradiction between this and what came from the Prophet ﷺ, if it is sound: ﴿almost the flash of its lightning goes near to taking away the sights﴾.

So this is among the signs of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, indicating the perfection of His power: the driving of this cloud between heaven and earth, its being mountains of hail, Allah's striking with it whom He wills and averting it from whom He wills. All of that is among the signs of Allah. For this reason Allah, Glorified and Exalted, placed them in the form of an interrogative indicating affirmation.

(﴿God alternates the night and the day﴾: meaning, He brings each of them in place of the other. ﴿Indeed in that alternation﴾ ﴿is a lesson﴾, an indication, ﴿for those of insight﴾ [al-Nur: 44], for those possessed of perception, of God's power.)

His words, ﴿God alternates the night and the day﴾: taqlib (alternation) means changing a thing from one state to another.

Is the alternation meant here the sensory alternation that the author pointed to, meaning that this comes in place of that and that in place of this, or is what is meant more comprehensive, both sensory and figurative alternation?

The answer: Yes, what is meant is more general than the sensory alternation.

The sensory alternation is that God turns the earth from light and day into night, then back into day, and so on.

The figurative alternation is what occurs in these days of events and changes, of honour and victory, of humiliation and abandonment, as God the Exalted says: ﴿And these days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140].

The correct view regarding alternation here is that it is not restricted to the sensory alternation, which is making night in place of day and day in place of night. Rather, it is more general than that and includes the sensory and the figurative.

Among alternation is also the alternation of the seasons, when the night and the day lengthen at one time in winter and at another time in summer. All of this is alternation. The important point is that you must know that this alternation is general to every change that occurs in the night and the day, whether sensory or figurative matters. This is the aspect of the lesson: ﴿Indeed in that alternation is a lesson for those of insight.﴾ "Al-absar" (those of insight) means the possessors of perception, not that "absar" means the sight of the eye. Every possessor of perception knows what the alternation of night and day contains of the power of God the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Say: Have you considered, if God made the night perpetual for you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you light?﴾ [al-Qasas: 71]. If all of creation gathered to make the sun rise at midnight, for example, could they? Can they or can they not? They cannot. And if they all gathered to make the night come at midday, they could not find a way to do so. And if God made the time always night or always day, all of creation could not change this condition. For this reason God made clear His favour upon His servants: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73].

Likewise, what occurs in the night and the day of events and changes of affairs also contains a lesson. For example, you find this kingdom belonging to this man, a complete, full sovereignty and abundant blessings, then that sovereignty turns into humiliation and captivity. And you find these people in honour, victory and establishment, and then suddenly the matter is reversed. All of this is what the intelligent person of insight derives as evidence of God's power over the alternation of affairs and of His wisdom in their management.

His words, ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of insight﴾: If you do not take a lesson from that, and you do not find in yourself any movement in response to this alternation and this change, then know that you are not among those possessed of insight. This is because the speech of God, glorified and exalted, is firm and does not change, and He has informed that in that alternation [there is a lesson]. What is it? A lesson for those of insight. So if there is no lesson for you in that, then know that you are not among the possessors of insight. Therefore you must treat yourself until you reflect upon the lessons in this alternation and take heed from it. Do not think this is merely a phrase uttered, ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of insight﴾, and that is all. What makes a person one of insight? He knows the power and wisdom of God in that. But you must take heed. If you do not take heed yourself, then you are not among the possessors of insight.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has created every moving creature from water﴾ [An-Nur 45], after He mentioned the signs of Allah the Glorified and Exalted in the upper world, He mentioned His sign in the lower world, which is His saying:
(﴿And Allah has created every moving creature﴾, i.e., every animal, ﴿from water﴾, i.e., from a drop of semen).
﴿Created﴾ means brought into existence. ﴿Every moving creature﴾: the dabbah (moving creature) is everything that crawls upon the earth, although it may be customarily applied to those that walk on four legs. He said: the dabbah is that which walks on four. This is the common and customary usage. For this reason, a human being is not called a dabbah in common usage; if a person says to you, "O dabbah!", you may end up quarreling with him. But linguistically, everything that crawls upon the earth is a dabbah. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And there is no moving creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud 6].
As for His saying: ﴿from water﴾, this is the origin of the creation of moving creatures: from water. The author's statement "from a drop of semen" is not correct, because not every moving creature is from a drop of semen; rather every moving creature is from water, whether a drop of semen or otherwise. As for what reproduces sexually, its water is a drop of semen; and as for what is spontaneously generated, its water is moisture.
