That is, these things that are spontaneously generated arise from decay and moisture. As for what reproduces, yes, it reproduces from a drop of semen, which Allah creates from it. So the phrase ﴿from water﴾ is more general than the word "drop of semen," and it is obligatory to keep the verse on its generality, so that it includes what is spontaneously generated and what reproduces. Is that clear?
And this verse is part of His saying: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [Al-Anbiya 30]. Which of them is more general?
* Student: ﴿And We made from water﴾.
* The Shaykh: Because ﴿every living thing﴾ includes animals and non-animals, even trees and the like, from water.
Now, His saying: ﴿from water every living thing﴾. People cite the verse for something other than what Allah intended by it. What do they cite it for?
* Student: Water.
The Shaykh: For the claim that water is essential for the continuation of life. That is not the matter; rather, the verse indicates that the origin of these living things is from water. And if the intended meaning were what people cite it for, He would have said: "And We made from water every thing living," meaning: We made it living by water. But the verse is undoubtedly about the fact that the origin of these living things is water. And from another angle, we say: if their origin is water, then they are in need of it, because its growth too can only occur through water.
﴿And Allah has created every moving creature from water, and of them is that which walks on its belly﴾ [An-Nur 45] (like snakes and insects).
﴿Of them﴾: this specification indicates that the moving creatures referred to are rational beings, ﴿of them﴾. Otherwise, He would have said "of it", meaning of these creatures. However, the scholars said that there is a case of prioritization here: prioritizing whom? The rational beings. For this reason He said ﴿of them﴾, i.e., of these creatures.
﴿That which walks on its belly﴾. Does one who walks on his belly walk or crawl? He crawls, but this walking is crawling, like snakes and insects. What are insects? Snakes are well known, but what are insects?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It appears to me that the author's statement is open to question, because among insects some walk on their bellies, some walk on two legs, and some walk on four. So using them as an example is questionable. As for snakes, yes, they walk on their bellies, and likewise worms such as the sirar and others walk on their bellies.
(﴿And of them is that which walks on two legs﴾, like humans and birds). Humans walk on two legs, and birds walk on two legs. Is there a bird that walks on more than two legs?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes? We do not know; perhaps there is. We do not know. But we know that birds have only two legs.
(﴿And of them is that which walks on four﴾ [An-Nur 45], like beasts and livestock). This is clear. Now, does this division serve to restrict (ḥaṣr) or not? Is it a matter of ḥaṣr or of qaṣr?
* Student: It is qaṣr.
* The Shaykh: It is qaṣr, meaning limiting oneself to some things; because among animals or moving creatures there are some that walk on more than four. Is that not so? There is a creature they call "forty-four legs," which exists, and there are things with fewer; some have six legs, and there are things with more than that. This division is not for ḥaṣr, but for qaṣr, meaning it only mentions some types. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Allah creates what He wills; indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾. ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ means among those mentioned, from walking on the belly, on two legs, on four, or on more than that. No one can restrain Allah the Glorified and Exalted; He creates what He wills according to what His wisdom, blessed and exalted, requires.
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾. Power (qudrah) is an attribute by which the capable one is described, so that he does what he wills without incapacity. This differs from strength (quwwah), by which one does what he wills without weakness. So strength is contrasted with weakness, and power is contrasted with incapacity. Consider His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾ [Ar-Rum 54], and consider His saying: ﴿And Allah is not to be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44].
So He placed power in contrast to incapacity. Because of His power, He is never incapacitated, the Glorified and Exalted. In any case, power is an attribute by which the capable one is described, such that he does what he wills without incapacity.
For example, a man prays standing but with difficulty; what do we say? Is he capable or strong?
* Student: Capable.
* The Shaykh: Capable. And there is a person who prays standing and it does not trouble him; what do we call him?
* Student: Strong.
* The Shaykh: Strong and capable too.
There is a person who lifts this rock as if it were a feather, without trouble; and there is a person who lifts this rock, with effort... The first?
* Student: Strong.
* The Shaykh: Strong. And the second?
* Student: Capable.
* The Shaykh: The second is capable, because he does it but with exertion and hardship; he is capable of lifting.
And there is also a third: when it came from it (...), this one is neither strong nor capable.
As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾ [An-Nur 45], there is a phrase among people; they say: "He is competent over whatever He wills." You should not say this phrase, because if you restrict power by will, a deficiency results; it would mean His power is only over what He wills and not over what He does not will, whereas Allah is capable of what He wills and of what He does not will. What He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. So whoever says "He is competent over whatever He wills" must be prohibited from it, and it should be said: "Say: He is competent over all things," not only over what He wills. Especially since when you say "He is competent over what He wills," and you front the object, what does fronting the object indicate?
* Student: Restriction (ḥaṣr).
* The Shaykh: Restriction. You have restricted power to what He wills only, and this is not correct. What is obligatory for a person is to affirm the attribute of power for Allah as Allah affirmed it for Himself, and to say: "He is competent over all things," as Allah described Himself, not restricting it by what He wills.
As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is, when He wills, competent to gather them﴾ [Ash-Shura 29], the will here is not a restriction on power, but a restriction on the gathering. That is, if He wills this act, He is not incapable of it. Allah said this in response to those who denied resurrection and said it is impossible for Allah to gather people after they have been scattered in the earth and become dust.
Similarly, what is reported in a hadith in Muslim concerning the man whom Allah commanded to enter Paradise after he had been [ordered]... Allah said to him: «Indeed I am capable of whatever I will» [Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. Here He addresses him concerning the doing of something that occurred, as if He said: I am capable of that if I will it. For this reason He used "qadir" (capable) rather than "qadir" in the intensive form (qadeer), because qadeer is more emphatic in description, whereas qadir may be linked to the doing of a specific thing.
In any case, what a person should do is not this; rather, he must affirm the attribute of power whenever he describes Allah with it, saying: "He is competent over all things," only, and not restrict it by will.
﴿Allah creates what He wills; indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾.
* * *
(﴿Certainly, We have sent down verses that are clear﴾, i.e., clear signs, which is the Qur'an, ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills to a path﴾: a way, ﴿straight﴾, i.e., the religion of Islam).
﴿Certainly, We have sent down﴾: the discussion of similar expressions has preceded several times, and we said: this sentence is emphasized with how many emphasizers? Three emphasizers: the oath, the lam, and "qad", because "laqad" originally is "wallahi laqad" (by Allah, indeed), so the sentence here is emphasized by these three emphasizers.
As for His saying: ﴿mubayyinat﴾, i.e., clear: there is no doubt that this explanation does not match the word being explained, because "mubayyinat" is more eloquent than "bayyinat". The mubayyin is that which is clear in itself and makes others clear, so it is manifest in itself and manifests others, whereas the bayyin is manifest in itself only. The former is more eloquent. Therefore the author's explanation is considered deficient.
The correct view is that "mubayyinat" means clear in itself and clarifying to others. So these verses that Allah sent down are mubayyinat. What do they clarify? They clarify everything related to the interests of the servants: they distinguish good from evil, truth from falsehood, the righteous from the defiant, and the attributes of the Creator from the attributes of the created.
Everything people need and that relates to their interests in their religion and worldly life, these verses have clarified it. But clarification has ways: sometimes it is clarification in detail, and sometimes in summary. Sometimes the Qur'an's clarification is detailed, and sometimes it is summary.
For example, if you ponder the verses on the obligatory shares (the division of inheritance), you find that these verses are clear in detail. And if you ponder other verses such as: ﴿Establish prayer﴾, ﴿give zakah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 43], you find they are summary, but a person knows them from other evidences. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation for all things﴾ [An-Nahl 89]; nothing is left except that this Qur'an has clarified it.
I have related to you what is reported about Shaykh Muhammad 'Abduh, may Allah have mercy on him, that he was in a restaurant in one of the cities of Europe, and there was a Christian man with him, who said to him: "The Qur'an is an explanation for everything; has it explained how this food is made?"
Of course, we do not see that the Qur'an includes such things, that when you cook food you put onions, salt, meat, and so on; this is not present. But he said: "Yes, this Qur'an has explained to us how to make this food." The Christian was astonished and said: "How so?" Then he called the owner of the restaurant and said to him: "How did you make this food?" He said: "I made it with such and such and such," and he explained its components to him. He said: "So it is in the Qur'an," for Allah says: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [An-Nahl 43].
So the Qur'an did not explain that in detail, but it guided us how to reach knowledge of matters: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾. Of course, this verse does not mean the people of remembrance in the sense of cooking; rather, either we say: the people of remembrance are the people of knowledge, and each knowledge is according to its kind; or we say: the people of knowledge of the Sharia, and we analogize all knowledge other than the Sharia sciences to the Sharia sciences, which would be a case of general meaning (al-'umum al-ma'nawi) in the verse; for if the verse does not include this by its verbal generality, it includes it by its general meaning.
By the way, verbal generality (al-'umum al-lafzi) is that which enters the speech verbally, and the speech indicates it by direct implication (dalalat al-mutabaqah). General meaning (al-'umum al-ma'nawi) is that which the speech indicates by analogy, meaning it does not enter the wording, but is analogized to it, because analogy (qiyas) is the sharing of the analogized and the basis of analogy in what?
* Students: In the cause ('illah).
* The Shaykh: In the cause for which the ruling was established. This is general meaning. For this reason you will find in the scholars' statements: "This issue is included by the text in its verbal generality," meaning it is an individual of that generality; and sometimes it is included in its general meaning, meaning it is analogized to what the text indicates.
Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills﴾. After describing the state of the verses, does everyone benefit from these clear verses? No. He said: ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills﴾. That is, despite the verses being clear and explanatory, not everyone is guided by them; rather, Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
This verse is like many others, such as His saying: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾, and after it: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. He made the invitation general, but guidance is specific: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. This verse is similar. The verses are clarifying and explanatory of matters, but not everyone is guided by them; Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
Now, the word ﴿whom He wills﴾: the discussion has already passed that everything Allah restricts by His will is connected with wisdom. So Allah guides whom His wisdom requires to be guided (...), and that a person should reflect on the cosmic signs of Allah in order to take a lesson from them, since taking a lesson from them necessitates worshipping Allah the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds﴾ and so on to the end [An-Nur 43]. Allah established this so that a person would look at this thing, and rather take a lesson from this thing he looks at and knows, in order to derive from it the power of the Doer, and thereby His worship, because the Capable One deserves to be worshipped. For this reason Allah said: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah 21] (...).
To its end, the means of locomotion differ in it: among them is one that walks on its belly (...) that Allah the Glorified and Exalted has absolute disposal over His creation: ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾.
* And in it: the affirmation of power and its generality, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾. We pointed out in the explanation, or in the commentary, that what some people use, restricting power by what He wills, is an error, and that the obligation is to affirm the attribute of power without restriction. We answered His saying: ﴿And He is, when He wills, competent to gather them﴾ [Ash-Shura 29], and the hadith in which: «Indeed I am capable of whatever I will» [Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. We said that this will is connected to the act, not to the attribute. So the attribute is unrestricted, and the act is what is restricted by will: if He wills, He does; and if He wills, He does not.
* And also in it, from earlier: the explanation that the verses Allah sent down are clarifying and explanatory, for what?
* Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, [the verses are] clarifying (mubayyinah) of everything: of truth from falsehood, of the people of goodness from the people of evil, of the rulings that govern people, and other things besides. But despite their being clarifying, has every person been guided by them? No. Only the one whom God wills to guide is guided by them. ﴿Indeed We have sent down clear verses﴾ [al-Nur 46], yet not everyone is guided by them. ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Nur 46].

There is also in this a proof that a person should not rely on himself for guidance; rather, he should always ask God to guide him and then to make him firm. Is that not so?

Students: Yes.

Shaykh: Since it is God who guides, you should not consider yourself independent in guiding yourself. So always ask God for guidance, then for steadfastness in it, and do not be deceived by the faith you possess, for example, since that may be taken from you. This is especially so when a person becomes pleased with his own deeds, for a person's self-admiration with his deeds may lead to their being nullified and voided.

There is also in this a proof that the whole Sharia, which is the religion of Islam, is straight, with no crookedness in it, based on His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow [other] ways, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153], meaning the ways that veer to the right and to the left, ﴿they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

If we say that guidance is from God, Mighty and Majestic, and that it is contingent upon His will, ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾, does this guidance have a cause?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Yes, and what is it?

Student: Seeking the truth.

Shaykh: Seeking the truth. A person's seeking of the truth is one of the causes of guidance. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5]. The evidence is also what comes in the verses after these, which point to what we have mentioned: that the cause of guidance is a person's desire for the truth and his seeking of it. So when he desires it and seeks it, God Most High guides him to it; but when he turns away and disregards it, God Most High does not guide him to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has created every moving creature from water﴾ [An-Nur 45], after He mentioned the signs of Allah the Glorified and Exalted in the upper world, He mentioned His sign in the lower world, which is His saying:
(﴿And Allah has created every moving creature﴾, i.e., every animal, ﴿from water﴾, i.e., from a drop of semen).
﴿Created﴾ means brought into existence. ﴿Every moving creature﴾: the dabbah (moving creature) is everything that crawls upon the earth, although it may be customarily applied to those that walk on four legs. He said: the dabbah is that which walks on four. This is the common and customary usage. For this reason, a human being is not called a dabbah in common usage; if a person says to you, "O dabbah!", you may end up quarreling with him. But linguistically, everything that crawls upon the earth is a dabbah. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And there is no moving creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud 6].
As for His saying: ﴿from water﴾, this is the origin of the creation of moving creatures: from water. The author's statement "from a drop of semen" is not correct, because not every moving creature is from a drop of semen; rather every moving creature is from water, whether a drop of semen or otherwise. As for what reproduces sexually, its water is a drop of semen; and as for what is spontaneously generated, its water is moisture. That is, these things that are spontaneously generated arise from decay and moisture. As for what reproduces, yes, it reproduces from a drop of semen, which Allah creates from it. So the phrase ﴿from water﴾ is more general than the word "drop of semen," and it is obligatory to keep the verse on its generality, so that it includes what is spontaneously generated and what reproduces. Is that clear?
And this verse is part of His saying: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [Al-Anbiya 30]. Which of them is more general?
* Student: ﴿And We made from water﴾.
* The Shaykh: Because ﴿every living thing﴾ includes animals and non-animals, even trees and the like, from water.
Now, His saying: ﴿from water every living thing﴾. People cite the verse for something other than what Allah intended by it. What do they cite it for?
* Student: Water.
The Shaykh: For the claim that water is essential for the continuation of life. That is not the matter; rather, the verse indicates that the origin of these living things is from water. And if the intended meaning were what people cite it for, He would have said: "And We made from water every thing living," meaning: We made it living by water. But the verse is undoubtedly about the fact that the origin of these living things is water. And from another angle, we say: if their origin is water, then they are in need of it, because its growth too can only occur through water.
﴿And Allah has created every moving creature from water, and of them is that which walks on its belly﴾ [An-Nur 45] (like snakes and insects).
﴿Of them﴾: this specification indicates that the moving creatures referred to are rational beings, ﴿of them﴾. Otherwise, He would have said "of it", meaning of these creatures. However, the scholars said that there is a case of prioritization here: prioritizing whom? The rational beings. For this reason He said ﴿of them﴾, i.e., of these creatures.
﴿That which walks on its belly﴾. Does one who walks on his belly walk or crawl? He crawls, but this walking is crawling, like snakes and insects. What are insects? Snakes are well known, but what are insects?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It appears to me that the author's statement is open to question, because among insects some walk on their bellies, some walk on two legs, and some walk on four. So using them as an example is questionable. As for snakes, yes, they walk on their bellies, and likewise worms such as the sirar and others walk on their bellies.
(﴿And of them is that which walks on two legs﴾, like humans and birds). Humans walk on two legs, and birds walk on two legs. Is there a bird that walks on more than two legs?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes? We do not know; perhaps there is. We do not know. But we know that birds have only two legs.
(﴿And of them is that which walks on four﴾ [An-Nur 45], like beasts and livestock). This is clear. Now, does this division serve to restrict (ḥaṣr) or not? Is it a matter of ḥaṣr or of qaṣr?
* Student: It is qaṣr.
* The Shaykh: It is qaṣr, meaning limiting oneself to some things; because among animals or moving creatures there are some that walk on more than four. Is that not so? There is a creature they call "forty-four legs," which exists, and there are things with fewer; some have six legs, and there are things with more than that. This division is not for ḥaṣr, but for qaṣr, meaning it only mentions some types. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Allah creates what He wills; indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾. ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ means among those mentioned, from walking on the belly, on two legs, on four, or on more than that. No one can restrain Allah the Glorified and Exalted; He creates what He wills according to what His wisdom, blessed and exalted, requires.
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾. Power (qudrah) is an attribute by which the capable one is described, so that he does what he wills without incapacity. This differs from strength (quwwah), by which one does what he wills without weakness. So strength is contrasted with weakness, and power is contrasted with incapacity. Consider His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾ [Ar-Rum 54], and consider His saying: ﴿And Allah is not to be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44].
So He placed power in contrast to incapacity. Because of His power, He is never incapacitated, the Glorified and Exalted. In any case, power is an attribute by which the capable one is described, such that he does what he wills without incapacity.
For example, a man prays standing but with difficulty; what do we say? Is he capable or strong?
* Student: Capable.
* The Shaykh: Capable. And there is a person who prays standing and it does not trouble him; what do we call him?
* Student: Strong.
* The Shaykh: Strong and capable too.
There is a person who lifts this rock as if it were a feather, without trouble; and there is a person who lifts this rock, with effort... The first?
* Student: Strong.
* The Shaykh: Strong. And the second?
* Student: Capable.
* The Shaykh: The second is capable, because he does it but with exertion and hardship; he is capable of lifting.
And there is also a third: when it came from it (...), this one is neither strong nor capable.
As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾ [An-Nur 45], there is a phrase among people; they say: "He is competent over whatever He wills." You should not say this phrase, because if you restrict power by will, a deficiency results; it would mean His power is only over what He wills and not over what He does not will, whereas Allah is capable of what He wills and of what He does not will. What He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. So whoever says "He is competent over whatever He wills" must be prohibited from it, and it should be said: "Say: He is competent over all things," not only over what He wills. Especially since when you say "He is competent over what He wills," and you front the object, what does fronting the object indicate?
* Student: Restriction (ḥaṣr).
* The Shaykh: Restriction. You have restricted power to what He wills only, and this is not correct. What is obligatory for a person is to affirm the attribute of power for Allah as Allah affirmed it for Himself, and to say: "He is competent over all things," as Allah described Himself, not restricting it by what He wills.
As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is, when He wills, competent to gather them﴾ [Ash-Shura 29], the will here is not a restriction on power, but a restriction on the gathering. That is, if He wills this act, He is not incapable of it. Allah said this in response to those who denied resurrection and said it is impossible for Allah to gather people after they have been scattered in the earth and become dust.
Similarly, what is reported in a hadith in Muslim concerning the man whom Allah commanded to enter Paradise after he had been [ordered]... Allah said to him: «Indeed I am capable of whatever I will» [Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. Here He addresses him concerning the doing of something that occurred, as if He said: I am capable of that if I will it. For this reason He used "qadir" (capable) rather than "qadir" in the intensive form (qadeer), because qadeer is more emphatic in description, whereas qadir may be linked to the doing of a specific thing.
In any case, what a person should do is not this; rather, he must affirm the attribute of power whenever he describes Allah with it, saying: "He is competent over all things," only, and not restrict it by will.
﴿Allah creates what He wills; indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾.
* * *
(﴿Certainly, We have sent down verses that are clear﴾, i.e., clear signs, which is the Qur'an, ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills to a path﴾: a way, ﴿straight﴾, i.e., the religion of Islam).
﴿Certainly, We have sent down﴾: the discussion of similar expressions has preceded several times, and we said: this sentence is emphasized with how many emphasizers? Three emphasizers: the oath, the lam, and "qad", because "laqad" originally is "wallahi laqad" (by Allah, indeed), so the sentence here is emphasized by these three emphasizers.
As for His saying: ﴿mubayyinat﴾, i.e., clear: there is no doubt that this explanation does not match the word being explained, because "mubayyinat" is more eloquent than "bayyinat". The mubayyin is that which is clear in itself and makes others clear, so it is manifest in itself and manifests others, whereas the bayyin is manifest in itself only. The former is more eloquent. Therefore the author's explanation is considered deficient.
The correct view is that "mubayyinat" means clear in itself and clarifying to others. So these verses that Allah sent down are mubayyinat. What do they clarify? They clarify everything related to the interests of the servants: they distinguish good from evil, truth from falsehood, the righteous from the defiant, and the attributes of the Creator from the attributes of the created.
Everything people need and that relates to their interests in their religion and worldly life, these verses have clarified it. But clarification has ways: sometimes it is clarification in detail, and sometimes in summary. Sometimes the Qur'an's clarification is detailed, and sometimes it is summary.
For example, if you ponder the verses on the obligatory shares (the division of inheritance), you find that these verses are clear in detail. And if you ponder other verses such as: ﴿Establish prayer﴾, ﴿give zakah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 43], you find they are summary, but a person knows them from other evidences. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation for all things﴾ [An-Nahl 89]; nothing is left except that this Qur'an has clarified it.
I have related to you what is reported about Shaykh Muhammad 'Abduh, may Allah have mercy on him, that he was in a restaurant in one of the cities of Europe, and there was a Christian man with him, who said to him: "The Qur'an is an explanation for everything; has it explained how this food is made?"
Of course, we do not see that the Qur'an includes such things, that when you cook food you put onions, salt, meat, and so on; this is not present. But he said: "Yes, this Qur'an has explained to us how to make this food." The Christian was astonished and said: "How so?" Then he called the owner of the restaurant and said to him: "How did you make this food?" He said: "I made it with such and such and such," and he explained its components to him. He said: "So it is in the Qur'an," for Allah says: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [An-Nahl 43].
So the Qur'an did not explain that in detail, but it guided us how to reach knowledge of matters: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾. Of course, this verse does not mean the people of remembrance in the sense of cooking; rather, either we say: the people of remembrance are the people of knowledge, and each knowledge is according to its kind; or we say: the people of knowledge of the Sharia, and we analogize all knowledge other than the Sharia sciences to the Sharia sciences, which would be a case of general meaning (al-'umum al-ma'nawi) in the verse; for if the verse does not include this by its verbal generality, it includes it by its general meaning.
By the way, verbal generality (al-'umum al-lafzi) is that which enters the speech verbally, and the speech indicates it by direct implication (dalalat al-mutabaqah). General meaning (al-'umum al-ma'nawi) is that which the speech indicates by analogy, meaning it does not enter the wording, but is analogized to it, because analogy (qiyas) is the sharing of the analogized and the basis of analogy in what?
* Students: In the cause ('illah).
* The Shaykh: In the cause for which the ruling was established. This is general meaning. For this reason you will find in the scholars' statements: "This issue is included by the text in its verbal generality," meaning it is an individual of that generality; and sometimes it is included in its general meaning, meaning it is analogized to what the text indicates.
Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills﴾. After describing the state of the verses, does everyone benefit from these clear verses? No. He said: ﴿and Allah guides whom He wills﴾. That is, despite the verses being clear and explanatory, not everyone is guided by them; rather, Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
This verse is like many others, such as His saying: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾, and after it: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. He made the invitation general, but guidance is specific: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. This verse is similar. The verses are clarifying and explanatory of matters, but not everyone is guided by them; Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
Now, the word ﴿whom He wills﴾: the discussion has already passed that everything Allah restricts by His will is connected with wisdom. So Allah guides whom His wisdom requires to be guided (...), and that a person should reflect on the cosmic signs of Allah in order to take a lesson from them, since taking a lesson from them necessitates worshipping Allah the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds﴾ and so on to the end [An-Nur 43]. Allah established this so that a person would look at this thing, and rather take a lesson from this thing he looks at and knows, in order to derive from it the power of the Doer, and thereby His worship, because the Capable One deserves to be worshipped. For this reason Allah said: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah 21] (...).
To its end, the means of locomotion differ in it: among them is one that walks on its belly (...) that Allah the Glorified and Exalted has absolute disposal over His creation: ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾.
* And in it: the affirmation of power and its generality, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is competent over all things﴾. We pointed out in the explanation, or in the commentary, that what some people use, restricting power by what He wills, is an error, and that the obligation is to affirm the attribute of power without restriction. We answered His saying: ﴿And He is, when He wills, competent to gather them﴾ [Ash-Shura 29], and the hadith in which: «Indeed I am capable of whatever I will» [Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. We said that this will is connected to the act, not to the attribute. So the attribute is unrestricted, and the act is what is restricted by will: if He wills, He does; and if He wills, He does not.
* And also in it, from earlier: the explanation that the verses Allah sent down are clarifying and explanatory, for what?
* Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, [the verses are] clarifying (mubayyinah) of everything: of truth from falsehood, of the people of goodness from the people of evil, of the rulings that govern people, and other things besides. But despite their being clarifying, has every person been guided by them? No. Only the one whom God wills to guide is guided by them. ﴿Indeed We have sent down clear verses﴾ [al-Nur 46], yet not everyone is guided by them. ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Nur 46].

There is also in this a proof that a person should not rely on himself for guidance; rather, he should always ask God to guide him and then to make him firm. Is that not so?

Students: Yes.

Shaykh: Since it is God who guides, you should not consider yourself independent in guiding yourself. So always ask God for guidance, then for steadfastness in it, and do not be deceived by the faith you possess, for example, since that may be taken from you. This is especially so when a person becomes pleased with his own deeds, for a person's self-admiration with his deeds may lead to their being nullified and voided.

There is also in this a proof that the whole Sharia, which is the religion of Islam, is straight, with no crookedness in it, based on His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow [other] ways, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153], meaning the ways that veer to the right and to the left, ﴿they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

If we say that guidance is from God, Mighty and Majestic, and that it is contingent upon His will, ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾, does this guidance have a cause?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Yes, and what is it?

Student: Seeking the truth.

Shaykh: Seeking the truth. A person's seeking of the truth is one of the causes of guidance. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5]. The evidence is also what comes in the verses after these, which point to what we have mentioned: that the cause of guidance is a person's desire for the truth and his seeking of it. So when he desires it and seeks it, God Most High guides him to it; but when he turns away and disregards it, God Most High does not guide him to it.

Allah the Exalted says: ("﴿And they say﴾" means the hypocrites. "﴿We believe﴾" means: we affirm as true. "﴿In Allah﴾" means: in His oneness. "﴿And in the Messenger﴾" means Muhammad (ﷺ). "﴿And we obey﴾" both of them in what they have decreed. "﴿Then a party of them turns away﴾" means: turns aside, "﴿after that﴾" from it. "﴿And those are not﴾" the ones who turn away "﴿believers﴾" [An-Nur 47], the known believers, whose hearts agree with their tongues.)

"﴿They say﴾" is a report about a group, whether they were hypocrites, as the author said, or others.

"﴿And they say: We believe in Allah and in the Messenger﴾": the author explained faith (iman) as affirmation (tasdiq). It has already been mentioned that this explanation is deficient, and that faith is affirmation together with something added. What is that? Acceptance and submission: that a person accepts what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought and submits to it. Mere affirmation is not faith.

For this reason we know that Abu Talib affirmed the Prophet (ﷺ), and he himself acknowledged this about himself. He said:

They have known that our son is not a liar among us,
and he is not concerned with worthless speech.

And he said:

Indeed I know that the religion of Muhammad
is among the best religions of mankind, a religion we follow.

But he was not a believer despite his affirmation. Why? Because he did not submit and did not yield. He did not submit to the Messenger (ﷺ) nor yield to him. Likewise the disbelievers about whom Allah reports: "﴿If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: Allah﴾" [Luqman 25]. Are they affirmers of Allah or not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: They believe in Him and affirm Him, but since they did not accept what the Messenger brought and did not submit to him, they were not believers. So defining faith in the Sharia merely as affirmation is an incomplete definition. Rather, we say: faith is affirmation together with acceptance and submission, and there must be both.

As for His saying "﴿We believe in Allah and in the Messenger﴾": He repeated the preposition "﴿and in the Messenger﴾" because faith in the Messenger is a separate faith. That is, a person must believe in Allah with complete faith and in the Messenger with complete faith, just as obedience to Allah is complete obedience, and obedience to the Messenger is likewise.

Compare His saying: "﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾" [An-Nisa 59]. He said "﴿obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾", then said "﴿and those in authority among you﴾", joining them to the obedience of Allah and the Messenger without repeating the governing verb. This indicates that obedience to rulers follows obedience to Allah and His Messenger, whereas obedience to the Messenger is independent. And "﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾" [An-Nisa 80], and obedience to Allah is likewise.

Similarly with belief in Allah and in the Messenger: when the preposition appears, its meaning is that this is an independent faith, as if these people were saying: we believe with complete faith in Allah, the Exalted, and we believe with complete faith in the Messenger that he is the Messenger of Allah.

The author's statement "(﴿We believe in Allah﴾: in His oneness)" is also deficient. Rather, faith in Allah includes tawhid (affirmation of His oneness) and other things: His oneness, His disposal of affairs, His governance, His legislation, and other matters. It includes all of this, and likewise His attributes, since faith in Allah is not complete without faith in His attributes. This is necessary.

His saying "﴿And we obey﴾" is this submission, meaning that we are believers and also obedient, carrying out commands. And what is obedience? They said its meaning is conformity to the command, meaning that you do not depart from the one who commands you and do not oppose him, but conform to his command. If it is a positive command, then by doing it; if it is a prohibition, then by refraining. This is obedience. For this reason the word "obedience" includes doing commanded acts and abstaining from forbidden acts, because its meaning is conformity to the command.

So the meaning of "﴿we obeyed﴾" is: we conformed to the command of Allah and His Messenger, and we will not depart from it. After this statement, "﴿then a party of them turns away after that﴾", after their acknowledgment of belief in Allah and His Messenger, a party of them turns aside.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "﴿And those are not believers﴾", meaning: those who turn away are not truly believers. But is this negation a negation of the very root of faith, or a negation of its completeness?

* Students: Its completeness.

* The Shaykh: No, there is detail. If the turning away is absolute, then it is a negation of faith entirely, of its root. If the turning away is not absolute but concerns some matters, then the matters differ. In some matters, if a person abandons them and turns away from them, he is a disbeliever; in others, he is a believer with deficient faith. The main point is that his turning away contradicts the faith they claimed.

This is clear evidence that if a person says he is a believer while turning away and refusing, he is lying in his claim. Either he is not a believer at all, or he is a believer with deficient faith.

He says: "﴿Then a party of them turns away after that﴾". "﴿A party﴾" means a group. "﴿Of them﴾" means of these speakers. Another party remains upon faith and obedience and does not turn away, so their claimed faith is real.

Allah, the Exalted, says: "﴿And those are not believers﴾". Let us look at the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this sentence.

"﴿Ma ulaika﴾": what is "ma"? "Ma" is a negating particle, but among the Hijazis it functions like "laysa" (is not): it raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative. "Ulaa'" is its subject, but it is not marked with a damma, because it is indeclinable (mabni). All demonstrative nouns are indeclinable: "haa'ulaa'" and "ulaa'" and similar words are all indeclinable.

As for His saying "﴿bi-l-mu'minin﴾": the "ba'" is a superfluous preposition (harf jarr za'id). Is it superfluous in terms of grammar or in terms of meaning?

* Students: Grammar.

* The Shaykh: In terms of grammar. As for meaning, it adds emphasis to the negation in "﴿ma ulaika﴾".

As for "﴿al-mu'minin﴾", it is the predicate of "ma". But the grammarians say it is its predicate, yet not put in the accusative by it, because the superfluous "ba'" is the one that governs, since its governing effect is evident by its direct attachment to the word. So: the "ba'" is a superfluous preposition, and "﴿al-mu'minin﴾" is a noun governed by the "ba'", and its sign of genitive is the "ya'" in place of the kasra, because it is a sound masculine plural.

Some say: "﴿al-mu'minin﴾" is the predicate of "ma", put in the accusative by it, and its sign of accusative is a hidden "ya'", its appearance prevented by the position being occupied by the superfluous preposition.

In any case, this is excessive depth and there is no need for it. What we must know is that "ma" is a negating particle in meaning, the "ba'" is a superfluous preposition, and its purpose is?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Emphasis of the negation: that is, the negation of faith from those who said "we believe and we obey" and then turned away. They are therefore not believers. You have understood that the negation of faith here is either a negation of its root or a negation of its completeness.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. In the language of the Hijazis, according to all grammarians, it functions like "laysa". But the dialect of the Banu Tamim does not make it function like "laysa". In the Qur'an: "﴿This is not a human﴾" [Yusuf 31]: here it functions like "laysa", but the verse does not say "ma hadha bashar-un" (with a damma). If it did not function, it would be "ma hadha bashar-un". The poet says:

A slender-waisted one, I said to him: declare your lineage.
He answered: "The killing of a lover is not forbidden."

What do you make of this? Is he a Hijazi or a Tamimi?

* Students: Hijazi.

* Another student: Tamimi.

* The Shaykh: Tamimi. When he was told "declare your lineage", he did not say "I am Tamimi" but answered: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden." Now you know he is Tamimi. If he had been Hijazi he would have said "the killing of the lover is not forbidden" with the accusative, because it functions like "laysa".

* Student: Was there Tamim here?

* The Shaykh: There were Tamim here. But in our time, no. We Hijazis and Tamimis are all one, and they do not make it function.

* Student: So only the Tamimis do not make it function?

* The Shaykh: No, the Hijazis are the ones who make it function. But what is meant is the early Arabs whose tongues had not changed. As for now, no, because the language has changed.

* Student: And the Kufans (...)?

The Shaykh: In fact, the Kufans and the grammarians are not a description of the Arabs who spoke Arabic. It is a description of the scholars who took charge of the study of grammar.

[Quran 24:48] He says: "When they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away."

"When they are called": the pronoun refers to those sayers who say, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger and we obey," then turn away.

(﴿When they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾ – i.e., to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who conveys from Him – ﴿that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ from coming to him).

"When they are called": i.e., when their opponent calls them to Allah and to His Messenger so that he may judge between them, they turn away.

As for His saying, "When they are called to Allah": does it mean that they are called to Allah, the Exalted, so that they reach Him above His Throne? No. And what is the calling to Allah? It is calling to His Book, because the Book of Allah is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; so calling to Allah is calling to the Book of Allah.

And as for His saying, "and His Messenger": does it mean that they reach the Prophet (ﷺ) in his house, or in his mosque, or in his market?

* Student: To his Sunnah.

* The Shaykh: No, we say: during his lifetime, to him; to him personally in the mosque, or in the house, or in the market; and after his death, to his Sunnah, because his Sunnah is his saying, his action and his tacit approval, so it is as though we see him when we call to his saying, or to his action, or to his approval.

As for His saying, "that he may judge between them": the lam is for causation, meaning they were called for this purpose, "that he may judge between them."

Does the pronoun in "that he may judge between them" refer to Allah or to the Messenger (ﷺ)? It cannot refer to both of them; if it referred to both, it would have to be in the dual form: "to Allah and His Messenger, that they both may judge between them." Rather it refers to one of them. To the Messenger?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, to the Messenger, because he is the nearest mentioned. But as for Allah, the Exalted, either we estimate a clause like this one, meaning: "to Allah, that He may judge between them, and His Messenger, that he may judge between them," just as we said regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [At-Tawbah 62], where He did not say "that they should please them both," but said "they have more right that they should please Him." They said the estimate is: "And Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger has more right that they should please Him." Or it is said that the judgment of the Messenger (peace be upon him) is the judgment of Allah, and the author's statement points to this: "– i.e., to the Messenger of Allah – (who conveys from Him)." So if the Prophet (ﷺ) is the one who conveys from Allah, his judgment becomes the judgment of Allah.

In reality, who is the direct judge? The Messenger (ﷺ). So when disputes arise during his lifetime, we return to him directly.

Therefore we say: "that he may judge" – the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). Why? Because he is the nearest mentioned. Then he says: the judgment of the Messenger (ﷺ) is the judgment of Allah, because he conveys from Him and judges only by what Allah has judged. These people, ﴿when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾. The grammarians call "idha" (إذا) here "sudden" (fujaʼiyyah), meaning for surprise. Here we have the first "idha," ﴿when they are called to Allah﴾ – what is the first "idha"?

* Students: Conditional.

* The Shaykh: Conditional. Its response is ﴿behold, a party of them﴾, but it is introduced by the sudden "idha," because it is a nominal sentence, and a nominal sentence must be introduced by "fa" or by the sudden "idha."

So the second "idha" is sudden. What does "sudden" mean? It means it indicates surprise: the surprise of what follows regarding what preceded. These people, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, do they think and consider whether to accept or not? What is the answer?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, they reject immediately – and we seek refuge with Allah – they do not deliberate on the matter, saying "We will think about it." ﴿behold, a party of them turn away﴾ straight away, without any deliberation. As if they were prepared from the outset for anything – to reject the judgment of Allah and His Messenger?

﴿behold, a party of them turn away﴾, and this – we seek refuge with Allah – is more arrogant and more defiant than a man who says, "I will take my time," even though both are equal in their ruling, since it is obligatory to accept what Allah and His Messenger judge. But when a person is caught off guard by it, this is evidence that he is arrogant and does not at all wish to submit to the truth. That is why He said: ﴿behold, a party of them turn away﴾. Observe the qualifications in the Quran: in the first verse: ﴿then a party of them turn away﴾ [An-Nur 47], because not everyone who says "We believe in Allah and we obey" turns away; rather among them is one who is truly a believer and does not turn away. Likewise, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, do they all turn away?

Student: No.

* The Shaykh: No. Among them are those who submit to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, bring their dispute to Allah and His Messenger, and accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. That is why He says: "a party of them turn away, and they are turning away from coming to him, or from his judgment?" Observe: "turn away" while "they are turning away" – the turning away is physical, and the aversion is of the heart, because one who turns away may turn away while hoping to return; but when one turns away while averse – we seek refuge with Allah – and the averse one dislikes what he was called to, he has turned away from it only because he hates it. This is more severe... So turning away is of the body, and aversion is of the heart, meaning they turn away and their intention is not to do what?

* Students: Return.

* The Shaykh: Return – they turn away with no intention of returning.

* The verse is evidence against those who are zealously attached to a madhhab, or to the view of one scholar, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger and it is said: "This is the Book of Allah, and this is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The obligation is to refer to both and return to both. Some people say: "No, the madhhab says such-and-such, and such-and-such scholar said so," and similar things. This has a resemblance to those hypocrites who, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, you find them turning away and averse.

And some people – we seek refuge with Allah – are never patient at all; they immediately become angry and get up, saying: "We absolutely do not want this; we want to follow so-and-so." Well, is so-and-so the Messenger? No. So-and-so is a human being who takes from the saying of the Messenger (peace be upon him); sometimes he errs and sometimes he is right.

If it is said: "And you too err and are right?" I say: "True, I err and am right, but this is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Examine it yourself. I do not oblige you to adopt what I have understood from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger; but I do oblige you to look at the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), then look at whether the view of the one you follow agrees or disagrees. But to turn away from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger and say, 'Never will I look at them, because I follow so-and-so and so-and-so,' this I do not agree with."

So here is a difference between my calling you to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger so that you look into it and follow it, and my saying: "This is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, but you must adhere to what I understand from them" – this I do not oblige you with, because if I obliged you with it, I would have called you to what I forbid you: I would have called you to my own taqlid. Rather we call you to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). The important thing is that you do not confine yourself and say, "I follow only so-and-so." (...) what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, whether it agrees with the opinion of the one you follow or disagrees. But the calamity, the whole calamity, is the matter of pure taqlid.

Yet – praise be to Allah – we give you good news, as you see now, that this has begun to weaken among people. I mean pure taqlid, which persists even when the truth has become manifest and clear. This has begun – praise be to Allah – to weaken among people, and people have started seeking the opinions that are preponderant according to the indication of the Book and the Sunnah, regardless of whether so-and-so adopted them or not. Yes indeed.

* Student: The ones informed (about)?

The Shaykh: "The one who conveys" (al-muballigh).

* Student: The ones informed about them?

* The Shaykh: "About him" – about Allah.

* Student: About him.

* The Shaykh: About him? No, that is wrong, (...), "the one who conveys from him"; from Allah. The author said this in order to clarify that the judgment of the Messenger (ﷺ) is the judgment of Allah, so that no confusion arises regarding His saying "that he may judge," even though they are called to Allah and His Messenger.

* In this verse is evidence that judgment belongs to whom? To Allah and His Messenger, and referring disputes to Allah and His Messenger. Allah, the Exalted, has sworn an emphatic oath that a person cannot believe until he makes the Prophet (ﷺ) judge in what is disputed among them: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves﴾ [An-Nisa 65]. This is one stage.

The second stage: ﴿then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided﴾ – these are two stages, meaning there is no tightness or aversion in one's self toward what the Messenger (peace be upon him) has judged.

The third stage: ﴿and submit with complete submission﴾ [An-Nisa 65], meaning they submit fully. People each fulfil one stage: some do not make the Messenger (peace be upon him) judge at all, and this one has not entered the three stages from the outset. Some make the Messenger (peace be upon him) judge but find discomfort within themselves at the judgment of Allah and His Messenger because it contradicts their desires, so you find the one who is distressed walks with the judgment but with tightness and discomfort; this too is not a believer. Some make the Messenger (peace be upon him) judge and have no discomfort in their hearts about his judgment, but they do not submit; there is hesitation and laxity, or shortcoming in some of the implementation; this too is not a believer. The three matters are necessary: taking the judgment, absence of discomfort, and submission.

Consider His saying "submission" (taslīman) – "and submit with submission" – an indication that it is complete submission. This is why the grammarians call this noun an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid), meaning they submit with complete submission, with no twisting or aversion whatsoever. This verse is similar to it.

Then He said: ﴿And if the right is theirs, they come to Him willingly, submissive﴾. "Submissive" (mudh'inin) — what is it? (Hastening, obedient.) There is a note here which I do not know what it is, by Allah: "And Allah is mentioned to magnify Him, or so, or: the mention of Allah is to magnify Him, after (the one who conveys from Him)."

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Do you not have this? It is written in my copy and written (yasihh, "is correct"). Otherwise we would say: a marginal note (hashiyah). Put this marginal note, if it has any basis, that His saying: ﴿to Allah and His Messenger﴾, that the mention of Allah here is not intended but is for magnification, to magnify the judgment of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, because the one who will judge is the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. But this has no basis.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if the right is theirs, they come to Him willingly, submissive﴾. That is: (hastening, obedient). If the right is on their side in the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, they do not turn away; rather they hasten and submit. This indicates that they do not want the truth, but want only what agrees with their desires. If the right is with them, they accept and submit; if the right is against them, they turn away and refuse.

Indeed, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they turn away in two situations: when the right is against them, and when it is neither for them nor against them; for they only submit when the right is theirs. When the right is theirs, they submit. In reality, is this their obedience and submission for the sake of the truth or for the desire of their own souls?

* Students: For the desire.

* The Shaykh: For the desire of their own souls, not for the truth. This is also the state of some people. You find that when the Book and the Sunnah indicate what he desires and wants, his chest expands, and he submits and accepts. When the Book and the Sunnah indicate something contrary to what he wants, you find that there is constriction in his soul, and perhaps he adds to that turning away and refusal. This, in reality, is not a believer; he only follows from the truth what agrees with his desire. As for the believer, he has another state, which will come, God willing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 50–53 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾: disbelief. ﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ meaning: they doubt his prophethood. ﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ in judgment, meaning they would wrong them in it. No; ﴿rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [an-Nur 50] by turning away from it.) Allah the Mighty and Majestic, clarifying the state of those who reject what Allah and His Messenger have judged, says that they do not escape these three conditions:

﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ The disease (maraḍ) is an ailment that afflicts what is healthy so that it leaves its balance. This is the disease, and this definition of disease includes both bodily disease and heart disease. Bodily disease is in reality an ailment that afflicts the body so that it leaves its balance; likewise heart disease is an ailment that afflicts the heart, taking it out of balance until it deviates and does not accept the truth. So what is the disease intended here?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. The author explained it as disbelief. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that what is meant is an evil intention, as shown by the division (that follows), whether it is disbelief, or hypocrisy, or something else. The point is that the disease is an evil intention that turns them away from accepting the truth.

﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ This is doubt, and it is the disease of misgiving (shubhah). For it has passed us many times that the causes of deviation from the truth are either shubhah or shahwah (desire). That is, either a person desires something that contradicts the Shariah and follows it, or he has a misgiving about this truth and so refrains from it.

So we say here: with what should the disease be explained? With an evil intention, which is desire, that is, craving what contradicts the Shariah.
(﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ meaning they have doubted.) This is the disease of misgiving that afflicts a person so that the truth does not become clear to him. Let us give an example: a man is commanded to do something, to pray, but he puts a worldly matter before his prayer. What disease is in his heart? The disease of desire.
Another is commanded to pray but doubts the benefit of prayer, or doubts its existence, or something similar. This has the disease of misgiving.
So what we have here: ﴿disease﴾ means an evil intention, and ﴿or do they have doubt﴾ is this doubt, may Allah protect us.

The third matter: ﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ That is, they do not have an evil intention, nor doubt about the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, but they have another doubt. What is it? Doubt about the justice of Allah and His Messenger. Therefore they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to them, so they dread inclination and injustice.
In reality, the inclination and injustice lie with them, not in the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, the judgment of Allah and His Messenger is upon truth and justice, but injustice is in their own scale, because they are the ones who have deviated from what they ought to be in terms of compliance and obedience.
﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Rather (bal)﴾ here is for transition (idrab). But what is your view of this idrab? Is it idrab of cancellation (ibṭāl) or idrab of transition (intiqāl)? What does the author see?
He said: (No), ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease, or have they doubt, or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ (No), then he said: ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ in the Qur'an. So the author's statement implies that the idrab here is of cancellation, and for this reason he estimated (No) after the three preceding possibilities.
But in my view the idrab here is not of cancellation; it is of transition. For the reality of the matter is that whoever does not accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger does not go beyond these three matters: either he has an evil intention, or doubt, or fear. We cannot imagine a fourth matter beyond these three possibilities.
Furthermore, describing them as wrongdoers does not go beyond these three possibilities either. Whoever has a disease in his heart is a wrongdoer, whoever has a misgiving in his heart is a wrongdoer, and whoever fears that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to him is a wrongdoer.
So the matter is one of transitional idrab, not cancelling idrab.

The phrase ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease, or have they doubt, or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ — is (am) in these places the equalizing (taswiyah) meaning "or," or the idrab meaning "rather"?
* Student: It admits both.
* The Shaykh: It admits both? How is that?
* Student: Or it could be (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, is this in the sense of "rather" or in the sense of "or"?
It has passed us earlier that the one meaning "or" is the one that comes after the interrogative of equalization (hamzat al-taswiyah), such as: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6], and ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. These are the ones meaning "or," and they are called connected (muttasilah). As for the one meaning "rather," it is the one not preceded by the hamzat al-taswiyah, and it is called disconnected (munqatiʿah).
On this basis, the (am) in ﴿or have they doubt, or do they fear﴾ is disconnected, meaning "rather," and it occurs frequently at the end of Surat at-Tur: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman.﴾ What follows it? ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, we await for him the misfortunes of time"? Say: "Wait, for I am with you among those who wait." Or do their minds command them to this, or are they a transgressing people? Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ to the end [at-Tur 30–33]. Many instances are in the end of Surat at-Tur, disconnected in the sense of "rather," with the interrogative hamzah.
So here it is disconnected, not connected, because the connected is the one that comes after the hamzat al-taswiyah and means "or," while the disconnected is the one that does not come after the hamzat al-taswiyah and means "rather."
As for His statement ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾, here He recorded wrongdoing upon them and emphasized it with two kinds of emphasis. What are they?
* Student: Huwa (they).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl).
* The Shaykh: With the pronoun of separation, and with the sentence being nominal with both parts definite; for when a sentence is nominal with both parts definite, it conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). Here ﴿ulā'ika﴾ is the subject, and it is definite because it is a demonstrative noun; ﴿al-ẓālimūn﴾ is the predicate, and it is definite because it has the article (al). On this basis Allah emphasized their wrongdoing with two kinds of emphasis: the sentence being nominal with both parts definite, and the pronoun of separation. As for the benefits of the pronoun of separation, which occurs frequently in the Qur'an and outside it, what are its benefits?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Wait. For emphasis, we all must be keeping it in mind, because I have just told you in the explanation that this sentence is emphasized with two kinds of emphasis: one of them is the pronoun of separation, and the second is that it is a nominal sentence with both parts definite. We ought to all know this; it does not need repeating. That is one point.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They came to him submitting, that is, compliant and obedient, so they follow only their desires. He showed the state of the believers, and said: ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, to judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾

First: in the parsing of His statement ﴿the saying of the believers﴾ — ﴿innamā kāna qawla al-mu'minīn﴾ — it is in the accusative. It is known that kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, and here the word after it is accusative. The answer is that this is its predicate, placed first: ﴿qawla al-mu'minīn﴾ is its predicate, fronted; and its subject is the verbal noun formed from (an) and the verb in His statement ﴿that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾, meaning: their saying was only this saying: ﴿"We hear and we obey."﴾

As for His statement ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning ﴿when they are called to Allah﴾: to His Book, and to His Messenger; to Him personally during his life, and to his Sunnah after his death. ﴿To judge between them﴾: what was said about its counterpart in the verse in the previous lesson applies here.
The pronoun in ﴿to judge﴾ returns to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ. The judgment is attributed to him because his judgment is a conveying from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, so his judgment is also aligned with the judgment of Allah, since he is the one who conveys from Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
His statement ﴿to judge between them﴾ includes disputes that they have disagreed over and rulings on which they differ; the judge is the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, both in the disputes that arise between litigants and in the rulings on which people differ. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 10], and He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [an-Nisa 59].

So when the believers are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, their saying is: ﴿that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾ ﴿That they say "We hear"﴾ with our ears, ﴿and "we obey"﴾ with our limbs. They hear and submit. Obedience, as has passed, encompasses doing the commands and abandoning the prohibitions, encompassing both together. Unlike those who say "We hear" while they do not hear, or say "We hear and we disobey," so they say "We hear" but do not submit, or openly declare disobedience, saying "We hear and we disobey." The believers say, "We hear and we obey."

The author's statement: i.e., (the appropriate saying for them), means that their appropriate saying is this. The apparent meaning of the author's words is that the matter is by way of supposition and assumption: that it is only proper for them to say this. But the reality is that this is what actually occurs; it is not merely the appropriate saying, but the appropriate saying that actually takes place. So when they are ﴿called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, they say, "We hear and we obey,"﴾ as Allah described them, and they said: ﴿"We hear and we obey."﴾

Making this an appropriate saying, meaning supposed and assumed, and that this is what is appropriate for them, contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. For the saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, is: "We hear and we obey," hearing and obeying, and "upon the wide and ample." This is their appropriate saying that actually comes from them. When they are called to Allah and His Messenger, they do not say, "By Allah, so-and-so's opinion is otherwise, and so-and-so's opinion is otherwise, and people are otherwise," or similar things. They do not say such a matter; they say, "We hear and we obey."

Likewise it is obligatory upon every believer. Whoever does not say this is not a believer: either faith has been entirely negated from him, or his faith is deficient.
Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: and (﴿"We hear and we obey"﴾ by responding, ﴿and those﴾ then, ﴿they are the successful﴾ the saved).
﴿And those, they are the successful﴾: (they) is a pronoun of separation, and its three benefits have passed: restriction, emphasis, and distinguishing the predicate from the attribute.
﴿And those﴾ meaning: those who say "We hear and we obey" when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, ﴿they are the successful﴾. The author said: (i.e., the saved).
The more correct view is that success (falāḥ) is not merely salvation, but salvation from what is feared, and attaining or obtaining what is sought. The successful one is he who is saved from what he dislikes and attains what he loves. So these are those who were saved from what is feared, because disobedience is absent from them, and who attained what is sought, because complete obedience is achieved by them. So through acts of obedience comes the attainment of what is sought, and through avoiding sins comes salvation from what is feared.
Restricting success to these people indicates that whoever is other than them is not successful. But if faith is entirely absent from a person, all success is absent from him; and if some faith is absent from him, some success is absent from him. So the duty of the believer, when he is called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, or when he himself becomes aware of the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, is that he say: "We hear and we obey." He does not look right or left, or interpret, or distort. No; he says, "We hear and we obey," with complete submission and complete hearing, for by this faith is realized.
The person who submits to the judgment of Allah the Exalted with such ease and such conformity is the one who finds rest and no anxiety arises in him. For whoever accustoms himself to hesitation in accepting the legal rulings, even in a single ruling, the soul will compel him to hesitate in many legal matters. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-An'am 110].
So when a person accustoms himself to accepting the truth at the first moment, without any anxiety or hesitation in carrying it out, it becomes easy for him afterward to submit to all commands and not to look aside or hesitate. But if he does it once and hesitates about one of the matters of the legal rulings, that is, after it has become established for him (leave aside hesitation about establishment; hesitation about establishment is something else: he may hesitate about establishment if, for example, the hadith is weak in its chain, or similar), but if the ruling has become established for him that this is the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, then his hesitation in accepting it is extremely dangerous for him, because it leads to hesitation in other rulings in the future.
A similar principle applies to the decreed ruling as well. The person who does not train himself to be patient with the decrees of Allah, and His predestination, remains constantly anxious and weary of decrees that do not suit him.
So when he goes along with predestination and decree, so that if good befalls him he is reassured by it, and if harm befalls him he is patient with it, while he is going along with predestination and decree, then by that he finds rest and is never anxious. You will find that the person who wants Allah the Mighty and Majestic's decree and predestination to be what suits him is always in anxiety, because predestination is not as you wish, just as the Shariah is also not as you wish.
The Shariah is not as people wish, and predestination is not as people wish. Whoever goes along with both of them, these two rulings, will find success, tranquility, and a good life. Whoever is anxious about them, or about one of them, will remain in anxiety: if it concerns the decreed matter, he remains in anxiety and grief, because matters do not come as they should; and if it concerns the legal matters, likewise, the door of hesitation in accepting and implementing Allah's rulings opens for him.

* * *

(﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger and fears Allah﴾: fears Him, ﴿and is mindful of Him﴾ — with the ha' vowelled and with it unvowelled — by obeying Him, ﴿then those are the victorious﴾ with Paradise).
This verse is among the most comprehensive and concise verses.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ by submitting to the judgments of Allah and His Messenger. It has passed that obedience is conformity to what? To the command: whether it is a prohibition or a command, that is, a demand to bring about or a demand to abandon; it is conformity to the command. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, and fears Allah, and is mindful of Him﴾. Note that obedience to Allah and His Messenger, fear (khashyah) is worship, and taqwa is worship; they are for none but whom?
* Students: Allah.
* The Shaykh: None but Allah alone. For this reason He said: ﴿and fears Allah and is mindful of Him﴾. I say here: (with the ha' vowelled — ﴿yattaqihi﴾ — and unvowelled) with the ha' vowelled and unvowelled: ﴿wa yattaqihi﴾ or ﴿wa yattaqih﴾.
Now, ﴿fears Allah﴾: the author says (fears Him), but this explanation is insufficient, because khashyah is stronger than khawf (fear). The difference between them: khashyah is only from knowledge, as in His statement: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. So the scholar is the one who fears Allah, because he fears Him with knowledge of the reality of the one feared and the state of the one who fears; he knows the state of the one feared and knows the state of the one who fears.
Khashyah is only with knowledge, as His statement: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28].

**Second difference: with respect to the one feared and the one who fears.** Khashyah (awe-fear) arises from the greatness of the one feared, whereas khawf (fear) arises from the weakness of the one who fears. The difference between them is clear: khashyah exists because of the greatness of the one feared, even if the one who fears is great himself, while khawf comes from the weakness of the one who fears.

**Third difference: khashyah is fear accompanied by reverence, veneration and exaltation.** This difference branches off from the second one.

Khawf is not like this; it does not arise from reverence, veneration and exaltation. For this reason one says "khafa min al-dhi'b" (he feared the wolf), and one does not say "khashiya minhu" or "khashiyahu," except figuratively (ʿalā sabīl al-tawassuʿ).

These three differences make it necessary that khashyah not be synonymous with khawf in the strict sense of exact equivalence. However, approximately (ʿalā wajh al-taqrīb) it is acceptable: a person may say that khashyah means khawf in order to bring it closer to the understanding of the listeners, but not on the basis that khawf is the exact meaning of khashyah. Khashyah occurs together with awe, veneration and exaltation of the one feared, unlike khawf.

We say: ﴿وَيَخْشَى اللهَ﴾ ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾ and ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾. We are now discussing the readings that exist:

There is: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾.

And there is: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾.

And there is a third reading, the reading of Hafs, which the author did not mention, namely ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾ with the qaf sukun and the ha kasra.

As for the reading ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾, whether we lengthen the ha (ishbaʿ) or not, these are two readings as well: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ and ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ﴾; there are two readings, lengthening and not lengthening. This reading is clear and has no difficulty, because it conforms to the Arabic grammatical rules we know. Or not?

﴿يَتَّقِهِ﴾ is like (يَرْمِهِ) and is conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to the conditional verb, which is ﴿يُطِعِ﴾, and it is jussive (majzūm). And the conjoined element of a jussive is jussive. What is the sign of its jussive?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is the deletion of the weak letter (ḥarf al-ʿillah), that is, the deletion of the yā', and the kasra before it is evidence of it. ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾: the yā' is deleted and the kasra before it is evidence of it.

The ha in ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾ is the object of (يَتَّقِ), and it is a pronoun with kasra, built on kasra.

But on the reading ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾, the ha is sukun, contrary to what we know. We say it was made sukun for lightness, because ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾ is lighter than ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾, so it is sukun for lightness.

On the reading of Hafs, ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾, how was it made sukun, given that it is jussive by deletion of the weak letter? Because (يَتَّقِي) is undoubtedly a defective verb whose final letter is a weak letter, so how was it made sukun?

* Student: (...).
