On the reading of Hafs, ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾, how was it made sukun, given that it is jussive by deletion of the weak letter? Because (يَتَّقِي) is undoubtedly a defective verb whose final letter is a weak letter, so how was it made sukun?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is kasra. ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾ cannot be made sukun (...) a sukun before it cannot be pronounced, but the qaf is sukun. So the difficulty now is in making the qaf sukun, although the verb is defective, its final letter not being a sound letter, and the defective verb is jussive by deleting the weak letter. So why was it made sukun?

It is said: either it was made sukun for lightness, ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾, or it was made sukun by forgetting the weak letter, as if the weak letter was forgotten and it became a verb of what? A sound verb, and a sound verb is jussive by sukun.

Taqwa: we have often been told in the explanation of taqwa that it is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So what is the connection between it and khashyah? It is said: taqwa is in reality the result of khashyah, because whoever fears Allah guards himself against Him. Whoever fears someone with awe, veneration and exaltation must guard himself from him. So the connection between them is that taqwa is a branch of khashyah and its result. Whoever fears Allah guards himself against Him without doubt.

There is also a second question. You said: taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Is that not obedience (ṭāʿa)? What is the answer?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, in reality it is obedience. But let there be a rule you understand: some words are explained with one meaning when standing alone, and with another meaning when conjoined. Sometimes when standing alone they include that meaning, and sometimes when combined they are only part of it. Such examples are many.

For example, faqīr and miskīn: when standing alone, faqīr includes miskīn and miskīn includes faqīr. But when combined, faqīr is part of miskīn and miskīn is part of faqīr, in the sense that we say: faqīr is such-and-such, and miskīn is such-and-such, so that synonymy between the two words does not occur and the benefit of conjunction (ʿaṭf) is not lost. Understood?

Likewise here, obedience and taqwa: when obedience stands alone it means taqwa, and when taqwa stands alone it means obedience. When the two are combined, taqwa is restricted to avoiding prohibitions and obedience to doing commands. So whoever obeys Allah by doing His commands only, we restrict it to part of its meaning because it is conjoined with what? With taqwa, and taqwa here is only avoiding prohibitions, and we restrict it to part of its meaning. We do not say "and doing commands," why? Because it is conjoined with obedience. For this reason it is said (...).

When they are combined they separate, and when they separate they combine, in the sense that when separate they have one meaning, and when combined their meaning differs. What requires us to turn one of them into another meaning, or into part of the meaning, is so that they are not synonymous, and by that—that is, by their being synonymous—the benefit of conjunction would be lost. Yes indeed.

* Student: If they differ in meaning (...)?

* Shaykh: No, it is not necessary (...). There must be a connection, because as long as when standing alone each one means the second, that means there is a connection. The faqīr and the miskīn have a connection in reality, which is need, and taqwa means abandoning prohibitions, and obedience means doing commands. There is a connection between them, which is compliance (imtithāl).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What colour?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, but obedience is conformity to the command.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No. Khashyah contains veneration, and obedience, in most cases, is only from love, because whoever does not love a person does not obey him except out of fear of him, and then it is khashyah. So obedience in reality is not possible for a person in anything except from love for the commander, or for the thing commanded, or from fear of him. As for one who hates the commander, it is not possible for him to obey him while he is able (...).

In any case, we say: when obedience stands alone it means doing commands and abandoning prohibitions, and when combined with taqwa it is taken to mean doing commands, and taqwa to mean abandoning prohibitions, just as when taqwa stands alone it means doing commands and abandoning prohibitions.

This ruling, or this meaning, applies to many words of the Arabic language: when combined they separate and each has its own meaning, so that the benefit of conjunction is not lost; and when standing alone they combine and their meaning becomes one. Yes indeed.

* Student: Shaykh (...) is synonymy forbidden?

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, absolute synonymy can never exist.

* Student: Why?

* Shaykh: Because it is repetition without benefit, especially with conjunction present. Without conjunction, it may be verbal emphasis.

* Student: And is emphasis permitted with conjunction?

* Shaykh: No, because conjunction requires difference, and emphasis means that the second is the first.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, it requires difference: that the conjoined is other than the conjoined-to.

* Student: (...) the scholars of uṣūl (...) that all exceptions return, in the case of conjunction, to the excepted, because conjunction requires some resemblance?

* Shaykh: Agreement in the ruling and difference in meaning: the conjoined word is other than the word it is conjoined to, but the ruling is one. You say: Zayd and ʿAmr and Bakr and Khālid came; the ruling applies to all of them, but ʿAmr, Bakr and Khālid are other than Zayd. The difference in meaning remains; the ruling applied to the conjoined items together is necessary, but the essence of conjunction means that this has been joined to that and so has taken its ruling, yet this is other than that. That is, you cannot say: Zayd and Zayd came, meaning the second Zayd is the first. That is not permitted. But you may say: Zayd Zayd came, the second Zayd being the first by way of emphasis.

﴿وَمَنْ يُطِعِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَيَخْشَ اللَّهَ وَيَتَّقْهِ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْفَائِزُونَ﴾ [al-Nur 52]. The fa' in His words ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ is the response of the conditional clause. Why? Because the clause is nominal, and when a nominal clause is the response of a conditional, it must be preceded by fa'; the fa' is dropped only in cases of necessity, like the poet's words:

مَنْ يَفْعِلِ الْحَسَنَاتِ اللُّهُ يَشْكُرُهَا ∗∗∗ ...........................

He did not say: "fa-Allah yashkuruha."

As for His words ﴿هُمُ الْفَائِزُونَ﴾, what was mentioned before about the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) applies to it. What was that?

* Students: Affirming restriction.

* Shaykh: Restriction, exclusivity, and distinguishing the predicate from the attribute, and these belong to the pronoun of separation.

Good. ﴿الْفَائِزُونَ﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And restriction and exclusivity are restriction.

As for his words, "﴿الْفَائِزُونَ﴾ with Paradise": that means also salvation from the Fire, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿فَمَنْ زُحْزِحَ عَنِ النَّارِ وَأُدْخِلَ الْجَنَّةَ فَقَدْ فَازَ﴾ [Ali ʿImran 185]. The author's restriction to Paradise alone is because whoever enters Paradise has been saved from the Fire.

This verse is among the most comprehensive verses, because it gathers in summary the causes of success: these three matters, obedience to Allah, khashyah of Him, and taqwa of Him. Whenever these matters are present in a person, he succeeds, and the details are well known from the Book and the Sunnah.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: Because khashyah itself is worship and the root of taqwa. For a person to have in his heart fear of Allah, veneration of Him and dread of Him is one of the greatest acts of worship.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾, their utmost effort, ﴿that if you ordered them﴾ to jihad, ﴿they would go forth.﴾ Say [to them], ﴿Do not swear; [what is wanted is] known obedience﴾ to the Prophet ﷺ, better than your oath which you do not fulfil, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾).

﴿أَقْسَمُوا بِاَللَّهِ جَهْد أَيْمَانهمْ﴾ means they swore by Allah. ﴿لَئِنْ أَمَرْتَهُمْ لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾. This verse includes all the elements of an oath: every element of the oath is present, because an oath often omits some of its elements, but this verse includes all of them: the sworn by, the particle of oath, the verb of swearing, and the sworn to. Or not? This verse mentions all the elements of the oath.

The verb of swearing: ﴿أَقْسَمُوا﴾. The particle of oath: the bā' in ﴿بِاَللَّهِ﴾. The sworn by: ﴿اَللَّهِ﴾. The sworn to: ﴿لَئِنْ أَمَرْتَهُمْ لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾; this clause is the answer of the oath and is the sworn-to matter.

These people swore that if the Prophet ﷺ commanded them, that is, to jihad, they would go forth. The proof that jihad is meant is His words ﴿لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾, since it is presupposed that (...) in jihad. So they swore this oath: that if the Messenger commanded them, they would go out.

This oath is both an oath and a vow, because when an oath includes an obligation a person places upon himself toward Allah, it combines oath and vow. Accordingly, if someone said: "By Allah, I will pray two rak'ahs," and intended by it to bind himself, what does this become?

* Students: An oath and a vow.

* Shaykh: It becomes an oath and a vow, like: "It is incumbent upon me to Allah to pray two rak'ahs (...)," and ﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ عَاهَدَ اللَّهَ لَئِنْ آتَانَا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ﴾ [al-Tawbah 75].

But if a person intends by the oath to bring about the thing without binding himself to it, it is not a vow. The difference between the person who binds himself, seeing that his soul is obliged by this thing, and the person who wants to bring about the thing without seeing himself obliged, is like if he said: "By Allah, I will do such-and-such; I will go out to the market, I will wear the garment," and similar. He did not intend that it be binding; he intended to bring it about without being bound, that is, he says: I will do this, and affirms that he will do it. This is not an oath. So if the oath includes an obligation, what does it become?

* Student: An oath and a vow.

* Shaykh: An oath and a vow, or a vow sworn about.

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾: there is no need for you to swear, saying, "By Allah, if you command us we will go out." Rather, when you are commanded, go out without an oath. There is no need (...).

﴿طَاعَةٌ مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾: the author, according to his context, made ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾ its attribute, and its predicate omitted, its estimated meaning being: better than your oath.

But this is not apparent. Rather, the apparent reading is that ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ is the subject and the predicate is omitted, estimated as: upon you is known obedience; or ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ is the predicate and the subject omitted, meaning: your obedience is known obedience. The meaning of that: a person must obey with known obedience. What is known obedience from the believers: that he swears to do it, or does it without swearing?

* Students: He does it without swearing.

* Shaykh: Yes, he does it without swearing, because one who swears he will do it, as if he did not wish to do it, but he binds himself by compulsion.

So known obedience is compliance without an oath. This is better than the author's estimate, which is to say: upon you is known obedience, or your obedience is known obedience, meaning known obedience of the believers, which is adherence to the rulings of the Sharia without an oath.

(﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ meaning: of your obedience in words and your opposition in deeds.) This is not correct. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ means: of everything you do, whether you swore to it or did not swear to it.

And (ma ta'malun): "mā" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality, that is, all deeds. ﴿خَبِيرٌ﴾ means knowing, except that the difference between it and ʿalīm is that khabīr is the one who knows inner realities, so it is more precise than absolute knowledge: an awareness of inner matters.

﴿بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ is general, covering everything a person does in his heart, his tongue or his limbs; nothing of that is hidden from Allah the Glorified and Exalted.

* From these noble verses it is derived: the description of the believers' submission. The description of submission: when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, they say, "We hear and we obey," they do not hesitate or waver.

* And also in it: what follows from this hearing and obedience of success, which is attaining the sought and being saved from the feared.

* And also in it: evidence of the benefit that obedience, khashyah and taqwa, these three, have the benefit of success in Paradise and salvation from the Fire.

* And in them is evidence for the disapproval of vows, from His words ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾, and this is a prohibition. The scholars have differed on whether vowing is disliked (makruh) or forbidden (ḥarām)?

There are two opinions. Some scholars hold that vowing is disliked, and others hold that it is forbidden. It seems Shaykh al-Islam inclines to prohibition, and it is closer to the truth: the view of prohibition is closer than the view of dislike, because Allah the Exalted forbade it by His words ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾, and the basic meaning of a prohibition is prohibition. The Prophet ﷺ also forbade it and said: «Indeed it brings no good, and it is only extracted thereby from the miser» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6608), and Muslim (1639/4), with his wording, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.]].

The meaning also requires it: because a person is in well-being, so binding himself to a matter Allah did not oblige him with is imposing on himself what he was not charged with.

Furthermore, from the meaning it requires: many vowing people regret their vows, especially when the vow involves some hardship; like swearing: if Allah cures his sick person, he will fast ten days of every month, and Allah cures his sick person, (...) now he fasts ten days of every month unless there is an excuse, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him» [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]].

Many people who make vows do not fulfill them, because they see the vow as binding only once they have what they wanted. They say, "Praise be to God, I got what I asked for, God cured my patient, or I passed," and then they do not fulfill to God what God has fulfilled for them. God fulfills for them what they stipulated with their Lord, while they, may God protect us, do not obey Him. But what is the outcome and the consequence? A very great one: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God, saying, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and will surely be among the righteous." (75) But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it﴾ and did not give charity, ﴿and they turned away while they were refusing﴾, and they were not righteous. And what happened is ﴿so He followed it with hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they will meet Him, because they failed God in what they promised Him and because they used to lie﴾ [at-Tawbah 75–77].

This outcome, may God protect us, is a very great evil: that God should place hypocrisy in the heart of this vower who did not fulfill to God Most High what he pledged to God, because he pledged to God this thing.

As for one who vows an act of disobedience, it is not permissible to fulfill it, because there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. Your soul, even if it compels you to do it, do not obey it, just as you do not obey your ruler if he commands you with something that involves disobedience to God. Likewise, do not obey your soul if it compels you to something that involves disobedience to God. It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever vows to disobey God, let him not disobey Him" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of 'Aishah].

Nevertheless, the vower must pay an expiation for an oath, for the vower in reality is not free of a trial that binds himself; at least it is an expiation for an oath. Even if a person says, for example, "For God is a vow upon me," but he only spoke these words and did nothing else, what becomes obligatory upon him? The expiation of an oath becomes obligatory upon him. From this we know the seriousness of vowing.

As for what some people imagine, that a vow brings about the desired outcome, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, negated this illusion with his saying: "Indeed it does not bring any good" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6608) and Muslim (1639/4), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. How can it bring good? Your patient, God had decreed that he would recover before you vowed, and your vow is certainly not a cause of the recovery. God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Most Generous of the generous; His generosity does not depend on anything (...). A person (...) says, "I vow to You so that You cure my patient." No. If God bestows a blessing upon you, then thank Him for it in the manner the Sharia has prescribed. As for your saying (...), it is as if you are saying: "God does not obey me; He will not cure this patient unless (...) I vow for him so that He cures him." Then the trial comes, and the matter happens to him not through it. This is from the trial.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon you, indeed it is obligatory upon you, to warn people against vowing, and to say to people: "A vow does not bring any good." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who does not speak from desire in these matters, informed that it does not bring any good.

How many a student has vowed, "If God makes me pass, I will fast three days," and God makes him pass, yet he does not fast. He did not fast (...) for what reason? Because the soul, in reality weak in faith, does not care that it opposes (its vow); it says, "The desired outcome has been achieved," and not (...). In any case, the prohibition of this vow is derived from His saying: ﴿Do not swear oaths﴾.

* And in it: the obligation of restricting obedience to what is recognized (ma'ruf); that it be obedience that is recognized. What is the meaning of "recognized": is it among people, or from the Sharia? It is obedience recognized by the Sharia, not from people, because people may recognize as obedience something they think is obedience and it is not obedience.
* And it is derived from it: it is not permissible to exceed the Sharia in obedience, nor to fall short of it; due to His saying: ﴿reasonable obedience﴾, without excess or deficiency.
* And in it also: the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of everything; due to His saying: ﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, that is, of everything you do, present and future.

The benefit of mentioning God's knowledge of what we do is not merely that He informs us that He knows. Rather, the benefit of it is what? Is it encouragement or warning? Both, unless the context requires only one of them. Otherwise, your knowing that God knows everything you do means: He grants you success in worship (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 50–53 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾: disbelief. ﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ meaning: they doubt his prophethood. ﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ in judgment, meaning they would wrong them in it. No; ﴿rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [an-Nur 50] by turning away from it.) Allah the Mighty and Majestic, clarifying the state of those who reject what Allah and His Messenger have judged, says that they do not escape these three conditions:

﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ The disease (maraḍ) is an ailment that afflicts what is healthy so that it leaves its balance. This is the disease, and this definition of disease includes both bodily disease and heart disease. Bodily disease is in reality an ailment that afflicts the body so that it leaves its balance; likewise heart disease is an ailment that afflicts the heart, taking it out of balance until it deviates and does not accept the truth. So what is the disease intended here?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. The author explained it as disbelief. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that what is meant is an evil intention, as shown by the division (that follows), whether it is disbelief, or hypocrisy, or something else. The point is that the disease is an evil intention that turns them away from accepting the truth.

﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ This is doubt, and it is the disease of misgiving (shubhah). For it has passed us many times that the causes of deviation from the truth are either shubhah or shahwah (desire). That is, either a person desires something that contradicts the Shariah and follows it, or he has a misgiving about this truth and so refrains from it.

So we say here: with what should the disease be explained? With an evil intention, which is desire, that is, craving what contradicts the Shariah.
(﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾ meaning they have doubted.) This is the disease of misgiving that afflicts a person so that the truth does not become clear to him. Let us give an example: a man is commanded to do something, to pray, but he puts a worldly matter before his prayer. What disease is in his heart? The disease of desire.
Another is commanded to pray but doubts the benefit of prayer, or doubts its existence, or something similar. This has the disease of misgiving.
So what we have here: ﴿disease﴾ means an evil intention, and ﴿or do they have doubt﴾ is this doubt, may Allah protect us.

The third matter: ﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ That is, they do not have an evil intention, nor doubt about the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, but they have another doubt. What is it? Doubt about the justice of Allah and His Messenger. Therefore they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to them, so they dread inclination and injustice.
In reality, the inclination and injustice lie with them, not in the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, the judgment of Allah and His Messenger is upon truth and justice, but injustice is in their own scale, because they are the ones who have deviated from what they ought to be in terms of compliance and obedience.
﴿Or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Rather (bal)﴾ here is for transition (idrab). But what is your view of this idrab? Is it idrab of cancellation (ibṭāl) or idrab of transition (intiqāl)? What does the author see?
He said: (No), ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease, or have they doubt, or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ (No), then he said: ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ in the Qur'an. So the author's statement implies that the idrab here is of cancellation, and for this reason he estimated (No) after the three preceding possibilities.
But in my view the idrab here is not of cancellation; it is of transition. For the reality of the matter is that whoever does not accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger does not go beyond these three matters: either he has an evil intention, or doubt, or fear. We cannot imagine a fourth matter beyond these three possibilities.
Furthermore, describing them as wrongdoers does not go beyond these three possibilities either. Whoever has a disease in his heart is a wrongdoer, whoever has a misgiving in his heart is a wrongdoer, and whoever fears that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to him is a wrongdoer.
So the matter is one of transitional idrab, not cancelling idrab.

The phrase ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease, or have they doubt, or do they fear that Allah will be unjust to them and His Messenger?﴾ — is (am) in these places the equalizing (taswiyah) meaning "or," or the idrab meaning "rather"?
* Student: It admits both.
* The Shaykh: It admits both? How is that?
* Student: Or it could be (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, is this in the sense of "rather" or in the sense of "or"?
It has passed us earlier that the one meaning "or" is the one that comes after the interrogative of equalization (hamzat al-taswiyah), such as: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6], and ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. These are the ones meaning "or," and they are called connected (muttasilah). As for the one meaning "rather," it is the one not preceded by the hamzat al-taswiyah, and it is called disconnected (munqatiʿah).
On this basis, the (am) in ﴿or have they doubt, or do they fear﴾ is disconnected, meaning "rather," and it occurs frequently at the end of Surat at-Tur: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman.﴾ What follows it? ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, we await for him the misfortunes of time"? Say: "Wait, for I am with you among those who wait." Or do their minds command them to this, or are they a transgressing people? Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ to the end [at-Tur 30–33]. Many instances are in the end of Surat at-Tur, disconnected in the sense of "rather," with the interrogative hamzah.
So here it is disconnected, not connected, because the connected is the one that comes after the hamzat al-taswiyah and means "or," while the disconnected is the one that does not come after the hamzat al-taswiyah and means "rather."
As for His statement ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾, here He recorded wrongdoing upon them and emphasized it with two kinds of emphasis. What are they?
* Student: Huwa (they).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl).
* The Shaykh: With the pronoun of separation, and with the sentence being nominal with both parts definite; for when a sentence is nominal with both parts definite, it conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). Here ﴿ulā'ika﴾ is the subject, and it is definite because it is a demonstrative noun; ﴿al-ẓālimūn﴾ is the predicate, and it is definite because it has the article (al). On this basis Allah emphasized their wrongdoing with two kinds of emphasis: the sentence being nominal with both parts definite, and the pronoun of separation. As for the benefits of the pronoun of separation, which occurs frequently in the Qur'an and outside it, what are its benefits?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Wait. For emphasis, we all must be keeping it in mind, because I have just told you in the explanation that this sentence is emphasized with two kinds of emphasis: one of them is the pronoun of separation, and the second is that it is a nominal sentence with both parts definite. We ought to all know this; it does not need repeating. That is one point.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They came to him submitting, that is, compliant and obedient, so they follow only their desires. He showed the state of the believers, and said: ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, to judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾

First: in the parsing of His statement ﴿the saying of the believers﴾ — ﴿innamā kāna qawla al-mu'minīn﴾ — it is in the accusative. It is known that kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, and here the word after it is accusative. The answer is that this is its predicate, placed first: ﴿qawla al-mu'minīn﴾ is its predicate, fronted; and its subject is the verbal noun formed from (an) and the verb in His statement ﴿that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾, meaning: their saying was only this saying: ﴿"We hear and we obey."﴾

As for His statement ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning ﴿when they are called to Allah﴾: to His Book, and to His Messenger; to Him personally during his life, and to his Sunnah after his death. ﴿To judge between them﴾: what was said about its counterpart in the verse in the previous lesson applies here.
The pronoun in ﴿to judge﴾ returns to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ. The judgment is attributed to him because his judgment is a conveying from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, so his judgment is also aligned with the judgment of Allah, since he is the one who conveys from Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
His statement ﴿to judge between them﴾ includes disputes that they have disagreed over and rulings on which they differ; the judge is the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, both in the disputes that arise between litigants and in the rulings on which people differ. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 10], and He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [an-Nisa 59].

So when the believers are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, their saying is: ﴿that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾ ﴿That they say "We hear"﴾ with our ears, ﴿and "we obey"﴾ with our limbs. They hear and submit. Obedience, as has passed, encompasses doing the commands and abandoning the prohibitions, encompassing both together. Unlike those who say "We hear" while they do not hear, or say "We hear and we disobey," so they say "We hear" but do not submit, or openly declare disobedience, saying "We hear and we disobey." The believers say, "We hear and we obey."

The author's statement: i.e., (the appropriate saying for them), means that their appropriate saying is this. The apparent meaning of the author's words is that the matter is by way of supposition and assumption: that it is only proper for them to say this. But the reality is that this is what actually occurs; it is not merely the appropriate saying, but the appropriate saying that actually takes place. So when they are ﴿called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, they say, "We hear and we obey,"﴾ as Allah described them, and they said: ﴿"We hear and we obey."﴾

Making this an appropriate saying, meaning supposed and assumed, and that this is what is appropriate for them, contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. For the saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, is: "We hear and we obey," hearing and obeying, and "upon the wide and ample." This is their appropriate saying that actually comes from them. When they are called to Allah and His Messenger, they do not say, "By Allah, so-and-so's opinion is otherwise, and so-and-so's opinion is otherwise, and people are otherwise," or similar things. They do not say such a matter; they say, "We hear and we obey."

Likewise it is obligatory upon every believer. Whoever does not say this is not a believer: either faith has been entirely negated from him, or his faith is deficient.
Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: and (﴿"We hear and we obey"﴾ by responding, ﴿and those﴾ then, ﴿they are the successful﴾ the saved).
﴿And those, they are the successful﴾: (they) is a pronoun of separation, and its three benefits have passed: restriction, emphasis, and distinguishing the predicate from the attribute.
﴿And those﴾ meaning: those who say "We hear and we obey" when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, ﴿they are the successful﴾. The author said: (i.e., the saved).
The more correct view is that success (falāḥ) is not merely salvation, but salvation from what is feared, and attaining or obtaining what is sought. The successful one is he who is saved from what he dislikes and attains what he loves. So these are those who were saved from what is feared, because disobedience is absent from them, and who attained what is sought, because complete obedience is achieved by them. So through acts of obedience comes the attainment of what is sought, and through avoiding sins comes salvation from what is feared.
Restricting success to these people indicates that whoever is other than them is not successful. But if faith is entirely absent from a person, all success is absent from him; and if some faith is absent from him, some success is absent from him. So the duty of the believer, when he is called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, or when he himself becomes aware of the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, is that he say: "We hear and we obey." He does not look right or left, or interpret, or distort. No; he says, "We hear and we obey," with complete submission and complete hearing, for by this faith is realized.
The person who submits to the judgment of Allah the Exalted with such ease and such conformity is the one who finds rest and no anxiety arises in him. For whoever accustoms himself to hesitation in accepting the legal rulings, even in a single ruling, the soul will compel him to hesitate in many legal matters. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-An'am 110].
So when a person accustoms himself to accepting the truth at the first moment, without any anxiety or hesitation in carrying it out, it becomes easy for him afterward to submit to all commands and not to look aside or hesitate. But if he does it once and hesitates about one of the matters of the legal rulings, that is, after it has become established for him (leave aside hesitation about establishment; hesitation about establishment is something else: he may hesitate about establishment if, for example, the hadith is weak in its chain, or similar), but if the ruling has become established for him that this is the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, then his hesitation in accepting it is extremely dangerous for him, because it leads to hesitation in other rulings in the future.
A similar principle applies to the decreed ruling as well. The person who does not train himself to be patient with the decrees of Allah, and His predestination, remains constantly anxious and weary of decrees that do not suit him.
So when he goes along with predestination and decree, so that if good befalls him he is reassured by it, and if harm befalls him he is patient with it, while he is going along with predestination and decree, then by that he finds rest and is never anxious. You will find that the person who wants Allah the Mighty and Majestic's decree and predestination to be what suits him is always in anxiety, because predestination is not as you wish, just as the Shariah is also not as you wish.
The Shariah is not as people wish, and predestination is not as people wish. Whoever goes along with both of them, these two rulings, will find success, tranquility, and a good life. Whoever is anxious about them, or about one of them, will remain in anxiety: if it concerns the decreed matter, he remains in anxiety and grief, because matters do not come as they should; and if it concerns the legal matters, likewise, the door of hesitation in accepting and implementing Allah's rulings opens for him.

* * *

(﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger and fears Allah﴾: fears Him, ﴿and is mindful of Him﴾ — with the ha' vowelled and with it unvowelled — by obeying Him, ﴿then those are the victorious﴾ with Paradise).
This verse is among the most comprehensive and concise verses.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ by submitting to the judgments of Allah and His Messenger. It has passed that obedience is conformity to what? To the command: whether it is a prohibition or a command, that is, a demand to bring about or a demand to abandon; it is conformity to the command. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, and fears Allah, and is mindful of Him﴾. Note that obedience to Allah and His Messenger, fear (khashyah) is worship, and taqwa is worship; they are for none but whom?
* Students: Allah.
* The Shaykh: None but Allah alone. For this reason He said: ﴿and fears Allah and is mindful of Him﴾. I say here: (with the ha' vowelled — ﴿yattaqihi﴾ — and unvowelled) with the ha' vowelled and unvowelled: ﴿wa yattaqihi﴾ or ﴿wa yattaqih﴾.
Now, ﴿fears Allah﴾: the author says (fears Him), but this explanation is insufficient, because khashyah is stronger than khawf (fear). The difference between them: khashyah is only from knowledge, as in His statement: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. So the scholar is the one who fears Allah, because he fears Him with knowledge of the reality of the one feared and the state of the one who fears; he knows the state of the one feared and knows the state of the one who fears.
Khashyah is only with knowledge, as His statement: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28].

**Second difference: with respect to the one feared and the one who fears.** Khashyah (awe-fear) arises from the greatness of the one feared, whereas khawf (fear) arises from the weakness of the one who fears. The difference between them is clear: khashyah exists because of the greatness of the one feared, even if the one who fears is great himself, while khawf comes from the weakness of the one who fears.

**Third difference: khashyah is fear accompanied by reverence, veneration and exaltation.** This difference branches off from the second one.

Khawf is not like this; it does not arise from reverence, veneration and exaltation. For this reason one says "khafa min al-dhi'b" (he feared the wolf), and one does not say "khashiya minhu" or "khashiyahu," except figuratively (ʿalā sabīl al-tawassuʿ).

These three differences make it necessary that khashyah not be synonymous with khawf in the strict sense of exact equivalence. However, approximately (ʿalā wajh al-taqrīb) it is acceptable: a person may say that khashyah means khawf in order to bring it closer to the understanding of the listeners, but not on the basis that khawf is the exact meaning of khashyah. Khashyah occurs together with awe, veneration and exaltation of the one feared, unlike khawf.

We say: ﴿وَيَخْشَى اللهَ﴾ ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾ and ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾. We are now discussing the readings that exist:

There is: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾.

And there is: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾.

And there is a third reading, the reading of Hafs, which the author did not mention, namely ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾ with the qaf sukun and the ha kasra.

As for the reading ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾, whether we lengthen the ha (ishbaʿ) or not, these are two readings as well: ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ and ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ فَأُولَئِكَ﴾; there are two readings, lengthening and not lengthening. This reading is clear and has no difficulty, because it conforms to the Arabic grammatical rules we know. Or not?

﴿يَتَّقِهِ﴾ is like (يَرْمِهِ) and is conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to the conditional verb, which is ﴿يُطِعِ﴾, and it is jussive (majzūm). And the conjoined element of a jussive is jussive. What is the sign of its jussive?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is the deletion of the weak letter (ḥarf al-ʿillah), that is, the deletion of the yā', and the kasra before it is evidence of it. ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾: the yā' is deleted and the kasra before it is evidence of it.

The ha in ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾ is the object of (يَتَّقِ), and it is a pronoun with kasra, built on kasra.

But on the reading ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾, the ha is sukun, contrary to what we know. We say it was made sukun for lightness, because ﴿وَيَتَّقِهْ﴾ is lighter than ﴿وَيَتَّقِهِ﴾, so it is sukun for lightness.

On the reading of Hafs, ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾, how was it made sukun, given that it is jussive by deletion of the weak letter? Because (يَتَّقِي) is undoubtedly a defective verb whose final letter is a weak letter, so how was it made sukun?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is kasra. ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾ cannot be made sukun (...) a sukun before it cannot be pronounced, but the qaf is sukun. So the difficulty now is in making the qaf sukun, although the verb is defective, its final letter not being a sound letter, and the defective verb is jussive by deleting the weak letter. So why was it made sukun?

It is said: either it was made sukun for lightness, ﴿وَيَتَّقْهِ﴾, or it was made sukun by forgetting the weak letter, as if the weak letter was forgotten and it became a verb of what? A sound verb, and a sound verb is jussive by sukun.

Taqwa: we have often been told in the explanation of taqwa that it is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So what is the connection between it and khashyah? It is said: taqwa is in reality the result of khashyah, because whoever fears Allah guards himself against Him. Whoever fears someone with awe, veneration and exaltation must guard himself from him. So the connection between them is that taqwa is a branch of khashyah and its result. Whoever fears Allah guards himself against Him without doubt.

There is also a second question. You said: taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Is that not obedience (ṭāʿa)? What is the answer?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, in reality it is obedience. But let there be a rule you understand: some words are explained with one meaning when standing alone, and with another meaning when conjoined. Sometimes when standing alone they include that meaning, and sometimes when combined they are only part of it. Such examples are many.

For example, faqīr and miskīn: when standing alone, faqīr includes miskīn and miskīn includes faqīr. But when combined, faqīr is part of miskīn and miskīn is part of faqīr, in the sense that we say: faqīr is such-and-such, and miskīn is such-and-such, so that synonymy between the two words does not occur and the benefit of conjunction (ʿaṭf) is not lost. Understood?

Likewise here, obedience and taqwa: when obedience stands alone it means taqwa, and when taqwa stands alone it means obedience. When the two are combined, taqwa is restricted to avoiding prohibitions and obedience to doing commands. So whoever obeys Allah by doing His commands only, we restrict it to part of its meaning because it is conjoined with what? With taqwa, and taqwa here is only avoiding prohibitions, and we restrict it to part of its meaning. We do not say "and doing commands," why? Because it is conjoined with obedience. For this reason it is said (...).

When they are combined they separate, and when they separate they combine, in the sense that when separate they have one meaning, and when combined their meaning differs. What requires us to turn one of them into another meaning, or into part of the meaning, is so that they are not synonymous, and by that—that is, by their being synonymous—the benefit of conjunction would be lost. Yes indeed.

* Student: If they differ in meaning (...)?

* Shaykh: No, it is not necessary (...). There must be a connection, because as long as when standing alone each one means the second, that means there is a connection. The faqīr and the miskīn have a connection in reality, which is need, and taqwa means abandoning prohibitions, and obedience means doing commands. There is a connection between them, which is compliance (imtithāl).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What colour?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, but obedience is conformity to the command.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No. Khashyah contains veneration, and obedience, in most cases, is only from love, because whoever does not love a person does not obey him except out of fear of him, and then it is khashyah. So obedience in reality is not possible for a person in anything except from love for the commander, or for the thing commanded, or from fear of him. As for one who hates the commander, it is not possible for him to obey him while he is able (...).

In any case, we say: when obedience stands alone it means doing commands and abandoning prohibitions, and when combined with taqwa it is taken to mean doing commands, and taqwa to mean abandoning prohibitions, just as when taqwa stands alone it means doing commands and abandoning prohibitions.

This ruling, or this meaning, applies to many words of the Arabic language: when combined they separate and each has its own meaning, so that the benefit of conjunction is not lost; and when standing alone they combine and their meaning becomes one. Yes indeed.

* Student: Shaykh (...) is synonymy forbidden?

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, absolute synonymy can never exist.

* Student: Why?

* Shaykh: Because it is repetition without benefit, especially with conjunction present. Without conjunction, it may be verbal emphasis.

* Student: And is emphasis permitted with conjunction?

* Shaykh: No, because conjunction requires difference, and emphasis means that the second is the first.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, it requires difference: that the conjoined is other than the conjoined-to.

* Student: (...) the scholars of uṣūl (...) that all exceptions return, in the case of conjunction, to the excepted, because conjunction requires some resemblance?

* Shaykh: Agreement in the ruling and difference in meaning: the conjoined word is other than the word it is conjoined to, but the ruling is one. You say: Zayd and ʿAmr and Bakr and Khālid came; the ruling applies to all of them, but ʿAmr, Bakr and Khālid are other than Zayd. The difference in meaning remains; the ruling applied to the conjoined items together is necessary, but the essence of conjunction means that this has been joined to that and so has taken its ruling, yet this is other than that. That is, you cannot say: Zayd and Zayd came, meaning the second Zayd is the first. That is not permitted. But you may say: Zayd Zayd came, the second Zayd being the first by way of emphasis.

﴿وَمَنْ يُطِعِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَيَخْشَ اللَّهَ وَيَتَّقْهِ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْفَائِزُونَ﴾ [al-Nur 52]. The fa' in His words ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ is the response of the conditional clause. Why? Because the clause is nominal, and when a nominal clause is the response of a conditional, it must be preceded by fa'; the fa' is dropped only in cases of necessity, like the poet's words:

مَنْ يَفْعِلِ الْحَسَنَاتِ اللُّهُ يَشْكُرُهَا ∗∗∗ ...........................

He did not say: "fa-Allah yashkuruha."

As for His words ﴿هُمُ الْفَائِزُونَ﴾, what was mentioned before about the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) applies to it. What was that?

* Students: Affirming restriction.

* Shaykh: Restriction, exclusivity, and distinguishing the predicate from the attribute, and these belong to the pronoun of separation.

Good. ﴿الْفَائِزُونَ﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And restriction and exclusivity are restriction.

As for his words, "﴿الْفَائِزُونَ﴾ with Paradise": that means also salvation from the Fire, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿فَمَنْ زُحْزِحَ عَنِ النَّارِ وَأُدْخِلَ الْجَنَّةَ فَقَدْ فَازَ﴾ [Ali ʿImran 185]. The author's restriction to Paradise alone is because whoever enters Paradise has been saved from the Fire.

This verse is among the most comprehensive verses, because it gathers in summary the causes of success: these three matters, obedience to Allah, khashyah of Him, and taqwa of Him. Whenever these matters are present in a person, he succeeds, and the details are well known from the Book and the Sunnah.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: Because khashyah itself is worship and the root of taqwa. For a person to have in his heart fear of Allah, veneration of Him and dread of Him is one of the greatest acts of worship.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾, their utmost effort, ﴿that if you ordered them﴾ to jihad, ﴿they would go forth.﴾ Say [to them], ﴿Do not swear; [what is wanted is] known obedience﴾ to the Prophet ﷺ, better than your oath which you do not fulfil, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾).

﴿أَقْسَمُوا بِاَللَّهِ جَهْد أَيْمَانهمْ﴾ means they swore by Allah. ﴿لَئِنْ أَمَرْتَهُمْ لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾. This verse includes all the elements of an oath: every element of the oath is present, because an oath often omits some of its elements, but this verse includes all of them: the sworn by, the particle of oath, the verb of swearing, and the sworn to. Or not? This verse mentions all the elements of the oath.

The verb of swearing: ﴿أَقْسَمُوا﴾. The particle of oath: the bā' in ﴿بِاَللَّهِ﴾. The sworn by: ﴿اَللَّهِ﴾. The sworn to: ﴿لَئِنْ أَمَرْتَهُمْ لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾; this clause is the answer of the oath and is the sworn-to matter.

These people swore that if the Prophet ﷺ commanded them, that is, to jihad, they would go forth. The proof that jihad is meant is His words ﴿لَيَخْرُجُنَّ﴾, since it is presupposed that (...) in jihad. So they swore this oath: that if the Messenger commanded them, they would go out.

This oath is both an oath and a vow, because when an oath includes an obligation a person places upon himself toward Allah, it combines oath and vow. Accordingly, if someone said: "By Allah, I will pray two rak'ahs," and intended by it to bind himself, what does this become?

* Students: An oath and a vow.

* Shaykh: It becomes an oath and a vow, like: "It is incumbent upon me to Allah to pray two rak'ahs (...)," and ﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ عَاهَدَ اللَّهَ لَئِنْ آتَانَا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ﴾ [al-Tawbah 75].

But if a person intends by the oath to bring about the thing without binding himself to it, it is not a vow. The difference between the person who binds himself, seeing that his soul is obliged by this thing, and the person who wants to bring about the thing without seeing himself obliged, is like if he said: "By Allah, I will do such-and-such; I will go out to the market, I will wear the garment," and similar. He did not intend that it be binding; he intended to bring it about without being bound, that is, he says: I will do this, and affirms that he will do it. This is not an oath. So if the oath includes an obligation, what does it become?

* Student: An oath and a vow.

* Shaykh: An oath and a vow, or a vow sworn about.

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾: there is no need for you to swear, saying, "By Allah, if you command us we will go out." Rather, when you are commanded, go out without an oath. There is no need (...).

﴿طَاعَةٌ مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾: the author, according to his context, made ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾ its attribute, and its predicate omitted, its estimated meaning being: better than your oath.

But this is not apparent. Rather, the apparent reading is that ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ is the subject and the predicate is omitted, estimated as: upon you is known obedience; or ﴿طَاعَةٌ﴾ is the predicate and the subject omitted, meaning: your obedience is known obedience. The meaning of that: a person must obey with known obedience. What is known obedience from the believers: that he swears to do it, or does it without swearing?

* Students: He does it without swearing.

* Shaykh: Yes, he does it without swearing, because one who swears he will do it, as if he did not wish to do it, but he binds himself by compulsion.

So known obedience is compliance without an oath. This is better than the author's estimate, which is to say: upon you is known obedience, or your obedience is known obedience, meaning known obedience of the believers, which is adherence to the rulings of the Sharia without an oath.

(﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ meaning: of your obedience in words and your opposition in deeds.) This is not correct. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ means: of everything you do, whether you swore to it or did not swear to it.

And (ma ta'malun): "mā" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality, that is, all deeds. ﴿خَبِيرٌ﴾ means knowing, except that the difference between it and ʿalīm is that khabīr is the one who knows inner realities, so it is more precise than absolute knowledge: an awareness of inner matters.

﴿بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ is general, covering everything a person does in his heart, his tongue or his limbs; nothing of that is hidden from Allah the Glorified and Exalted.

* From these noble verses it is derived: the description of the believers' submission. The description of submission: when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, they say, "We hear and we obey," they do not hesitate or waver.

* And also in it: what follows from this hearing and obedience of success, which is attaining the sought and being saved from the feared.

* And also in it: evidence of the benefit that obedience, khashyah and taqwa, these three, have the benefit of success in Paradise and salvation from the Fire.

* And in them is evidence for the disapproval of vows, from His words ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾, and this is a prohibition. The scholars have differed on whether vowing is disliked (makruh) or forbidden (ḥarām)?

There are two opinions. Some scholars hold that vowing is disliked, and others hold that it is forbidden. It seems Shaykh al-Islam inclines to prohibition, and it is closer to the truth: the view of prohibition is closer than the view of dislike, because Allah the Exalted forbade it by His words ﴿قُلْ لَا تُقْسِمُوا﴾, and the basic meaning of a prohibition is prohibition. The Prophet ﷺ also forbade it and said: «Indeed it brings no good, and it is only extracted thereby from the miser» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6608), and Muslim (1639/4), with his wording, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.]].

The meaning also requires it: because a person is in well-being, so binding himself to a matter Allah did not oblige him with is imposing on himself what he was not charged with.

Furthermore, from the meaning it requires: many vowing people regret their vows, especially when the vow involves some hardship; like swearing: if Allah cures his sick person, he will fast ten days of every month, and Allah cures his sick person, (...) now he fasts ten days of every month unless there is an excuse, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him» [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]].

Many people who make vows do not fulfill them, because they see the vow as binding only once they have what they wanted. They say, "Praise be to God, I got what I asked for, God cured my patient, or I passed," and then they do not fulfill to God what God has fulfilled for them. God fulfills for them what they stipulated with their Lord, while they, may God protect us, do not obey Him. But what is the outcome and the consequence? A very great one: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God, saying, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and will surely be among the righteous." (75) But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it﴾ and did not give charity, ﴿and they turned away while they were refusing﴾, and they were not righteous. And what happened is ﴿so He followed it with hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they will meet Him, because they failed God in what they promised Him and because they used to lie﴾ [at-Tawbah 75–77].

This outcome, may God protect us, is a very great evil: that God should place hypocrisy in the heart of this vower who did not fulfill to God Most High what he pledged to God, because he pledged to God this thing.

As for one who vows an act of disobedience, it is not permissible to fulfill it, because there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. Your soul, even if it compels you to do it, do not obey it, just as you do not obey your ruler if he commands you with something that involves disobedience to God. Likewise, do not obey your soul if it compels you to something that involves disobedience to God. It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever vows to disobey God, let him not disobey Him" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of 'Aishah].

Nevertheless, the vower must pay an expiation for an oath, for the vower in reality is not free of a trial that binds himself; at least it is an expiation for an oath. Even if a person says, for example, "For God is a vow upon me," but he only spoke these words and did nothing else, what becomes obligatory upon him? The expiation of an oath becomes obligatory upon him. From this we know the seriousness of vowing.

As for what some people imagine, that a vow brings about the desired outcome, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, negated this illusion with his saying: "Indeed it does not bring any good" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6608) and Muslim (1639/4), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. How can it bring good? Your patient, God had decreed that he would recover before you vowed, and your vow is certainly not a cause of the recovery. God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Most Generous of the generous; His generosity does not depend on anything (...). A person (...) says, "I vow to You so that You cure my patient." No. If God bestows a blessing upon you, then thank Him for it in the manner the Sharia has prescribed. As for your saying (...), it is as if you are saying: "God does not obey me; He will not cure this patient unless (...) I vow for him so that He cures him." Then the trial comes, and the matter happens to him not through it. This is from the trial.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon you, indeed it is obligatory upon you, to warn people against vowing, and to say to people: "A vow does not bring any good." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who does not speak from desire in these matters, informed that it does not bring any good.

How many a student has vowed, "If God makes me pass, I will fast three days," and God makes him pass, yet he does not fast. He did not fast (...) for what reason? Because the soul, in reality weak in faith, does not care that it opposes (its vow); it says, "The desired outcome has been achieved," and not (...). In any case, the prohibition of this vow is derived from His saying: ﴿Do not swear oaths﴾.

* And in it: the obligation of restricting obedience to what is recognized (ma'ruf); that it be obedience that is recognized. What is the meaning of "recognized": is it among people, or from the Sharia? It is obedience recognized by the Sharia, not from people, because people may recognize as obedience something they think is obedience and it is not obedience.
* And it is derived from it: it is not permissible to exceed the Sharia in obedience, nor to fall short of it; due to His saying: ﴿reasonable obedience﴾, without excess or deficiency.
* And in it also: the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of everything; due to His saying: ﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, that is, of everything you do, present and future.

The benefit of mentioning God's knowledge of what we do is not merely that He informs us that He knows. Rather, the benefit of it is what? Is it encouragement or warning? Both, unless the context requires only one of them. Otherwise, your knowing that God knows everything you do means: He grants you success in worship (...).

(﴿فَإِنَّمَا عَلَيْهِ مَا حُمِّلَ﴾ من التبليغ، ﴿وَعَلَيْكُمْ مَا حُمِّلْتُمْ﴾ من طاعته، ﴿وَإِنْ تُطِيعُوهُ تَهْتَدُوا وَمَا عَلَى الرَّسُول إلَّا الْبَلَاغ الْمُبِين﴾ أي: التبليغ البين).

Allah Most High says to the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding him to tell the people: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾. It has already been mentioned that obedience (ṭāʿah) means conforming to the command by carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden; this is obedience.

His words ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ repeat the governing particle (al-ʿāmil, the word that governs the case of what follows), which shows that obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) is an independent obedience, and that what he brought is like what came from Allah. For this reason the scholars said: what is made obligatory by the Sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is like what is made obligatory by the Qur'an, whether a command or a prohibition. This is clear, because He made obedience to the Prophet (ﷺ) an independent obedience when He said: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾.

His words ﴿the Messenger﴾: the definite article (al-) here is for a known reference (al-ʿahd), and it is a mental reference (ʿahd dhihnī), meaning: the Messenger who is known among you, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is not like His words: ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 16], because His words ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾ refer to a reference already mentioned (ʿahd dhikrī), as in ﴿We sent to Pharaoh a messenger. But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15–16]. As for this verse, it is a mental reference: meaning the Messenger who is known to you and whom you recognise.

(﴿فَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ عن طاعته، بحذف إحدى التاءين خطاب لهم) ﴿But if they turn away﴾. The author says: the meaning of ﴿tawallaw﴾ is "turn away" (taʿarrod), that is the meaning of turning away: refusal. But in terms of the wording, its original form is tatawallaw, for "tatawallaw" is addressed to the people, meaning: "And if you, O people, turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with," and so on. But one of the two tāʾs has been deleted.

The grammarians (naḥwiyyūn) disagreed over which was deleted: is it the tāʾ of the present tense (tāʾ al-muḍāraʿah, the prefixed tāʾ that marks the present-tense verb), or the tāʾ that is part of the verb's root?

Some said it is the tāʾ of the verb itself, because the tāʾ of the present tense was brought in for a purpose, so it should not be deleted. Others said it is the tāʾ of the present tense, because the tāʾ of the verb is original, while the tāʾ of the present tense is an addition, and so it is more fitting to delete it than an original letter.

In any case, the disagreement here is verbal; it has no effect on the meaning. What is intended is: tatawallaw.

A parallel to the deletion of one of the two tāʾs is His words: ﴿Therefore I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [al-Layl 14]. ﴿Talaẓẓā﴾ means ﴿tatalaẓẓā﴾, and ﴿talaẓẓā﴾ is not a past-tense verb, for otherwise it would say ﴿talaẓẓat﴾. Rather it is a present-tense verb from which one of the two tāʾs was deleted.

﴿But if they turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾. ﴿Upon him﴾ means upon the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿What he has been charged with﴾ means the conveying, the clarifying and the calling (to Islam). He (ﷺ) conveyed the message clearly and also called people, as in: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf 108].

So the Prophet (ﷺ) had two duties, and the author mentioned only one of them. What was obligatory upon him was to convey and to call, and he did so (ﷺ): he conveyed to the people and called them to Allah, and he fulfilled what was required of him.

﴿And upon you is what you have been charged with﴾. What is it that we have been charged with? We have been charged with obeying him and following him. On this basis, if he fails in what is upon him, he becomes deserving of the consequences of that; and if you fail in what is obligatory upon you, you become deserving of the requital for that.

The Prophet (ﷺ) delivered the clear message, so he fulfilled what he was charged with. But those who turned away did not fulfil what they were charged with. In this there is evidence that the Messenger (ﷺ) is not obliged to guide them.

This is frequent in the Qur'an: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 22]; ﴿Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus 99]; ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and Ours is the reckoning﴾ [al-Raʿd 40]. So he is not obliged to guide them. Rather, Allah forbade him to have constriction, narrowness and grief in his chest: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of what they plot﴾ [al-Naḥl 127]; and He said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 3], meaning: destroying yourself because they do not believe.

Likewise, whoever inherits from the Prophet (ﷺ), namely the scholars, is only obliged to convey and to call. As for guiding creation, that belongs to their Creator, blessed and exalted is He; it is not your responsibility to guide them.

Allah Most High said, encouraging obedience to Him: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. If you obey the Messenger (ﷺ), you will be guided. In this there is an indication of what was mentioned earlier: that what the Sunnah has brought is an independent ruling which must be obeyed and followed, just as what came in the Qur'an is. For this reason He said: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. Guidance is what is sought. So when the Prophet (ﷺ) commands something, it is not permissible for us to say: "Is there a basis for this in the Qur'an or not? If it has a basis, we accept it; if it has no basis, we do not accept it." That is forbidden, and it is disbelief in the Qur'an itself, because Allah says: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, and then He says ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. This shows that everything he brought is truth and guidance, and that there is nothing in it of falsehood or misguidance.

Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾. Is this restriction (ḥaṣr) real or relative? In ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the conveyance﴾, is the restriction real?

* Student: Real.
* Shaykh: Real? How can it be real, when it is obligatory upon him to pray, to pay zakah and to fast?
* Student: It is a relative restriction.
* Shaykh: A relative restriction, is that right?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Real. When it is said "a real restriction," it means that anything other than it is negated. Can we say here that the Messenger (ﷺ) is only obliged to convey to the people, and as for performing acts of obedience himself, nothing of that is obligatory upon him?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not possible, since there is no qualifier.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. This restriction is considered relative; that is, with respect to what is obligatory upon him towards you. If He had said: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾ and ﴿Upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, and ﴿And upon the Messenger, with respect to you, is only the clear conveyance﴾, but as for guiding you and compelling you to the truth, that is not his responsibility, as Allah Most High said: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 272]. So this restriction indicates what is obligatory upon him towards his community: he is obliged only to the clear conveyance.

* Student: A real restriction with respect to (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, with respect to what is obligatory upon him, not with respect to everything in general. But a real restriction is one that applies to everything, not (...) other than this. The meaning of his saying "relative" is that it is relative to a certain circumstance. If you say, for example, "There is no generous man except so-and-so," this is a restriction meaning that there is no generous man other than him, even though many generous men exist besides him. But it means "there is no generous man except so-and-so," that is, with respect to his tribe for example, or relative to his town, or something similar.

So the restriction is relative. It is not real in meaning, but it is relative to something. When the restriction means "relative to such-and-such," it is relative. When the restriction applies to all, it is?
* Students: Real.
* Shaykh: Real.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed: real and relative.

He says: ﴿upon the Messenger is only the conveyance﴾. "Conveyance" (balāgh) means conveying (tablīgh). The root meaning of balāgh is reaching an end; it is said "balagha kadhā," meaning "he reached." So the one who conveys brings people to a goal, which is the guidance that Allah, glorified and exalted, wants His servants to attain.

The author's statement "al-mubīn (the clear) in the sense of al-bayyin (the evident)" is open to question. It has already been established that al-mubīn can mean al-bayyin (evident in itself), and it can mean "making clear to others," that is, clarifying for others. This depends on the context. Here, balāgh means "clear," or "making clear what was conveyed," meaning: he made clear and manifest what he called to and conveyed. So here al-mubīn means "one who makes manifest," not "evident" as the author said. Which is more eloquent: al-mubīn in the sense of "one who makes manifest," or al-mubīn in the sense of "evident"?
* Student: In the sense of "one who makes manifest."
* Shaykh: In the sense of "one who makes manifest," because al-mubīn in the sense of "one who makes manifest" is evident in itself and makes others clear, whereas al-bayyin alone is evident in itself; it may or may not make others clear. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾.

(﴿وَعَدَ اللَّه الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنْكُمْ وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَات لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ فِي الْأَرْض﴾ بدلًا عن الكفار، ﴿كَمَا اسْتَخْلَفَ﴾ بالبناء للفاعل والمفعول، ﴿الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلهمْ﴾ من بني إسرائيل بدلًا عن الجبابرة، ﴿وَلَيُمَكِّنَن لَهُمْ دِينهمْ الَّذِي ارْتَضَى لَهُمْ﴾ وهو الإسلام؛ بأن يظهره على جميع الأديان ويوسع لهم في البلاد فيملكوها، ﴿وَلَيُبَدِّلَنهُمْ﴾ بالتخفيف والتشديد، ﴿مِنْ بَعْد خَوْفهمْ﴾ من الكفار، ﴿أَمْنًا﴾ وقد أنجز الله ما وعدهم).

﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land﴾, in place of the disbelievers, ﴿as He made successors those before them﴾ (the verb may be read in the active or passive voice), ﴿from the Children of Israel, in place of the tyrants; and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾, which is Islam, by making it prevail over all other religions and by widening the lands for them so that they possess them; ﴿and He will surely change [their state] after their fear﴾ of the disbelievers ﴿to security﴾. Allah has fulfilled what He promised them.

﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Promise (waʿd) means granting a person what pleases him, while threat (waʿīd) means warning him of what he dislikes. There is a difference between promise and threat: promise is for what is hoped for of what is loved, and threat is for what is feared of what is dreaded. The poet said:

*And indeed I, even if I threaten him, I am one who breaks my threat and fulfils my promise.*

﴿Allah has promised﴾: that is, He, glorified and exalted, has committed Himself to them in what they love. ﴿Those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: that is, those who combine faith and righteous deeds. Faith has its place in the heart, and righteous deeds have their place in the limbs. Faith alone is not sufficient, and deeds alone are not sufficient, and no deed is righteous unless it is based on faith. Even if its outward form is that of righteousness, if it is not founded on faith, it is not righteous. The matter revolves around both: faith and righteous deeds, and this promise belongs to both of them.

﴿He will surely make them successors in the land as He made successors those before them﴾. This is a promise. The meaning of ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ is that He will make them successors to others: they will succeed others in the land. The word ﴿in the land﴾ here refers to the genus, not one specific land, but the land in general: in truth, all the earth, the whole land. This is because the earth is Allah's earth: ﴿Indeed, the earth is Allah's; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 128].

His words ﴿to whom He wills of His servants﴾ are well known: He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills. ﴿And We have already written in the Psalms (al-Zabūr, the book given to David) after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 105]. On this basis, for example, the land of the Arabs does not belong to the Arabs, the land of the Persians does not belong to the Persians, and the land of the Romans does not belong to the Romans. To whom does the land belong?
* Students: To Allah.
* Shaykh: To Allah. He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills, namely the righteous servants who believe and do righteous deeds. Whoever disbelieves in Allah and rebels against His obedience has no right to the land; the right belongs to someone else. Allah gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His righteous servants.

On this basis, if the Children of Israel say: "The land of al-Sham is ours, because Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Māʾidah 21]," then Allah has prescribed it for them here. If the Children of Israel say this, we say: Yes, Moses said this, because at that time you were the people of righteousness, and you were the righteous servants of Allah. The land belongs to Allah, who gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants. So it was yours at that time, without doubt. But when Islam came and you disbelieved in it, you were no longer worthy of it, and its people became whom?
* Students: The righteous.
* Shaykh: The righteous: those who believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and follow him.

So when the Muslims were expelled, before that, it was occupied after the Jews by whom? By the Christians, the Romans, because they were the righteous after the Jews. Then after the Romans it was occupied by whom? It was occupied by the Muslims, because they were the righteous servants of Allah. So the land, the land of al-Sham, had been written for whom? For the righteous: ﴿And We have already written in the Psalms after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾. The Children of Israel inherited it from the tyrants because they were upon the truth, meaning the Jews, I mean. Then the Christians inherited it from the Jews because they were the people of truth. Then the Muslims inherited it from the Christians because they were the people of truth.

On this basis, the Jews now have no right to Palestine or to any other part of Allah's land. They have no right to the land ever, neither they nor any disbeliever, because the land is deserved only by whom? By the righteous servants of Allah.

But if the Muslims become righteous and return to their true religion, through which Allah gives them His land as inheritance, then we affirm with certainty that they will regain the land: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land as He made successors those before them﴾ [al-Nūr 55]. So we affirm with certainty that if the Muslims now truly return to the religion of Allah, with faith and righteous deeds, they will drive the Jews out of the land. Indeed, they will drive the Americans out of their places, and the Russians out of their places. Do we affirm this with certainty or not?

But as long as they (the Muslims) remain in this condition, according to the legal principles and the texts, they do not deserve victory, because they have not struggled against themselves, let alone struggled against others to bring them into Islam. We say: Now establish Islam among yourselves, establish the religion of Allah among yourselves; then afterward Allah will give victory to His religion if you uphold it. For He does not give victory to a person because he is so-and-so, or to this group because they are Arabs, or to that group because they are (...). He gives victory to whoever upholds this religion. Was Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi of Arab origin or not?
* Students: Not Arab.
* Shaykh: Not Arab. Nevertheless Allah gave him victory over the Christians, because he upheld the religion of Allah. The religion itself is what gives victory. It is (...) of itself (...). It is a weapon even if it is not carried. Do not say: Islam is a weapon by which one can decide victory with whatever weapon is in his hand, never. If there is (...) a weapon in Islam in a person's hand, then for us the material weapon remains; that is, with whatever is most powerful in material terms.

It is well known that the Muslims are, at the present time, the weakest of nations in material terms, because they are scattered and dispersed nations, and the enmities among them are many, and the hatred among them is great. This one calls to such-and-such, and that one calls to such-and-such, and this one has a particular school of thought; they are all divided. Allah Most High has said: ﴿Indeed, those who divide their religion and become sects, you have nothing to do with them﴾ [al-Anʿām 159]. This matter applies completely to the Muslims at the present time. There is no unity upon Islam, and no upright religion established among the Muslims. There may be a small faction in which there is some righteousness, of faith and righteous deeds, but even that is weak.

In summary: this promise which Allah has made is true, but to whom? To those who believe and do righteous deeds. These are the righteous servants of Allah about whom Allah said: ﴿And We have already written in the Psalms after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 105].

So when those who are now fighting the Jews say: "We will drive out the Jews, and establish on these blessed lands which they have occupied (...) an Islamic state that leads people by the religion of Allah, by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ)," and they first exemplify that themselves before they conquer these lands, then at that point we will be certain of their victory. Otherwise, victory is not guaranteed; rather it may be the opposite, and defeat is what is guaranteed, because whoever undertakes something and struggles for it while acting contrary to it, that is a kind of deception of Allah, mighty and majestic. And whoever deceives Allah, He deceives him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verses 54–58 (part 2 of 7):**

﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾. It was said: what is meant by "the earth"?
* Students: The genus (all lands).
* The Shaykh: The genus. That is, it is not a specific land, such as the land of Makkah, where Allah makes the emigrants successors in place of the polytheists. It is all the earth.

﴿as He made successors those before them﴾. His saying, ﴿as He made successors﴾, is in reality like His saying: ﴿"Yes, but that my heart may be at rest"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:260]. That is, it is mentioned for the sake of emphasis and to reassure the one promised of what he was promised. It is as if He said: look at this promise that Allah made to you; it has been fulfilled among those before you.

﴿as He made successors those before them﴾. Like whom? (...) Like the Children of Israel, who succeeded the tyrants. Correct. And also the Children of Israel who succeeded the Pharaohs, for Allah the Exalted says: ﴿"Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:59].
