* Shaykh: Yes indeed, in it is that hardship brings ease. Let us look at the author's words, since he has a comment on this verse.
He says: (The verse of seeking permission (istī'dhān) is said to be abrogated (mansūkha, naskh), and it is said: no, but people were lax in abandoning seeking permission.) The two opinions we pointed to. The correct view is that the verse is muḥkam (firm, not abrogated), remaining in effect, and that abandoning seeking permission is either due to negligence or due to the cause requiring permission having ceased. As for saying that legal rulings are abrogated by people's abandonment of acting upon them, this has no basis.
* Student: The Shaykh says: "in abandoning," "people were lax in abandoning"?
* Shaykh: In abandoning seeking permission.
* Student: He did not say: they were lax in doing it.
* Shaykh: No, in abandoning it. People were lax in abandoning it, meaning they abandoned it. You mean that what should be said is "they were lax in doing it." That would be if he said "in abandoning it." It is also acceptable to say: "people were lax." In what were they lax, or what was the cause of their laxity? It is the abandonment, the abandonment of seeking permission. Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, from disobedience or violation. If he is negligent, we restricted it. What did we restrict it to? If he is negligent in raising and disciplining him. But if he is not negligent, then no.
* Student: Even if he is mature?
* Shaykh: Where?
* Student: We mentioned (...).
* Shaykh: No. If he is mature, he has become independent in himself. But if he reaches maturity, he becomes like others: if he is able to change the evil he has committed, it becomes obligatory upon him.
We also discussed yesterday the matter of His saying: ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ وَلَا عَلَيْهِمْ جُنَاحٌ بَعْدَهُنَّ﴾ (laysa 'alaykum wa-lā 'alayhim junāḥun ba'dahunna, "there is no blame upon you or upon them after these [times]") [An-Nur 58]. We said the verse has a manṭūq (explicit meaning) and a mafhūm (implicit meaning). Its manṭūq presents no difficulty, namely the negation of blame, since blame is negated. But its mafhūm is that there is blame upon them at these three times.
[That is] upon the guardians and upon the young children. This is problematic, because young children are not morally responsible (mukallafīn), so that they would bear blame for their disobedience.
* Student: The manṭūq has multiple individual instances, and it is true in one of the instances.
* Shaykh: In one of the instances, yes. We say: the mafhūm does not have generality, so it is true with the existence of one case of the generality, even a single case.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 59:

Then he said: (﴿And when the children among you reach puberty﴾ [An-Nur 59], O free ones, ﴿let them ask permission﴾ at all times, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾, i.e., the free adults).

When they reach puberty, the author says: (﴿among you﴾, O free ones). This is because slaves, as was previously mentioned, only need to ask permission at the three times, whether they are adults or children; for this reason the author restricted it to free persons, in accordance with the implication of the first verse.

As for his words, "reach ﴿puberty﴾" (al-hulm), al-hulm is a metaphor for puberty through emission (al-inzal). Al-hulm may mean the experience of wet dreams (al-ihtilam) or it may mean reason (al-'aql), because of the completeness of their intellects; but the first is more appropriate, because full mental maturity is not a condition for this, and full mental maturity is attained at the completion of forty years.

As for his words, "when they reach al-hulm," "let them ask permission": Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned only reaching al-hulm. It is well known that there are two other things by which puberty is attained: the completion of fifteen years of age, and the growth of pubic hair (in'at al-'anah). However, these two matters are disputed among the scholars. Some of them hold that there is no puberty except by emission, and that completing fifteen years is not a sign of puberty but a sign of a person's ability to fight in jihad, because those who adopted it relied only on the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Uhud and was not permitted, and was presented to him on the day of the Trench and was permitted, and he was fifteen years old on the day of the Trench[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2664), and Muslim (1868 / 91).]].

However, in a narration of al-Hakim he said: "He did not permit me and did not see me as having reached [maturity]," and in the second: "He permitted me and saw me as having reached [maturity]"[[Al-Hakim recorded it in al-Mustadrak (6501) from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]][[Previously cited.]]. But the word "reached" (balaghtu): does it mean that he reached the age of legal responsibility, or that he reached the condition in which he could fight? There is a possibility of both. However, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, wrote to his governors that they should assign stipends to whoever had reached fifteen years and was seen to have reached [that stage][[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2664), and Muslim (1868 / 91).]]. He said: "If this age is the limit of their fitness for fighting, then it is the limit of their puberty."

Some scholars, such as Abu Hanifa, hold that the limit of puberty is eighteen years, not fifteen. This is the view followed by the system of work and workers here, because the one who drafted it, as far as appears, was a foreigner who did not know any school other than the well-known school prevalent among most Muslims, which is the school of Abu Hanifa that restricts it to eighteen years. The schools of the three other imams hold that puberty is attained at fifteen years.

As for the growth of pubic hair, the same disagreement applies. Those who said it is not a sign of puberty said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ examining the garment of the Banu Qurayza and killing whoever had grown [pubic hair] does not prove that he was legally responsible; rather, it is evidence that he was among those fit for fighting, so the Prophet ﷺ would kill him. However, the well-known position of the school is what is known to you, that puberty is attained by one of three things.

He said: ﴿So let them ask permission﴾. Note ﴿So let them ask permission﴾: the address is directed to them, because when they reach al-hulm they become fit for legal responsibility and the address is directed to them.

As for his words, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾, i.e., from the general people who ask permission at all times.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾. ﴿Thus﴾ means: like that clarification, He clarifies. We have said that the kaf is a noun meaning "like," and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of ﴿yubayyinu﴾. Here the noble verse is like the verse before it, except for the difference in His words ﴿āyātihi﴾ instead of ﴿al-āyāt﴾. Perhaps this, and Allah knows best, is a matter of variation in address or style; otherwise their meaning is the same.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage﴾ [al-Nur 60]) They have ceased to menstruate and to bear children because of their old age. ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾ due to that. ﴿there is no blame upon them for removing their outer garments﴾ such as the jilbab, the rida', the qina' and the khimar, ﴿provided they do not display adornment﴾ by showing hidden adornment such as a necklace, bracelet and anklet. ﴿But it is better for them to be modest﴾ ... and so on to the end.

﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is the plural of qa'idah. His words ﴿min al-nisa'﴾ [from among women] explain al-qawa'id, because the (al-) in ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul). When al- is prefixed to a derived noun, whether an ism maf'ul or an ism fa'il, it is a relative pronoun. So ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ means "those who have sat (ceased)" (al-lati qa'adna).

His words ﴿min al-nisa'﴾ are an explanation of "qawa'id". But they have ceased from what?

The author says: (from menstruation and child-bearing). (...) The meaning of ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is those who no longer bear children or menstruate because of their old age.

It is said: ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ are those who remain in their houses because of their old age, since they do not go out due to their weakness and frailty, so they are qawa'id.

It is also said that ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is a name for old women in general, as we say "ajuz" (old woman), derived from 'ajz (incapacity). We also say qa'idah meaning one incapable of standing, going and returning.

His words ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾: ﴿allati﴾ is an adjective of what? Of al-qawa'id or of al-nisa'?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it is an adjective of (al-qawa'id), because if you said ﴿from among women who have no hope of marriage﴾, it would mean that among the qawa'id there are women who hope for marriage, and that is not the case. So his words ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾ are an adjective of (al-qawa'id).

His words ﴿have no hope﴾: how is "la yarjun" (have no hope) when they are feminine, while "yarjun" is a masculine verb?

Student: The nun is the nun of the feminine plural.

Shaykh: And the waw.

Student: The waw (...).

Shaykh: Yes, indeed. The waw is the waw of the verb, and the nun is the nun of the feminine plural.

The meaning of ﴿la yarjuna nikahan﴾ is: they do not desire it, because of their old age. For they do not expect that anyone will marry them, since old women are not desired by anyone.

﴿there is no blame upon them for removing their outer garments﴾. There is no doubt that the meaning of ﴿removing their garments﴾ is not all garments, meaning that they remain naked. This cannot be said.

So what is meant by garments? The outer garments that customarily are worn, such as the jilbab.

The author's words: "the rida', the qina' and the khimar" are outer things. So it is permissible for the old woman to wear a miqta' (a short garment), showing her hands, head, face, feet and shins. But on condition that she does not display adornment ﴿not displaying adornment﴾. It is as if she intends to show adornment, because some old women, if they do not desire marriage, like to appear like young women: you find her, for example, wearing a bracelet and an anklet and sitting boastfully among people. But this is conditional on her not being in this state. If she is in this state it is not permitted. But if the matter is natural, it is permissible for her to remove her garments.

Student: What if she is in the presence of a non-mahram man?

Shaykh: Yes, even if she is in the presence of a non-mahram man, because she does not hope for marriage (...) desiring. It will come, God willing, in the mention of the benefits, with more than this.

Student: ﴿adornment﴾ (...) ﴿not displaying adornment﴾ (...).

Shaykh: Yes, it means there is no tabarruj except through adornment.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: There is no tabarruj except through adornment; I say this as a description of the reality.

Student: A description of the reality.

Shaykh: A description of the reality, yes.

Student: O shaykh, do we always link the request (...)?

Shaykh: What do you mean?

Student: ﴿al-qawa'id min al-nisa'﴾, does (...)?

Shaykh: If she is an old woman, there is no objection. That is, if a person brings an old woman as a servant to the house, it is permissible for her to uncover, there is no prohibition.

Student: (...) mahram?

Shaykh: No, the mahram is not required. The hadiths are general: it is not permitted to travel except with a mahram.

Student: (...) is present in the house.

Shaykh: No, it is not a condition, because when the house has no seclusion (khalwa), there is no objection.

Student: (...) fifteen from puberty, or fifteen from the beginning..

Shaykh: No, his puberty is completed at fifteen.

Student: So his entering the sixteenth year?

Shaykh: Yes.

* * *

Student: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Peace be upon you and the mercy of God and His blessings.

A letter from the honourable (name), dated the twenty-second of Ramadan this year, (...) and praise be to God for that. Your congratulations on the Feast of Fitr; for you, from us, the same, and we ask God to accept from all of us.

You remember that you looked through a treatise on ablution, bathing and prayer, and that the way of placing the right hand between the two prostrations drew your attention.

O beloved, what is in the treatise is what the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ requires, as Muslim narrated..

Shaykh: Listen, my brothers. This is a jurisprudential benefit, not a matter (...).

Student: As Muslim narrated [(579/113)] from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. He said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ sat to supplicate, he placed his right hand upon his right thigh and his left hand upon his left thigh, and he pointed with his index finger, and placed his thumb upon his middle finger, and he would place his left palm upon his knee." And in another narration: "When he sat in prayer." [Narrated by Muslim (579/112).]

And it is narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "He, meaning the Prophet ﷺ, when he sat in prayer, placed his right palm upon his right thigh, closed all his fingers, pointed with the finger next to the thumb, and placed his left palm upon his left thigh." [Narrated by Muslim (580/116).] And there is no report, as far as I know, distinguishing between sitting for the tashahhud and sitting between the two prostrations. What shows that there is no difference between the two sittings is what Imam Ahmad narrated in the Musnad, page three hundred and seventeen, part four, from the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr who said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ say the takbir and raise his hands when he said the takbir." [(18858).] He mentioned the hadith, and in it: "And he prostrated and placed his hands level with his ears. Then he sat, spreading his left leg, then placed his left hand on his left knee, and placed his right forearm on his right thigh, then he pointed with his index finger and placed the thumb on the middle finger, and closed the rest of his fingers. Then he prostrated, and his hands were level with his ears."

Shaykh: What is this?

Student: It is between the two prostrations.

Shaykh: (...), because it is between the two prostrations (...).

Student: And in another narration: "He made thirty (with his fingers) and released one, and pointed with his index finger." [(18850).]

Shaykh: How many did he make?

Student: Thirty.

Student: And he mentioned the hadith in al-Fath al-Rabbani, the arrangement of the Musnad, page one hundred and forty-seven, part three, and he said in its chain: good. [(3/149).]

It was narrated in a similar form by Abu Dawud [(726)], and he said in it: "And he closed two, and made a circle (halqah)"; meaning he made a circle with the thumb and the middle finger. By this it becomes clear that there is no difference between the sitting of the tashahhud and the sitting between the two prostrations. As for restricting the sitting, in some narrations of the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, to the sitting for the tashahhud [narrated by Muslim (580/115)], this does not contradict the general wording, because mentioning some instances of the general ruling in a way that matches the general ruling does not necessitate restricting it, although it may suggest restriction if no evidence establishes the generality.

And in a narration: "He placed his hands upon his knees and raised his right finger which is next to the thumb and supplicated with it, and his left hand upon his left knee, spreading it upon it." [Narrated by Muslim (580/114).] Its apparent meaning is that he raised it for supplication with it, and this is a raising beyond the mere pointing mentioned in the first narration and in the hadith of Ibn al-Zubayr [previously cited]. On this basis the index finger is raised in the manner of pointing; when he mentions the supplicatory phrase he raises it additionally, indicating the exaltedness of the One he supplicates, who is God, exalted is He. This is supported by the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr: "Then he raised his finger, and I saw him moving it, supplicating with it." [Narrated by al-Nasa'i (889) and al-Darimi (1397).] In the hadith of Ibn al-Zubayr in al-Darimi: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ supplicate like this in prayer," and Ibn 'Uyaynah pointed with his finger. Narrated by al-Darimi [(1377)].

Shaykh: Leave this book with you, and review the Musnad and al-Fath.

Student: The statement (...) made thirty.

Shaykh: The apparent thing is that it is an error in the Musnad (...). Abu Dawud: "He made two."

Student: (...) thirty (...).

Shaykh: I say: thirty. Apparently it is an error in the Musnad. Apparently it is like the narration of Abu Dawud: "He made two."

Student: The judgment on the author of al-Fath al-Rabbani (...).

Shaykh: By God, apparently there is no harm in it, and I have not seen anything wrong with its narrators.

Student: O shaykh, is pointing during supplication other than in tashahhud reported?

Shaykh: Yes. In supplication in the Friday sermon: "The Messenger used to point when he supplicated" [narrated by Muslim (874/53) from the hadith of 'Umarah ibn Ruwaybah]. Except in the rain prayer (istisqa'), when he raised his hands [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1031), Muslim (896/7), from the hadith of Anas]. Likewise it is also reported that the Messenger pointed when he said: "O God, bear witness" [narrated by Abu Dawud (1905), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah] in the sermon of 'Arafah (...).

* * *

Indeed God, glory be to Him, commanded children, when they reach puberty, to seek permission as those before them did; that is, at all times. As for before that, they need only seek permission at three times only. That is because they move among us frequently, and seeking permission each time is burdensome, and God has not placed in this religion any hardship upon this community. Then it was also previously stated that God removed blame from the qawa'id who have no hope of marriage, that they may remove their garments, meaning the outer garments, on condition that they do not display adornment, and He made clear that their modesty is better for them. This is what we will begin now, God willing.

He said: (﴿And as for women past child-bearing﴾) meaning the old women who have "sat" (ceased). The author says: (from menstruation and child-bearing because of their old age). Rather also from work: they have ceased from work, menstruation and child-bearing because of their old age, and they remain in their houses and their places. So it is the plural of qa'idah.

His words ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾ mean they do not desire it, because of their old age and because people have no desire for them. He says ﴿there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning, there is no sin.

(﴿that they may remove their garments, provided they do not display adornment﴾ by showing hidden adornment such as a necklace, bracelet and anklet.) Tabarruj means display and showing, and from it come the "buruj" in the sky, because of their height and elevation. So the meaning of ﴿mutabarrijat﴾ is "those who make themselves prominent".

The author's words, may God have mercy on him: "displaying" (mudhhirat). This is interpretation by a necessary consequence (al-tafsir bi-al-lazim), since tabarruj means making oneself prominent, which necessarily entails displaying adornment.

His words ﴿with adornment﴾ mean with hidden adornment which they display when they remove those garments.

He then said: (﴿But it is better for them to be modest﴾ by not removing them) ﴿better for them﴾ because in that is distance from the places of temptation. As it is said: "Every fallen thing has a picker-up." Such a woman may not herself hope for marriage because of her age, but a man may still become attached to her while she is in this state. Therefore He said: ﴿But it is better for them to be modest﴾.

(﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾ of your speech ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what is in your hearts.) He concluded the verse with hearing and knowledge, because the context may call for speech, as in His words: ﴿So do not be soft in speech﴾ [al-Ahzab 32], and for knowledge, because His words ﴿not displaying adornment﴾ have their seat in the heart, and their object is knowledge, since what is in the heart is not heard or seen, but is known by knowledge. So He is All-Hearing, glory be to Him, of what is said to them or what these qawa'id say, and All-Knowing of what is in their hearts and the hearts of those who look at them, of inclination and temptation.

Student: Is its seat the heart or the limbs?

Shaykh: What?

Student: "Mutabarrijat" (displaying).

Shaykh: No, the limbs. This is not related to knowledge; it is related to sight.

Student: (...) mutabarrijat.

Shaykh: Yes, because she may display adornment without intending tabarruj, so there is no intention in that.

* In this verse are benefits:

* First: The ruling apparent from it: old women who have despaired of marriage because of their old age are permitted to remove the outer garments, such as the jilbab, the rida', the khimar and what is similar. That is, these outer garments may be removed by old women, because they do not hope for marriage and so do not fear temptation.

* Second: That women other than the qawa'id must wear outer covering clothing. A woman may not say, "I want to go out in a miqta' and without a khimar," and similar things. No: women other than the qawa'id must keep their outer garments on them, because of the concealment in that, and because its absence falls under the authentic hadith: "There are two kinds of the people of the Fire, whom I have not yet seen: a people who have whips like cow-tails with which they strike people, and women who are clothed yet naked, inclining and causing others to incline, their heads like the humps of the Bukht camels leaning. They will not enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance, though its fragrance is found from such and such a distance." [Narrated by Muslim (2128/125) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] For a woman who has clothing on, but which describes the parts of her body and does not remove temptation, is clothed yet naked.

* And also in it: those who are not desired because of extreme ugliness are analogous to the qawa'id, for whoever is not desired because of extreme ugliness, such as old women, since she does not hope for marriage and no one desires her. For this reason the scholars joined this category of women to the qawa'id.

* Fourth: That tabarruj with adornment is forbidden for old women, by His words ﴿not displaying adornment﴾. This condition, if violated, makes it sinful for them, and this indicates prohibition. If tabarruj is forbidden for old women, then we say:

* The fifth benefit: The prohibition of tabarruj applies to whom? To young women, who are the locus of temptation. Is this analogy one of greater priority (qiyas awlawiyyah) or of equality?

* Students: Greater priority.

* Shaykh: Greater priority, known. Because if the qawa'id who have no hope of marriage are forbidden, then others who hope for marriage and to whom temptation attaches are more so.

* Sixth: That the ruling revolves with its cause, existence and absence. How is that? Because God only permitted the removal of garments for these qawa'id because temptation is remote in them. From this is taken that the whole matter depends on fear of temptation in such matters, so the ruling revolves with its cause in existence and absence.

* Seventh benefit: What many people of knowledge have pointed out, that even on the view that permits uncovering the face and hands, if that is a means to temptation and laxity, it is forbidden. Accordingly, this view has no place in our age. Why? Because women cannot be controlled at all; they cannot be controlled. For this reason, you find that societies which adopted this view have become unable to free themselves from the open tabarruj into which they have fallen, which this view has no connection with at all. The matter did not stop at the face and the two hands, but progressed to the head, the neck, the chest, the forearm, even the upper arm at times, the shin and the foot. All of this is because women now, and indeed Muslim societies, unfortunately cannot be restrained by the legal limits, since they have turned away from the religion, except those whom God wills.

Accordingly, we say this view which some people who love unveiling (sufur) mutter about has no place in this age, because one of its conditions is not displaying adornment and that temptation not be feared from it, and this exists and is established: temptation exists and tabarruj exists. For this reason, the qawa'id whom God permitted to remove garments were made subject to this condition: ﴿not displaying adornment﴾.

And we find that many of the women of these people do display adornment without doubt: they redden the cheeks and lips, darken the eyes with kohl, and pluck and shape the eyebrows. All of this shows that the matter has now become of no consequence at this time.

* Student: The seventh benefit.

* Shaykh: No, the correct view is that it has no limit.
* Student: The seventh benefit you mentioned.
* Shaykh: Eh, what about the seventh benefit?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. The ruling revolves around its cause ('illah), and from it branches this issue: whenever there is fear of temptation (fitnah) from uncovering the face and hands, based on the view that permits it, then it is not permissible, as many scholars have pointed out.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: There is no doubt that it has no basis, but we said: on the view that permits it, at this time it cannot be applied, because the temptation is present, and its being a means to laxity is also present.
* And in it: evidence that it is better to keep away from suspicion and from the place of temptation, even if it is remote. His saying ﴿And that they refrain is better for them﴾ shows that. It is permissible for them to remove their garments when the temptation regarding them is remote, but nevertheless, the further a person stays from the causes of temptation, the better it is for him. A person may feel that he is far from temptation and then fall into it. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded whoever hears of the Dajjal to keep far away from him, because he will come to him while thinking himself a believer, and he will keep throwing at him doubts and misgivings until he follows him.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4319) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn.]]
* The ninth benefit: establishing the varying degrees of deeds (tafadul al-a'mal). His saying ﴿is better for them﴾ means better than not refraining, which shows that some deeds are better than others. From this follows, or branches from it, the varying degrees of faith (iman), since deeds are part of it. When the difference in degrees among deeds is established, the difference in degrees of faith is established, and that it increases and decreases. This is the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah.
* "And in it:" establishing two of Allah's names: ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, and the attributes they include, which are hearing (sam') and knowledge ('ilm). It has already passed with us that the purpose of Allah's names and attributes is not merely knowing those names and attributes, but rather the purpose and aim is to worship Allah in accordance with what they require. When you know that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, you act on every word that pleases Him and avoid every word that displeases Him: you act on every word that pleases Him because you know He hears you and will reward you for it, and you avoid every word that displeases Him because you know He hears you and will be displeased with you. The same applies to knowledge, and likewise to all the other attributes and names. The aim is not that you merely know this name and attribute and their meaning, but that you act for Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and worship Allah in accordance with that name and that attribute. This is why the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) says: "Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2736) and Muslim (2677/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] The enumeration of them has three aspects: preserving their wording, their meaning, and worshipping Allah in accordance with what they require. A person knows the wording and the meaning and worships Allah by what these names require (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 61–63 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ [al-Nur 61] concerning eating with those who are their companions) (...).
* * *
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of "they do not hope for marriage"? Are people not inclined toward them?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So you are saying that an old woman has no desire? And this ugly young woman has desire? Yes, indeed. But Allah the Exalted did not say, "And the women who have no marriage," rather He said: ﴿those women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage﴾. That means they have despaired of marriage, because they know that people have no desire for them. If He had said, "the women among whom there is no marriage, or among whom there is no desire," that would be correct, but it would not be permissible to extend the ruling to the ugly, hideous woman. But since He said: ﴿who do not hope for marriage﴾, it means they do not aspire to marriage, not merely because there is no desire in them, but because people have no desire for them (...).
(...) those who have no husbands, ﴿who do not hope for marriage﴾ in any way.
* Student: Which scholar (...)?
* The Shaykh: I do not know. Has anyone said it? But as for (...) faith, this is attested and the view is well known. As for the graduation of deeds (in merit), I do not know, and I do not know of anyone who holds it now.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. In fact the Murji'ah exclude all deeds from faith.
* Student: That is, they say deeds (...).
* The Shaykh: No. But they do not say, for example, that prayer is like fasting, and fasting is like such-and-such. They hold that some deeds are better than others. Only they say that they are not included within faith; they exclude them from faith. I do not know that they say the deeds are equal in their merit; I do not know that, and I do not think anyone holds it. But the matter of excluding them from faith is what led them to say that the faith of Abu Bakr and the faith of the most wicked of people are one and the same. That is, for them faith is merely acknowledgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while the matter of submission is outside faith.
﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ [al-Nur 61]. "The blind" (al-a'ma): is this an elative (ism al-tafdil) or an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah)? It is an attributive adjective, because it describes his state, and it does not mean that he is blinder than someone else. The elative is that which means "more so" and has a "more so than" comparison. As for al-a'ma, al-a'raj and the like, these are attributive adjectives, which they call al-sifat al-mushabbahah, meaning in the sense of the active participle.
As for His saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way﴾ [al-Isra 72], its apparent meaning is that the second "a'ma" is an elative, meaning more blind and further astray from the way. But what is well known, especially among the Basrans, is that this is an attributive adjective, and that it is not permissible to form an elative on the pattern af'al from a thing that is an attributive adjective. The Kufans, however, say there is no harm, and they hold that there is no harm in saying: "So-and-so is more lame than so-and-so, and so-and-so is more blind than so-and-so." Their view is more correct, because this is something that sound taste accepts and there is no objection to it. What is meant here by "the blind" is the attributive adjective: the one who cannot see.
﴿nor upon the lame﴾: the lame is the one who does not walk in a straight manner.
﴿nor upon the sick﴾: the sick is the one whose health has departed from its balance. Everyone whose health has departed from balance is sick, and illnesses differ. But in what did the author say: (concerning eating with those who are their companions)? The counterpart of the blind is the one who sees, the counterpart of the lame is the sound one, and the counterpart of the sick is the healthy one. That is, there is no blame upon the blind if he eats with the one who sees; there is no blame on him. Is there anything in this?
* Student: This is clear.
* The Shaykh: This is a clear matter that does not need the removal of blame from them. But it may be said that they used to feel uneasy about eating with the blind, saying: "Because if we eat with him (...)." And on the other hand, the blind man also feels uneasy about eating with the one who sees, because he says: "If I eat, I fear I will eat more than him."
According to the first opinion: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾, meaning there is no blame on the blind man in eating with him.
Likewise, the sick: there is no blame on the sick if he eats with whom? With the healthy. It is not said that there is blame in it, because the healthy man eats more. Likewise the lame: there is no harm if he eats with the healthy, and no blame on him, because the lame man may say: "My leg is bent, and if I sit, the one nearest to me will eat (...)." There is no blame on him. This is what some have held: that what is meant is that there is no blame on them in eating with others. On this view, "upon" (ʿalā) in ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ means "in": that is, there is no blame in the blind man, that is, in eating with him, nor in the lame, nor in the sick.
Others said: what is meant is jihad. ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾, meaning in abandoning jihad; ﴿nor upon the lame﴾, in abandoning jihad; ﴿nor upon the sick﴾, in abandoning jihad. They said: the evidence for this is that Allah mentioned after this verse His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾ up to the end of the verses [al-Nur 62], for these are about jihad. And these verses serve as an introduction to the mention of jihad. But the verse about eating from the houses was placed before it either as a preparation, a paving, and an alert, because when a statement comes out of its expected place, a person must pay attention and inquire what the reason is, unlike when speech comes in a single flow, when one may be carried along with it and not grasp the meanings.
It has already passed for us that one of the benefits of iltifat (shift of address) is to alert the addressee or listener.
Also: this sentence, ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾, was placed before the verses of jihad are mentioned in this place, so that the reader would be alerted, since the matter has come out of what is familiar and expected. This is one view.
Another view: what is meant is that there is no blame on them in what? In abandoning jihad. They said: this is like His saying in Surat al-Fath: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ [al-Fath 17], which is undoubtedly about jihad, as in Surat al-Fath.
Others said: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ in abandoning any act of worship which these excuses prevent. Any worship that these excuses prevent them from, there is no blame on them in abandoning it. Understand this, O people: the verse is more general than jihad and other things; rather, for every act of worship whose abandonment or deficiency is caused by one of these three attributes, there is no blame on them in it. They said: this is the implication of the legal evidences: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj 78].
So if a person abandons an act of worship or falls short in it due to the excuse of blindness, there is no blame on him; due to the excuse of sickness, there is no blame on him; due to the excuse of lameness, there is no blame on him. Thus the verse is general in eating (companionship at meals), as the author said.
Likewise, it also applies to abandoning jihad, and likewise to what requires walking, for one who is lame and cannot, or sick and cannot, or blind and cannot, as with what requires sight. In all of this there is no blame on them. But on these last two views, as we pointed out, there remains the question: what is the connection between this statement, or this verse, and what follows it, the beginning of the verse with its end? What is the aspect of connection between them?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, the connection is that, as is known, these people have no blame in what requires soundness from these illnesses; likewise there is no blame upon you in what follows. So the purpose is a preparation for removing blame in what comes next. That is, just as it is known that these things are excuses that remove blame without any dispute, likewise there is no blame upon you in eating from your houses, and so on.
So is ﴿and upon yourselves that you eat﴾ connected to what precedes it or not? No, because if it were connected to what precedes it, the meaning would be: there is no blame on the blind that he eats from your house, nor on the lame that he eats from your house. But we have said that the verse is general, meaning there is no blame on these people in what these defects are an excuse for them to abandon.
Then he said: (﴿nor﴾ blame ﴿upon yourselves that you eat from your houses﴾, i.e., the houses of your children).
The author said: (﴿from your houses﴾) and said: (i.e., the houses of your children). Why did he not make the verse general? ﴿from your houses﴾ means the houses of yourselves.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed; because there is no need (...) for blame in it.
But someone may say: at the end of the verse there is something that indicates that the houses of a person themselves are meant, namely His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately﴾, and the removal of blame concerning eating from the houses would be in terms of their being ﴿together or separately﴾, not for eating in general. Do you understand, O people?
I say: the author understood the verse to mean that the houses of a person are the houses of his children, while we say there is no objection to meaning by it his own house and the house of his child. If someone asks: what is the benefit of removing blame from his eating from his own house?
We say: it is for the sake of what is mentioned at the end of the verse, namely: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately﴾. That is, there is no blame upon you that you eat from your house, whether you and your family eat together or you eat separately, although eating together is better, as we will mention, God willing, at the end of the verse. Nevertheless, there is no blame: a person has no blame if he eats, lunching alone, while his family lunches on their own, or he and his wife eat separately, or the like; and there is no harm either if he eats with them all together. There is no harm in either.
There remains the consideration: ﴿or the houses of your fathers﴾ and so on to the end. He did not mention the houses of the children! We say: they are included in His saying: ﴿from your houses﴾, for a child's house is a house for his father, by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed the best of what you eat is from your earnings, and indeed your children are from your earnings,"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3528), al-Tirmidhi (1358), al-Nasa'i (4449), and Ibn Majah (2290) from 'A'ishah; the wording is that of al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.]] and by his saying: "You and your wealth belong to your father."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3530) from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, and Ibn Majah (2291) from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah; the wording is that of Ibn Majah.]] Therefore the child's house is a house for the father. We did not criticise the author for including the children's houses among a person's houses, for this is correct; we criticised his restricting the houses to the children's houses, what does he say? To the children's houses. So we say: ﴿from your houses﴾ means the houses of yourselves, and the houses of your children with respect to a man's own house, its benefit is what is mentioned at the end of the verse, and with respect to his child's house it is more general than that.
﴿or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers﴾: ﴿fathers﴾ includes the nearer and the more remote father, for the grandfather is a father, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham; He named you Muslims before this﴾ [al-Hajj 78]. Allah called Abraham a father to us, though he is a distant grandfather. Likewise ﴿your mothers﴾ includes the mother who bore the person and the more remote mothers, who are the grandmothers.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it does not include foster-relations or adoption, because the rights of kinship are not attached to them by the rights of nursing.
﴿or the houses of your brothers﴾: full siblings or those by the same father or the same mother.
﴿or the houses of your sisters﴾: but on condition that she is not married. If she is married, the house becomes her husband's, since the property is his, not hers. But if the sister has a house of her own, there is no harm in a person eating from that house.
﴿or the houses of your paternal uncles or the houses of your paternal aunts﴾: what is said of ﴿your aunts﴾ is like what we said of ﴿your sisters﴾; that is, as long as the aunt is not married, a person does not eat from the house of her husband, because it is his and not hers.
﴿or the houses of your maternal uncles or the houses of your maternal aunts﴾: regarding paternal and maternal uncles and aunts, it includes the nearer of these and the more remote: the nearer paternal uncle is your father's brother, and the more remote is your grandfather's brother however far up he goes; and regarding the maternal uncle, the nearer is your mother's brother, and the more remote is your grandmother's brother however far up he goes, he is still your maternal uncle.
(﴿or what you possess the keys of﴾) i.e., (what you have stored for others). The phrase ﴿mafatihahu﴾: the "mafatih" means treasuries; that is, what you possess the treasuries of. It has also been said that it means keys, which are the things by which something is opened. The singular "miftah" (key) differs from "miftah" (a larger key/opener); the plural of "miftah" is "mafatih", the plural of "miftah" is "mafatih"... Some say that "miftah" is applied to "key" and "mafatih" to "keys". Others say no: "mafatih" means treasuries and "mafatih" the keys by which something is opened. But the Qur'an supports the first view, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We gave him of treasures whose keys would be a burden to a band of strong men﴾ [al-Qasas 76]. On this basis, in this noble verse, ﴿mafatihahu﴾ means its treasuries or the keys of its treasuries.
And His saying: ﴿what you possess the keys of﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿what you possess the keys of﴾?
That is: its keys have been placed in your hands, and they are the treasuries. So there is no blame on a person in eating from them, but in a reasonable manner. For example, if a man owns fruit and gave you the key to the storeroom intending that you keep it and its keys safe, then one day you entered this storeroom, it is permissible that you eat from it, for example, but on condition that it is done in a reasonable manner, that you do not take (...) frequent it constantly, unless he is pleased with that.
* Student: What if it were state property?
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: What if it were state property?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, even if it were state property; because as long as you have been entrusted with it, it is general, and it is permissible.
He said: (﴿or your friend﴾, who is one who is sincere to you in his affection. The meaning is that it is permissible to eat from the houses of those mentioned, even if they are not present, i.e., when their approval is known.) Note that the author says it is permissible to eat from the houses of these people even if they are not present, and this is correct.
As for his saying: (i.e., when their approval is known), this is not correct. For when the owner's approval of your eating is known, there is no difference between whether he is one of these or one of others: if approval is known, then one may eat from the houses of these people as long as their disapproval is not known.
The categories are three:
The first category: you know their approval, the owner's approval of your eating; this is permissible, from these houses and from others. Is it permissible or not? It is permissible, from these houses and from others.
The second category: you know their disapproval, that he would not be pleased; then do not eat, neither from these houses nor from others, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his free consent."[[Narrated by Ahmad (20695) and al-Daraqutni (2886) from the paternal uncle of Abu Hurrah al-Raqashi.]]
The third category: you neither know his approval nor his disapproval. This is the case in which a distinction is made between those mentioned and others, so it is said: you may eat from the houses of these people, because usually they are pleased, due to the connection between you and them of kinship, friendship, or trust; for the reality of the matter is that these houses go back to three causes: either kinship, or trust, or friendship.
Kinship is those mentioned; trust is in His saying: ﴿what you possess the keys of﴾; and friendship is in His saying: ﴿or your friend﴾. In the case of not knowing approval or disapproval, we say: it is permissible to eat from these houses and not from others. As for the author's stipulation of knowing approval in these houses, there is no basis for it, for if we stipulated that, there would be no difference between them and other houses.
Suppose a friend of yours brought you into his house and you found food in the coffee-room and ate without asking permission: is that permissible or not? Yes, it is permissible; we say it is permissible. This is the meaning of the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 61–63 (part 2 of 5):

The author holds that it is not permissible unless you know that he would be pleased with that, but the correct view is that knowledge of his consent is not a condition. However, if we know that this man is stingy and would never be pleased for you to eat anything from his property except what he has served you, then in this case it is not permissible to eat, on account of the hadith we have pointed to (...).
No, but this is dangerous, because (...). Merely because he honours you and brings you in, for example, with a feast, it is not permissible for you to sit down to it without his permission. But a close friend, whether he invited you or did not invite you, and whether he intended to show you hospitality or did not intend it, if you enter your friend's house, then you may eat so long as you do not know that he would not be pleased by that.
In His saying: ﴿your friend﴾ there is evidence that friendship carries a right, and so it does; the basis for it is the connection between you and him.
What is your opinion regarding in-laws (al-sihr) and foster kinship (silat al-radá'): do they fall under kinship by blood (silat al-nasab), or under friendship, or under neither?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They fall under friendship if he is a friend, because many people may have a foster brother with whom there is enmity between you, and many people may have an in-law with whom there is enmity between you. So the point is: if there is no friendship between the in-law and his in-law, or between the foster child and the one who nursed him, then it is not permissible to eat from his house.
(﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together﴾ gathered together ﴿or separately﴾ dispersed, plural of shatt. Shatt and ashtat are like sabab and asbab, except that sabab is not assimilated (idghām), whereas shatt is assimilated.)
He said: (It was revealed concerning those who were reluctant to eat alone, and if they did not find anyone to eat with, they would abstain from eating.) It is said that this was a custom among some of the Arabs: if they did not find anyone to eat with them, they would not eat anything at all. They would die of hunger rather than eat until they met someone to eat with. This is undoubtedly evidence of generosity, but it is a generosity carried to excess.
The point is that you eat with others and you eat alone, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately﴾. This is in terms of permissibility; as for what is better, it is to eat together, as the Prophet ﷺ commanded, and he informed that there is blessing in it. A man complained to him that he would eat and not be satisfied, so the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to him: «Perhaps you eat separately?» He said: Yes. He said: «Gather together over your food, and it will be blessed for you»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3764) and Ibn Majah (3286), from the hadith of Wahshi ibn Harb.]]. So people gathering to eat is among the causes of blessing, and it is also among the causes of familiarity and affection. For the members of a household, for example, are scattered in their work; if there is nothing to bring them together, which is the meal, then when will they gather? Unfortunately, this Sunnah has now disappeared among many people. You find the father eating alone, the eldest son eating alone, and the middle one eating alone; the only ones who may gather are the women of the household. As for the men, their gathering, as far as I can see, is rare. But this is contrary to the Sunnah.
The Sunnah is that people gather to eat. And praise be to Allah, some of them wait for one another. Is there any harm if someone is delayed a quarter of an hour waiting for his companion? What harm is there? Because their gathering together and conversing brings affection and familiarity. But if a son never sees his father: at night the son stays up and his father sleeps early, and by day the father seeks a livelihood while the son studies, and at mealtime the father prays with the congregation while the son is sitting to have lunch, for example, or something similar. Then when is there gathering? And when is there familiarity among people?
Is it now better for a man and the people of his household, men and women, to eat? Yes, this is the better course: that they all eat together, including the men with the women. We have seen among the earlier generations those who would eat together, he and his father. When we were with our maternal uncles, whenever we arrived at their house, we would find them all gathered together (...).
* * *
That is: sin and hardship. We mentioned the disagreement of the scholars on this (...); that is, the blind, the lame and the sick, and that they mentioned three opinions regarding it, which are what?
* Student: That it concerns jihad.
* Shaykh: That it concerns jihad.
* Student: Or that it is general in everything.
* Shaykh: Or that it is general in everything.
* Student: That it concerns eating.
* Shaykh: That it concerns eating together with them. The general meaning is preferable: there is no hardship upon them in matters where these illnesses or defects are a cause of incapacity, whether from jihad or otherwise, so there is no blame on them. This serves as a preamble to what is mentioned afterwards: just as these people bear no blame, neither do you bear blame in ﴿that you eat from your houses﴾ and so on to the end.
﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together﴾, that is, gathered together for the meal, ﴿or separately﴾, dispersed.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾. (﴿houses﴾ belonging to you, with no people in them: ﴿greet one another﴾, that is, say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," for the angels return your greeting; and if there are people in them, greet them.)
In His saying: ﴿When you enter houses﴾, ﴿houses﴾ is indefinite in the context of ﴿when﴾. What is ﴿when﴾? It is conditional, and it occurs in the context of a condition, so it is general, covering a person's own houses and the houses of others.
And His saying: ﴿greet one another﴾: if there are people in the house and it belongs to someone else, they greet those in it. It is called greeting "one another" even though it is directed at others, because believers are one soul, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, mercy and compassion is like the likeness of one body; when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6011) and Muslim (2586/66), from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]]. If the houses are empty with no one in them, a person greets himself, saying: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," because this is the greeting the Prophet ﷺ taught his community to use on themselves, as in the prayer.
His saying: ﴿greeting﴾ is a verbal noun from (ḥayyā), meaning: you are greeted with a greeting.
His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾: Allah attributed it to Himself because He is the One who legislated it. ﴿From Allah﴾ means: this greeting is from Allah, or it is from Him because He is the one who legislated it, or because He is its ultimate goal, meaning it is sought from Him, since you say "Peace be upon us" or "Peace be upon you," and it is requested from Him. So He is its goal or its legislator; its attribution to Allah is because He is the Legislator who commanded it, ﴿from Allah﴾, or because He is its ultimate end, that is, the one to whom this greeting ultimately leads, so that He may reward for it and respond to it.
His saying: ﴿blessed﴾: what is the meaning of blessed? It means possessing blessing, and blessing, as already explained, is abundant and enduring good.
His saying: ﴿good﴾: the author said: (for which you are rewarded). This is part of goodness, that it be rewarded; but goodness also includes that it conform to the Law of Allah, because righteous and good deeds mean that they conform to the Shari'ah, by being sincere in them for Allah and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in them.
His saying: (﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾, that is, He explains to you the landmarks of your religion ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that you may comprehend that).
﴿Thus makes clear﴾: we have already noted that we parse the (kāf) as a noun meaning "like" functioning as an absolute object of ﴿yubayyin﴾, that is, "like that clarification". And ﴿the signs﴾: it has already been explained that what is meant is both the legislative and the cosmic signs; the legislative ones are what the messengers brought, and the cosmic ones are the creations of Allah that we see and hear.
His saying: ﴿so that you may understand﴾: (la'alla) here expresses purpose, that is, in order that you may understand. The meaning of "reason" (ʿaql) here is understanding, according to what the author adopted; but the more correct view is that it is more general than that: it is understanding and good conduct. For reason, as we have already learned, is of two types: what are they?
* Student: Perception.
* Shaykh: And reason of conduct. Perceptive reason is the basis of accountability, and it is present in the Muslim and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. Reason of conduct is good conduct: that a person behaves in a manner founded on reason. This excludes the disbeliever and the sinner, for they do not conduct themselves well, so they are not reasonable. That is why Allah, glorified and exalted, always denies reason to the disbelievers, even though they are among the cleverest and most understanding of people; but they do not have the reason of conduct, they have only perceptive reason. What a person is praised for is the reason of conduct; as for the first type, a person is not praised for it, since it is not something he has acquired.
* Student: Reason in the sense of (...).
* Shaykh: In the sense of what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, he has reason, because it comes from 'iqal (tethering), since it restrains its possessor toward good conduct. The conduct of a madman is not like the conduct of this man.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Perceptive reason. The reason by which a human being is distinguished from the madman is perceptive reason. The point is that what is meant by reason here is not merely understanding; for if we explain it as mere understanding, we reduce it to perceptive reason alone, and perceptive reason is not the basis of praise; rather, the basis of praise is the reason of conduct by which a person conducts himself well. This is what is meant by this verse: ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that is, you comprehend that and conduct yourselves well in accordance with these verses which Allah has made clear to you.
* Benefits drawn from this verse:
* First: the demonstration of Allah's mercy, the Mighty and Majestic, in removing hardship from those who do not deserve it, as in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾.
* Second: the demonstration of the ease of this Shari'ah in removing hardship from those who do not deserve for it to befall them.
* Third: that rulings revolve around their causes: when the cause exists the ruling is established, and when it ceases the ruling ceases. For the removal of hardship from these people is for what reason? For this cause which is in them. So if the sick person recovers, the lame man's gait is straightened, and Allah restores sight to the blind, this ruling ceases in regard to them, and what applies to the sound becomes established for them.
* And in it: permissibility of eating from the houses of those mentioned, whether with permission or without, unless we know that they are not pleased, in which case it is not permissible to eat from their houses.
* And in it is evidence that a man's child's property is considered his property. How so?
* Student: (...) if he benefits, meaning: what you have eaten.
* Shaykh: «Indeed the best of what you eat».
* Student: Indeed the best of what you eat and your children.
* Shaykh: «And indeed your children are from your earnings»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3528), al-Tirmidhi (1358) with this wording, al-Nasa'i (4449), and Ibn Majah (2137), from the hadith of 'A'isha.]]. And here, what is the point of evidence from the verse?
* Student: (...) here ﴿from your houses﴾, and he did not mention, meaning..
* Shaykh: The children. He did not mention the children, which shows that what is meant by "houses" is your houses and the houses of your children.
* And in it is also evidence for: the reliance on custom in matters; for permission to eat from these houses was given only because custom and convention indicate consent to that. It is known that these relatives, friends, and keyholders are all people among whom custom has established leniency regarding eating. However, it has already been said that a person does not carry anything away; he may eat but not take. That is why Allah only permitted eating.
* And also in the verse is evidence for: permissibility of eating together or separately, by His saying ﴿together or separately﴾; but what is better, as already explained, is gathering together.
* And also in it is evidence for: the legislated nature of greeting upon entering houses, by His saying: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet yourselves﴾. This was the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ, except that a person begins with something before the greeting, which is the siwak: when he enters his home he first begins with using the siwak[[Narrated by Muslim (253/43), from 'A'isha.]], then he greets his family[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2698), from Anas, and its wording is: "O my son, when you enter upon your family, greet them; it will be a blessing upon you and upon the people of your house."]].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, before this, before the greeting; because usually in our time they are not at the door, but if they are at the door, then greet them before.
* And also in it is evidence for: the virtue of the greeting, since Allah the Exalted described it as: a greeting from Him, blessed and good; three attributes. This is undoubtedly evidence of its excellence, and it shows that it is better than a person saying "Ahlan wa sahlan" and the like. It also shows that if a person answers a greeting with "Ahlan wa sahlan" it will not suffice, because "Ahlan wa sahlan" is not described as ﴿a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾.
As for "Peace be upon you" or "Upon you be peace," it is described as ﴿a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾. That is why you find this is the guidance of the prophets in the hadith of the Ascension (mi'raj). When the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, greeted a prophet he met in the heavens, that prophet returned the greeting and said: «Welcome, the righteous son» regarding Adam and Abraham, and «the righteous brother» regarding others: «Welcome, the righteous brother and the righteous prophet». They welcome him after returning the greeting. His saying in the hadith: «He returned the greeting and said» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3887), with this wording, and Muslim (164/264), from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a.]] is evidence that this is not part of returning the greeting, and this is well known. But unfortunately people have now abandoned this, and most people, when you greet them, say to you: "Ahlan wa marhaban," or "Hala" or "Marhaban"; this does not suffice, and it is not permissible to limit oneself to it.
* Student: (...) the telephone.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, the telephone greeting: whenever you call someone, greet him, because the reality of the telephone is face-to-face contact, though it is unseen. So you say: "Peace be upon you." But it is also regrettable that people, young and old, perhaps we can say: their learned and their ignorant, do not do this; they say: "Alo, alo, I hear you (...)."
* * *
Then He, the Exalted, said, disciplining His servants: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur 63]
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That he says: "May Allah forgive you; depart, may Allah forgive you," or "O Allah, forgive them."
He said: (﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾, by saying: "O Muhammad!" Rather, say: "O Prophet of Allah! O Messenger of Allah!", with gentleness, humility and lowered voice), and so on to the end.
His saying: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾: ﴿calling (du'a')﴾, according to the author's statement, means "summoning" (nida'), as in your saying: "I called so-and-so," meaning I called out to him. On this basis, ﴿calling﴾ is a verbal noun annexed to its object, since ﴿calling﴾ is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with its subject omitted. The implied meaning is: "Do not make your calling of the Messenger [like that]," this being the original form; the subject was dropped and the verbal noun was annexed to its object, that is, "your calling of the Messenger." This is the original form.
His saying: ﴿like the calling of some of you to others﴾: this is annexed to its subject and object, ﴿some﴾ meaning: as when some of you call others. When we call one another we say: "O so-and-so." But the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has such a right and dignity that it is not fitting for us to call him by his name; rather we say: "O Prophet of Allah! O Messenger of Allah!" The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, adhered to this courtesy, and they would address the Prophet ﷺ by his title of prophethood or messengership. Whatever reports contrary to this from the statements or supplications of the Companions exist, they either predate the prohibition or come from an ignorant person, like what occurs from some of the Bedouins.

This is the view of the author and some of the exegetes. Others said: what is meant by "the summoning of the Messenger" (du'a' al-Rasul) is the Messenger's summoning of you, so the verbal noun is attributed to its agent: "Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like the summoning of some of you to others" — if you wish, you respond, and if you wish, you leave it. Rather, responding to the Prophet ﷺ is obligatory, and so when he commands us to something or calls us to a matter, responding to him is obligatory upon us; it is not like others, where if we wish we respond and if we wish we leave. On this view the verse contains a prohibition against disobeying the Messenger ﷺ and a command to obey him: ﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like the summoning of some of you to others.﴾

This is supported by His saying: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind others. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [An-Nur 63]. The context of the verse supports this view. If it is said that the verse includes both meanings, is that permissible or not? It is permissible; we may take it to include both meanings, because we have established a principle in this regard: if a verse can bear two meanings without contradiction, it is to be understood as both of them together. But if it bears two meanings and the meaning of each contradicts the other, then one must seek a preponderance (tarjih) that favors one of the two meanings, and that is acted upon. And if it is suitable for both and there is no conflict between them, then the obligation is to understand it as both meanings together.

So we say: this is part of the etiquette in addressing the Messenger ﷺ and the etiquette in responding to him. In addressing him, we do not make his address and our summoning of him like the summoning of anyone else; and in responding to him, we do not make his summoning and his request for any matter like the request of others. Hence the scholars said: if the Prophet ﷺ calls someone while he is praying, is it obligatory for him to respond or not? It is obligatory to respond. If his father calls him while he is praying, then if it is an obligatory prayer he does not respond, and if it is a voluntary prayer he responds, unless he knows his father's contentment with that, such that the father makes him feel that he is praying and it does not matter to him that he does not respond; in that case he does not respond. But if his father is among those who do not excuse (such matters), and likewise his mother, then he responds in the voluntary prayer and breaks his prayer.

Al-haraj (hardship): that is, sin and hardship. We have mentioned the disagreement of the scholars regarding this negation concerning the blind, the lame and the sick, and that they mentioned three opinions regarding it. What are they?
* Student: That it refers to jihad.
* Shaykh: That it refers to jihad.
* Student: Or that it is general in everything.
* Shaykh: Or that it is general in everything.
* Student: That it refers to eating.
* Shaykh: That it refers to eating together with them, but the generality is preferable. The meaning: there is no hardship upon them in whatever these illnesses or defects prevent them from doing, such as jihad or other things; so there is no hardship upon them. This serves as a preparation for what is mentioned afterward; that is, just as these have no hardship upon them, neither is there hardship upon you in eating from your houses, and so on.

(﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾ [An-Nur 61] — that is, eating in groups, or ﴿separately﴾, scattered.)

Then Allah the Most High said: (﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ — houses belonging to you with no one in them — ﴿greet one another﴾, that is, say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," for the angels return your greeting. If there are people in them, greet them.)

His words: ﴿When you enter houses﴾ — ﴿houses﴾ is an indefinite noun in what context?
* Student: (After) "idha."
* Shaykh: "Idha" — what is "idha"?
* Student: Conditional.
* Shaykh: Conditional; it is in the context of a condition, so it is general, covering a person's own houses and the houses of others.

His words: ﴿greet one another﴾ — if there are people in it who belong to someone else, he greets them, that is, those within it. It is called a greeting upon "one another" though it is directed to others, because believers are one soul, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, mercy and compassion is like the likeness of a single body: when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6011) and Muslim (2586) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]

If the houses are empty with no one in them, then the person greets himself, saying: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," because this is the greeting the Prophet ﷺ taught his community, that they greet themselves as in the prayer.

His words: ﴿a greeting﴾ is a verbal noun of (haya), meaning: you greet with a greeting. His words: ﴿from Allah﴾ — Allah attributed it to Himself because He is the one who legislated it. ﴿From Allah﴾ means this greeting is from Allah, or that He is its ultimate object, meaning it is sought from Him, since you say "Peace be upon us" or "Peace be upon you," so it is sought from Him. He is its ultimate goal or its legislator. Its attribution to Allah is because He is the legislator who ordained it, so He is the one who commanded it ﴿from Allah﴾, or because He is its ultimate end, that is, the one to whom this greeting ultimately goes, so that He rewards for it and answers it.

His words: ﴿blessed﴾ — what is the meaning of ﴿blessed﴾? It means possessing blessing, and blessing, as has passed, is abundant and enduring good.

His words: ﴿good﴾ — the author said: "rewarded for it." This is indeed part of goodness, that it be rewarded; but it is also part of goodness that it conform to the law of Allah, because righteous and good deeds mean that they conform to the Shari'ah, by being sincere in them for Allah and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in them.

His words: "﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, that is, He explains to you the landmarks of your religion, ﴿that you may understand﴾, so that you may comprehend that."
﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾ — it has passed that we parse the kaf as a noun meaning "like," as an absolute object of ﴿yubayyinu﴾; that is, like that clarification, He makes clear.
﴿The verses﴾ — it has been mentioned that they refer to both the legislative and the cosmic: the legislative is what the messengers brought, and the cosmic are the creations of Allah that we observe and hear.
His words: ﴿that you may understand﴾ — "la'alla" here expresses purpose, meaning: so that you may understand. The meaning of intellect ('aql) here is understanding, as the author followed, but the more correct view is that it is more general than that: it is understanding and good conduct. As has passed with us, intellect is of two kinds. What are they?
* Student: The intellect of perception.
* Shaykh: And the intellect of conduct.
So the intellect of perception is the basis of accountability, and it is present in the Muslim and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. The intellect of conduct is good management of one's actions, so that a person acts in a manner founded on reason; this excludes the disbeliever and the sinner, since they did not conduct themselves well, so they are not truly intelligent. For this reason Allah the Most High always negates intellect from the disbelievers, even though they are among the cleverest and most perceptive of people, but they lack the intellect of conduct. They have only the intellect of perception, while what a person is praised for is the intellect of conduct; as for the first, one is not praised for it, since it is not one's own acquisition.
* Student: O Shaykh, does "intellect" have a root in language, custom or the Shari'ah?
* Shaykh: Yes, it has a root.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Because it is from "'iqal" (the tether), since it restrains its possessor through good conduct; the conduct of a madman is not like this.
* Student: From which category?
* Shaykh: From the intellect of perception. The intellect by which a person is distinguished from the madman is the intellect of perception.
The point is that intellect here does not mean mere understanding, because if we interpret it as mere understanding we reduce it to the intellect of perception only, and the intellect of perception is not the basis of praise; rather, the basis of praise is the intellect of conduct by which a person conducts himself well. This is what is meant by this verse: ﴿so that you may understand﴾ — that you perceive that and act well in accordance with these verses which Allah has made clear to you.

* Benefits from this verse: First, the display of Allah the Most High's mercy in negating hardship from those who do not deserve it, as in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾.
* Second: the ease of this Shari'ah, by negating hardship from those who do not deserve to be burdened.
* Third: that rulings revolve around their causes; when the cause exists the ruling is established, and when it is absent the ruling is removed. The negation of hardship from these people is because of the cause present in them; so if the sick person recovers, the lame walks straight, and Allah restores sight to the blind, this ruling is removed from them and what applies to the able-bodied applies to them.
* And in it: is it permissible to eat from the houses of those mentioned, with or without permission? Except when we know—
* Student: Their dissatisfaction.
* Shaykh: Their dissatisfaction. So if we know they are not pleased, then it is not permissible to eat from their houses.
* And in it is evidence that a person's child's wealth is his own wealth. How so?
* Student: "﴿Or from your houses﴾," and the Messenger said, meaning... "Indeed the best of what you eat..." with its meaning...
* Shaykh: "Indeed the best of what you eat."
* Student: Meaning the best of what you eat, and your children...
* Shaykh: "And indeed your children are from your earnings." [Abu Dawud (3528), al-Tirmidhi (1358), al-Nasa'i (4450), Ibn Majah (2290), from 'A'ishah.]
And what is the point of proof from the verse here?
* Student: It says here "﴿from your houses﴾" and does not mention the children.
* Shaykh: It does not mention the children, so this shows that "houses" means your houses and the houses of your children.
* And in it is also evidence for relying on custom in matters; because eating from these houses was permitted to us only because custom and convention indicate consent to that; these relatives, friends, and keyholders are known to be lenient about eating. But it has been mentioned that a person does not carry anything away; he eats but does not carry; for this reason Allah permitted only eating.
* In the verse is evidence for the permissibility of eating together or separately, from His saying: ﴿together or separately﴾, but the better is, as has passed, to eat together.
* Also in it is evidence for the legislated nature of greeting upon entering houses, from His saying: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾, and this was the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ, except that a person begins before the greeting with something, which is—
* Student: The siwak.
* Shaykh: The siwak. When he enters his house he begins first with the siwak, then greets his family.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, before this, before the greeting; because nowadays people are usually not at the door, but if they are at the door, then greeting them comes first.
* Also in it is evidence for the virtue of greeting, since Allah the Most High described it as a greeting from Him, blessed and good: three attributes. This is without doubt evidence of its excellence, and it shows that it is better than a person's saying "Ahlan wa sahlan" and the like.
And that if a person answers a greeting with "Ahlan wa sahlan," it does not suffice, because "Ahlan wa sahlan" is not described as a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. But "as-salamu 'alaykum" or "wa 'alaykumu as-salam" is described as a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. For this reason you find this is the guidance of the prophets in the hadith of the Mi'raj: when the Messenger ﷺ greeted the prophet he encountered in the heavens, that prophet returned the greeting and said: "Welcome, the righteous son," regarding Adam and Abraham, and "the righteous brother" regarding the others: "Welcome, righteous brother and righteous prophet." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3887), Muslim (164/264), the wording of al-Bukhari, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah.] They welcome after returning the greeting, and his saying in the hadith "he returned the greeting and said" is evidence that this welcome is not part of returning the greeting, and this is well known.
But unfortunately people have now abandoned this; most people, when you greet them, say: "Ahlan wa marhaban," or "Hala," or "Marhaban." This does not suffice, and it is not permissible to limit oneself to it.
* Student: O Shaykh, does this apply to (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, the greeting you mean?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Whenever you address someone, greet him, because in reality the telephone is a form of direct address, though unseen; so you say "as-salamu 'alaykum." But it is also regrettable that people now, young and old, perhaps we can say scholars and ignorant, do not do this; they say "Alo," and I hear that "alo" is an English greeting.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: A problem. The state of people—may Allah guide us and them—they do not notice these matters.
As for "telephone," I see that the foreign names used are not a problem to leave as they are, because arabized names exist in the Arabic language since long ago; so there is no harm in saying "telefon," and it is not necessary to say "hatif," for example. Likewise we say "radio," and it is not necessary to say "mudhi'," but the problem is a thing that contradicts the Shari'ah; that is, replacing a legislated word used in such a context with a non-legislated word. That is the problem. Or the matter of names that come from others, because they made them and named them this, so we are not responsible for them. Although some scholars say: no, they named it this to observe the meaning, not merely the craft; so they say, for example, that "radio," I think, means "hatif" among them.
* Student: "Radio" means "mudhi'."
