If his father calls him while he is praying, then if it is an obligatory prayer he does not respond, and if it is a voluntary prayer he responds, unless he knows his father's contentment with that, such that the father makes him feel that he is praying and it does not matter to him that he does not respond; in that case he does not respond. But if his father is among those who do not excuse (such matters), and likewise his mother, then he responds in the voluntary prayer and breaks his prayer.

Al-haraj (hardship): that is, sin and hardship. We have mentioned the disagreement of the scholars regarding this negation concerning the blind, the lame and the sick, and that they mentioned three opinions regarding it. What are they?
* Student: That it refers to jihad.
* Shaykh: That it refers to jihad.
* Student: Or that it is general in everything.
* Shaykh: Or that it is general in everything.
* Student: That it refers to eating.
* Shaykh: That it refers to eating together with them, but the generality is preferable. The meaning: there is no hardship upon them in whatever these illnesses or defects prevent them from doing, such as jihad or other things; so there is no hardship upon them. This serves as a preparation for what is mentioned afterward; that is, just as these have no hardship upon them, neither is there hardship upon you in eating from your houses, and so on.

(﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾ [An-Nur 61] — that is, eating in groups, or ﴿separately﴾, scattered.)

Then Allah the Most High said: (﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ — houses belonging to you with no one in them — ﴿greet one another﴾, that is, say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," for the angels return your greeting. If there are people in them, greet them.)

His words: ﴿When you enter houses﴾ — ﴿houses﴾ is an indefinite noun in what context?
* Student: (After) "idha."
* Shaykh: "Idha" — what is "idha"?
* Student: Conditional.
* Shaykh: Conditional; it is in the context of a condition, so it is general, covering a person's own houses and the houses of others.

His words: ﴿greet one another﴾ — if there are people in it who belong to someone else, he greets them, that is, those within it. It is called a greeting upon "one another" though it is directed to others, because believers are one soul, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, mercy and compassion is like the likeness of a single body: when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6011) and Muslim (2586) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]

If the houses are empty with no one in them, then the person greets himself, saying: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," because this is the greeting the Prophet ﷺ taught his community, that they greet themselves as in the prayer.

His words: ﴿a greeting﴾ is a verbal noun of (haya), meaning: you greet with a greeting. His words: ﴿from Allah﴾ — Allah attributed it to Himself because He is the one who legislated it. ﴿From Allah﴾ means this greeting is from Allah, or that He is its ultimate object, meaning it is sought from Him, since you say "Peace be upon us" or "Peace be upon you," so it is sought from Him. He is its ultimate goal or its legislator. Its attribution to Allah is because He is the legislator who ordained it, so He is the one who commanded it ﴿from Allah﴾, or because He is its ultimate end, that is, the one to whom this greeting ultimately goes, so that He rewards for it and answers it.

His words: ﴿blessed﴾ — what is the meaning of ﴿blessed﴾? It means possessing blessing, and blessing, as has passed, is abundant and enduring good.

His words: ﴿good﴾ — the author said: "rewarded for it." This is indeed part of goodness, that it be rewarded; but it is also part of goodness that it conform to the law of Allah, because righteous and good deeds mean that they conform to the Shari'ah, by being sincere in them for Allah and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in them.

His words: "﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, that is, He explains to you the landmarks of your religion, ﴿that you may understand﴾, so that you may comprehend that."
﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾ — it has passed that we parse the kaf as a noun meaning "like," as an absolute object of ﴿yubayyinu﴾; that is, like that clarification, He makes clear.
﴿The verses﴾ — it has been mentioned that they refer to both the legislative and the cosmic: the legislative is what the messengers brought, and the cosmic are the creations of Allah that we observe and hear.
His words: ﴿that you may understand﴾ — "la'alla" here expresses purpose, meaning: so that you may understand. The meaning of intellect ('aql) here is understanding, as the author followed, but the more correct view is that it is more general than that: it is understanding and good conduct. As has passed with us, intellect is of two kinds. What are they?
* Student: The intellect of perception.
* Shaykh: And the intellect of conduct.
So the intellect of perception is the basis of accountability, and it is present in the Muslim and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. The intellect of conduct is good management of one's actions, so that a person acts in a manner founded on reason; this excludes the disbeliever and the sinner, since they did not conduct themselves well, so they are not truly intelligent. For this reason Allah the Most High always negates intellect from the disbelievers, even though they are among the cleverest and most perceptive of people, but they lack the intellect of conduct. They have only the intellect of perception, while what a person is praised for is the intellect of conduct; as for the first, one is not praised for it, since it is not one's own acquisition.
* Student: O Shaykh, does "intellect" have a root in language, custom or the Shari'ah?
* Shaykh: Yes, it has a root.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Because it is from "'iqal" (the tether), since it restrains its possessor through good conduct; the conduct of a madman is not like this.
* Student: From which category?
* Shaykh: From the intellect of perception. The intellect by which a person is distinguished from the madman is the intellect of perception.
The point is that intellect here does not mean mere understanding, because if we interpret it as mere understanding we reduce it to the intellect of perception only, and the intellect of perception is not the basis of praise; rather, the basis of praise is the intellect of conduct by which a person conducts himself well. This is what is meant by this verse: ﴿so that you may understand﴾ — that you perceive that and act well in accordance with these verses which Allah has made clear to you.

* Benefits from this verse: First, the display of Allah the Most High's mercy in negating hardship from those who do not deserve it, as in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾.
* Second: the ease of this Shari'ah, by negating hardship from those who do not deserve to be burdened.
* Third: that rulings revolve around their causes; when the cause exists the ruling is established, and when it is absent the ruling is removed. The negation of hardship from these people is because of the cause present in them; so if the sick person recovers, the lame walks straight, and Allah restores sight to the blind, this ruling is removed from them and what applies to the able-bodied applies to them.
* And in it: is it permissible to eat from the houses of those mentioned, with or without permission? Except when we know—
* Student: Their dissatisfaction.
* Shaykh: Their dissatisfaction. So if we know they are not pleased, then it is not permissible to eat from their houses.
* And in it is evidence that a person's child's wealth is his own wealth. How so?
* Student: "﴿Or from your houses﴾," and the Messenger said, meaning... "Indeed the best of what you eat..." with its meaning...
* Shaykh: "Indeed the best of what you eat."
* Student: Meaning the best of what you eat, and your children...
* Shaykh: "And indeed your children are from your earnings." [Abu Dawud (3528), al-Tirmidhi (1358), al-Nasa'i (4450), Ibn Majah (2290), from 'A'ishah.]
And what is the point of proof from the verse here?
* Student: It says here "﴿from your houses﴾" and does not mention the children.
* Shaykh: It does not mention the children, so this shows that "houses" means your houses and the houses of your children.
* And in it is also evidence for relying on custom in matters; because eating from these houses was permitted to us only because custom and convention indicate consent to that; these relatives, friends, and keyholders are known to be lenient about eating. But it has been mentioned that a person does not carry anything away; he eats but does not carry; for this reason Allah permitted only eating.
* In the verse is evidence for the permissibility of eating together or separately, from His saying: ﴿together or separately﴾, but the better is, as has passed, to eat together.
* Also in it is evidence for the legislated nature of greeting upon entering houses, from His saying: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾, and this was the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ, except that a person begins before the greeting with something, which is—
* Student: The siwak.
* Shaykh: The siwak. When he enters his house he begins first with the siwak, then greets his family.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, before this, before the greeting; because nowadays people are usually not at the door, but if they are at the door, then greeting them comes first.
* Also in it is evidence for the virtue of greeting, since Allah the Most High described it as a greeting from Him, blessed and good: three attributes. This is without doubt evidence of its excellence, and it shows that it is better than a person's saying "Ahlan wa sahlan" and the like.
And that if a person answers a greeting with "Ahlan wa sahlan," it does not suffice, because "Ahlan wa sahlan" is not described as a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. But "as-salamu 'alaykum" or "wa 'alaykumu as-salam" is described as a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. For this reason you find this is the guidance of the prophets in the hadith of the Mi'raj: when the Messenger ﷺ greeted the prophet he encountered in the heavens, that prophet returned the greeting and said: "Welcome, the righteous son," regarding Adam and Abraham, and "the righteous brother" regarding the others: "Welcome, righteous brother and righteous prophet." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3887), Muslim (164/264), the wording of al-Bukhari, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah.] They welcome after returning the greeting, and his saying in the hadith "he returned the greeting and said" is evidence that this welcome is not part of returning the greeting, and this is well known.
But unfortunately people have now abandoned this; most people, when you greet them, say: "Ahlan wa marhaban," or "Hala," or "Marhaban." This does not suffice, and it is not permissible to limit oneself to it.
* Student: O Shaykh, does this apply to (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, the greeting you mean?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Whenever you address someone, greet him, because in reality the telephone is a form of direct address, though unseen; so you say "as-salamu 'alaykum." But it is also regrettable that people now, young and old, perhaps we can say scholars and ignorant, do not do this; they say "Alo," and I hear that "alo" is an English greeting.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: A problem. The state of people—may Allah guide us and them—they do not notice these matters.
As for "telephone," I see that the foreign names used are not a problem to leave as they are, because arabized names exist in the Arabic language since long ago; so there is no harm in saying "telefon," and it is not necessary to say "hatif," for example. Likewise we say "radio," and it is not necessary to say "mudhi'," but the problem is a thing that contradicts the Shari'ah; that is, replacing a legislated word used in such a context with a non-legislated word. That is the problem. Or the matter of names that come from others, because they made them and named them this, so we are not responsible for them. Although some scholars say: no, they named it this to observe the meaning, not merely the craft; so they say, for example, that "radio," I think, means "hatif" among them.
* Student: "Radio" means "mudhi'."
* Shaykh: It means "mudhi'," so as long as they observe the meaning, it is necessary that we use a word in our language that indicates this meaning. The matter is simple; but the discussion concerns what contradicts the Shari'ah. As for these matters, they are easier.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Encouragement to—?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Perhaps it is derived from it, and perhaps it is said that the unrestricted greeting contains blessing, and that is preferable; because restricting it to the case when one says "wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuhu" would be restricting something that is broad. The Prophet ﷺ always greeted saying "as-salamu 'alaykum" [al-Bukhari (4739), from 'A'ishah]. Nevertheless, we say that the better is "wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuhu," without doubt. But if one limits himself to the first, it is correct for us to say: ﴿a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾, because this is a description of the greeting, not a description of its wording; that is, the greeting itself is blessed and good, and it is not a description of its form, that it contain the word "blessing" and the word "good," or that he says afterward "and His good things."
* And in this verse is also evidence of Allah the Most High's care for creation, in that He makes the signs clear to them, so that they act as intelligent people do and follow His law: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, that you may understand﴾. It has passed with us that this clarification regarding the legislative signs is known only by believers who believed in them and understood them; as for the cosmic signs, even a disbeliever may believe in them: disbelievers believe that Allah is the creator of the heavens and the earth, that the dominion of the heavens and the earth is in His hand, that He sends down rain, and so on.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Nothing authentic from the Messenger at this exact place is known, but it is reported that he taught the words "as-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibadillahi as-salihin" in the prayer [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (831), Muslim (402/55), from Ibn Mas'ud]. As for the angels returning the greeting, there is no established report; that the angels return your greeting—there is no narration from the Prophet ﷺ about it. But they say: when there is no one in them, Allah the Most High said: ﴿greet one another﴾, so we take from this generality that we greet those within it, and they, being believers, are like ourselves; and if there is no one in them, we greet ourselves specifically: "as-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibadillahi as-salihin," which is what the Shari'ah has prescribed in the prayer.
* Student: (...)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 61–63 (part 4 of 5):

* The Shaykh: This is possible, but it is at a distance, and you have greeted yourself, because you are the cause of his returning it, and the one who causes something is like the one who does it directly, as in the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "A man curses the father of another man, and he curses his father," when they said: "Would a man curse his own parents?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5973), Muslim (90 / 146), and Abu Dawud (5141), with his wording, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr.]] This can be understood as the sense in which it is on ourselves: when we greet, he returns the greeting to us, but in reality it may not happen if he does not return it. So when you greet him, you have greeted yourself, whether he returns it or not, and even if it is assumed that he did not return it to me, you have still complied with the command. Yes indeed.
* Student: Now we have said that we excuse the blind and the lame because of these disabilities. Do we say the same of (...) one with weak eyesight, or of one who is between the sighted, with ordinary vision, and this blindness? That is, do we say, for example: one with weak sight (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. For example, if we suppose that a person is obligated to write: writing is obligatory when a person is called to it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So let him write﴾ [al-Baqarah 282]. That is, if someone calls you to write a document between them and you are able, then Allah has commanded you to write. If he has weak sight and cannot do so, there is no blame on him, unless he is not blind at all. In any case, these disabilities, if they are complete, the person is excused completely, and if they are partial, then according to their degree. The ruling revolves around its cause.
* Student: (...) on the basis of restriction (ḥaṣr), or on the basis of (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, on the basis of restriction. This is the benefit of explicitly mentioning each one; otherwise the verse would read: "Nor on yourselves that you eat from your houses or the houses of your relatives." But these are specifically mentioned. That is, for example, the son of your maternal aunt, you may not eat from his house, and the son of your paternal aunt, you may not eat from his house, because they are specifically mentioned. This is the benefit of mentioning each one individually.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the son of the paternal aunt is not a house belonging to you.
* Student: By analogy (qiyas).
* The Shaykh: No, and it is not valid as an analogy, because if you wanted to analogize it to ﴿from your houses﴾, you would make it higher than the paternal aunt; that is, you would place it in a more fitting position to be eaten from than the paternal aunt, if you include it in ﴿your houses﴾.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not included. Apart from these specifically mentioned persons, you may not eat from his house unless he permits it; that is, he and the stranger are equal.
* Student: His saying: ﴿or the houses of your mothers﴾ (...) general (...) the absence of disobedience (ʿuqūq)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, but the mother has greater claim; that is, she is more obligatory in dutifulness. The closer one is, the more obligatory it is, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then the nearer, then the nearer."[[Narrated by Muslim (2548 / 2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* Student: That she should be in the position of the mother.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. For this reason it is obligatory to be dutiful to her and to spend on her, and everything that is established for the mother is established for her, except that the mother is more entitled and more deserving. Likewise, with regard to the grandfather, he is like her, except that the grandfather differs from the father in some matters, such as the matter of appropriating (tamalluk). Those who say it is permissible for a father to take from his child's property restricted it to the nearer father, because the reality is that the issue is weak; one does not reach the conclusion that the grandfather and whoever is above him may appropriate. Even the father is disputed regarding his appropriating from his child's property.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾ [al-Nur 62]. ﴿Innama﴾ (only) is a particle of restriction. ﴿Innama al-mu'minun alladhina amanu billahi wa rasulihi﴾: restriction establishes the ruling for what is mentioned and negates it for what is other than it. Accordingly, faith is established for those who are described by these attributes, and is negated for whoever lacks any of them.

First: ﴿alladhina amanu billahi wa rasulihi﴾. Faith in Allah and His Messenger, as we have previously stated, is not faith unless it includes acceptance (qabul). What comes next?
* Student: And submission (idhan).
* The Shaykh: And submission. It must include acceptance and submission. Mere affirmation of truth is not faith. So if a person affirms Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, but does not accept what he brought nor submit to it, he is not a believer. For this reason, Abu Talib affirmed the Prophet ﷺ, yet he was not a believer in him, because he did not accept what he brought nor submit to it. ﴿Alladhina amanu billahi wa rasulihi﴾ means faith that is correct, including acceptance and submission.

And His saying: ﴿wa idha kanu ma'ahu﴾ (and when they are with him). With whom? He says: (﴿ma'ahu﴾, i.e., the Messenger ﷺ; ﴿ala amrin jami'in﴾, such as the Friday sermon; ﴿lam yadhhabu﴾, due to some excuse arising for them; ﴿hatta yasta'dhinuhu﴾).

﴿idha kanu ma'ahu ala amrin jami'in﴾, that is, on a matter general to the Muslims: from jihad, consultation, Friday prayer and others. Every common matter general to the Muslims, not a matter specific to them. When they gather, they do not leave until they seek his permission, because leaving without permission leads to disorder and disruption of order.

Suppose it is announced: "The prayer is gathered" (al-salah jami'ah), and people gather to consult on a matter, then one person, after the people have arrived, rises and leaves without permission. We say: this is forbidden and not permissible, because it leads to the disintegration of this gathering and to disorder and lack of order.

So when the Muslims gather on a common matter, that is, general to the Muslims such as the Friday sermon and others, it is not permissible for anyone to leave except with an excuse and after seeking permission, because of the weakness that results and the weakening of the rest. For when they see one person rise, a second rises, a third rises, a fourth, and so on. Without doubt, as we see ourselves now, when one person rises from a gathering, people follow him, and this is like a wall from which a breach has been made, which will not hold together afterward. The common people have a saying for this: "If one stone falls from the well's side, all will fall." The well (rakiyah) is the well; if one pebble falls from it, what remains? It collapses; you cannot hold it except that it falls.

The conclusion: the true believers are those who, when they are with the Messenger ﷺ on a common matter, and what does "common" mean? That is, comprehensive and general, such as gathering for jihad, gathering for consultation, and gathering for an important matter concerning the Muslims in general, they do not leave the place of gathering until they seek permission from the Prophet ﷺ.

Then the author also qualifies it with a necessary condition, saying: (for some excuse arising for them). Likewise, they do not leave except for an excuse, so an excuse is necessary, and an excuse is a hidden matter that is not known, so seeking permission is necessary, so that their excuse may become clear to all those present, and there be no harm to them in that.
* Student: Shaykh, is this specific to the Messenger ﷺ?
* The Shaykh: No, this is general to every gathering.
* Student: All gatherings?
* The Shaykh: All general gatherings that are for the benefit of Islam and the Muslims. It is not permissible for anyone to leave except for an excuse and after seeking permission.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, this is not among the benefits of the Muslims.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is not among the benefits of the Muslims. The discussion concerns those with benefits for the Muslims. ﴿amrin jami'in﴾ means it gathers the Muslims for their benefits. As for going out (...) how? Whoever enters, enters. Although it is not proper for a person to stray from his station, one cannot say it is forbidden, because this does not harm Islam at all. The most that can be said is that it disturbs this gathering (...) they enjoy (...) how? There is nothing wrong with it.

﴿Indeed those who ask your permission, those are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Without doubt, the structure of the sentence in this way indicates nobility and elevation of rank, by His saying: ﴿Indeed those who ask your permission, those are...﴾. For ("ula'") is a demonstrative pronoun indicating the exaltation of the one referred to; therefore it came in the form of the distant: ﴿ulaika﴾, indicating the height of their status. Then it came emphasized with ("inna"), then it came as a nominal sentence: ﴿Indeed those who ask your permission, those are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Thus faith in Allah and His Messenger is restricted to those who seek the permission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when they are with him on a common matter, seeking his permission before they leave.

(﴿fa-idha istadhanukum li-ba'di sha'nihim﴾ their matter, ﴿fa'dhan liman shi'ta minhum﴾ to depart, ﴿wastaghfir lahumu Allah, inna Allaha ghafurun rahim﴾).

﴿Idha istadhanukum li-ba'di sha'nihim fa'dhan liman shi'ta minhum﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, stipulated that the seeking of permission be for some affair; that is, for a matter of their concerns for which they are excused from being absent from the gathering. Then He said to the Messenger: ﴿fa'dhan liman shi'ta﴾, making him also free to grant permission or not. ﴿fa'dhan liman shi'ta﴾. Is this choice a choice of desire and absolute will, or a choice of benefit?
* Student: A choice of benefit.
* The Shaykh: A choice of benefit.

What is the criterion distinguishing a choice of benefit from a choice of desire and absolute will? If the choice is for the sake of ease for the obligated person, it is a choice of desire, as found in some expiations, such as the expiation for oaths: ﴿its expiation is feeding ten needy persons, from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾ [al-Ma'idah 89], and as in His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah 196].

So if the purpose of the choice is to facilitate ease for the obligated person, it is of the category of desire: whatever you desire, do it. If the choice is for a general or particular benefit, it is a choice of benefit, and that is when it concerns others. For example, the guardian of an orphan's choice in selling his property, or withholding it, or lending it or not lending it, is of the category of choice of benefit, because he acts on behalf of another.

Likewise, the Prophet's choice here ﴿fa'dhan liman shi'ta﴾ is a choice of benefit: if the Messenger's permission to these people does not harm the gathering, and there is also a clear benefit for them greater than the benefit of their remaining, then it is determined?
* Students: The permission.
* The Shaykh: The permission is determined. If it is feared that by granting them permission the seekers would multiply and this gathering would collapse, or that their staying in the gathering is better for them than going about their affairs, then it is determined that he should not grant them permission. So the Prophet's choice here returns to benefit: if benefit requires permission, he grants it; otherwise, not.

His saying ﴿li-ba'di sha'nihim﴾ uses "some" (ba'd) as an indication that if they seek permission for something important, even if it is not one of their many affairs, it is an excuse permitting them to seek permission and be granted it.

Then, with that, He said: ﴿wastaghfir lahumu Allah﴾. This seeking of forgiveness for them is to console their hearts when they leave this gathering and miss its reward, so the Messenger ﷺ seeks forgiveness for them, and their hearts are comforted in leaving and no discomfort or anxiety remains in their hearts. This is one aspect. On the other hand, ﴿wastaghfir lahum﴾ because in their seeking permission there may be a matter for which they are not excused: they thought it an excuse and sought permission on its account, but it is not an excuse before Allah, and your seeking forgiveness for them erases whatever shortcoming or negligence may be in that.

His saying: ﴿inna Allaha ghafurun rahim﴾. This has been discussed many times before, and we said that forgiveness pertains to the side of sins, and mercy pertains to the attainment of what is sought; in forgiveness is deliverance from what is disliked, and in mercy is the attainment of what is desired.

Then Allah the Exalted said, disciplining His servants: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur 63].
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: That one says: "May Allah forgive you; depart, may Allah forgive you," yes, or "O Allah, forgive them."

He said: (﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾, by saying: "O Muhammad," but rather say: "O Prophet of Allah, O Messenger of Allah," in softness, humility and lowered voice) and so on.

His saying: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾. ﴿Du'a'a﴾ according to the author's explanation means "call" (nida'), from which your saying: "I called (da'awtu) so-and-so," that is, I called out to him. On this basis, ﴿du'a'a﴾ is an verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its object, since "du'a'" is a masdar annexed to its object, and its subject is omitted. The estimate is: "Do not make your calling the Messenger..." This is the origin; then the subject was deleted and the verbal noun was annexed to its object, that is, "your calling the Messenger," this is its origin.

His saying: ﴿ka-du'a'i ba'dikum ba'da﴾ is annexed to its subject, and its object is ﴿ba'da﴾; that is, as when one of you calls another, for when we call one another we say: "O so-and-so." But the Prophet ﷺ has such right and honor that it is not fitting for us to call him by his name; rather we say: "O Prophet of Allah, O Messenger of Allah." The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, adhered to this courtesy, and they would address the Prophet ﷺ by his prophethood or messengership. Whatever is reported contrary to this from the sayings or calls of the Companions is either before the prohibition, or from one ignorant, like what occurs from some Bedouins. This is what the author and some exegetes have taken.

Others said: what is meant by ﴿du'a'a al-rasul﴾ is the Messenger's calling you (du'a' al-rasul iyyakum), so the verbal noun is annexed to its subject; that is: do not make the Messenger's calling you, when he calls you, like the calling of one of you to another. If you wish, you respond; if you wish, you leave. Rather, the Prophet's ﷺ response is obligatory. Accordingly, when he commands us with a matter or calls us to a matter, his response is obligatory upon us; it is not like others: if we wish we respond, and if we wish we leave. On this basis, the verse contains a prohibition against disobeying the Messenger ﷺ and a command to obey him: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Allah already knows those of you who slip away, concealed by others. So let those who oppose His command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them﴾. The context of the verse supports this view.

If it were said that the verse includes both meanings, is that permissible or not? It is permissible to make it include both meanings, because we have previously stated a rule in this: if a verse can bear two meanings without contradiction, it is interpreted by both together. But if it can bear two meanings and the meaning of each contradicts the other, then it is necessary to seek the preponderance that favors one of the two meanings, and act on it. And if it is suitable for both and there is no conflict between them, then it is obligatory to interpret it by both meanings.

Accordingly, we say: this is part of the courtesy in addressing the Messenger ﷺ and the courtesy in responding to him. In addressing him, we do not make his calling us like the calling of others, and in responding to him, we do not make his call or request for any matter like the request of others.

Hence the scholars said: if the Prophet ﷺ calls someone while he is praying, is it obligatory for him to respond or not? It is obligatory to respond. And if his father calls him while he is praying: if it is an obligatory prayer, he does not respond; if it is a voluntary prayer, he responds, unless he knows his father's pleasure in that, in that his father makes him feel that he is praying, so it does not matter if he does not respond. In that case he does not respond. But if his father is one of those who do not excuse, and likewise his mother, then he responds in the voluntary prayer and breaks his prayer.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: He shortens the obligatory prayer if he knows his father has business, but not in a way that spoils it.

He said: (﴿Allah already knows those of you who slip away, concealed by others﴾ [al-Nur 63], that is, they leave the mosque during the sermon without permission, secretly, hiding behind something; and ﴿qad﴾ is for emphasis of certainty).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 24, verse 61–63 (part 5 of 5):

His words: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind one another﴾. "Tasallul" (slipping away stealthily) means leaving secretly; this is the meaning of tasallul. His words ﴿liwadhan﴾ mean taking cover behind something, and it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal); that is, he slips away and takes cover behind something, such as a pillar, or like another person who stands there and then goes off from behind and sneaks away, and similar things.

The author's words "(during the Friday prayer)" are based on the view that the intended "common matter" (amr jami') is the Friday sermon. If we say that what is meant is something more general, such as slipping away from the place of gathering, whether in the Friday prayer or otherwise, then Allah the Exalted knows those who slip away taking cover behind something, because they have departed from what the Muslims were upon and from what it is obligatory for them to be upon.

His words ﴿Allah already knows﴾: the author said, "(qad) is for emphasis (tahqiq)." He specified this because it is well known in the science of grammar that "qad," if it precedes a past-tense verb, is for emphasis, and if it precedes a present-tense verb, it is for diminution (taqlil): "The miser sometimes gives generously (qad yajud al-bakhil), the dullard sometimes understands (qad yafhamu al-baleed), the weak sometimes overtakes (qad yasbiqu al-'ajiz)," and similar examples. This is for diminution, but it sometimes comes for emphasis, as in this verse ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind one another﴾, and as in the Exalted's words ﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder others and those who say to their brothers﴾ [al-Ahzab 18]. The present tense is used here so as to make clear that this knowledge is not only of what has passed but also of what is yet to come. So Allah's knowledge of these slipping away hypocrites is not knowledge only of those who have already slipped away, but of those who have already slipped away and of those who (...).

* * *

﴿A greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ [al-Nur 61]. That is among the signs which Allah the Exalted has made clear to His servants and explained to them, because of what it brings of affection, love and good. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the giving of greetings of peace and said: "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not inform you of something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the greeting of peace among you." [Reported by Muslim (54/93) from Abu Hurayrah.]

Also previously mentioned: Allah restricted faith to ﴿those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a common matter, they do not leave until they seek his permission﴾, meaning with the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿on a common matter﴾, a general and comprehensive matter. He explained that those who seek permission are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and that those who slip away stealthily without seeking permission are those who do not believe in Allah or His Messenger. He threatened them for that by saying that He knows this action of theirs, and His informing them that He knows it is evidence that He will recompense them for it, since there is no benefit in informing of knowledge except that recompense follows it.

* The verse is evidence that faith is divided into deficient and complete. Failing to seek permission in a common matter does not necessitate disbelief, but it is a disobedience that is incompatible with the perfection of faith. Faith may be meant in an absolute sense (mutlaq al-iman) and may be meant as complete faith (al-iman al-mutlaq). The difference is that "mutlaq al-iman" applies even with deficient faith, while "al-iman al-mutlaq" is... faith?
* Student: The complete.
* The Shaykh: The complete. So distinguish between "mutlaq al-iman," where you add "mutlaq" to "iman," and describing faith as "mutlaq." "Al-iman al-mutlaq" means complete, while "mutlaq al-iman" means that a person has the basic faith even if it is not complete. In His words concerning the expiation for killing: ﴿a blood-money delivered to his family and the freeing of a believing slave﴾ [al-Nisa 92], is the intended meaning of faith here the absolute or the mutlaq?
* Student: Mutlaq al-iman.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because it is not required in freeing a slave that the freed person be of complete faith; it suffices that he be a believer, even if he has only the basic faith.
In His words ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, like this verse, and in His words ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal 2], what is the intended meaning of faith?
* Student: The absolute.
* The Shaykh: Complete faith; that is, complete faith is that which has these attributes.
* The verse is evidence that the ruler must make things easy for those under his authority; due to His words ﴿so when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, grant permission to whomever you will of them﴾.
* It is also evidence that permission sought without an excuse is not accepted; due to His words ﴿when they ask your permission for some of their affairs﴾. As for when they ask permission merely because they want to abandon the work, permission is not granted to them.
* It is also evidence for delegating the matter to the one who holds authority; due to His words ﴿to whomever you will﴾. However, this delegation, as we indicated in the lesson, is delegation for the sake of the public interest, not merely for whim and desire. Rather, when he sees that granting them permission serves the interest, he grants it; if he sees that the interest lies in not granting it, it is not permissible for him to grant it.
* It is also evidence of Allah's care for His believing servants, in that He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to ask forgiveness for them, so that they might be reassured about this departure.
* It is also evidence that it is better for a person not to seek permission even if he has a matter to attend to, because the command to seek forgiveness is evidence that there was some shortcoming (tafrit) for which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to ask forgiveness; and this is undoubtedly correct: it is better to remain with the congregation, and seeking permission to leave may involve a sin. For this reason Allah commanded His Prophet to ask forgiveness for them, saying: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them from Allah﴾.
* It is also evidence that a person benefits from the supplication of another; due to His words ﴿and ask forgiveness for them from Allah﴾, and the proofs of this in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ) are many. But does a person benefit from the deeds of others other than supplication, or not?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The answer: if the deed of another has an effect on that act, he certainly benefits from it; such as when he is the one who initiated this practice, that is, he began the act among the people and guided them to it, since the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." [Reported by Muslim (1017/69) from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.] Likewise if he has an effect on the doer, such as being a parent to him, for "the best of what you eat is from your earnings, and your children are from your earnings." [Reported by Abu Dawud (3528), al-Tirmidhi (1358), al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (4450), and Ibn Majah (2290) from 'A'ishah.] So a parent benefits from the deed of his child if the child gives it to him as a gift. That is why "a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, my mother died suddenly and had she been able to speak she would have given charity; shall I give charity on her behalf? He said: Yes." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1388), Muslim (1004/51) from 'A'ishah.]
Likewise the woman who "asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about her mother who had a month of fasting owed; may she fast on her behalf? The Prophet (ﷺ) permitted her." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1953), Muslim (1148/154) from Ibn 'Abbas.]
Likewise the pilgrimage, when "a woman asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Her father had reached the age when Allah's obligation of pilgrimage was due upon His servants, but he was an old man who could not sit on a mount; may she perform the pilgrimage on his behalf? He said: Yes, and that was during the Farewell Pilgrimage." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1513), Muslim (1334/407) from Ibn 'Abbas.]
So if the recipient of the gift, or the person, has an effect on the deed or on the doer, he benefits from it. But if there is no effect on either, such as when a relative gives a righteous deed to his relative or a friend to his friend, is that valid or not?
The scholars differed on this. Some hold that it is valid, and that if a person does a righteous deed and makes its reward for a Muslim, whether living or dead, that person benefits; this is the well-known position of the school of Imam Ahmad, that any act of worship or obedience by which the servant draws near to Allah, and whose reward he makes for a living or dead Muslim, benefits him.
Their evidence is analogy of others to children: they say, if the deed of someone other than the person can reach him, then there is no difference between a child and a non-child; the question is whether a person benefits from another's deed.
Those who held the prohibition said: a child is not like others, because a child is from a person's effort and earnings and actions, and is not like a brother, relative, friend, or the like.
As for supplication for Muslims, this is agreed upon, and there is a text on it in the Book, the Sunnah and consensus, and no one disagrees on it.
If someone asks: which is better, that I pray two units and give their reward in charity to one of my relatives other than my father, or that I supplicate for this person in my prayer?
We say: it is better that you supplicate for him in your prayer, because this is something agreed upon as beneficial; but giving him in charity the reward of your prayer is disputed. Some scholars permit it, and some say it is not permissible and not legislated, and that the dead do not benefit from it.
This applies to one who is hired to perform a righteous deed in order to give it to another, such as hiring some reciters to recite the Qur'an for the dead; this the dead person certainly does not benefit from, because this reciter who reads for money has read for the worldly life, and whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, for him there is no share in the Hereafter.
Accordingly, this reciter has no reward; and if he has no reward, does the deceased benefit from that? Since the deceased benefits only from the reward, not from mere recitation. So if we say this reciter has no reward, because he intended worldly gain by an act of the Hereafter, the deceased remains without benefit from that recitation.
* Student: (...) and said: O Allah, this is on behalf of (...)?
* The Shaykh: This may be cited as evidence, but this is in the category of charity, which is wealth, and not of purely physical acts of worship.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: But he gave the reward as a gift, seeking nearness to Allah: ﴿Their flesh will not reach Allah, nor their blood, but piety from you will reach Him﴾ [al-Hajj 37]. The reward that he obtained by this slaughter, this slaughter is a financial act, not a purely physical act; it is financial, so it is like charity. As for a purely physical act, such as a person praying, glorifying, saying "la ilaha illa Allah," or reciting, it is not like this.
* Student: (...) charities?
* The Shaykh: (...) righteous deeds.
* Student: Even physical acts (...) gives charity while (...) on behalf of so-and-so.
* The Shaykh: This is permissible according to most scholars, because they cite the hadith of "the man who said: My mother died; shall I give charity on her behalf? He said: Yes." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1388), Muslim (1004/51) from 'A'ishah.]
They also cite the sacrifice: that the Messenger (ﷺ) sacrificed on behalf of his community, among whom were living and dead, and he was not their father.
But one may say: the Messenger (ﷺ) is a father to the believers, so he is like a man who sacrifices on behalf of his household.
So the matter is not one in which a person can be confident that every deed benefits the dead if gifted to them, or benefits the living if gifted to them; it is not a matter in which a person can be reassured of this view. For this reason we hold that supplication for the dead is better than gifting acts of worship to them, except where a text has been reported, which is then followed.
But the majority, as you know, who say it is permissible, analogize everyone other than children to children, and analogize non-financial acts to financial acts, and say: the important thing is that the reward reaches the dead from another; this is the absolute position. The ones who prohibit say children are not like others and are not analogized to others, because a child is from a person's earnings.
It was also previously mentioned that Allah forbade the believers to make the Messenger's supplication among them like their supplication to one another.
* It is derived from this: the obligation of respecting and honoring the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it is not permissible for a person to address him as he addresses other people, because of his exalted status and honor.
* It is also, according to the second interpretation of the verse: the Prophet's (ﷺ) summons of the community is not like the summons of others. So if the Prophet (ﷺ) calls you to a matter or commands you to it, it is obligatory upon you not to treat that call as you would another's call, because responding to it fulfills the command of Allah and His Messenger.
* It is also a warning against those who slip away in common matters without excuse or permission; due to His words ﴿Allah already knows﴾.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah an-Nur, verse 64 (part 1 of 6):

With the emphatic (inna) particle.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [an-Nur 64]. This was brought after His saying: ﴿So let those who oppose His order beware﴾ [an-Nur 63], as evidence that what Allah threatened of trial or painful punishment is a matter that cannot overpower Allah; because Allah, Most High, possesses the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever possesses the dominion of the heavens and the earth is not incapable of carrying out and inflicting what He has threatened.

(﴿﴿He already knows what you are upon﴾﴾ O you who are obligated [to religious duties], ﴿upon it﴾ of faith and hypocrisy, and He knows ﴿the Day they are returned to Him﴾﴾) and so on to the end.

﴿He already knows﴾. It has passed with us that (qad) when it enters upon the present-tense verb, it conveys...?
* Student: Diminution (taqlil).
* The Shaykh: It conveys diminution, as in their saying: "qad yajūd al-bakhīl" (the miser may be generous). But it indicates certainty (tahqiq) when context shows that, and here ﴿He already knows what you are upon﴾ cannot be taken as diminution, because Allah's knowledge is established and permanent, so (qad) in this verse is for certainty.

He did not say "qad 'alima ma antum 'alayhi" (He knew what you were upon), indicating what they will do in the future, and that He is knowing of what has occurred and what will occur. So here the future tense relates not to the knowledge but to the known: it is not that His knowledge is future, for Allah's knowledge is pre-eternal and prior, but rather that the known, which these people will do, Allah knows it continuously.

His saying: ﴿what you are upon﴾. He says: the address is to the obligated (﴿﴿what you are﴾﴾ O you who are obligated). Yet it would have been better to make it general to people: "what you, O people, are upon," so as to include the obligated and the non-obligated, because the non-obligated also receive reward for the righteous deeds they do, and no evil deeds are recorded against them. On this basis, Allah, Most High, knows what they are upon, even the non-obligated.

His saying: (from faith and hypocrisy). This should be understood as an example and not as a restriction, because Allah knows what we are upon not only of faith and hypocrisy, but of faith and hypocrisy, righteous deeds and evil deeds, ease and hardship, and other things. Everything we are upon of states and actions, Allah, Most High, knows it.

(And He knows ﴿﴿the Day they are returned to Him﴾﴾.) When Allah mentioned what we are upon in this world, He mentioned what we will return to on the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿and the Day they are returned to Him﴾, meaning: (and He knows ﴿﴿the Day they are returned to Him﴾﴾). So His knowledge of our conduct in this world at the time of action, and the Day we are returned to Him at the time of reckoning and recompense, He knows both states.

He, Most High, said: (﴿﴿and the Day they are returned to Him﴾﴾ contains an iltifat (shift) from address, i.e., when will it be?)
This is acceptable (...) his saying "when will it be", but we have an objection to it.
His saying "contains an iltifat from address": how from address? "I know what you are upon" is address, and the context requires saying "and the Day you are returned to Him," but it shifted from address to the third person. What is the benefit of the iltifat?
* Student: Alerting.
* The Shaykh: To alert the addressee, because when the style changes, the addressee must pay attention, unlike when the style is uniform, where a person grows accustomed to it and finds nothing that calls for attention.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, alerting. It also has other benefits, but these are understood from context; the important constant one is alerting, though there may be other benefits as we mentioned.

In His saying, Most High: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds (2), the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful (3), Sovereign of the Day of Recompense (4)﴾ [al-Fatihah 2-4], all of this is third person. ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah 5] is address. Its benefit is alerting.

The second benefit: when you describe Allah with those attributes, it is as if He is now before you, so you address Him with the address of one present, saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah 5].

﴿He already knows what you are upon, and the Day they are returned to Him﴾ [an-Nur 64]. His saying "when will it be" is open to question, because the intended meaning is not only that Allah, Most High, knows when they will be returned to Him, but that He knows their state at the time they are returned to Him, along with His knowledge of when they will be returned to Him. That He knows when they will return to Him is beyond doubt, but the context does not support it; rather it supports that He knows them at the time of their deeds and at the time of recompense for their deeds. Like: "and He knows the Day they are returned to Him, what state they will be in," just as knowledge of when they return, whether a general return like the Day of Resurrection or a particular one like a person's death, also refers back to Allah, Most High.

His saying: (﴿﴿so He will inform them﴾﴾ in it, i.e., on this day, ﴿of what they did﴾ of good and evil, ﴿and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ of their deeds and other things.)
﴿so He will inform them﴾: He will tell them ﴿of what they did﴾ of good and evil.

The benefit of informing: it is to establish, i.e., to make them stand firm, so that their recompense is in the form of justice which they themselves acknowledge. So they do not say, "We were wronged," but Allah says, "You did such and such, and you did such and such," until they acknowledge it. After this acknowledgment, recompense follows, either as bounty or as justice, because recompense is either bounty, or justice, or oppression.

The last of these three is negated of Allah, and the first two are established, for His recompense, Most High, is between justice and bounty. The recompense for good deeds...?
* Students: Bounty.
* The Shaykh: Bounty, by way of bounty; and the recompense for evil deeds is by way of justice if He repays each evil deed with its equivalent, and if He pardons, Most High, it is by way of bounty.

His saying: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾.
﴿of all things﴾ is general: all things of the deeds of the children of Adam, great and small, and of other things too; Allah, Most High, knows them. Knowledge is the perception of a thing as it is, perceiving it...?
* Students: Decisively.
* The Shaykh: Decisively. So Allah, Most High, perceives every thing with decisive perception; in His knowledge there is no doubt or conjecture, but all His knowledge is certain knowledge.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, (ynabbi'uhum): informs them, to make them firm, i.e., so that He may establish them until they acknowledge it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: You mean making ﴿the Day they are returned to Him﴾ dependent on (yunabbi'uhum)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: That is not suitable, because the (fa') prevents it. This (fa') prevents what precedes it from being dependent on what follows it; had there been no fa', "the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them" would have been sound, but the fa' is what prevents what precedes it from being a complement of what follows.
* Student: Here the (fa') is conjunctive.
* The Shaykh: Here the (fa') is conjunctive.

* In this verse there are benefits: verbal benefits and meaningful benefits.
* As for verbal ones: it is appropriate to emphasize important matters and to draw attention to them, that important matters be stressed with what affirms and alerts to them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Our knowledge of that, our acknowledgment of it, and our belief in it is an important matter; for this it is emphasized with (alā) and (inna).
* Also in it: the generality of Allah's dominion over what is in the heavens and what is in the earth: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.
* In it: the generality of His knowledge, by His saying: ﴿He already knows what you are upon﴾, and that His knowledge, blessed and exalted, covers the present and the future, by His saying: ﴿and the Day they are returned to Him﴾: and He knows the Day they are returned to Him.
* In it: affirmation of the return and resurrection, by His saying: ﴿and the Day they are returned to Him﴾.
* Also in it: affirmation of reckoning, by His saying: ﴿so He will inform them of what they did﴾. Then, is this informing a questioning (munaqasha) or merely a telling?
* Student: A telling.
* The Shaykh: The answer here is that there is no questioning; it is merely a telling, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is questioned in the reckoning is punished," or he said: "is destroyed" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6536), Muslim (2876/79) from 'A'ishah]; because if he were questioned, it would be said to him, for example: "You did such and such righteous deeds, and that was established for you," then these deeds would be weighed against some blessing; the blessing would encompass them and exhaust them, and the person would remain accountable.
This is the meaning of questioning, but the deeds are presented so that the servant acknowledges them, and after that Allah arranges the recompense as He wills and as He pleases.
As for the disbelievers, they are not reckoned in the manner of one whose good and evil deeds are weighed, because they have no good deeds; rather their deeds are presented to them in a manner of shame and disgrace, may Allah protect us, until they acknowledge them and say: ﴿What is this book that leaves out nothing small or great but has recorded it?﴾ [al-Kahf 49], and after that their final abode is the Fire.
* Also in it: evidence of the generality of Allah's knowledge, by His saying: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾. What is the benefit of mentioning the generality of knowledge?
* Student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: A warning against disobedience, because whoever knows that you are obedient or disobedient, He will recompense you for it; so if the matter is like this, then in every verse containing the affirmation of knowledge there is a warning against disobeying Allah, Almighty and Majestic, lest a person fall into what angers Allah, Most High.
* Also in it, a verbal benefit: the shifting of address from third person to second person, or from second person to third person, which the rhetoricians call...?
* Student: Iltifat.
* The Shaykh: The rhetoricians call it iltifat, and this carries a benefit, which is alerting the addressee, and other benefits added to it according to what the context requires (...).

* * *

Additional benefits: ...that a group, even if what they agree upon is false, has influence; the influence of a group or a people when they gather, even if what they have adopted is false.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander﴾ are from among the believers, by His saying: ﴿from among you﴾ [an-Nur 11].
* The Shaykh: No, this is not necessarily so, because among them there were believers and among them hypocrites; but (...) those who came with the slander are people from among the believers, by His saying: ﴿from among you﴾, and the basic assumption is that the attribution is genuine.
* Student: Shaykh, is there not an indication (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not (...).
* Student: (...) since among those who came with the slander are hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Since among those who came with the slander...?
* Student: Hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Hypocrites, and yet Allah made them of us: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group from among you﴾ [an-Nur 11]; because the Prophet ﷺ treated the hypocrites according to the outward appearance of their state, treating them as Muslims; for this reason he did not separate them from their wives, nor kill them, nor take jizyah from them or anything.
The benefit he indicated (...) may be taken that they did not leave faith by this slander. But since we said that it is understood from it that the hypocrites are among the believers in terms of the outward, i.e., it is not suitable to take from it (...), either we take (...) faith and leave (...) the rights of hypocrites, or we take the hypocrites and leave that they did not leave faith, since we said the hypocrite may be (...) believers in terms of his outward appearance, then (...).
* Student: (...) they did not leave faith (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is not possible, since we said the attribution may be according to outward appearance (...) only. So either you take it as according to outward appearance, and then we say: perhaps these people did leave faith but their outward state is that they are Muslims, so he takes the ruling of the outward; that is, it is not certain that they did not leave faith. Since we said the attribution may be according to outward appearance, it is not established that they did not leave faith.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...) righteous people who believe (...).
* The Shaykh: No, (...) because it is possible (...) but what he, Abdullah, said means (...).
* Student: He said (...) they spread the slander, he said: it came from their own selves (...).
* The Shaykh: Correct? What is the benefit in it; meaning it is a summary of something (...) of their misguidance, by His saying: they came with it; that is, He did not say that those who, for example, transmitted or conveyed or the like. Is that possible?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: If we said that, it would not include those who spread it and those who transmitted it without originating it; this would not include them (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of the wording ﴿they came with the slander﴾ [an-Nur 11]?
* Student: (...) they originated it outright and did not transmit it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this does not contradict (...) but its origin (...) does it have a source or was it from their own selves?
* Student: No, it was from themselves (...).
* The Shaykh: It is taken from His saying: they came with it, so the origin of those who spoke it is that they came with it from their own selves; they did not build on known realities. Rather, the matter of Safwan, may Allah be pleased with him, does not necessitate that the matter be as they said.
* Student: Then does the verse include those who spread it or not?
* The Shaykh: No, it includes those who spread it and those who came with it (...) ﴿you received it with your tongues﴾ [an-Nur 15], so this one receives it from those who came with it (...).
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: This...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) this matter; some scholars say: slandering the Mothers of the Believers is like slandering other women, i.e., it entails the prescribed punishment for slander, and it entails disbelief only for one who slanders 'A'ishah with what she was accused of, for he becomes a disbeliever. What is the disagreement?
* Student: Opposing the clear text of the Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: Because he denies the Qur'an. For this reason some scholars said: whoever slanders 'A'ishah with what Allah cleared her of is a disbeliever. They restricted the matter to 'A'ishah and to what Allah cleared her of, and gave the rest the ruling of other women, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes﴾ [an-Nur 4]. But the correct view is that one becomes a disbeliever not because of slandering the woman herself, but because of the right of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. In any case, this benefit (...) is not correct.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. His saying: ﴿do not think it bad for you﴾ [an-Nur 11]; what benefit is derived from it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) from the verse. The benefit: a person is accountable for his assumption which he is certain of; for this (...) ﴿do not think it bad for you﴾, otherwise He would not forbid them; that is, He would leave them to their assumption. Do you agree with this benefit or not?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. In reality we do not know whether they assumed it to be evil, or whether Allah forbade them from a matter expected to (...) ﴿do not think it⦆ means: what has happened, do not assume it, i.e., in the future. Yes?
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: There is a possibility; it is not explicit that they assumed it evil, it is not explicit, but there is a possibility that they assumed it, or it was expected that they would assume it evil for you.
* But there is another benefit besides this: that good may be in what a person expects to be evil, and from it is His saying, Most High: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 216], because His saying ﴿that you dislike a thing﴾ is general; many things a person dislikes in (...) this world, and it becomes clear to him that good is in them. In any case, the benefit of this, about which there is no objection, is that he said: what? What did we say last?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: That good may be for a person in what he expects to be evil. Yes.

This is correct. For this reason you find that Allah, glorified and exalted, said in Surah al-Munafiqun: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun 4]. ﴿They are the enemy﴾, as we established yesterday (...). What does it contain?

**Student:** Restriction (al-hasr, exclusivity).

**Shaykh:** It contains restriction, because the subject and predicate form a nominal sentence whose two parts are?

**Student:** Two definites.

**Shaykh:** And when a nominal sentence has two definite parts, it indicates restriction. ﴿They are the enemy﴾ means as if no one is more emphatic than them in enmity, so as if there is no enemy other than them. This is correct. There is no doubt that the enmity of the hypocrites is more grievous than the enmity of the disbelievers. Because the disbeliever says: "I am your enemy." You guard against him, you can rid yourself of him, you fight him and combat him until (...). But can this hypocrite be rid of? Eh?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** He cannot be rid of, because he is a direct affliction. When a person has a disease in his stomach (...), he cannot see his stomach and take it out. For this wisdom, the punishment for sodomy became execution in every case, whether the doer and the one done to were married or unmarried. The reason is that one cannot guard against it.

Likewise, the punishment for the assassin who kills by ambush (ghilah) became execution in every case, even if the heirs of the one killed say: "Leave him, we forgive him." The killing is not lifted if it was by ambush, because he came upon him unawares and killed him. Even if the heirs of the one killed say: "By Allah, we want peace, we forgive, we do not want blood money or retaliation," or they say: "We want blood money, not retaliation," it is still obligatory to kill him. The reason is that this cannot be guarded against.

Sodomy cannot be guarded against, because a man walks with another man. What would you say: do not walk with him? You cannot. Since guarding against it is difficult, its punishment is cutting off this germ from the earth.

Likewise the assassin, since guarding against him is difficult, he comes unawares (...). This differs from two men fighting each other and one killing the other. That is not objectionable, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has a murdered relative has the choice between two options."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (112) and Muslim (1355 / 447), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

In any case, my intention in this matter is that a distinction is made between matters that can be guarded against and those that cannot, and each has its own ruling.

So, O people, there is a problem. What is the difference between the witness and the slanderer? That is, if the witnesses are four, and a man wants to testify, does he become a slanderer?

**Shaykh:** No. The witness must say: "I testify that he committed adultery with her, and that I saw his member in her private part." It is not enough to say: "He committed adultery with her."

**Student:** Shaykh, this is a real case.

**Shaykh:** Even the slanderer may be claiming this.

**Shaykh:** It has in reality occurred to my mind just now, and I have not reviewed anything on it. But it becomes clear to me that the difference between the slanderer and the witness is this: the slanderer spreads adultery as a matter of defamation and disparagement, while the witness testifies to it before the judge. For this reason the jurists said: there is no difference whether these four witnesses come to the ruler together or separately. Those who said that if they come separately they become slanderers were noting that there is no difference between the slanderer and the witness. Because if one comes in the morning before the judge and testifies, and another comes in the forenoon, and the third after that, and the fourth after noon, there is no difference. That is, it is valid to rule by their testimony and establish the hadd. But the apparent difference between them is this: the slanderer describes the accused with adultery as a matter of defamation and disparagement. Therefore he does not go to the judge and say that so-and-so committed adultery, or anything of this sort. But the witness testifies to it before the judge, and does not speak of it among the people or expose his honor. He testifies before the judge to establish the hadd upon him, not for his defamation and disparagement. This is what has become clear to me now, and the matter needs verification and examination of the words of the scholars on this subject. But this is what is clear to me now.

Do we say that this verse affirms causes, the affirmation of legislated causes, or not?

Affirmation of legislated causes: that a thing may be a cause of punishment. This is in contrast to one who denies that a cause is effective by itself. It has passed with us that some of the Ash'aris (the followers of al-Ash'ari) deny that a cause is effective by itself, to the extent that they said: the burning of fire is not by the fire; rather the burning occurs at its presence, not by it. Do you agree with this? The saying of the Ash'aris?

I say: in this verse is the affirmation that causes are effective by themselves, the affirmation that causes are effective by themselves, in contrast to those who say there is no effect for them, that the effect occurs at them and not by them.

This includes the fatwa, the ruling, the testimony, and widely spread reports. A person says nothing except with knowledge. And as we said, the prohibition of a muqallid's fatwa is known to be forbidden, because it is without knowledge. But if people are compelled and find only a muqallid, what do they do? Seeking a fatwa from a muqallid is better than asking someone ignorant who has no acquaintance with knowledge at all, meaning, nor with the sciences of the people.

Which of them, in your own mind, is closer to the correct?

**Shaykh:** Okay. If we find only a muqallid in the society, what do we do? Do we say: do not ask people? Let these ignorant ones issue fatwas to one another?! Allah says: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him﴾ [Al-Baqarah 173].

And when it is qualified, like ﴿and they say within themselves: why does Allah not punish us﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 8], it becomes a person's speech to himself. So His saying ﴿you said: it is not...﴾ means that a person must declare publicly that this is a matter no believer could say.

**Student:** The greatness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of 'Ā'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) (...), due to the Exalted's saying: ﴿Glory be to You! This is a great slander﴾, where (...) the Messenger (ﷺ) or 'Ā'ishah is a diminishing of the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

**Shaykh:** That is, declaring Him free of what (...).

This is clear: the greatness of the status of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and that the wisdom of Allah refuses that such a thing should occur on the bed of the Prophet (ﷺ), due to His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾. This indicates that it is not fitting for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that such a thing should happen on the bed of the Prophet (ﷺ). And this is what made them say: ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾, because it contradicts the wisdom of Allah.

**Student:** If two interests combine, the interest of others and the interest of the individual, which do we give precedence to?

**Shaykh:** No, the public interest takes precedence.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** As for himself, he does what benefits himself and benefits others. But if we want to observe interests, we give precedence to public interests. Even in the Sharia and in qadar (divine decree), public interests take precedence. That is why we flog the adulterer, or stone him until he dies, for the public interest. Otherwise, is it in his interest that we offer him repentance or not? The rain falls, and it may ruin some farms that are not suited to rain, but it fell for the public interest. The observance of public interests in the Sharia and in qadar is a known matter. As for whether a person prefers his own interest over the interest of another in a matter that is not one of authority or management, this goes back to the legislative rules on that. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, says: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support." [Narrated by Muslim (977/41) from the hadith of Jabir, with similar wording.]

And sometimes it is obligatory on a person to prefer the public interest over his own, as in single combat, ransom, and what is similar to that, as happened with the believing man who said to the king: "If you want to kill me, take an arrow from my quiver, then shoot me with it, and say: 'In the name of the Lord of this boy.'" [Narrated by Muslim (3005/73) from the hadith of Suhayb ibn Sinan.] This one wants to kill himself, but for an interest.

As for administration and authority: if a person is entrusted with a matter, he must take the public interest into account and give it precedence over the interest of the individual. And as for a person's dealing with himself, in itself, this is according to what the legislative evidences require. A person may be trustworthy and God-fearing in himself, as if he had food and with him were ten hungry people while he himself is hungry. We do not tell him: give it to them, divide it among them while you die of hunger. We say: no, begin with yourself. And sometimes, as has come, the public interest takes precedence; the public interests should be observed.

When it becomes specifically obligatory on you, suppose it becomes specifically yours, it becomes a communal obligation (fard kifāyah). But there is someone who will stand in the mosque, so here there is no conflict. We say: seeking knowledge is preferable, because the mosque is not an end in itself if you do not become imam.

**Shaykh:** Complete this verse, because the time has ended.

**Student:** A Muslim should glorify Allah the Exalted when (...) Allah for him.

**Shaykh:** When it occurs to his mind or he hears: all of it, which does not imply belittling Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So he should glorify Allah until what is in his soul disappears.

**Student:** (...), due to His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ (...). A question mark (...).

**Shaykh:** Where is the interest of praise? Does it not fit here at all? (...) let alone (...).
